News.title: Third runway at Heathrow Airport would drive growth, Healey says
News.content:
Chancellor John Healey has said building a third runway at Heathrow Airport has "always been a case for growth" after Prime Minister Andy Burnham refused to say if he backed the expansion.

Healey said airport expansion, including at Heathrow, had been "a big part of jobs and growth" in recent decades, speaking at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Bangkok.

His comments came after Prime Minister Andy Burnham was more sceptical, telling the BBC last month it was "a matter for London and Londoners".

Healey's predecessor Rachel Reeves had put the airport's expansion at the centrepiece of an argument that Britain was open for business.

Earlier this week Heathrow's chief executive Thomas Woldbye warned that not building a third runway at the UK's busiest airport would be a "huge missed opportunity".

Healey told reporters: "The case for a third runway at Heathrow has always been a case for growth."

He added: "The formal position now is that the consultation is closed, led by the Transport Department.

"We're reviewing those, and then further decisions and announcements will follow."

The third runway been debated for decades, with the project facing opposition from residents, politicians and climate campaigners.

Last year, Reeves announced the government-backed expansion, saying "a third runway is badly needed", and the government could not "duck the decision any longer".

Asked about the project in September, Burnham suggested it was an argument for London to decide.

"I think we ought to hear the voice of people there first. It's not right for me to just jump straight in on the back of the consultation," he added.

The Department for Transport has said it is "considering the appropriate next steps" following the public consultation on its National Policy Statement, which provides the basis for deciding whether to grant a new runway at Heathrow.

The airport's consortium of owners has said they need explicit backing from Burnham before the end of the year in order to proceed with the project.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme earlier this week, Woldbye said it would be "good to know" the government's position on the project.

He said he hoped the prime minister would "come along" with the project, adding that a third runway was "not just for Londoners".

"Benefits will be felt all over the country because our supply chain reaches all the way from the north all the way to the south of the UK," Woldbye said.

Heathrow serves more than 80 million travellers a year with its four passenger terminals and two runways. The number of flights, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average, if a third runway is built.

The project, which has an estimated price tag of Â£33bn, would see hundreds of homes demolished, rivers diverted and the M25 motorway rerouted through a tunnel between junctions 14 and 15.

The new runway was scheduled to open by 2035, subject to plans being submitted and approved, but Heathrow has since suggested it would be delayed by four years to 2039 due to planning and regulatory issues.

News.title: Analysis: Zacharia was thrown into a whirlwind - and failed at a critical time for Trump
News.content:
The White House press secretary job is a challenging one, even under the best of circumstances.

These were not the best of circumstances.

Katie Zacharia was thrown into the whirlwind, joining the White House team as press secretary just weeks away from what polls suggest could be a difficult midterm congressional elections for President Donald Trump and his Republican Party.

In just five days, she was out â the result of a disastrous press conference that lasted all of 14 minutes, followed by a series of halting media appearances and questions about whether she had mischaracterised her legal credentials over the course of her career.

The axe dropped on Friday, with the news delivered â in a roundabout way - by Trump himself before the gathered media at the White House, as he recounted a conversation he had with Zacharia earlier in the day.

"Honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider," Trump said he told Zacharia. "Katie, do you need this? I don't think you need this."

He later added that maybe the press secretary job "is not for her".

In case there was any doubt, the White House quickly confirmed to the BBC that Zacharia would be "transitioning" out of her current job.

News.title: Five days, one briefing: How Katie Zacharia’s short tenure unfolded
News.content:
The White House says Katie Zacharia is "transitioning out" of the role of press secretary just days after taking the job. It comes after US President Donald Trump said on Friday he suggested to Zacharia she should "reconsider" the job.

Trump went on to say that Zacharia has been treated "very, very badly" by the media in recent days.

The BBC's Sarah Smith, who was in the room at Zachariaâs first briefing, breaks down how her short tenure unfolded.

News.title: Faisal Islam: What I learned from a week with the world's top finance leaders
News.content:
When it comes to the future direction of the global economy there is a bit of a tug of war going on.

There are starkly opposing forces. On the one hand holding back growth are the familiar, recurring crises from the energy shock, trade conflict and actual war. This is reflected most clearly in the sharply rising interest rate costs for the world's advanced economies.

Pulling in the other direction is the boost from massive spending on AI, and the frankly astonishing resilience shown especially by smaller economies, as new routes for trade, including for oil and gas, have been established out of necessity.

At the IMF meetings in Bangkok this week these themes came up again and again, including among those at the very top table. But not even they know which way things are going to go.

In the meantime it's a sportsman's bet where the roving eye of the bond markets will focus next. Currently they seem to be looking at the US and France.

However, the French finance minister, Roland Lescure, has been telling the world he has had no problem selling debt, though it was more expensive, and that his Budget would be fine. He also suggested he had helped save the G7 group of advanced nations, which was at risk of collapsing a year ago amid Donald Trump-inspired tensions.

In some ways it is a miracle there has not been a global recession, or a debt crisis in a major emerging economy. Indeed the Thai finance minister was boasting to me of how little his borrowing costs had gone up, especially in relation to the US.

Another surprise is the UK being taken off the bond markets' naughty step, and instead being named model pupil by the IMF. The IMF has taken the government's Budget plans at face value and on trust. The reality is that the rest of the G7 lack even this. And beauty is relative, especially when it comes to borrowing.

And this moment gave Chancellor John Healey the chance of a hearing, to highlight that the UK's actual growth data has continued to outperform expectations and so far in 2026 can now be described as strong. Healey told me that he saw the figures as the first sign that AI and tech investment was starting to increase UK economic growth. The bond financiers milling around the IMF meetings seem to be taking another look at the UK after years of crisis.

News.title: Miranda's tears, joy and dance moves steal show as deadly boredom sets in on The Celebrity Traitors
News.content:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode six of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

For a show that likes to keep participants and viewers on the edges of their seats, gripped by suspense and skullduggery, it was ironic that Friday's episode of The Celebrity Traitors came down to which one of its stars would die of boredom.

The climactic final scene switched between a series of faces as we waited to see which of the famous faithful would... yawn.

Some dramatic editing and music attempted to build fevered anticipation, but this was a slow-motion, low-energy premise for a murder in plain sight.

The trio of traitors had been tasked with being as boring as possible, and yawned theatrically in one of the castle's communal rooms in the hope that their apparent fatigue would be contagious.

News.title: Toxic algorithms wouldn't let them go - now Australia wants an off switch
News.content:
Warning: This article contains an account of living with an eating disorder

Varsha Yajman was already self-conscious about the way she looked when she joined social media as a 13-year-old.

Endless workout videos making impossible promises filled her feeds. Through the screen, girls she'd never met urged her to sign up to dangerous calorie challenges. Others proudly promoted their height and weight - even the number of times they had been sent to hospital - on their profiles in a form of twisted competition.

Every night as she fell asleep, Varsha would watch a stranger on the internet diarising what they'd consumed that day.

"I was like, 'I don't need to eat. I can just watch other people eat'," Varsha tells the BBC.

"I would find that I'd be down these really deep rabbit holes... it was like no matter how hard you tried to get out, you couldn't."

Now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, Varsha says she is still served weight loss content on social media - despite having every safety setting turned on, and an exhaustive list of banned words.

News.title: Why people who have never smoked are getting hooked on vaping
News.content:
When vaping first took off at Gracey Mungulu's school, she was vocal about the fact she found it as repulsive as smoking.

"I literally used to tell people like, 'Er, why are you doing that?'" she says.

But Gracey says the habit became so common among her classmates that by the age of 16 she too had taken it up, even though the first time left her coughing rather than inhaling.

"The more you see it, the more you start trying it a bit more," Gracey says, "and then eventually I just got used to it and I was just doing it all the time."

Now 21, she buys a refillable vape every day, using it whenever her hands aren't busy with her work as a hairdresser and in a school.

Gracey is among the more than one million people in the UK who say they have never smoked but now vape, according to recent Office for National Statistics (ONS) survey data â and that number has risen year-on-year.

When vaping first came to the market it was seen as a way to help smokers quit cigarettes.

Vaping nicotine, a highly addictive substance, is less harmful than cigarettes, but the long-term effects are not yet clear, according to the NHS.

News.title: Not sure what to wear for Halloween? These outfits are set to be the most popular this year
News.content:
If you're still on the hunt for the perfect Halloween costume, then you might want to look to gargoyles, Freaky Nikki and Dolly Parton for inspiration - they are all predicted to be popular outfit choices for 2026.

"People don't necessarily want to look frightening - they want to look extraordinary," says costume designer Tamar Zaig, who runs a fancy dress hire shop in London and says she's seeing a "real appetite for escapism, glamour and a bit of dark humour" right now.

And as usual, the year's major film and TV releases, as well as news and pop culture trends, are also driving outfit choices.

So, here are some spooky ideas to try.

News.title: Chris Mason: Burnham and Swinney tussle over where power lies in Scotland
News.content:
UK political debate has had a distinctly Scottish feel these last few days.

As the Scottish National Party has gathered for its annual conference at the Event Complex on the outskirts of Aberdeen, the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has been in Paisley and Edinburgh and the prime minister has been in Motherwell.

The SNP is buoyant, its activists gathering for the first time since it won, in May, a fifth consecutive Scottish Parliament election, albeit with fewer seats than they won in 2021.

Next year will mark the moment the party has been in devolved power at Holyrood for 20 years.

It is quite the contrast with where the SNP found itself just two years ago, pulverised by the landslide at the general election in 2024 where Labour gained 36 seats from the SNP.

As I wrote a year ago, the SNP's critics point to what they see as a dismal domestic record, on the NHS and the number of deaths among drug addicts, for instance.

The SNP counter Scotland has more police officers per person than England and Wales and the highest spend per school pupil in the UK.

No matter the arguments, the result in May was clear - the SNP leader and First Minister John Swinney has his own mandate. Little wonder, given the state of the party when he took the job, that the conference brochure has a front page photo of a smiling Swinney cradling a glass of whisky.

And remember it wasn't just an electoral pummelling the SNP was dealing with, but the jaw dropping details which culminated in the jailing of Peter Murrell, the party's former chief executive - and estranged husband of the former First Minister Nicola Sturgeon - for embezzling more than Â£400,000 from the party.

Swinney now looks ahead to a parliamentary term with all that behind them and a new prime minister to deal with in Downing Street.

Burnham and Swinney share a diagnosis that Westminster has failed to deliver and political power is better administered closer to people than it ever has been.

But, crucially, the prime minister sees the "drama" of the constant questions around Scottish independence as a distraction.

For Swinney, independence has been and remains his lifelong political goal.

We have had a glimpse this week as to how that dynamic between the two men may play out.

Burnham's critics, including the SNP, have seen this former Mancunian mayor's devolutionary instincts as having a distinctly English flavour. The prime minister, on his trip to New College Lanarkshire, sought to counter that.

"I do want a good growth in every postcode here, and in the rest of the UK, and I want to work with the first minister to deliver it. We won't agree on everything, but we can agree on something," he said.

"I want us to design a new model together of regional economic empowerment across Scotland, one that puts control in the hands of local people."

Burnham has offered to devolve powers on localised employment support, currently held by the Department of Work and Pensions.

Both he and the Secretary of State for Scotland, Douglas Alexander, said Scotland was "one of the most centralised nations in Europe", an assertion flatly rejected by Swinney.

News.title: Man jailed for Starmer-linked arson attacks is deported
News.content:
A man who plotted to carry out arson attacks on property connected to Sir Keir Starmer has been deported, the Home Office says.

Stanislav Carpiuc, 28, was one of two men convicted over the attacks, which took place in May last year and targeted a car and two houses.

The Ukrainian-born Romanian national was sentenced to two years in prison in June. The Home Office said he had been removed from the UK, without specifying where he had been sent.

The BBC revealed the attacks were ordered on behalf of Russia, with an anonymous handler known as EL promising payment to Carpiuc's accomplice, Roman Lavrynovych.

Lavrynovych, a 22-year-old Ukrainian national, was sentenced to seven years imprisonment in June.

A Home Office spokesperson said: "This was an abhorrent attack and the conviction and imprisonment of these men should send a clear message to anyone blinded by the promise of money from strangers. You will be caught and face severe consequences.

"This individual has now been deported from the UK," it added, referring to Carpiuc.

News.title: Woman says she was left 'bewildered and confused' by alleged Russell Brand assault
News.content:
The complainant told jurors on Friday she met Brand in 2001 when she worked at MTV.

She said she recognised him straight away and said there was "banter" between them initially.

After noticing his "distinctive T-shirt" with the words "I am Spartacus", she told Brand she "loved it" and wanted it.

"He said, 'you can have it'", the woman told the jury, to which she said she replied: "Make sure it gets a good wash first."

Brand then asked her for directions to the bathroom.

The woman, who was in her thirties at the time, said she offered to show him the way because she was going in the same direction.

Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC asked her what happened next.

She said his "demeanour changed" when they got to the bathroom door.

"He grabbed my forearm, he was leaning into the door and he was quite forceful," she said, adding that it took her "unaware".

Asked by the prosecutor what she meant by his demeanour changing, the witness said: "He grabbed me by the arm, started to pull me in."

She said Brand then said to her "come on" while still holding her forearm.

The woman said while Brand was trying to pull her into the bathroom, she was trying to pull herself away.

"I said to him, 'What are you doing, are you mad, let me go'... and then he started to... plead almost," she said.

The woman told the court she managed to "wrench" herself from Brand's grip because of her own strength.

She told jurors Brand went from "jovial, affable, friendly to suddenly turning into this wild-eyed manic so I was quite confused this was happening, as anyone would be".

Asked by the prosecutor why she did not report what had happened to her employer, she said: "I was scared... I thought it would be my word against his."

But she did tell two of her colleagues, she said.

Jurors heard that she reported the allegation to the police in 2023 after watching a Channel 4 documentary about Brand.

"I thought it was the right thing to do to come forward," she told the court.

Brand's barrister challenged the complainant on the fact that she did not report Brand for what he had allegedly done until after watching the documentary.

"You didn't think there was any need to report him," Ian Winter KC said.

"It would have been my word against his," she replied. "He didn't manage to rape me. I managed to get out of the situation."

The defence barrister said: "It was only after you saw the television programme that you think he was trying to rape you in the toilet."

The woman responded: "Why else would you drag someone into the toilet if you weren't going to assault them."

Winter KC continued: "Twenty-two years before that, you hadn't thought he was trying to get you in there to rape you..."

The woman denied that, adding: "You don't grab someone by the arm. You don't grip someone and try to drag them in, that's not consensual."

News.title: Nurse stole £750k from 99-year-old woman for cosmetic surgery and home improvements
News.content:
A nurse who stole Â£750,000 from a vulnerable 99-year-old and spent the money on cosmetic surgery and home improvements has been struck off.

Rebecca Louise Burwood exploited the resident who was living at Bryn Yr Haul Care Home in Mold, Flintshire, where she was deputy manager, for her own personal and financial gain.

She coerced the pensioner from 2017 to 2023 and also bought a car and campervan with the stolen money, as well as obtaining ownership of the woman's home.

A Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) hearing found Burwood's fitness to practise was impaired by reason of misconduct and imposed a striking-off order, meaning she will be removed from the nursing register.

The NMC hearing was told Burwood had a longstanding relationship with the woman before she moved into the home in 2018.

The panel heard the resident had no family members and was vulnerable after a fall. She was dependent on Burwood for friendship and social contact.

It found that, between 2017 and 2023, Burwood abused a position of trust and power, becoming the resident's lasting power of attorney, while also overseeing her care.

Burwood withdrew money from the woman's bank account, accepted ownership of her house and received thousand of pounds, which was used for her own benefit, including for building work and the purchase of vehicles.

Evidence presented showed more than Â£370,000 had left the resident's account over five years, with Â£160,000 of that from making large cash withdrawals at ATMs.

She also took the resident to the solicitors and got her to transfer the ownership of her Â£400,000 house.

The hearing was told there was "evidence to show Mrs Burwood used the funds for house improvements, utility bills and council tax", and there were "allegations that Mrs Burwood used some of the funds for personal cosmetic surgery".

She convinced the resident to pay Â£20,000 for a car and Â£9,000 for a campervan, which she said was purchased so the pair could go on days outs.

Burwood claimed the work on her home had been so the elderly woman could live with her in the event of another outbreak of Covid - however it had been paid for before any Covid lockdown in the UK.

News.title: Why hasn't the UK had any named storms yet?
News.content:
With November already on the horizon the UK is yet to see its first named storm of the season.

Deep Atlantic lows responsible for more turbulent conditions have been steered away by dominant areas of high pressure.

This year the headlines have been about worsening drought rather than the impact of gales.

However, could this be the calm before the storms as the Met Office predict a growing chance that late autumn and early winter will turn wetter and windier as El NiÃ±o strengthens in the Pacific.

News.title: Burnham invites Swinney to work together on 'deeper Scottish devolution'
News.content:
The prime minister has invited the Scottish government to work together to put "power back in the hands" of regions - but insisted they must "move beyond" the constitutional question of Scottish independence.

Andy Burnham said he wanted to start work on a new deal for regional economic development in the next few months, including an offer of devolution from the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP).

Speaking at an event in Motherwell, Burnham called on first minister John Swinney to cede further powers from Holyrood to local areas before that happened.

SNP minister Stephen Flynn said the party had asked for increased devolution since the Smith Commission report was published in 2014.

The prime minister said devolution "was never supposed to stop at the doors of the Scottish Parliament" when Holyrood opened in 1999.

He said it was meant to be the "start of something deeper" where "communities had more of a say in their own future".

News.title: 'Law change will be my sons' legacy - I hope they're proud of me'
News.content:
Claire Throssell missed seeing her sons by five minutes. She was on her way back from work when they set off for a visit to see their father.

When police knocked on her door later that night, her first thought was: "What has he done?"

Her estranged husband, Darren Sykes, had started a fire in his home while Jack, 12, and Paul, nine, were inside the attic looking at a train set, then locked them in.

The unsupervised access visit had been sanctioned by the family court despite evidence that Sykes had abused both his sons and Claire, and was capable of harming them.

Paul died on that same night, 22 October 2014, and Jack passed away a few days later, believing he had saved his younger brother's life.

Claire made Jack a promise while he lay in her arms in hospital - and this week she feels like, more than a decade on, she kept that promise.

Claire, from Penistone near Barnsley, has spent 12 years campaigning to change the law around presumption of parental involvement, which assumes children benefit from contact with both parents after separation, and on Tuesday she saw the Courts and Tribunals Bill go through its final stages in the Commons.

That means it will become the law she has spent so long fighting for.

I remember sitting in her front room more than a decade ago, nearly a year to the day after the boys were killed.

Some people's nightmares stay with you for a long time.

But Claire has gone through what happened to her, Jack and Paul, thousands of times, in incredibly intricate detail, with hundreds of different journalists.

All because she wanted to keep doing her best to keep her promise.

"There are many days when they are dark. I can sit and think 'how do I get through the next minute?' Never mind the next hour or the next day.

"But then I remind myself that that are dozens of children that don't have that day tomorrow and I've kind of made it my mission to try and educate other people.

"For anyone at risk of harm there is only today, there is no tomorrow and if we can do something better, do it today."

Twelve years on, 2026 marks the year that Jack has been dead for as long as he was alive.

"The right thing to do is love. The right thing to do is take the boys' love and move it forward and share it with the world. Make difference in their names and make a legacy that will last," Claire explains.

"This year, Jack will have been sleeping as long as he was alive. It never feels like a victory, how can it because the boys are not here anymore.

"But it does fell like this is a step to the future, to give generations of children to come, a safe, happy life, free from fear."

News.title: Dad fined after son, 2, died in Cyprus hotel fall
News.content:
A father whose two-year-old boy fell from a fourth floor window of a Cyprus hotel has been fined â¬3,000 (Â£2,500) for causing his death.

Joshua Foster thought the window was closed when he placed his son on a sill to show him the view of a waterpark and "lost control" of him, Paphos District Court previously heard.

The toddler fell nearly 40ft (12.1m) at the five-star King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort on 12 July, the first day of the family's holiday in Chlorakas.

Foster, 37, from Essex, admitted causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act and was sentenced earlier.

He told reporters afterwards: "Thank you for the support. I'm looking forward to going home and being with my wife and daughter."

Later, the family said in a statement: "We are relieved that this process is now over, but for our family, the consequences of this tragedy will never end.

"Our son was deeply loved and will be forever missed. His loss is something we carry with us every day."

Foster, an auditor, arrived in Cyprus hours before the incident with his wife, two children and in-laws.

They enjoyed various activities and swimming, before getting ready for dinner in the evening.

News.title: Teenage boy and pensioner killed in Scotland plane crash
News.content:

Two people, including a teenager, have died after a light aircraft crashed in Scotland, police have said.

Emergency services were called at around 4.45pm on Friday, with a 16-year-old teenager boy and a 80-year-old man pronounced dead at the scene.

Following the crash, temporary airspace restrictions are in place over the Drymen area.

These are likely to be in place to allow the Air Accidents Investigation Branch to investigate, police said.

More follows on this breaking news story

News.title: White House’s Katie Zacharia sitting down for ‘interview with Wall Street Journal when fired by Trump’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

White House press secretary Katie Zacharia had been sitting down for an interview with the newspaper The Wall Street Journal when she discovered she had been fired just five days into her role, reports say.

Donald Trump’s latest press secretary had made a disastrous debut on Tuesday, taking only three questions from friendly outlets, reading from a script and speaking for only 14 minutes.

The 42-year-old had also faced scrutiny over her legal background after the US president described her as an attorney - despite her confirming that she had never passed the bar exam.

The Journal wrote that they had been interviewing Ms Zacharia at her desk in the West Wing at 1pm on Friday, when she received a knock on the door from Jason Miller, a senior adviser to the president.

“JD wanted to chat with us real quick,” Mr Miller had said, referring the JD Vance, the vice president.

open image in gallery Donald Trump told reporters he had told her to ‘reconsider’ her position ( Reuters )

Minutes later, Mr Trump told reporters at his helipad that he had told Ms Zacharia: “I said, ‘Is this for you Katie? Because honestly, you don’t need this’”.

He added: “Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider.”

The Journal noted that Ms Zacharia, who had previously worked on the conservative radio programme The Clay Travis and Buck Sexton Show, failed to return to the interview.

“I did everything in my power to effectuate a briefing in the limited time and information I had,” she later told The Journal on Friday night, hours after her firing, according to the outlet. “My goal was to serve President Trump and the American people to the best of my ability.”

In a post on social media, she said: “President Trump is a kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man. I wish more Americans appreciated him.

“No one will ever make America great the way he has and continues to. It was an honor to work for him.”

Ms Zacharia had faced scrutiny over her first White House press conference, in which she had appeared visibly nervous and referred to her husband as the president.

During the briefing, she was asked by a reporter about where she passed the bar exam, and replied that she had done so while living in China.

However on Thursday, under pressure from the media, she admitted that she did not pass the bar exam but had practiced international transaction law in China with the “appropriate credentials”.

open image in gallery In her first press briefing, she only spoke for 14 minutes and took three questions ( AFP/Getty )

In an interview with conservative talking head Sean Hannity on Fox News, she faced particularly tough questioning, with the host asking: “Why didn’t you just say, ‘I never practiced the law?”

When she described how quickly she had taken on the role of press secretary, following Karoline Leavitt’s departure, he asked: "Am I hearing that you think the staff should have better prepped you?"

Her early exit is the quickest among the president’s White House press team, after Anthony Scaramucci left his post as communications director after only 10 days during Mr Trump’s first term.

Her departure also means that the crucial communications role is vacant just three weeks ahead of the midterm elections, with polls suggesting that Mr Trump could see a dramatic turn in favour amongst the American public over the cost of living crisis and the Iran war.

News.title: Celebrity Traitors 2026 lineup – Meet all the contestants competing on series two
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

After the huge success of The Celebrity Traitors’ smash-hit inaugural series last year, host Claudia Winkleman is back with a fresh crop of famous faces in the Scottish castle.

And once again, the BBC has booked an all-star line-up, with award-winning actors, chart-topping musicians and no less than five (five!) comedians among the celebrities playing as either Faithfuls or Traitors.

There’s a huge prize up for grabs too, as those who are victorious will win up to £100,000 for a charity of their choice.

Get to know the celebrities taking part in the ultimate game of deception below...

Michael Sheen – Faithful

open image in gallery Michael Sheen on ‘Celebrity Traitors’ ( BBC )

Stage and screen star Michael Sheen began his career with increasingly prominent theatre roles in the 1990s, culminating in Laurence Olivier Award nominations in 1998 and 1999, for his performances in Amadeus and Look Back In Anger, respectively. The Welsh star expanded his on-screen career in the Noughties, notably playing Tony Blair in three films penned by Peter Morgan (The Crown). His other film credits include the Oscar-nominated Frost/Nixon, British hit The Damned United and Woody Allen’s Midnight In Paris.

In recent years, Sheen has appeared in TV shows including of Good Omens, Quiz (in which he played Chris Tarrant), and A Very Royal Scandal. He has also become known for his activism, thanks to documentaries including Michael Sheen's Secret Million Pound Giveaway and Buried with Michael Sheen. He was announced as the new host of House of Games earlier this year, taking over from Richard Osman.

Maya Jama – Traitor

open image in gallery ‘Love Island’ host Maya Jama ( ITV )

Love Island host Maya Jama is swapping cameo appearances in the ITV villa for a stint in the BBC Traitors castle.

She’s hosted Love Island and its various spin-offs since 2023. Bristol-born Jama moved to London to pursue an acting career in 2012, but soon realised she’d be better suited to presenting. After joining MTV as a presenter in 2014, she went on to front a series of Channel 4’s The Circle, ITV’s Saturday night gameshow Cannonball and BBC Three’s competition series Glow Up: Britain’s Next Make-Up Star.

Jama’s other hosting jobs include the Mobo Awards and the Brit Awards, and she also previously enjoyed a stint in the Radio 1 studios, fronting her one twice-weekly show between 2018 and 2020. Her love life – including past high-profile relationships with rapper Stormzy, NBA player Ben Simmons and Portuguese footballer Rúben Dias – has also made headlines over the years.

Ross Kemp – Faithful

open image in gallery Ross Kemp is best known for playing Grant Mitchell ( BBC/Jack Barnes/Kieron McCarron/PA Wire )

Ross Kemp is best known for playing EastEnders hardman Grant Mitchell from 1990 to 1999, and he has reprised the role multiple times since first leaving Walford. Most recently, Grant was back in E20 in April to say farewell to his longtime friend Nigel Bates. Kemp’s other acting credits include a mid-Eighties stint in Emmerdale and a phenomenal guest appearance in Ricky Gervais’s Extras.

He has also made a name for himself as a presenter and journalist, fronting documentaries such as the Bafta-winning Ross Kemp on Gangs, Ross Kemp in Afghanistan and Sky’s Extreme World, which ran for six series. Kemp has presented daytime quiz show Bridge of Lies on BBC One since 2022 and went viral online over the summer after he shared increasingly passionate Instagram videos to cheer England on during the World Cup.

Julie Hesmondhalgh – Banished Faithful

open image in gallery Julie Hesmondhalgh won an Olivier in 2025 ( Getty )

Coronation Street legend Julie Hesmondhalgh played Weatherfield’s Hayley Cropper for 14 years. The much-loved Hayley arrived on the cobbles in 1998 and was the first regular transgender character to appear in a British soap. Viewers were left devastated when Hesmondhalgh decided to leave the ITV programme in 2014. The emotional exit storyline saw Hayley take her own life after receiving a cancer diagnosis; the actor had asked bosses to kill her character off so she wouldn’t be tempted to return to the soap.

Hesmondhalgh has since landed TV roles in the likes of Russell T Davies’ Cucumber, Happy Valley and Broadchurch, as well as branching out into theatre, winning an Olivier Award for her performance in James Graham’s 2025 play Punch. In January last year, she played subpostmaster Alan Bates’s wife Suzanne Sercombe in ITV’s groundbreaking drama Mr Bates vs The Post Office.

Rob Beckett – Murdered

open image in gallery Comedian Rob Beckett ( Getty )

Rob Beckett was cast as one of five comedians in the Traitors castle. With his cheeky chappy persona, the south-east London born star soon won over fans when he started out on the stand-up circuit in 2009, and went on to appear on panel shows Mock the Week, 8 out of 10 Cats and the latter’s Countdown spin-off. In 2017, he won the third series of Taskmaster.

Beckett has also dipped his toe into the world of reality television on more than a few occasions, hosting three seasons of ITV’s I'm a Celebrity spin-off show, providing the voiceover for Celebs Go Dating and taking part in Celebrity Bake Off.

Together with Strictly Come Dancing host Josh Widdicombe, he fronts the podcast Parenting Hell. And Beckett is also part of a hugely popular double act with another of this year’s Celebrity Traitors contestants…

Romesh Ranganathan – Faithful

open image in gallery Comic Romesh Ranganathan ( PA Wire )

Former maths teacher Romesh Ranganathan began his comedy career while he was still working full-time in the classroom. After a brief flirtation with freestyle rap, Ranganathan found his footing on the comedy circuit and enjoyed a huge boost in popularity when he appeared on the BBC’s Live at the Apollo in 2013.

Since then, he’s appeared on the likes of Taskmaster, Would I Lie To You?, Have I Got News For You and QI. Ranganathan has also fronted quiz shows including Sky’s A League of Their Own and the BBC’s The Weakest Link revival. He’s channelled his love of music into a weekly Radio 2 show, For The Love of Hip-Hop, and took over the station’s Saturday lunchtime slot from Claudia Winkleman in April 2024.

Beckett and Ranganathan have landed a number of joint gigs, with the former’s chirpy attitude being balanced out by the latter’s often sarcastic and deadpan musings. The pair have a popular Sky series, Rob and Romesh Vs…, and co-hosted the TV Baftas in 2023 and 2024.

Jerry Hall – Faithful

open image in gallery Wildcard booking Jerry Hall ( AFP/Getty )

One of this year’s truly wildcard bookings, supermodel Jerry Hall is bringing old-school glamour to the castle.

Hall’s modelling career began in the 1970s, when she appeared as a mermaid on the cover of Roxy Music’s album Siren. She became synonymous with the glamour of the Seventies disco era, appearing on magazine covers for the likes of Vogue UK, Cosmopolitan and Interview, and often being photographed at Studio 54 with close friend Andy Warhol, who counted Hall as a muse, and then-boyfriend Mick Jagger.

Hall and the Rolling Stones frontman remained together until 1999, with the pair welcoming four children during that time. Throughout their relationship, Hall continued to expand her career and moved into acting, landing roles in Tim Burton’s Batman, TV series Cluedo and a Broadway production of The Graduate.

Hall married media mogul Rupert Murdoch in a low-key London ceremony in 2016. The couple remained together until 2022, when Hall filed for divorce citing irreconcilable differences.

Joe Lycett – Banished Faithful

open image in gallery Comedian Joe Lycett ( Getty )

Birmingham-based funnyman Joe Lycett’s comedy has become increasingly surrealist and absurd over the years – with a touch of Martin Lewis thrown in for good measure. He’s appeared on all of the major comedy and panel shows on British television (think Taskmaster, 8 out of 10 Cats, Last One Laughing UK) and fronted his own consumer rights show Joe Lycett's Got Your Back, Channel 4’s Travel Man and The Great British Sewing Bee.

In 2023, he began hosting his very own live variety show, Late Night Lycett. The star has also leaned in to comedic stunts in recent years, legally changing his name to Hugo Boss to draw attention to the fashion brand’s use of cease and desist letters against small businesses.

James Blunt – Faithful

open image in gallery Singer James Blunt ( Getty )

James Blunt made the unlikely journey from British Army captain to chart-topper when he released “You’re Beautiful” in 2005, three years after leaving the forces. The single went straight to the top of the UK charts, and boosted the popularity of his debut album Back to Bedlam, which had actually been released a year before. With the record top of the charts, Blunt also also released “Goodbye My Lover” as a single.

At the 2006 Brit Awards, he was named best british pop act and best british male solo act, and a follow-up album, All the Lost Souls, followed in 2007. He has since released five more albums, with another – titled Airplane Mode – coming out in November this year. When he’s not in the studio, Blunt is a keen user of X and has frequently gone viral thanks to self-deprecating, sarcastic and pithy comebacks.

Bella Ramsey – Murdered

open image in gallery Bella Ramsey in ‘The Last of Us’ ( HBO )

Bella Ramsey was just 11 years old when they began filming Game of Thrones. The child star played Lyanna Mormont, the young ruler who found herself at the head of her family following her mother’s death. After appearances in CBBC’s The Worst Witch, Phillip Pullman adaptation His Dark Materials and anthology series Time, Ramsey landed a leading role in HBO’s The Last Of Us.

Adapted from the hugely popular PlayStation game of the same name, The Last Of Us sees Ramsay’s Ellie attempting to survive alongside unlikely guardian Joel (Pedro Pascal). The show and its leading stars both received awards nods for the first two seasons, with Ramsey nominated for an Emmy, a Critics’ Choice award and a Golden Globe. Two series of The Last Of Us have so far aired, with a third set to arrive in 2027.

Richard E Grant – Banished Traitor

open image in gallery Actor Richard E Grant ( AFP/Getty )

Legendary actor Richard E Grant has one of the most impressive CVs in the business. The Swazi-English actor made his debut as the titular character in 1987’s Withnail and I, and is also known for films including The Portrait of a Lady, Gosford Park, The Iron Lady, Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker and Emerald Fennell’s controversial Saltburn. He received an Academy Award nomination for 2018’s Can You Forgive Me?, a biographical drama about American author Lee Israel.

On the small screen, his credits include Doctor Who, Frasier, A Series of Unfortunate Events and Game of Thrones. In 2022, he released a best-selling memoir, A Pocketful of Happiness, which chronicled his 40-year marriage to dialect coach Joan Washington, and her death from cancer in 2021.

Leigh-Anne Pinnock – Faithful

open image in gallery Singer Leigh-Anne Pinnock ( Getty )

Singer Leigh-Anne Pinnock rocketed to fame as one fourth of Little Mix, the first group to ever win The X Factor. Pinnock triumphed with bandmates Jade Thirlwall, Perrie Edwards and Jesy Nelson in 2011 and Little Mix went on to become the UK’s most successful girlband since the Spice Girls, with hit singles including “D.N.A”, “Shout out to my Ex”, “Black Magic” and “Power”.

Nelson departed the group in 2020 and Little Mix continued as a trio until 2022, when they announced an indefinite hiatus. Pinnock has since pursued a solo career and initially signed with Warner Records, before leaving after the label decided against releasing her debut album. Pinnock then moved to Virgin and My Ego Told Me To came out in February this year. The singer and her husband Andre Gray are parents to twin daughters, and announced in May this year that a third child is on the way.

James Acaster – Traitor

open image in gallery James Acaster thinks comedians have a disadvantage on ‘Celebrity Traitors’ ( BBC )

James Acaster has said he’s worried previous winner Alan Carr’s success in the Traitors castle has “tainted” this year’s comedians. “I think we’re going to be the first ones under the magnifying glass being looked at – particularly at the beginning when you have absolutely nothing to go on,” he told the BBC.

The comedian is another of this year’s recruits who cut their teeth in stand-up, and has taken multiple shows to the Edinburgh Fringe Festival, with Repertoire also being released on Netflix. He hosts the popular foodie podcast Off Menu with Traitors Uncloaked host Ed Gamble and has written two books about music, James Acaster’s Classic Scrapes and Perfect Sound Whatever.

Miranda Hart – Faithful

open image in gallery Miranda Hart in her mega-hit BBC sitcom ( BBC )

Actor, comedian and writer Miranda Hart is best-known for her self-titled BBC sitcom, which landed multiple TV Bafta nominations and British Comedy Award wins across its three seasons. She also appeared as midwife Camilla “Chummy” Fortescue-Cholmondeley-Browne in Call the Midwife and made her Hollywood debut opposite Mellisa McCarthy in the action comedy Spy.

She’s release numerous books, including 2012’s Is it Just Me?, which merged anecdotes from her life with advice, and The Girl With The Lost Smile. In 2024, she released the memoir I Haven't Been Entirely Honest with You, revealing on the book’s promotional tour that she had secretly married at the age of 51. The book also recounted how she’d been experiencing a decades-long struggle with Lyme disease, which turned into ME (Myalgic encephalomyelitis), also known as chronic fatigue syndrome.

Amol Rajan – Murdered

open image in gallery Amol Rajan recently left the ‘Today’ programme ( PA )

Broadcaster Amol Rajan got his start in journalism at this very publication in 2007, and moved up the ranks before serving as editor between 2013 and 2016. After leaving, he became the BBC’s first media editor, before joining the Today programme’s presenting team in 2021 – a role he recently left.

On the small screen, Rajan has hosted University Challenge since 2023, and appeared on the likes of The One Show, Have I Got News For You and House of Games.

Joanne McNally – Faithful

open image in gallery Comedian Joanne McNally ( Getty )

Completing the series’ quintet of comedians, it’s Irish star Joanne McNally.

After years on the comedy circuit, McNally took her her dark one-woman show Bite Me, about her bulimia, to Edinburgh Fringe Festival in 2017. She hit the road with her Prosecco Express show in 2022 and the tour was extended multiple times. By the time it was done and dusted, McNally had performed a record-breaking 78 sold-out shows at Dublin’s Vicar Street venue, while her crowd at the London Palladium broke the 118-year old venue’s record for most alcohol sold.

McNally followed it up with the Pinotphile tour, which began in 2025, squeezing in appearances on Taskmaster and Channel 4's The Big Fat Quiz of Everything in between. She co-hosts the popular My Therapist Ghosted Me podcast with close pal Vogue Williams.

Sharon Rooney – Faithful

open image in gallery Sharon Rooney in ‘My Mad Fat Diary’ ( Channel 4 )

Scottish actor Sharon Rooney landed her breakthrough role in Channel 4’s acclaimed comedy My Mad Fat Diary back in 2013. Subsequent television roles have included parts in Sherlock, The Capture and Finding Alice, as well as appearing as series regular Sophie in Two Doors Down.

On the big screen, Rooney popped up in Greta Gerwig’s Barbie film, as a lawyer version of the famous doll, and played Miss Atlantic in Disney’s live-action remake of Dumbo, performing the track “Baby Mine”.

King Kenny – Traitor

open image in gallery King Kenny in the ring ( Getty )

While he’s not technically a comedian, social media star King Kenny loves to bring the laughs with pranks and stunts. Kenny, full name Kenny Oghenovo Ojuederie, is a former boxer who primarily fought other influencers, before quitting the sport earlier this year due to injury.

He’s built a huge audience on TikTok and YouTube, with almost three million followers across the two platforms. Kenny’s most popular videos include pranks – often involving his younger brother – and gaming-related videos. He was previously part of the Beta Squad collective with fellow pranksters including Niko Omilana, who appeared in the first series of Celebrity Traitors but went out early.

Professor Hannah Fry – Banished Traitor

open image in gallery Professor Hannah Fry ( PA Wire )

Broadcaster and mathematician Professor Hannah Fry has been making television and radio appearances for more than 10 years. Some of her most notable cameos include the BBC Two series The Secret Genius Of Modern Life, the post-pandemic documentary Unvaccinated and number-crunching for Channel 4 during their general election coverage in 2024.

Fry also hosts The Rest Science podcast alongside Michael Stevens and has a huge following online, with more than 100 million views on her YouTube channel.

Sebastian Croft – Faithful

open image in gallery Actor and musician Sebastian Croft ( Getty )

Actor and musician Sebastian Croft is another Traitors star who has had a brush with Westeros – as a child star, he played a young Ned Stark in two episodes of Game of Thrones. Croft’s more recent credits include Netflix’s Heartstopper and Amazon Video romcom How to Date Billy Walsh.

On the music front, Croft has independently released two singles, “Toyko” and “Better than ever”. The star identifies as queer and in 2022, he designed a t-shirt featuring “two gay dinosaurs kissing, reminding everyone that Queer has always been here”, with profits from sales going to two charities that support LGBT+ refugees.

Myha’la – Banished Faithful

open image in gallery Myha’la ( Getty )

American actor Myha’la Herrold, known just by her first name, is best known for playing chaotic antihero Harper Stern in Industry.

Born and raised in California, the star began her acting career with a string of theatre roles, including parts in Shrek the Musical and a touring production of Book of Mormon. Myha’la has also appeared in the Loch Henry episode in series six of Charlie Brooker’s Black Mirror, the New York Times-inspired series Modern Love, and films Dumb Money and Leave the World Behind.

News.title: Reform councillor resigns after being filmed making racist remarks
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A Reform councillor who was filmed by an undercover journalist calling Asian homeowners “parasites” has resigned over his “completely unacceptable” remarks.

Alan Feeney, who held posts on Solihull Council and Birmingham City Council, was one of several Reform members featured in an ITV investigation, and was also recorded saying no more than 1 per cent of the UK population should be non-white.

In a post on Facebook, he announced he had stepped down from his post, saying: “My remarks were wrong, offensive and completely unacceptable. They do not reflect the standards that the public rightly expects from an elected representative, and I take full responsibility for what I said.

“The comments do not reflect my true beliefs or opinions, particularly of the communities mentioned in the report. These are communities I have supported countless times in my personal and professional life over many years, many of whom I have been lucky enough to call friends.”

He continued: “There is no excuse for my comments. With responsibility comes accountability, and it is for that reason that I have resigned every post I hold on both Solihull borough council and Birmingham city council.”

open image in gallery Nigel Farage said in 2024 ‘we don't want extremists, we don't want bigots’ ( Getty )

Mr Feeney had been appointed deputy mayor of Solihull after winning seats in the Shard End ward of Birmingham and the Castle Bromwich ward of Solhill metropolitan borough council.

He added: “Byelections will be held on a timescale laid out by those councils in the due course. I hope that in time these councils, and the communities they serve can heal and move on.”

After ITV published the first part of their investigation on Wednesday, Mr Feeney said he was leaving Reform for “personal reasons” but would remain as an independent councillor.

He has now resigned, while the Ministry of Justice has also suspended him from his job with the prison service, describing his comments as “despicable”.

The footage, part of a documentary by ITV Exposure to be screened on Sunday night, followed Reform UK election candidates and councillors across England and Wales during the May local elections and four by-election campaigns in 2025 and 2026.

It also recorded Mr Feeney saying of Asian people: “Drag them out of their homes, stick them on planes and f*** them off to Pakistan.”

Speaking about a female Reform candidate, another Reform male councillor, Chris Whelan, said: “If she was my daughter, it would still be bath night on a Thursday”.

Councillor Whelan also resigned from Reform for personal and health reasons. In a statement, responding to the issues raised in the ITV documentary, Solihull Borough Council said: "There is no place for this disgusting racist discriminatory and misogynistic language in public life, and these comments do not represent the values of Solihull Council or its residents.

"We have received a resignation from Mr Whelan and will be investigating the complaints made against councillor Feeney”.

Mr Whelan has been approached for comment.

A spokesperson for Reform UK said: "Not all individuals covertly recorded by ITV are members of Reform UK. Where members, activists and councillors have clearly behaved inappropriately, investigations have commenced. In some cases, there have been suspensions and due process must be followed.”

Reform UK also said it had improved its vetting procedures “but from time to time, a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting. This is the same for all organisations.”

The investigation came “at a time when Nigel Farage and other members of Reform are being targeted by individuals who wished them harm and caused a security issue which was documented during the course of the undercover investigation”, but was not included in the report, the party said.

In September 2024, Nigel Farage promised he would improve the party’s vetting process saying “we don't want extremists, we don't want bigots, we don’t want people who think that way, because we represent the silent, decent majority of this great country that we live in.”

News.title: The Fabio Wardley fear motivating mission for revenge against Daniel Dubois
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

As a battered and bruised Fabio Wardley made his way to the back following his war with Daniel Dubois in May - right eye closed shut, nose splattered, the white of his Ipswich Town-themed trunks now pink - the now-former WBO world champion had one thought and one thought only: “Get me back in.”

Wardley had just been on the losing end of a firefight that he could have had in the bag inside 15 seconds. His first-round knockdown of Dubois was followed up by another two rounds later, as the 31-year-old consigned criticism of being a slow starter to the scrapheap once and for all. Alas, it was during the third round where one sharp Dubois overhand right turned the tides. A torrent of ‘Dynamite’ punishment ensued, proving his heart beyond doubt, and Wardley was eventually stopped in the 11th.

It was a brutal way to be dealt a first career loss. But Wardley didn’t want to wallow in his failure; not for a second. Asked at what point he requested the rematch, which goes down at London’s O2 Arena this Saturday, Wardley said: “Immediately. I was sat in the changing room and I think I was asking for Frank [Warren, his promoter]. I was like, ‘Someone go get Frank and tell him we're doing this again in November,’ immediately.

open image in gallery A battered and bruised Fabio Wardley immediately asked his promoter Frank Warren to set up the Daniel Dubois rematch ( Getty )

“What else am I gonna do? Just go, ‘No,’ and run off in a different direction or, ‘No, I think I need two or three fights to build me back up. I need my confidence back.’ F*** that. No. Get me back in. I'll sort it out myself. I'll right the wrongs. I'll fix it, and we'll go again.”

Wardley was back in the gym within two weeks. As bad as the optics were, he insists it was business as usual within hours of the fight being waved off. He was back on dad duty by 4am on Sunday morning. “I know it sounds really weird to say, but I was fine,” he said. “I had a swollen eye and a cut nose, and I was a little bit tired and whatever else. But overall, I was fine. I still had a lump of a baby on my shoulder bouncing around, and I stood there for half an hour getting her down and whichever else. I was still able to turn up in that capacity.”

He is expecting another child in December, giving him a bit more breathing room post-fight than he had for his first-born, who arrived a week after his win over Justis Huni in June 2025. He says neither were planned: “They just keep popping up!”

Some fighters use their children as a motivation. Others become more aware of their health and the perils of fighting in parenthood. Wardley seemed to be falling into the latter camp after the insane Huni fight, saying he wanted to avoid being in so many wars that “keep taking years off my life”. He’s about to re-enter the ring with a man with whom he shared the biggest war of his career. “I don’t listen to myself,” he conceded.

To be both Wardley the fighter and Wardley the father, he has to separate the two. “There’s a Jekyll and Hyde going on, they’re two different people,” he explained. “I love my child dearly with every bit of my heart, but I guess in the nicest way, she is no consideration to me whatsoever when I'm in the middle of the ring, because she can't be. That can’t be a factor in my brain, otherwise I'm not gonna achieve big things.”

open image in gallery Wardley (right) will go to war with WBO world heavyweight champion Dubois (left) again this Saturday ( Getty )

Moving on from the setback of five months ago required Wardley to do something he’d never done before: watch back a fight he’d lost. To start, he was doing this alone in the dead of night, waiting for his partner and baby to go to sleep before poring over the footage: “I knew my missus doesn’t really enjoy it.” He has since learned where he needed to adjust, and while he obviously wasn’t going to share that information before fight night, he believes his malleability will shine through in their rematch.

“I think we can all be very plain and honest here that the room for growth between the pair of us is exponentially in my favour,” Wardley proclaimed. “That's not to take away from Daniel at all. He's a good fighter. He does things very well, and he has done for a number of years.

“But the room for change and growth and adjustment in style [is something] which I've proven across different fights against different fighters. I've not looked the same in all my fights. I've been able to adjust and change things around. That's already ticked off and proven in my books. I just need to apply it again to this fight.”

open image in gallery Wardley says the scope for growth is far greater for him than Dubois ( PA )

Wardley has continued to repeat the same summation of his first fight in the build-up to the second: “I was a victim of my own success.” He lacked the composure necessary when Dubois was there for the taking. But as he heads into fight week, Wardley is at ease; that night in Manchester confirmed to him that he has the fundamentals of beating Dubois already down.

He can hit him hard enough. “I’ve ticked that box, I can knock you down - and not just the once, the twice. It doesn’t prove it’s a fluke; it’s a consistent action, it’s something I can do,” Wardley said. But he can also get hit. Asked about Dubois’s haymakers, he denied being particularly taken aback: “I’m not gonna disrespect the man by saying he’s not a big puncher or that I didn’t feel it. I did - I just wasn’t... that bothered by it.”

Wardley is confident he will this time find a way to get through Dubois in the cauldron of the O2 Arena. Redemption has been on his mind from the moment he was beaten. But it’s not just personal revenge that has motivated his quick turnaround. There is a changing of the guard at heavyweight; Wardley refuses to become a side character of the new generation.

open image in gallery Wardley says he wasn’t ‘that bothered’ by Dubois’s power ( Getty )

“We've seen how quickly the division can be turned on its head. [Oleksandr] Usyk vacating the belts threw the division upside down, and all of a sudden there was all these fights being made and all these things going on. If I'm just sat at the wayside, I can be left, lost in the dark,” he said.

In his quest to fill an Usyk-shaped hole at the very top, diving straight back into this rematch comes with a huge risk. Back-to-back defeats could send Wardley plummeting out of the world title picture. On the difficulty of building Wardley back up in the event of another loss, Warren said, “It depends how he loses,” before the Queensberry chief - who also promotes Dubois - quickly hinted there will only be one outcome: “It ain’t gonna go the distance. Not these two.”

This will not just be a slugfest spectacle; there are career-altering stakes at play. Dubois succeeded when tasked with bouncing back from failure before, doing so against Wardley. No longer surrounded by the mystique of being undefeated, Wardley now gets his turn to prove he belongs.

Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley meet again tonight, with boxing fans expecting another chaotic classic between the British heavyweights.

In May, Dubois climbed off the canvas twice – including in the first 20 seconds – to stop Wardley on his feet as the towel came in in round 11.

With that dramatic victory in Manchester, Dubois won the WBO title, which he will defend against Wardley in tonight’s main event in London.

open image in gallery Fabio Wardley (left) and Daniel Dubois during first fight, in May ( PA Wire )

Wardley had never lost as a professional before his 11th-round defeat by Dubois, so has he learned the relevant lessons to exact revenge?

Or will Dubois extend his second world-title reign and close in on a unification fight?

When is the fight?

Dubois vs Wardley 2 will take place on Saturday 17 October at the O2 Arena in London. The main card is due to begin at 7pm BST (11am PT / 1pm CT / 2pm ET), with main-event ring walks at around 10.30pm BST (2.30pm PT / 4.30pm CT / 5.30pm ET).

The event will stream live exclusively on DAZN pay-per-view at a cost of £24.99, and on DAZN Ultimate Tier – which is priced at £24.99 per month. You can purchase the fight or an Ultimate Tier subscription here.

News.title: Top 10 heavyweight fighters in boxing as Dubois and Wardley rematch before Fury vs Joshua
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Heavyweight boxing continues to be a compelling draw in the sport with two monster fights on the horizon as Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley rematch and Tyson Fury finally meets Anthony Joshua in the highly-anticipated bout between the two generational British fighters.

That fight, to bring an end to 2026, should set up a fascinating 2027 with a number of contenders, including newly-crowned champions Agit Kabayel and Filip Hrgovic. While super talent Moses Itauma will hope to regroup after a shock first defeat of his career.

Then there is the king of the division: Oleksandr Usyk, patiently waiting for one final payday and an attraction to showcase his exceptional skill on the way out of what has been a legendary career.

Honourable mentions should go out to Murat Gassiev, who holds the WBA regular belt, while Efe Ajagba, Justis Huni, Frank Sanchez, Bakhodir Jalolov and Deontay Wilder remain live contenders.

Here, Independent Sport glosses over the contenders and ranks the fighters on both credentials and their present ability in the ring, as the division takes shape and hurtles towards another unification bout in 2027.

10. Rico Verhoeven (1-1-0)

A controversial selection, perhaps, the great Dutch kickboxer is ranked in the top 10 by the WBC and top 15 by the WBA after his impressive display to get on top of Oleksandr Usyk in Cairo, only to be ground down and stopped late, even if there was some debate over the premature nature of the stoppage. A fight with Deontay Wilder has been floated, on the undercard of Fury v Joshua, which would offer insight into Verhoeven’s ability to mix it with lesser competition in the sport. A rematch with the Ukrainian legend is surely a priority, yet Verhoeven against any of the fighters on this list would be compelling from a competition standpoint, which legitimises his presence in this list.

open image in gallery Rico Verhoeven and Oleksandr Usyk touch gloves ( Getty )

9. Joseph Parker (36-4-0)

After reports that Parker’s positive test for cocaine before his defeat to Fabio Wardley in October last year was caused by a nutritionist, Parker appears to be in the clear to fight again. And while he was exhausted and overpowered by the heavy-handed Wardley last time out, he held his own and showed his exceptional skill to box and move, piling up the rounds and moving to the brink of victory before that dramatic 11th round conclusion. If back and healthy, Parker will be a live opponent for anybody on this list.

8. Moses Itauma (14-1-0)

The aforementioned Parker, rusty after a long lay-off, could make for a fine test for Itauma off the back of his stunning upset defeat to Filip Hrgovic. The promise and potential remain immense, but lessons must be learned, despite dominating the Croatian until his unfortunate and abrupt demise in the ninth round in August. A straight rematch appears too risky for a 21-year-old, but there’s no way back now and a big name to headline will be required next in a highly-anticipated comeback.

7. Anthony Joshua (30-4-0)

Finally set to mix it with great rival Tyson Fury in a fight that might be decided by who has more left in the tank. Joshua’s immense power could point to great hope, with the cliche that it is always the last asset to go for a fighter. The turmoil of that first round against Kristian Prenga casts doubt on ‘AJ’ and his stature in the division, yet his prowess and heart, let’s not forget from his gripping contest with Daniel Dubois in 2024, show how dangerous he remains.

open image in gallery Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua will be fighting in the early hours of the morning ( PA Wire )

6. Filip Hrgovic (21-1-0)

Rocketing up these rankings after a stunning win as a massive underdog to Itauma to snatch the IBF world title, Hrgovic is eager to snatch a world title in the coming months. Since a bloody loss to Dubois in 2024, Hrgovic dispatched Joe Joyce, David Adeleye and Dave Allen, with the patient, yet ruthless defeat of Itauma showing he is ready for another big test in the near future as the belt holder.

5. Agit Kabayel (27-0-0)

The WBC champion, undefeated, might consider himself unlucky not to be a little higher on this list, considering he dealt with Arslanbek Makhmudov in better fashion than Tyson Fury and then put away Frank Sanchez and the past-his-prime Zhilei Zhang before a soft win over Damian Knyba to pick up the interim belt before being elevated. Nelson Hysa might not convince the doubters yet, but Kabayel deserves a big unification fight in 2027, perhaps with the winner of Dubois v Wardley 2.

4. Tyson Fury (36-2-1)

Finally in the ring with Joshua to conclude 2026, Fury will hope to shake off the rust displayed against Makhmudov and then again with the glorified sparring session with Mariusz Wach to tune up for ‘AJ’. The pedigree still warrants respect and there is less vulnerability than Joshua to ensure he holds a lofty ranking here. Fury is adamant he will fight Usyk once more, but he’ll need to look dominant in Cardiff to convince fans a third fight sets pulses racing.

3. Fabio Wardley (20-1-1)

Had Dubois hurt and in trouble on a few occasions before succumbing to the brutal, bruising nature of a heavyweight classic. Showed his power carries deep into fights, but a more cautious or slippery performance is surely needed to avoid another sickening end to the rematch. Maybe the most exciting heavyweight in the world and ready to prove doubters wrong as an “underdog” in the rematch.

2. Daniel Dubois (23-3-0)

An outstanding resume all of a sudden, despite two losses to Usyk. Stopped Hrgovic, who has since made that win look even better after stunning Itauma, then destroyed Joshua at Wembley before recovering from a second Usyk defeat to claim the WBO title with a crushing 11th round come-from-behind victory over Wardley. Another dominant display puts the division in an awkward position: does anybody want to see a third fight with Usyk? Does Usyk deserve one or two more showcase fights? If so, then Dubois is essentially the No 1 fighter in the division that remains active and open to all challengers.

open image in gallery Daniel Dubois suffered two stoppage losses to Oleksandr Usyk ( Getty )

1. Oleksandr Usyk (25-0-0)

Usyk remains the king of the heavyweights, but for how much longer? Verhoeven perhaps showed the cracks or the inevitable signs of Father Time gradually imposing itself on the legendary Ukrainian. A rematch against the Dutch kickboxer? A trilogy with Fury? There doesn’t appear to be an obvious fight for Usyk left, even if he will gladly pick up one last payday.

News.title: Canada end England’s 41-match unbeaten streak with first defeat in four years
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

England were stunned by a late charge from Canada as the Red Roses lost their 41-match unbeaten run that stretched back four years.

Last month, Canada snapped England’s 39-game winning streak with a 26-26 draw against the World Cup champions in Exeter.

And Canada finally earned revenge for their defeat to England in last year’s World Cup final at Twickenham as they won 24-21 in front of a record crowd in Toronto.

Shoshanah Seumanutafa came off the bench to score the match-winning try in the 77th minute, bringing England’s dominant run to an end.

The Red Roses had not lost a match since their previous World Cup final against New Zealand in 2022, a loss that started their unbeaten run to becoming world champions.

England’s head coach John Mitchell said he was focused on taking what positives he could out of the defeat and the Red Roses will play Canada again next Saturday in Ottawa.

It will be the second encounter of the two-game Rugby Rematch Tour between the growing rivals and Mitchell said the defeat will allow him to learn even more about his group.

“We’re not driven by outcome,” Mitchell said. “We’re disappointed by the result but there was some very good things in our performance tonight. So we’ll stick to our processes.

open image in gallery ( Getty )

“I guess (the loss) frees us up and allows us all to find more. I know this group has got more in them but sometimes it requires the context that we’ve just received to dig deeper and find something more.

“Maybe everyone in the group can probably review their ‘why’s and re-establish those as well because I’m sure they’re changing and evolving as they experience what we’re going through.”

Canada looked up for the challenge early as they opened the scoring through Savannah Bauder in the 15th minute.

Quickfire tries to Maddie Feaunati and Zoe Harrison just before half-time put England ahead 14-5 at the break.

open image in gallery Canada's Shoshanah Seumanutafa (23) dives to make a try ( AP )

The points kept flowing as both teams crossed just after play resumed, but DaLeaka Menin’s 63rd-minute try kept the door open for Canada.

A raucous home crowd exploded for Shoshanah Seumanutafa’s match-winner shortly after, with Canada able to hold on from there and quell England’s historic run.

The crowd of ⁠18,621 set a record for a women’s rugby union match in North America and Red Roses captain Meg Jones said England came away taking “huge pride” in their unbeaten run.

“We're the biggest advocates for the game," Jones said. “So we're always going to try and grow the game as much as we can, and Canada definitely did that in tenfold today.”

Includes reporting from agencies

News.title: Wallabies left wondering if Bledisloe pain will ever end after All Blacks thrashing
News.content:
New Zealand blew Australia off the field in an extraordinary first-half display in Sydney as they claimed a 13th successive win against the Wallabies and completed a 2-0 Bledisloe Cup clean sweep.

The annual series had already gone New Zealand’s way for a 24th successive year at Eden Park last weekend, but Australia did enough in a highly competitive first half in Auckland to suggest they could give the All Blacks a game on their home turf. And in a breathless opening six minutes in Sydney, it looked as if they might.

The ball-in-play time during that opening spell was incredible as both teams committed to fast, attacking rugby, offloading from everywhere. Like two heavyweights going toe-to-toe in the opening round of a boxing contest, throwing haymakers to see who would get knocked out first.

Ryan Lonergan produced an excellent turnover for the Wallabies to trigger an Australia counter, the irrepressible Peter Lakai responded with one for the visitors, as the ball travelled from one end of the pitch to the other in one long unbroken spell.

But after New Zealand wing Josh Moorby finally broke the deadlock, it was Australia who found themselves out on their feet, punch drunk.

News.title: ‘The boats don’t stop’: The deadly coastline that has become a trafficking superhighway
News.content:
The fishing village of Khor Angar does not look like a site on one of the world’s main maritime migrant smuggling routes.

Nestled between the desert and the Red Sea, the whitewashed buildings seem to slumber in the searing heat and give no indication of the life-and-death drama witnessed along this coastline.

Maps claim there is a road from the town of Obock 40 miles away, but the occasional cars and bikes must instead venture over baked sand and mudflats to get there. Camels watch as they pass.

But if you scan the remote beaches along this stretch of northern Djibouti’s coastline clues to the scale of its intercontinental human traffic emerge.

Half buried in the sand are abandoned shoes, clothes and even identity documents.

The dropped personal possessions are reminders of hurried embarkations in the surf, or of terrible panicked capsizings in a perilous strait known as the ‘Gate of Tears’.

On some beaches there are mass graves of those who have drowned, marked out by stones among the sand dunes.

News.title: Asia’s vaccine self-sufficiency drive gets $650m boost
News.content:
An “innovative” partnership to boost vaccine security across Southeast Asia will inject up to $650 million into regional manufacturing, in a bid to reduce reliance on imported shots.

The five-year initiative, announced at the annual meetings of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund in Bangkok on Friday, will see major lenders, non-profits, and the private sector come together to invest in the region’s vaccine industry.

Currently Southeast Asia’s production base remains limited and exposed. The majority of shots are imported, and any capacity the region does have is highly concentrated – one analysis this year estimates 60 to 90 per cent sits with a single vaccine manufacturer.

Even before Covid-19 hit, this vulnerability was recognised. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), a regional bloc of 11 countries, endorsed a vaccine security and self-reliance initiative in 2019, driven by Thailand’s National Vaccine Institute (NVI).

These concerns have mounted since the pandemic, but up until now investment as well as political will has been lacking. The partnership announced on Friday, led by NVI, hopes to remedy this, and develop a model that can be copied worldwide.

​​“If we can do it here in Asia, then that really provides a model for the world,” said Aurélia Nguyen, deputy CEO of the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (Cepi), a a vaccine research non-profit. “We can build it out in Africa, in Latin America, and that really gives us the resilience that we want the next time we have a major epidemic.”

Cepi has committed up to $20 million of “catalytic funding” for the programme, which is backed by the World Bank as well as organisations like the Singapore-based AVPN investment network.

In all, the package of loans and grants will include at least $174m in public financing, and up to $460m in private capital mobilisation for regional vaccine manufacturing. Further details, including recipients, have not yet been announced.

But Paschal Donohoe, the managing director and chief knowledge officer of the World Bank Group, told a panel in the Thai capital that “we believe this has the ability over time to mobilise up to $650m of finance”.

He added that the group would use public loans and grants alongside investments by its private-sector arm, the IFC, while its guarantee arm, MIGA, would help cover investors against risk.

“It’s really important because each element of the World Bank Group is involved in it,” Donohoe said. “We’re not just talking the talk, but walking the walk.”

Speaking to the Telegraph after the event, Nguyen added: “Innovative models and partnerships like this, where we’re each bringing a piece to de-risk scientific technology, [allow us] to leverage larger quantities of capital.

“But I think what’s also helpful in this model is, beyond the financing, [we] have a sort of coordinating umbrella through Asean,” she said. “So you can be smart and [avoid] duplicating investments, which brings commercial sustainability and resilience for health systems.”

Nakorn Premsri, the director of NVI, added that the investment model will help “build a more sustainable and resilient regional vaccine ecosystem, to meet both routine needs and the demands of health emergencies”.
