Hyron and his wife Maiglin along with one of their sons are pictured here

Confirming Andrews’ passing, the Lions said in a statement: ‘The Lions Rugby Company is deeply saddened by the passing of player Hyron Andrews while on tour with the 10bet Lions ahead of their Investec Champions Cup and Vodacom United Rugby Championship fixtures.

'This devastating news has sent shockwaves through the international rugby community. The former Sharks and Sale Sharks lock forward was a valued member of the Lions family and his loss will be felt profoundly by his team-mates, coaches, supporters and all who had the privilege of knowing him. Our deepest and most heartfelt condolences go to Hyron’s wife, Maiglin, their young sons, and the entire Andrews family. We hold them in our thoughts during this time of unimaginable grief and ask that their privacy be respected as they mourn.’ The Lions have confirmed that their scheduled clash with La Rochelle will go ahead with the team’s players keen to pay tribute to Andrews on the field.

Reports in the French media said a psychological support unit had been set up for the Lions franchise's players and staff, as well as the hotel personnel.

Rudolf Straeuli, Lions chief executive, said: ‘We are heartbroken by the passing of Hyron. He was not only a gifted rugby player, but also a cherished member of our Lions family having recently joined us this season.

'On behalf of our chairman, Mr Altmann Allers, the board and everyone at the Lions, I extend our deepest sympathies to Maiglin, their young sons Hendrix and Emerson and the entire Andrews family. We stand with them in their sorrow and will remember Hyron with great affection and respect.’

The Lions added: ‘The Lions Rugby Company will communicate further details regarding an appropriate tribute in due course. In honour of Hyron, the 10bet Lions will fulfil their opening match of the Investec Champions Cup against La Rochelle tomorrow evening South African time. May Hyron rest in peace.’

Andrews' former employers Sale said: 'Everyone at Sale Sharks is devastated to learn of the death of our former player Hyron Andrews. Hyron was a much-loved member of the squad during his time with us and everyone at the club is united in sending their love, thoughts and heartfelt condolences to his wife Maiglin, their beautiful boys and the rest of his family and friends and everyone at Lions Rugby.'

PREM Rugby also said in a statement: 'Everyone at PREM Rugby and our clubs is deeply saddened by the passing of Hyron Andrews and we extend our heartfelt sympathies to his family and friends.

'Our thoughts are also with Hyron’s team-mates past and present, everyone at the Lions and Sale Sharks, and the wider South African rugby community at this very difficult time.'

Hyron Andrews career Andrews spent the majority of his career playing in his native South Africa with the lock having joined the academy of Durban-based the Sharks in 2014. He made his debut for the Sharks in 2016 and made 83 appearances for the team, scoring three tries. Andrews was part of the Sharks side that reached the quarter-finals of the Champions Cup in 2023. The 6’8 lock joined Sale Sharks on an initial short-term deal in the 2023-24 season. He ultimately stayed at the PREM Rugby side for a further two seasons, playing 45 times in total. Andrews left at the end of last season to return to South Africa with the Lions. Internationally, Andrews represented South Africa at the 2015 World Rugby Under 20 Championship in 2015. The junior Springboks were beaten in the semi-finals by England, but won the third place match against France.

Andrews was a former South Africa Under-20 international.

Mark Alexander, president of the South African Rugby Union, said: 'This is terrible and distressing news. Our hearts go out to Hyron’s family and the whole Lions rugby community.

'There are no words to adequately convey our shock and the depth of sympathy we feel for his wife Maiglin and for his extended family, friends, team-mates and loved ones during this time of immense sorrow.

'Hyron was a respected member of the rugby community whose contribution to the game and impact on those around him will be remembered with great fondness.

'His untimely passing is a devastating loss and we share in the grief of all who knew and loved him.

'The thoughts and prayers of the entire South African rugby family are with Maiglin and all those mourning his loss. May they find strength, comfort and peace in the memories they shared with him and in the support of those around them.'

In a bizarre coincidence, Andrews’ tragic passing occurred on the 10-year anniversary of the death of Munster legend Anthony Foley. A former Munster coach and captain, Foley died in his sleep on October 16, 2016, at the age of 42 in Paris on the eve of a European tie against Racing 92 after a heart condition caused fluid to build up in his lungs.

Ronan O’Gara, the current La Rochelle head coach, was an ex-Munster team-mate of Foley’s. Reports have suggested O’Gara headed to the team hotel of the Lions to offer the team’s grieving players and support staff emotional support. La Rochelle said they had learned of Andrews’ death with ‘immense sadness.’ They added: ‘The club extends its deepest condolences to his family, loved ones, team-mates, staff and the entire Lions family.

South African star Andrews played for Sale in England before leaving at the end of last season

‘To honour the memory of their team-mate and out of respect for La Rochelle and its fans, the Lions players and staff have decided, despite the circumstances, to play the match.

‘A minute's silence will be observed before kick-off. La Rochelle invites its supporters to join in this moment of reflection with the utmost respect.

‘La Rochelle remains by the side of the Lions in this ordeal.’

European Rugby organisers said: ‘It is with deep sadness that EPCR has learned of the tragic passing of 10bet Lions player Hyron Andrews while on tour ahead of their Investec Champions Cup and URC fixtures.’

The organisation’s chairman, Dominic McKay, said: ‘The thoughts of everyone at EPCR and the wider international rugby community are with Hyron’s wife Maiglin, his young sons, wider family, friends, team-mates, the 10bet Lions and all those who knew and loved him at this incredibly difficult time.’ In memory of Andrews, a moment’s silence will be held ahead of every Champions Cup and Challenge Cup match this weekend.

Those tributes began when Gloucester hosted French giants and current European champions Bordeaux on Friday night.

Sports.title: The fact Man United cannot drop Lisandro Martinez after his outburst just goes to show he was spot on about Sir Jim Ratcliffe's politburo of under-qualified, over-protected advisors, writes RIATH AL-SAMARRAI
Sports.content:
The fact Man United cannot drop Lisandro Martinez after his outburst just goes to show he was spot on about Sir Jim Ratcliffe's politburo of under-qualified, over-protected advisors, writes RIATH AL-SAMARRAI

Lisandro Martinez will be in the Manchester United squad when they face Leeds on Sunday. And of course he will, because he was right about that shambling wreck of a club.

If he was wrong, and United were indeed a functional, intelligent organisation, he wouldn’t be anywhere near the bus for Elland Road. Not after what he said the other night.

A proper recruitment system would have meant there was enough defensive cover to drop a dissenting voice in questionable form. But United don’t have that. Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s politburo of under-qualified, over-protected advisors messed up another transfer window, so kicking Martinez into the long grass wasn’t an option.

In other words, if Jason Wilcox was better at his job then Martinez would have lost his and here’s a little list to support the point: Cristiano Ronaldo, Jadon Sancho, Marcus Rashford.

In the past few years, all of them have spoken out about those above them at United. And with the exception of Rashford, their feet didn’t touch the ground. Straight red. Rashford got put in the freezer for 18 months.

Martinez’s comments were slightly different, of course. He didn’t go after his manager, like Ronaldo and Sancho, and he didn’t turn up late and then flash some leg to potential suitors, like Rashford.

But he did sing a similar song by tearing strips off the regime in public. That used to be a hard no-no at Old Trafford, irrespective of how much truth was in the pudding.

We know that everything Martinez said about Wilcox and the club’s lack of ambition was accurate. We also know that his performance at the microphone was better than anything he has shown on the pitch in quite some time. No one could score points off him for accuracy, only his wisdom in stating the obvious and his reliability as a witness.

Michael Carrick says the club have moved on from Lisandro Martinez's comments after the defeat by Atletico Madrid on Tuesday night

Sir Jim Ratcliffe brought in Jason Wilcox from Southampton in 2024

Michael Carrick’s position in all of this is quite interesting. Unlike Wilcox, he has to answer questions about rogue speakers, limited options and poor results and the links between them.

When the Martinez situation was put to him on Friday, he dealt with it the way he used to play, by taking the least fussy option – he managed upwards by not slapping his bosses and he limited his criticisms of Martinez to saying he made a ‘mistake’. Pinned into a tight space, he found a sensible pass.

Carrick couldn’t have done much better in that no-win scenario. But on some level, and in thoughts best kept to himself, he might even wish to thank Martinez. Because who else in-house has pinned United’s difficulties to the lapels of those who are largely responsible for this mess?

It won’t count for much in the long run, as it’s always the manager who carries the can. And some of the flak he has drawn in recent weeks is justified, of course. Same goes for the players.

But it is inconceivable to think Carrick, a smart man, would have supported the thinking behind a summer window in which United prepared for a return to a European workload by signing three midfielders and a back-up goalkeeper.

A window that offered no cover for a left-back in Luke Shaw, who has managed 25-plus Premier League games in four of his 12 seasons at United. A window that left Martinez and Harry Maguire as the first-choice centre-back pairing. A window that marked two years since they last signed a senior defender, the entirety of which has been spent under the watch of Wilcox, the director of directionless football.

Those are the decisions that shape seasons and what we are seeing from United is no surprise. We all called it a mile off. And we can all see Carrick’s points of exposure when Leeds are in the opposite corner.

Wilcox brought in Carlos Baleba from Brighton to complete United's transfer business this summer - he was the third midfielder they signed, after Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans

In many ways, they are the last thing he needs right now. They are a club that, for a number of reasons, highlight his shortcomings and those of United’s executive tier.

I was at their game against Arsenal and left with three main thoughts – Leeds dominated the champions for an hour, they are brilliantly organised by Daniel Farke and they know the value of a good defender.

Leeds didn’t have a spectacular window, but it was key to the building of a backline that is jointly the best in the Premier League so far. Nico Elvedi has been a good signing and Tarik Muharemovic an exceptional one; between them, they cost roughly the same as Youri Tielemans, with the difference being that Farke had a clear idea of how to use them.

It’s possible that Carrick will crack that code on Sunday – his team are good for attacking moments, if nothing else.

But it is also possible that Elland Road will prove the worst possible place for him to be, because so many of the areas where his side have under-performed are those where Farke has excelled.

A solid, physical midfield, a reliable defence, and a collective that operates with a detailed, well-understood plan has been shown so far this season by only one of the two clubs in the fixtures.

For Carrick, there is some blame to be swallowed there. But only some. The vast majority goes to higher planes, where the responsibility truly lies for United’s problems.

I would doubt Lisandro Martinez’s judgement in designating himself as the man to point it out. But he wasn’t wrong.

Sports.title: Fabio Wardley reveals why he wanted to get straight back into the ring with Daniel Dubois as he defends his team after they came under fire for not pulling him out earlier in first defeat
Sports.content:
Fabio Wardley reveals why he wanted to get straight back into the ring with Daniel Dubois as he defends his team after they came under fire for not pulling him out earlier in first defeat

Fabio Wardley is not supposed to be here again so soon.

Not, at least, according to those who watched him endure 11 gruelling rounds against Daniel Dubois in Manchester in May. Not according to those who questioned whether his corner should have pulled him out earlier, as his face became increasingly battered and his right eye swelled shut. And certainly not according to those who believe the punishment he absorbed makes a rematch a risk too far.

But Wardley has never been one to follow the script.

When the 31-year-old first faced Dubois, 29, he did so as the WBO heavyweight champion. He dropped his opponent twice in the opening three rounds, threatening to produce one of the biggest victories of his career before Dubois fought his way back into the contest and eventually stopped him in the 11th.

Now, with the WBO title back on the line, Wardley finds himself in more familiar territory in one respect: he is the challenger, the underdog and the man many expect to lose again.

And, as he explains when we sit down ahead of the rematch, he rather likes it that way.

Fabio Wardley is not supposed to be here again so soon but he's never one to follow the script

Dubois (right) and Wardley (left) will go toe-to-toe for a second time on Saturday evening

'It's been the staple of my career for as long as I can remember, well, since I started. It has been the main focal point. After the first five or six fights, when I started to step up the level, even incrementally, even slightly, people were saying I was going to lose, that it was a step too far, and all the rest of it. It's all the stuff everyone's heard before,' he says.

'It's a side of the coin I'm very much used to, and the pressure's off. I'm the challenger here. I'm expected to lose and expected to go even quicker, and Daniel's supposed to put on a better performance, and all the rest of it. So there's no pressure on me. There's nothing on my shoulders.'

It is a strikingly relaxed assessment from a fighter preparing to walk back into the ring with the man who inflicted the first defeat of his professional career.

Wardley, however, insists that defeat has done little to change him. He is not pretending that losing a world title is enjoyable, but nor does he regard it as a defining moment in his life.

'Not a lot has changed. I'm not that different. Don't get me wrong, a loss is never fun. It's never nice, it's never enjoyable. But for me, at least, it wasn't soul-crushing or devastating, and it hasn't had any effect on me as a person, my character or anything else.

'The job’s the job, the game’s the game. From the very beginning, I’ve accepted that getting through heavyweight boxing unscathed isn’t guaranteed, especially given the way I compete at the highest level and my desire to take on the biggest challengers out there.

'I think people forget that the first time around, I picked Daniel. I asked for that fight because I looked at the crop of heavyweights and thought, "That's the best one to challenge myself against."

'Knowing that about myself, and knowing that's my angle, was I ever going to get through this undefeated like Floyd Mayweather? Probably not. So, look, it comes how it comes. But as long as I'm happy with myself in terms of the performances, that I've given my all and all the rest of it, I can sleep at night.'

Their first fight in May was a brutal affair, with the contest being stopped in the 11th round

Wardley took a lot of punishment in the latter rounds of their first encounter in May (above)

It is that willingness to put himself in the firing line which has made Wardley such a compelling heavyweight. His fights are rarely short on drama, and the first meeting with Dubois was no exception. He started at a blistering pace, dropping DDD in the opening 10 seconds, only for the momentum to swing as the punishment began to accumulate.

By the later rounds, Wardley was absorbing heavy shots and fighting through considerable damage. His condition between rounds prompted questions about whether the contest should have been stopped sooner, with particular scrutiny falling on his corner for allowing him out ahead of the 10th.

Wardley disagrees with the suggestion that his team failed him. He regards the people around him as family and trusts them to put his welfare first, even when the decisions they make are questioned from the outside.

He is equally dismissive of the noise surrounding the timing of the rematch, arguing that those watching from the outside cannot know the full picture of his recovery. His position is that he and his team are best placed to judge the damage he sustained and whether he is ready to fight again.

For Wardley, the prospect of another brutal encounter is not something he has brushed aside or refused to think about. It is a reality he has had to confront with himself, knowing that by stepping back into the ring with Dubois, he is willingly putting himself in a position where he could once again withstand a frightening amount of punishment.

It is a remarkable thought process: to acknowledge the possibility of enduring the same damage all over again, to ask himself whether he is prepared to go through it, and then to make peace with the answer before he has even thrown a punch.

'It's a level of early acceptance. The second I triggered the rematch clause, even before that, I had to have a conversation with myself and ask, "This could go the exact same way. Are you ready for that? Are you OK with that?"

'As long as the answer is yes from me to me, then cool, let's go. But by now, it's nowhere near my brain as a question mark or something I'm having to deal with, battle with or anything else. It's already been ticked off, boxed and put away. It is what it is.'

Wardley was checked by the doctor and spoken to by the referee multiple times in the fight

As a result, Dubois became a two-time heavyweight champion and will now defend his belt

There is little melodrama in his delivery. When the possibility of going through the same ordeal again is put to him, Wardley does not attempt to dress it up as fearlessness or pretend that the risks do not exist.

'It's an acceptance of the game and the sport we got into, and especially the way I fight as well,' he says.

That approach is perhaps best illustrated by what goes through his mind when he is taking punishment in the ring. Wardley is not a heavyweight who is inclined to retreat quietly after being caught cleanly. His instinct is to make sure his opponent knows there will be a response.

'Especially in those moments, it's about getting back at them. All right, you took one… let your hands go. Don't just let them get away with it for free. At least let them know. Let them have it in their brain that if they get off a few shots, I'm not just going to take them, run away and roll over.'

It is a mindset that makes for spectacular viewing, but one which also places enormous demands on a fighter's corner.

Wardley describes those 60 seconds between rounds as almost too precious to waste on anything other than the information he needs to continue. With the clock ticking and another round approaching, he wants tactical instruction rather than an emotional check-in.

'No, I think it's 90 per cent tactical, 10 per cent everything else, because in those moments, compassion doesn't need to come into it. That's not where the compassion needs to be.

'Those 60 seconds are so precious, such a small moment. It feels like a click. It feels like nothing. It feels like it's done and gone so quickly that you're on your stool, you're off your stool and the next round has started.

'In that time, you need to get the information. It's not time for, "Oh, a little rub on the shoulder. Are you doing OK, Fab? Is everything alright? Are you going to be alright, mate? Do you want me to dab your face a bit?" No. Let me know what I need to know. Let's get this going again.'

Wardley knows that the rematch will be gruelling. He knows his durability will continue to be questioned. But he also knows why he wanted the first fight in the first place.

For Wardley, the pursuit of the biggest challenges has always mattered more than protecting an unbeaten record. Defeat by Dubois has not changed that. He is back because in his mind, the possibility of the same ending has already been accepted and because it’s a risk worth taking.

Sports.title: How Fabian Hurzeler turned Brighton from 'nice guys' to Champions League contenders: His ruthless pre-season edict, the Austrian boot camp, an All Blacks guru, Bart Verbruggen's coffee club and the 'best squad ever'
Sports.content:
How Fabian Hurzeler turned Brighton from 'nice guys' to Champions League contenders: His ruthless pre-season edict, the Austrian boot camp, an All Blacks guru, Bart Verbruggen's coffee club and the 'best squad ever'

It's only eight months since the low point not only of Brighton's season but also head coach Fabian Hurzeler’s tenure. A dismal 1-0 home defeat by rivals Crystal Palace was played out to chants of ‘sacked in the morning’ from Seagulls supporters after a run of one Premier League win in 12.

Sacked in the morning? As Daily Mail Sport revealed at the time, that was never going to happen. Owner Tony Bloom stood by his man, Hurzeler went back to basics and recalled James Milner, and Brighton won seven of the next 11 to climb from 14th to eighth and qualify for the Conference League.

On Sunday they welcome Palace again, this time third in the table after winning four and drawing one of their first six games. They have won their last three by an aggregate score of 10-0, including a complete domination of champions Arsenal.

Hurzeler was Manager of the Month for September, Pascal Gross Player of the Month and captain Lewis Dunk winner of Goal of the Month for his audacious 30-yard screamer in the 5-0 rout of Coventry. So how have they done it?

It all began with a pre-season like no other, partly spent in Austria, partly on the south coast. Club insiders rate it as 'elite level', not just on the grass but with every spare minute used for meetings and discussions with Hurzeler and senior staff.

The summer transfer window was also key. Brighton brought in players high in character who were already disciples of the Hurzeler way of playing and a work ethic that has required a serious buy-in from all.

Fabian Hurzeler celebrates another Brighton win with Ferdi Kadioglu in what has been a fantastic start to the season for the club

Brighton have scored more goals than any other team in the top flight, netting 18 times in their first six games

They also decided to introduce a ‘no more Mr Nice Guy’ attitude. Hurzeler wanted the team to be difficult to beat, ruthless in personal duels and Brighton to no longer be perceived as a 'nice' club. He relayed this to all staff.

Brighton have also been ruthless in front of goal and are the league’s top scorers with 18, despite selling their own top scorer last season, Danny Welbeck, to Chelsea. 'Who is going to score the goals?' was an oft-heard refrain after Welbeck’s departure, which the club did not seek out. The answer? Everyone else. Algeria left-back Jaouen Hadjam, a £10.3million summer signing from Swiss side Young Boys, became Brighton’s 12th different scorer this season in the 2-0 win at Sunderland on Saturday.

A visit to the club’s training ground helps to explain the feel-good factor. There is a coffee wagon parked up and goalkeeper Bart Verbruggen makes a point of buying everyone a hot drink whenever he keeps a clean sheet. He already has seven those this season of those in nine appearances in all competitions.

There is also new padel court for staff use, and next to go in might be a crown green bowls arena after the success of a staff tournament on Hove seafront. It was held as a way of building connections among staff and for Hurzeler – who didn't win the tournament – to say thank you to the people in the background at the club.

It was organised by Mike Anthony, the club’s head of player development and high performance. He spent 14 years with the All Blacks rugby team, filling a variety of senior performance roles in strength and conditioning, performance science, player development and elite culture building. In fact, 'culture' is a word you hear everywhere at Brighton.

'Bowls is more a game for, I would say, experienced persons, older persons,' Hurzeler said, 'and when we were there, we took the average age down a little bit.'

Bloom has hinted that he regards a top-five finish, and with it Champions League qualification, as within reach and says Brighton have their best-ever squad. Its depth will be tested in the coming weeks by the Thursday-Sunday grind of the Conference League. But Hurzeler could field two different teams of good quality and Brighton's starting XI against Palace may well bear little resemblance to the side they put out in a 4-0 win over Lithuanian outfit Kauno Zalgiris on Thursday.

Welbeck leaving allowed Greek striker Babis Kostoulas, 19, to move from bit-part player to main man. Injured wingers Yankuba Minteh and Kaoru Mitoma are yet to feature this season, but Belgium left-back Maxim De Cuyper has stepped forward into Mitoma’s berth on the left wing with two goals and two assists, while Paraguay forward Diego Gomez has taken Minteh’s place.

Bart Verbruggen buys every Brighton player a drink from the coffee wagon outside the training ground when he keeps a clean sheet - that's seven rounds in his nine appearances this season

Babis Kostoulas has been able to become the main man up front after Danny Welbeck's exit, and the Greece striker smashed in a fine goal in the hugely impressive 3-0 win over Arsenal

Maxim de Cuyper (left) has been converted from left-back to left winger and has proved a revelation, scoring twice and adding two assists

Few complained about the sale of Carlos Baleba to Manchester United for £70m after they saw his replacement, Spain Under 21s midfielder Chema 'Baby Rodri' Andres, signed from Stuttgart on deadline day for a fraction of the Baleba windfall.

It would be an exaggeration to claim that most Brighton signings are from the bargain basement. But for every £44m Luka Vuskovic, there is a £3.5m Yasin Ayari, while Andres (£15.5m), Gomez (£11m) and De Cuyper (£17.5m) hardly broke the bank by Premier League standards.

Players who struggled for game time last season, such as French defender Olivier Boscagli, are now regulars, while Malick Yalcouye has been a revelation in midfield after two years out on loan, earning an Ivory Coast call-up.

And of course, there is always Gross. The 35-year-old continues to defy Father Time, stepping seamlessly into Milner’s role since the latter’s retirement during the close season.

He still looks like the Premier League’s all-time bargain buy at a total profit to Brighton of £3.5m. They signed him from Ingolstadt for £3m in 2017, sold him to his boyhood club Borussia Dortmund for £8m in 2024 and bought him back last January for £1.5m. Last weekend he became the oldest player since Ryan Giggs to provide an assist in three successive Premier League matches, and along with Kostoulas and Andres, found the net in the 3-0 win over Arsenal.

Gross’s example inspires the relentless pressing of opponents that drove both Manchester United and Arsenal to distraction before the international break. For the press to work so well so often, everyone has to be committed.

'You have to be intense,' said Sweden midfielder Ayari recently. 'To play the way we play, you have to be fit. We emphasise this every day and we train hard to be able to play like this. Everyone knows the standards. When we started this summer, everyone was fit and had been doing their own training.'

The willingness to keep pressing until the final whistle depends on a team spirit and togetherness that appears to be off the charts. The substitutes and coaches rose as one to applaud Dunk’s goal at Coventry, and the bench cleared at the Stadium of Light as team-mates rushed to congratulate Hadjam on his first goal in English football.

Chema Andres, 21, celebrates scoring against Arsenal. The Spain Under 21s midfielder is known as 'Baby Rodri' and signed from Stuttgart on deadline day

The bench cleared at the Stadium of Light last weekend as team-mates rushed to congratulate Jaouen Hadjam on his first goal in English football

Pascal Gross looks like the Premier League’s all-time bargain buy at a total profit to Brighton of £3.5m

Not everything has been perfect. Chaos reigned at the back as Brighton went 3-0 down at Chelsea in a 4-3 defeat. Blooding several new faces all at once caused early confusion in a Carabao Cup tie away to Manchester United, but once a much-changed team had settled down, they recovered from 2-0 down to win 3-2.

And you have to wonder how many analysts at the other 19 clubs spent the international break working out how to beat them. Does Hurzeler have a Plan B if so?

'If you think you are perfect, then you are done,' he has said. 'It's about finding other solutions, it's always finding different approaches.

'There will always be some non-negotiables in our game but there are always different elements and different adaptations we need to do to stay competitive. You can never be satisfied, you can never stop.'

Sports.title: 'He's a dead man strutting': Inside Fulham's divided dressing room - as we reveal how Alvaro Arbeloa alienated his own players from day one, the 'disconnect' splitting stars and staff and why 'worried' owners don't want to pull trigger
Sports.content:
After just six Premier League matches as Fulham manager, Alvaro Arbeloa is a dead man walking. Or in the words of one source close to the dressing room, a ‘dead man strutting’.

It was always an extraordinary gamble for a mid-table Premier League club operating on a limited budget to hire a man who had only previously coached within the confines of the world’s mightiest club, Real Madrid, and then to purchase him three young products of the Spanish club’s La Fabrica academy.

So far that high-risk strategy is failing alarmingly. Fulham are bottom of the Premier League and winless, having tossed away the lead in three of those six matches.

Most glaringly at Ipswich Town last Saturday when Arbeloa’s team led until the 88th minute, only to concede twice after their manager made a series of baffling substitutions.

As a result of that ‘Farmageddon’ against the Tractor Boys, today’s home fixture against Hull City is pivotal for the Spaniard. Lose it and he will surely be sacked – with former Premier League managers Thomas Frank and Vitor Pereira in the running to replace him. Although Pereira is believed to be keener on the role than former Brentford and Tottenham boss Frank.

Draw and Arbeloa may limp on until next weekend’s trip to Coventry City – a third consecutive fixture against a newly-promoted club. That all three of those teams have all made decent starts only adds to the current sense of dread around Craven Cottage.

Alvaro Arbeloa has been described as a 'dead man strutting' by a source close to the Fulham dressing room

Fulham are bottom of the Premier League after six games and still waiting for their first win

Fulham owner Shahid Khan and his son Tony – who, while juggling other roles in wrestling and the NFL, is the club’s controversial director of football – are said to be ‘worried’ but also reluctant to make any early managerial change.

Especially given that they took such a leap of faith on Arbeloa, along with his three Real recruits – striker Gonzalo Garcia and the lightweight midfield duo of Cesar Palacios and Manuel Angel.

In the post-match press conference at Portman Road, Arbeloa further enraged large sections of the Fulham fanbase by playing the Real card.

Asked about the pressure of his predicament, he responded: 'Maybe you don't know me, but I have played for the best team in the world and I have coached the best team in the world. Maybe you don't know, but just to let you know that pressure is part of my life since I was a kid.'

Such confidence – bordering on arrogance – has been noted by his players, hence the ‘dead man strutting’ comment. While a struggling side need a manager to show self-belief, some players feel Arbeloa is covering up for the fact he is simply unsuited to the job at hand.

At Friday morning’s pre-match media conference, however, Arbeloa was far more contrite – insisting the Hull match is ‘not about me’ and admitting to his own errors against Ipswich.

Some senior players have had serious misgivings about Arbeloa’s tactics and training since the off – and these have only grown during a dismal start to the season.

Three players expressed dissatisfaction with the club on social media after the Craven Cottage crowd turned toxic in the aftermath of last month’s 3-2 home defeat by Crystal Palace, when Fulham twice squandered leads and conceded two shambolic second-half goals before supporters on the Hammersmith End erupted into cries of ‘what the f***ing hell was that?’ at the final whistle.

There is a general sense of dread at Craven Cottage at how the season is going to unfold

Fulham's players have not been impressed by Arbeloa's tactics and training methods

Alex Iwobi was booed by Fulham fans when he was withdrawn late on. He and fellow former Arsenal player Emile Smith Rowe took down all Fulham mentions from their Instagram accounts, while Brazilian winger Kevin posted a cryptic message of the three wise monkeys with the words ‘no hear, no speak, no see’. This post, in particular, is said to have angered Arbeloa.

A former Real and Liverpool defender, Arbeloa was part of Spain’s all-conquering side which won three straight major international tournaments between 2008 and 2012. His playing credentials were beyond doubt.

Yet as a coach, he progressed through Real’s age-group teams to manage second-string Castilla – who compete in the third tier of Spanish football. When Xabi Alonso left the Bernabeu in January, Arbeloa stepped up as manager for a four-month stint, yet Real ended the season without silverware, finishing eight points adrift of champions Barcelona and knocked out of the Copa del Rey by lower-league Albacete.

At Castilla, Arbeloa helped nurture Garcia, Palacios and Angel, who all played under him during his brief spell as Real’s first-team boss. There is a feeling among some Fulham players that he has shown too much faith in that inexperienced trio since arriving in west London.

Garcia, who is quick and strong but not a target man, has started every league match. He scored on his debut, a 3-2 home defeat by Chelsea, but has missed several decent chances while failing to find the net since.

Palacios, a slightly-built, technically-gifted midfielder, started the first three league matches – which all ended in defeat. Yet after a man-of-the-match display in a Carabao Cup win at West Ham, he has not featured in Fulham’s last two games.

The tiny Angel – officially 5ft 7in – was handed his Premier League debut as a substitute in the 71st minute at Ipswich, replacing the impressive and physical Shea Charles with Fulham attempting to defend a one-goal lead.

If that move was met with incredulity, then the subsequent decision to bring on a second striker, Rodrigo Muniz, and swich to a 4-4-2 formation while clinging to a slender lead, was even more difficult to fathom.

Fulham's Kenny Tete looks broken after his side conceded two late goals against Ipswich last weekend to lose 2-1

Cesar Palacios (right) put in a man-of-the-match display in a Carabao Cup win at West Ham but has not featured in Fulham’s last two matches

Fulham had been ahead on every metric until those changes, which led to their late collapse and have caused widespread alarm about Arbeloa’s in-game decision-making, including among some members of his squad.

After the match, goalscorer Ryan Sessegnon damningly spoke of a problem with the team’s ‘mentality’.

When asked about these substitutions on Friday, Arbeloa admitted: 'Maybe I was wrong. Maybe it was my fault that we lost the game – not because of the players but because of me, I can accept that analysis.'

Fulham had already surrendered leads against Palace and given up a late equaliser in a 1-1 draw with Manchester United.

All of Arbeloa’s senior coaching staff are Spanish and arrived at the club with him. Some speak of a ‘disconnect’ between them and Fulham’s players, staff and supporters. They trained the players especially hard in pre-season, with an expectation that Fulham would be one of the fittest, hardest-running and highest-pressing teams in the League.

That energetic, attacking style was apparent in the opening three matches but Arbeloa’s side were wide open defensively. A goalless draw at Anfield showed a willingness to compromise on his attacking ideals – but the Ipswich defeat has turned the majority of Fulham’s fanbase against the Spaniard.

Arbeloa succeeded Marco Silva, one of the most successful managers in Fulham’s recent history – who apparently blindsided the Khans by leaving to take charge at Benfica in June when the owners claim they had expected him to sign a new contract.

Alex Iwobi has taken down all Fulham mentions from his Instagram account after being booed by the fans

This is Fulham’s eighth Premier League campaign since the Khan takeover of 2013. In four seasons under Silva, they enjoyed four comfortable mid-table finishes. In the first three seasons under other managers, Fulham were relegated by a distance. In the fourth, they are winless and bottom.

In all four top-flight campaigns under Silva, Fulham threatened to qualify for Europe only to dip from March onwards and miss out. The Portuguese valued experience over youth and consistently fielded the oldest starting line-up in the Premier League.

And his three most expensive signings – Smith Rowe, Kevin and former Manchester City wide player Oscar Bobb, signed for a combined £94million – have all struggled to make an impact. Last season’s leading goalscorers, Harry Wilson and Raul Jimenez, left on free transfers in the summer.

So a refresh was certainly needed but a revolution based on the idea of turning London’s oldest professional football club into Real Madrid Lite always felt like a reckless punt.

Dave Kidd is the editor of Fulham site Saturday White Fever. Go to: saturdaywhitefever.counterpress.media

Sports.title: Revealed: Arsenal's plans to revamp London Colney training ground in arms race with Big Six rivals - from new gyms to state-of-the-art 'hub' and why they wanted 'mini-stadium' for academy teams
Sports.content:
Revealed: Arsenal's plans to revamp London Colney training ground in arms race with Big Six rivals - from new gyms to state-of-the-art 'hub' and why they wanted 'mini-stadium' for academy teams

Evolve or be left behind is the mantra ingrained at Mikel Arteta’s Arsenal.

From their commercial operation to recruitment, the champions are hellbent on revamping whatever they can to capitalise on a first Premier League title in 22 years and cement their place in Europe’s elite.

Next in their sights is their London Colney training base. Sources say there is an acceptance that Arsenal’s training facilities lag behind some of their Big Six rivals, which the club are focused on rectifying.

In February 2024, Arsenal made Dubai-based real estate developers Sobha Realty their first training ground sponsor. The club said the relationship would also help them explore development opportunities at the site, which are now kicking into gear with Sobha involved in the plans. But since that deal, the rest of the Big Six have left Arsenal behind.

Manchester United spent £50million on their Carrington redevelopment in August 2025, with improved gym and rehabilitation areas, nutrition facilities, an altitude-training room, sleep pods and dry-floating recovery equipment.

Chelsea are exploring further redevelopment of their facilities, while Liverpool’s AXA base remains state of the art after opening six years ago. Spurs began further upgrades to the first-team gym at their Hotspur Way training ground in July this year.

Arsenal are desperate to stay at the top of English and European football - and next in their sights to achieve that is revamping their Sobha Realty training ground

Tottenham's Hotspur Way facilities are some of the best in the world, and are regularly used by England for training camps

It’s understood Arsenal have undergone a refurbishment of their first-team gym and treatment amenities and also been granted planning permission for a temporary women's gym, which will kickstart the wider revamp.

Longer term, Arsenal are understood to be assessing whether they can build a new state-of-the-art men’s hub which would put their facilities among the best in Europe.

The women’s team would be able to train in the temporary gym for a maximum of three years and then – if a brand new men's hub is built – move into the facility that the men's team currently use.

It is understood that last season Arsenal were considering plans to erect stands around a pitch at Colney, to in effect create a mini-stadium for the Under 21s and Under 19s. It is believed the club had an informal talk with the local council before deciding not to pursue planning permission.

The Under 21s play at Meadow Park, the home of National League leaders Boreham Wood FC. The new stadium would have ended those journeys to Boreham Wood for youth-team players and their parents.

The pivot towards focusing on the training ground comes after resolving their more pressing matter of the Emirates Stadium, built in 2006. At the time, it was widely regarded as one of the most advanced football arenas in Britain, a benchmark for modern stadium design.

Since then, competitors have built or redeveloped stadiums with increasingly sophisticated hospitality, entertainment, retail and non-matchday offerings – none more so than their north London rivals Tottenham.

As reported by Daily Mail Sport in November 2024, options to expand the Emirates were keenly explored with architects from Populous – the firm which designed Arsenal’s stadium – consulted on the options available. Yet, earlier this month, Arsenal confirmed they had decided to pursue a ‘continued evolution’ of the stadium rather than an expansion.

Arsenal's Under 21s currently play at Boreham Wood FC, but plans were in the works to build a mini-stadium for them at Colney

Arsene Wenger oversaw the project to build London Colney back in 1999 and then the major upgrades from 2015 to 2017

Attention has instead turned to Colney. Built on a 143-acre site back in 1999 in a project overseen by Arsene Wenger and largely financed by the £25m sale of Nicolas Anelka to Real Madrid, the previous major upgrades began in 2015 and were completed ahead of the 2017-18 season.

This included a new player performance centre, which brought together fitness, medical, rehabilitation and player-support facilities for the women’s and academy teams. Recovery technology such as ice baths and a cryotherapy chamber were brought in, as were a 40-metre running track and dedicated analysis and scouting suites.

For Arsenal, the latest plans underline a growing recognition that staying competitive off the pitch is just as important as the results on it.

With rivals continuing to invest in their infrastructure, the challenge for Arteta and the club’s hierarchy is to ensure London Colney can keep up with their title-chasing ambitions.

Sports.title: Keep training fresh, find a hobby... and know when to let top players leave: what Mikel Arteta can learn from greats such as Sir Alex Ferguson, Bob Paisley and Graham Taylor as he bids to join the 10-year brigade and build an Arsenal dynasty
Sports.content:
A conversation between Sir Alex Ferguson and Rio Ferdinand nearly 20 years ago encapsulates why the former Manchester United’s manager’s longevity and success surpass those of anyone who has lasted a decade or more at the helm of a British football club.

Ferguson had just spent an evening away in Europe, scouting a player, and returned the following day having left morning training to his assistant Carlos Queiroz. Ferdinand sought him out at Carrington to ask where he’d been. ‘It’s not the same when you’re not here,’ he told him.

The manager took these words to heart, ensuring that from then on United always chartered him a plane for such trips, so he would be at the training ground, even if it meant getting to bed at 2am.

The significance resides both in Ferguson’s acceptance that a manager’s physical presence was important – ‘leaders are usually unaware, or underestimate, the motivating power of their presence. No one sees themselves as other sees them,’ he observed years later – and his willingness to weigh a player’s complaint.

Mikel Arteta may not feel he needs to take lessons on keeping things fresh and intense from an arch foe like United, though the small band of managers who’ve lasted a decade in post provide pointers as to how Arsenal’s manager might see his new contract to its end point and join that ten-year brigade.

Bill Shankly, at Liverpool’s bridgehead for 15 years, and Brian Clough, 18 years at Forest, were also the all-seeing eye – present at, though not controlling, training. For Shankly, there was a beauty in training sessions being unchanging, says Gordon Milne, who played in the mid-1960s Liverpool team and later enjoyed a very successful seven years as Coventry City manager.

‘Today, coaches are often lauded for the variety of their sessions,’ Milne writes in his excellent memoir Shankly, My Dad and Me.

Sir Alex Ferguson was willingness to adapt after hearing from his player Rio Ferdinand

Mikel Arteta's new deal at Arsenal will take him to a decade in charge

‘That wasn’t us. Success and stability thrived on repetition and although this may have appeared basic, we took these principles on board.

'And because Shanks was a great believer in principles (rather than rules, which he knew would be broken), it was nigh-on impossible not to be swept along.’

It was away from the training ground that managers who’ve lasted changed things up. Graham Taylor, who passed away in 2017, was constantly looking to freshen the environment during his ten years at Watford’s helm, occasionally cancelling training and inviting those players who had a dog to turn up with it at the appointed time. They would be embarking on a walk.

LONGEST PL MANAGERIAL REIGNS 1. Arsene Wenger , Arsenal 21 years, 8 months (1996-2018) 2. Sir Alex Ferguson , Man United 20 years, 11 months (1992-2013) 3. David Moyes , Everton 11 years, 3 months (2002-2013) 4. Pep Guardiola , Man City 10 years (2016-26) 5. Jurgen Klopp , Liverpool 8 years, 8 months (2015-24) 6. Joe Kinnear , Wimbledon 6 years, 11 months (1992-99) 7. MIKEL ARTETA , Arsenal 6 years, 10 months (2019-present) 8. Harry Redknapp , West Ham 6 years, 9 months (1994-2001)

’On a similar occasion, the players were asked to turn up with an overnight bag and to bring their passports,’ journalist and author Lionel Birnie, who worked on Taylor’s own excellent posthumous memoir, In His Own Words, tells Daily Mail Sport.

‘It turned out they were heading by ferry to the Isle of Wight. That was Graham. He kept the momentum going all those years by the depth of his engagement and his imagination.’

Common to some of those managers who have lasted and flourished is a resolve to refresh the backroom staff, so that the voices the players heard were changing.

David Pleat, who was at the Luton Town helm for eight years, always felt this was a secret of Ferguson’s success. Over time, the United manager employed Brian Kidd, Jim Ryan, Steve McClaren, Carlos Queiroz and Mike Phelan as his No 2s.

‘This constant change meant new ideas, a fresh voice in the dressing room and changing philosophies,’ Pleat wrote in his biography, Just One More Goal, published in 2024.

Pleat contrasts managers like Mark Hughes who always took the same backroom team everywhere with him.

Graham Taylor kept changing things up at Watford to keep his players engaged

‘Did they change their views and ideas as time progressed?’ he writes. ‘Did they adapt to the players? Did they keep their freshness as the training grounds changed? I wonder.’

Mauricio Pochettino was another who displayed such reluctance to employ new assistants, as a critical voice.

For David Moyes, whose first period at Everton spanned 11 years from 2002, longevity was built on learning and evolving as he went along and not presupposing that some of his earlier responses to situations were right.

As a 38-year-old in his early months at Everton, he let Wayne Rooney and Thomas Gravesen get away with letting off rockets in the gym. A mistake, he felt in retrospect.

But when one senior member of the squad he inherited repeatedly feigned injury before miraculously declaring himself fit for an attractive final game of the season against a former rival, Moyes flatly told him he would not be playing.

Moyes, who has received several calls from Arteta, including one last season, seems to view management as a constant form of self-improvement.

‘I’m really looking closely at the moment at what I could do to try to manage the players a bit better,’ he says in a TNT Sports interview this weekend. ‘I feel myself that I’ve had to be adaptable and try and change. I think about it a lot. I stress about it a lot.’

Bill Shankly - with his team of Liverpool coaches Bob Paisley, Ronnie Moran, Joe Fagan and Reuben Bennett - had a set of principles underpinning his 15-year spell at Anfield

John Coleman, whose two spells managing Accrington Stanley spanned 13 years and ten years respectively, puts longevity down to embedding a clearly defined culture.

‘It’s like a mother yeast,’ he tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘Once it’s going, you don’t have to alter or interfere with it, but you do have to evolve. You have to adapt to the times, or you get left behind. I’ve tried to meet people and exchange ideas and listen.’

Coleman, now assistant manager at Reading, thinks it helped that he was never a professional footballer himself. ‘I had to take it my own way and prove myself that way,’ he says. Coleman, like Ferguson, Shankly and Taylor, found delegation to be an article of faith.

Shankly’s innovative obsession with his players ‘living right, sleeping right, eating right, training right’, as Milne puts it, feels immensely modern, now, and his pursuit of new ways was never-ending. One of his 1960s projects was the purchase of a German electrical muscle stimulation device, first tested on midfielder Jimmy Melia.

Melia, lying prostrate on a treatment table with his left leg wired up to the machine’s electrodes, declared he could not feel anything, even when the dials were turned to ‘maximum.’

David Moyes admitted to mistakes in his early years at Everton, before replacing Ferguson at United in 2013

Someone in the room pointed out to Shankly that the plug had not been flicked – so someone immediately rectified this, without anyone thinking of turning down the dials.

The story of Melia’s leg shooting up from the table is one Shankly’s old players discuss to this day. He engendered a sense of adventure and fun through infectious enthusiasm and so his players loved him. ‘Players have to see how much it means to you,’ Coleman says. ‘You’ve got to be obsessed with the game.’

The brutally difficult, sometimes impossible, task is releasing players who had delivered so much. Shankly struggled with this in a way that Ferguson didn’t and endured six trophyless years from 1966 because of it.

‘The hardest thing is to let go of a player who has been a great guy – but all the evidence is on the field,’ Ferguson reflected from retirement. ‘I believe that the cycle of a successful team lasts maybe four years.’

Arsene Wenger laboured under a different kind of sentimentality, which wrecked the legacy he built in the glorious first eight of his 22 years at Arsenal. The money Arsenal spent building a new stadium gave opponents bigger spending power, but his obstinate insistence on attempting to replicate Barcelona’s aesthetic without the quality of player and in a far harder league was flawed.

That obstinacy was still evident on the occasion of his 1,000th game at Arsenal’s helm, in 2014. ‘Maybe I have an idea of making the players perfect, having the ideal game, the perfect game,’ he said that day. ‘I run after that happiness week after week.’

Perhaps the greatest challenge for Arteta, if he is to make it through a decade at Arsenal, is simply surviving the contemporary maelstrom.

Arteta has already shown he is willing to vary his methods to keep his players fresh

Shankly was desolate when stepping down in 1974 and Jurgen Klopp worn out by eight Anfield years in 2024. Clough was the most sadly diminished when he walked away in 1993. He never got over his split with Peter Taylor. He stopped laughing. 'Peter made me laugh,' Clough said in an interview, heartbreaking in retrospect.

There are already ample signs that Arteta is looking for his own idiosyncratic ways of ensuring that his Arsenal environment is kept fresh, five years into his tenure. The introduction of ‘Win’, the club’s chocolate labrador, to foster a family-orientated atmosphere. Having ‘pickpockets’ at club dinners to heighten players’ sensory awareness. Bringing a 150-year-old olive tree, symbolic of history and growth, into training.

But it is to the example of Ferguson he would be wise to turn, in search of how to maintain some sanity. And Ferguson would tell the Spaniard to find himself a hinterland, however small and insignificant.

‘I find horse racing is a release but I'm also learning to play the piano,’ he related, during his last stretch as manager. ‘I'm quite determined, you know. It’s a necessary release from the pressure.’

Sports.title: Man United WAGs 'forced to cancel night out' after Lisandro Martinez's bombshell outburst targeting club bosses - as Michael Carrick stresses both sides have 'moved on' after defender's public apology
Sports.content:
Partners of Manchester United stars reportedly cancelled a planned night out amid the fallout from Lisandro Martinez's explosive interview. A furious Martinez publicly criticised technical director Jason Wilcox and United’s top executives after defeat to Atletico Madrid for not backing manager Michael Carrick in the summer transfer window. Martinez looked to clarify his remarks with a statement on Instagram on Wednesday – the squad’s allocated day off following the 2-0 defeat to Atletico Madrid – before releasing a fresh statement after talks with Wilcox and the board. The Argentine was also fined over his comments. According to the Sun, wives and girlfriends of Man United stars decided to cancel a planned evening out on Thursday to keep a 'low profile'. The partners are believed to have cancelled a booking at the Italian restaurant Cibo in Hale, an eatery popular with Man United's players and managers alike. Partners of Man United stars reportedly cancelled a planned night out following the explosive interview given by Lisandro Martinez, left, in midweek (Source: Instagram/Muri Lopez) Harry Maguire's wife Fern Hawkins, left, was among those expected to attend the dinner at the Italian restaurant Cibo before the cancellation A floor of the restaurant was claimed to have been booked, but a decision was taken to cancel at the last minute. The report alleged that the decision was taken after advice was given from the club to keep a low profile as the Red Devils looked to move on from controversy. Martinez's partner Muri Lopez had reportedly been due to attend, along with Fern Hawkins and Ana Pinho, who are married to Harry Maguire and Bruno Fernandes respectively. On Friday, Man United boss Michael Carrick insisted the club has moved on from Martinez's comments. Carrick believes Martinez 'realised he has made a mistake' and insists the controversy will not distract Man United from turning their season around. 'We all understood the situation and what it meant. Lisandro obviously made his statement, and he acknowledges that it was a mistake from him, and that was it really. It's really not a drama for us as a group. We've genuinely moved on,' Carrick said on Friday. 'From our point of view, the acknowledgement of what's been done has certainly been enough. He's released his statement and he's realised he's made a mistake. I think that's enough for all of us to move on with. We're definitely not looking back at it now.' Martinez is set to be in the Man United squad for their clash with Leeds on Sunday.

Sports.title: Daniel Dubois accused of throwing illegal shots in Fabio Wardley fight
Sports.content:
Daniel Dubois accused of throwing illegal shots in Fabio Wardley fight

Dubois climbed off the canvas twice in the opening three rounds of the Brits’ brutal first clash in May and will look for a repeat against Wardley tonight

View 2 Images Daniel Dubois beat Fabio Wardley in May (Image: Richard Sellers/PA Wire)

Daniel Dubois has been accused of resorting to dirty tricks ahead of his rematch with Fabio Wardley.

‌



‌



Dubois climbed off the canvas twice in the opening three rounds of the Brits’ brutal first clash in May. He went on to dominate, leaving Wardley battled and bruised when the slugfest was finally stopped in the 11th round. Dubois was crowned heavyweight world champion for the second time and will defend his crown in tonight's sequel.

‌



But Wardley's manager, Michael Ofo, has claimed the Londoner was guilty of throwing illegal shots five months ago. "I believe Fabio is in a better place than he was and he's ready to go to war," he said. "The first fight was an amazing fight but there was also a lot going on in that fight that has not been talked about enough. The MMA rugby tackling; there was a lot leading with the head and a lot of rabbit punches. We are going to be applying a lot of pressure to make sure those things are not going to be happening."

‌



Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources

View 2 Images Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley face off (Image: Nick Potts/the Press Association)

‌



Wardley reigned for only 173 days before being relieved of his WBO belt. He immediately insisted on a rematch and will walk to the ring 161 days after his first career defeat. Doubts have been raised over his decision to return so soon, but Wardley said: "I gave myself four weeks away from it all. A whole lot is made of needing time off to recover but I know how I felt after the fight.

"I was wondering why I wasn't back in the gym and that we needed to hurry it along. There was a lot of cosmetic damage but it's heavyweight boxing. We're big men and we're going to end up with a few bumps and bruises. This feels like my more natural place, being the underdog who took the second fight too soon. That’s been the story my whole career, so I’m comfortable being back here. "A loss is never part of the plan but the thought is worse than the reality.

"I was never going to get through unscathed, undefeated like Floyd Mayweather, because I want to be in there with the best guys. And that jeopardy leaves lots of room for things to go wrong. I know where I went wrong, it didn't take long to realise where I messed up. We’ve made changes and adjustments for this fight and we’ll implement them on Saturday night.

Article continues below

I was over-zealous and confident in my power in the first fight. I probably believed too much that the right hand would land, but that’s easy to adjust. I have to be controlled and not just march forward and throw right hands. But if someone wants a war with me then I’m happy to oblige. Often I’m the instigator and once I smell blood, I’m getting him out of there."

Dubois will start as the favourite to deliver a repeat performance on home soil in London. And he added: “I’m ready to go to war. Of course I respect him, but I’m just ready to go out to battle. I’m feeling stronger than in the first fight. I’m grounded and ready to do my job. First I need to get through Saturday and then it’s on to bigger and better things.”

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua has role to play in Daniel Dubois vs Fabio Wardley rematch
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua has role to play in Daniel Dubois vs Fabio Wardley rematch

Fabio Wardley takes on Daniel Dubois again tonight having had Anthony Joshua back in the gym ahead of the heavyweight rematch

View Image Fabio Wardley with Anthony Joshua

Anthony Joshua has handed Fabio Wardley a late boost in his attempt to regain his heavyweight title.

‌



‌



Wardley will challenge Daniel Dubois in London tonight, five months after losing his crown to his fellow Brit. Joshua himself is preparing to take on bitter rival Tyson Fury in December and has opted to re-unite with Wardley's trainer Ben Davison. And the Ipswich man said: "He’s been back in the gym for a good while and it’s been good to see him.

‌



"He has a different energy; a different aura around him once he appears, and that gives the gym a little buzz and a different feel to it. He’s been straight back in the mix and he’s shoulder to shoulder with the boys like you’d expect." Davison was heavily criticised for not throwing in the towel during Wardley's bruising defeat by Dubois in May.

‌

Fabio Wardley inspired by Ipswich heroics ahead of Daniel Dubois rematch READ MORE :

But his charge insists Joshua's decision to return vindicates his own faith in his coach. "The whole conversation around Ben has always been incredibly frustrating," he added. "It’s so strange, because the levels at which people say he’s not done the right job have been at the absolute pinnacle of the sport.

Article continues below

"They’ve been with me, fighting for a world heavyweight title; they’ve been with Moses Itauma, fighting for a world heavyweight title; with AJ, fighting for a world heavyweight title. It’s going to be tough at the top; you might lose, you might win. That’s enough evidence to show that someone like Ben deserves to have someone like AJ.

"As a fighter, you know what works and what doesn’t work for you, especially Joshua – someone who’s bounced around quite a bit between trainers – so the proof’s in the pudding, really. He’s been bouncing around from trainer to trainer to trainer to trainer, and then has left one, went somewhere else, and gone ‘Actually I know where I felt best in myself and where I got the most out of it’. He has left and thought ‘The grass isn’t actually greener’ and come back."

Fabio Wardley and Daniel Dubois look set to deliver another heavyweight barnstomer again tonight.

Jalolov has not ruled out going for a third gold medal in Los Angeles in 2026 but needs a big win tonight if he is to prove he has world title credentials in the paid ranks. Dacres bounced back from his defeat by David Adeleye with a win over previously-unbeaten Vladyslav Sirenko last time out.

View 2 Images Bakhodir Jalolov takes on Solomon Dacres (Image: Getty Images)

Nelson Birchall vs Levi Giles - 7pm

One of three boxing brothers and one of two siblings on this card, Nelson Birchall will be looking to extend his unbeaten and winning record to 13. In what will be his fourth fight of the year, he could be tested by Levi Giles who took rising star Giorgio Visioli the distance in March.

‌



Tony Curtis vs Kerim Agius - 6.30pm

Tony Curtis suffered a defeat on his pro debut four years ago at the tender age of 16 but has been slowly rebuilding ever since. He has racked up 14 wins since 2022 and will step up slightly against Kerim Angus who also has one defeat to his name, albeit coming more recently when he was stopped by Marcus Sutherland.

Zayn Ahmed vs Kasey Bradnum - 6pm

Another one from the Frank Warren production line, 20-year-old Zayn Ahmed is one to watch and is unlikely to be troubled tonight in his fourth fight against Kasey Bradnum who has one win in 51 fights.

The other Birchall brother in action tonight, Leighton lags behind his brother in terms of experience and will walk to the ring for just the sixth time againt Mexican Alejandro Chazaro who has won nine of 20.

‌



Manny Safari vs Jake Pollard - 5pm

Manny Safara makes his professional debut and should enjoy a comfortable night against journeyman Jake Pollard who has lost 121 of his 123 outings and who currently has another four fights lined up this year, including three over the next three weekends.

Abdul-Fawaz Aborode vs Rashid Omar - 4.40pm

Abdul-Fawaz Aborode will look for his third professional victory tonight as he takes on Rashid Omar who has lost more often than not having switched from contender to journeyman.

Aaron Noriega vs Leonardo Baez - 4.20pm

American Aaron Noriega fights in the UK for the first time having previously been in action in Mexico. He should make light work of Leonardo Baez.

Sports.title: 'I was set to sign for Man Utd – but I had to say no for two reasons'
Sports.content:
'I was set to sign for Man Utd – but I had to say no for two reasons'

Manchester United have a huge pulling power but they don't always land every target

View 2 Images (Image: Leonardo Fernandez, Getty Images)

Clarence Seedorf has revealed how close he came to joining Manchester United. But the Real Madrid and AC Milan legend had two big reasons for turning the club down.

‌



‌



The former midfielder had a big decision to make when he left the Bernabeu at the turn of the millennium. Sir Alex Ferguson was trying to convince him to move to Old Trafford.

‌



However, the tantalising prospect of playing alongside Ronaldo (R9) and Christian Vieri was too good to turn down. So was the Italian weather.

‌



Speaking to Kobbie Mainoo on Amazon Prime Video Sport's YouTube channel, the 50-year-old admitted he "wanted to come here for a long time" and was "supposed to even play here."

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

When the young United star enquired why the transfer to Old Trafford never materialised, Seedorf elaborated: "I went to Inter Milan instead. Marcello Lippi, I don't know if you remember the coach, world champion with Italy.

‌



"He called me. He said, 'Uh, Clarence, you want to come and play behind Ronaldo R9 and Christian Vieri?' I said, 'Okay, let me just take my bags. I'm coming.' Italy was a bit more familiar. Probably was the reason why I chose to go there as well."

At that point, Seedorf had established himself as a creative force in Real's engine room, netting 20 goals and providing 35 assists across 159 outings.

View 2 Images Clarence Seedorf admitted a chat with Marcello Lippi changed his mind (Image: FC Internazionale/Inter via Getty Images)

‌



He secured the La Liga crown, two domestic cups and the Champions League.

He departed for Inter Milan following three campaigns in Spain, joining the Serie A outfit for approximately £20million (€24m).

While he failed to lift any silverware there, he did achieve glory in Italy - albeit with Inter's bitter rivals. Seedorf made 432 appearances for AC Milan, netting 62 goals, providing 67 assists and claiming nine trophies.

Article continues below

Among his haul were two Champions Leagues, two UEFA Super Cups, two Serie A titles and three domestic cups.

Following a decade of glory at AC Milan, Seedorf headed to Botafogo in Brazil to bring his playing days to a close. He hung up his boots in 2014 after clinching the league title with his final club.

Sports.title: 13 boxing icons predict Daniel Dubois vs Fabio Wardley result as clear victor emerges
Sports.content:
13 boxing icons predict Daniel Dubois vs Fabio Wardley result as clear victor emerges

Boxing greats have cast their predictions for Daniel Dubois vs Fabio Wardley 2 and a resounding consensus has emerged ahead of Saturday's rematch

View 4 Images Some of boxing's elite figures have made their predictions for Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley's rematch (Image: Getty Images)

The British boxing aristocracy has made its predictions for Saturday's rematch between Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley. 'Dynamite' blitzed his way to a late stoppage victory when these fighters first met in May to clinch the WBO heavyweight belt.

‌



‌



That result brought an end to Wardley's undefeated record in the first blemish of his boxing career. Dubois will hope to draw a line under their rivalry and cement back-to-back victories for the first time in more than two years.

‌



The rivals will face off once more at London's O2 Arena as the British boxing public watches on with anticipation. And Mirror Fighting has compiled a list of what every major figure has said about the outcome, with a very clear favourite emerging.

‌



Eddie Hearn - Dubois win

Hearn has had a change of opinion since the first bout. He recalled: “I backed Fabio to win that [first] fight, right? It was the first time I ever backed him to win in the last five fights that he has been in – and he lost, but he was incredible."

Changing his tune this time around, he added: “I think that he is a massive underdog in the second fight.”

Fabio Wardley explains mindset ahead of Daniel Dubois rematch READ MORE :

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

‌



Carl Froch - Dubois win

"When I look at Fabio Wardley, he took a lot of damage in that [first] fight, and Daniel Dubois actually finished strong, stood proud and was full of energy," he said on his Froch on Fighting YouTube channel. "In the rematch, I just think Daniel Dubois’ got an extra 10 per cent over Wardley and I think that’ll be enough.

"So Fabio Wardley, unfortunately, I don’t think will get this job done and he’ll probably get stopped again. Daniel Dubois’ going to be coming into this fight really confident."

You can make sure you don't miss any of the Dubois vs Wardley 2 action by accessing DAZN below.

‌



Watch Daniel Dubois vs Fabio Wardley 2 live on DAZN This article contains affiliate links, we will receive a commission on any sales we generate from it. Learn more £24.99 or £0 DAZN Order the fight here Product Description Daniel Dubois will defend his WBO world title in a rematch with Fabio Wardley on Saturday, October 17, at London's O2 Arena . Fans can order the fight on DAZN PPV for £24.99 or watch it at no extra cost with DAZN Ultimate.

Derek Chisora - Dubois KO

"I think that this is Wardley’s last fight," said 'War' on talkSPORT. "I don’t think that he wants to box anymore. This is his cash out.

"After three rounds, Daniel’s going to win it by knockout."

‌



David Haye - Wardley win

"[Wardley] is a very tough man, he's a warrior," said former unified cruiserweight champion and WBA heavyweight titleholder David Haye on Seconds Out. "We've seen that time and time again, win or lose, he's laying it all out on the line.

"So I think he'll be ready and if it's to be, if he's able to hold it together, then he's got a chance. But Dubois looked solid last time out. Got dropped a couple of times and was able to weather the storm. So you're gonna get fireworks. Fabio's obviously gonna come with something more this time around. He understands what it's about.

"Throwing that massive overhand right that's nowhere near the target constantly. He'll have watched videos of that and thought, 'What was I doing? I need to set up my big back hand.' And we're gonna get good action. I think it'll be a lot closer [this time]. I don't think Fabio will be making the same basic, novice mistakes he was making first time around.

‌



View 4 Images Former heavyweight world champion David Haye has backed Wardley to learn from the first fight (Image: Eric Espada/Getty Images)

"I don't think [Dubois] is gonna change that much, because he won the [first] fight. And when you win fights, you think, 'I've got it figured out.' So I think he's gonna be pretty much the same. He'll be a similar fighter that turned up.

"He got decked early but Fabio didn't know what he was doing, how to get someone out of there. I think Fabio, if the knockout he received, the punishment he received, if he's able to recover from that, he'll have a better shot in this return fight."

‌



Spencer Oliver - Dubois win

"My prediction for the fight is that Daniel Dubois wins the rematch much more comfortably than he did in the first fight," said former European super bantamweight champion Spencer Oliver on talkSPORT.

"He has grown as a fighter both physically and mentally, and he is going from strength to strength. It's going to be a tough night for Fabio Wardley."

Agit Kabayel - Dubois win

WBC heavyweight champion Agit Kabayel told Playbook Boxing: "I think maybe Daniel win but this is heavyweight boxing.

‌



"Definitely [Wardley has a chance] but I watched the reaction from Usyk for the fight with Fabio and Daniel and what Usyk said is correct, Fabio lost this fight on his jab. He forgot his jab, he came only with the right hand.

"When Fabio makes this better in the second fight, he can beat him. I don’t know if this is boxing politics but for the UK fans, this is the biggest fight in the heavyweight division.

"The winner of the fight, maybe he can fight with [Filip] Hrgovic or he fights with me for the belts. This is the way for everyone, but we will see."

‌



Tony Bellew - On the fence

Content cannot be displayed without consent

"I need to see what Fabio's got left," said ex-WBC cruiserweight champion Tony Bellew while speaking to DAZN. "That's a hard one...I'm not gonna lie, if Fabio comes back fully, he's a dangerous man, because he's so brave.

"And when Daniel is having success, he's a monster. It's a really, really hard fight. I wouldn't write either off of it. It's a killer. It's a brilliant, brilliant fight."

‌



Johnny Nelson - Dubois win

Former WBO cruiserweight king Johnny Nelson said on talkBOXING: "It's about levels and [their last fight] shows quite clearly that Daniel's is way above Fabio's. I think Fabio is going to box so much better but Daniel is going to step it up even more."

Darren Barker - Dubois win

"Fabio Wardley's an absolute machine, one of the toughest men out there. You'd want him on the front line," former IBF middleweight champion Darren Barker told DAZN. "You'd want him to be stood next to you in battle. The man’s an absolute soldier and has the ability to knock anyone out.

"Think back to the punches that dropped Daniel Dubois in the first fight. They were glancing blows. They weren't full — he didn't have full purchase on the shots. A couple of them glanced the top of the head. If he hits the target correctly, he's got every chance of getting the win.

‌



"But I just feel Dubois has found a new confidence. He's exorcised those demons from when the word ‘quit’ was being thrown around. Filip Hrgovic hit him with about 20 right hands a couple of years ago. He stayed there, kept digging in and found a way to win.

"He got dropped twice by Wardley but managed to get the victory. It was a very good fight, but it was kind of one-sided in big portions.

"I know Wardley loaded up, found big shots and made it exciting, but the boxing from Dubois was really good. As long as he's not complacent and doesn't get overconfident, I feel he'll have a bit too much for Wardley."

‌



George Groves - Dubois win

View 4 Images George Groves has tipped Dubois to finish off the rivalry if he's at his best (Image: Getty Images)

Speaking on Sky Sports' Toe2Toe podcast, former WBA super-middleweight titleholder George Groves said: "I've seen [Wardley] say, 'I caught him. I hurt him. It's my fault I blew it. It was mine to lose...'

"I don't think that's the case, to be honest. It was almost Dubois' to lose. Dubois is the better boxer, you know. [He has] better movement, faster hands. I mean they both can crack but you think Dubois has got crazy power.

‌



"I think they've both got great chins. You can't fault Wardley's chin...when you see him get caught on the button, the punches bounce off him.

"One thing I thought about is the mentality of Dubois, because sometimes he's on it and usually, sometimes, after a big win, he's not there. And I just think he's beat Wardley now. Does he think, 'Eh, I'm better than Wardley,' and he's not quite switched on... If he has [that mentality], he may come unstuck.

"Because let's get it straight, Wardley with no amateur pedigree, very limited boxer, but very effective with the way he is. Big, strong, powerful, game and maybe a slight awkwardness to his style. Dubois figured that out last time. If he shows up, he walks it."

‌



Steve Bunce - On the fence

"Wardley is taking an enormous gamble," commentator Steve Bunce wrote in his BBC Sport column. "His nose was badly damaged in the first fight, and the cut across its bridge is an old wound that has reopened before.

"He has also been through plenty of hard rounds throughout his career, sometimes unnecessarily against opponents he was expected to beat comfortably. That concerns me. But I've spoken to Wardley a couple of times in the build-up, and he makes a compelling argument for an immediate rematch...

"Dubois seems more sheltered than normal this week, which in his case translates into more focused. He knows how close he came to losing the first fight, having made mistakes and been dropped twice. This time he seems confident without being overconfident.

‌



"If he stops Wardley again in another spectacular fight, I would argue he becomes the most marketable heavyweight in the division."

Fabio Wardley - Wardley KO

View 4 Images Wardley is aiming to avenge his 11th-round stoppage defeat to Dubois (Image: Getty Images)

"I've not made a career out of going to points," said the challenger. "I've made a career out of finishing fights before the bell. I had it done almost in the first round of our fight, almost in the third round.

Article continues below

"We'll pick apart those moments, pick apart you stylistically, what worked and what didn't work, and within the first quarter of the fight, you'll be gone."

Daniel Dubois - Dubois win

Speaking ahead of Saturday's rematch, Dubois said: "A win by any means necessary. I respect you. You're a good gladiator, a good dance partner, but I'm going to win."

Final score: Dubois 9-2 Wardley
