Trump has dismissed the numerous calls to slow down the technology as “negative forces.”

The proposed legislation would also override certain state laws, such as those in force in California.

Anthropic wrote in June that “absent a strong federal law, states should retain full authority to legislate.”

Charlie Bullock of the Institute for Law & AI think tank praised the proposal as “pretty reasonable,” and “more than other frontier labs have done.”

But he said on X he considers it “weaker” than the FRONTIER Act, a competing bill introduced in the House of Representatives this summer.

World.title: Military kills 11 terrorists, arrests 22, rescues 25 kidnapped victims in one week
World.content:
By Kingsley Omonobi

Troops fighting to rid the nation of criminal gangs and enemies of the state in the different theatres across the nation neutralised 11 terrorists, rescued 25 kidnapped victims and arrested 22 terrorists, collaborators, logistics suppliers and gun runners, among others in the last week

Major General Michael Onoja, Director of Defence Media Operations, disclosed this in an update on clearance operations in the theatres, noting that about seven terrorist fighters and members of the families surrendered with weapons to troops during the week.

Detailing the encounters, he said, “In the North East geopolitical zone, troops of Operation Hadin Kai on 9 October 2026 took custody of a suspected terrorist family member, identified as Iyakura Umar, who surrendered with her one-year-old daughter at Dikwa–Gulumba, following their escape from Iyaganari, all in Dikwa LGA.

On 10 October, troops in collaboration with the Civilian Joint Task Force (CJTF), arrested two suspected terrorist logistics suppliers named Abubakar Modu and Alhaji Bura in Monguno town, Monguno LGA of Borno State, with supplies intended for Kwatan Dowoshi in Kukawa LGA.

On 12 October, troops in Gubio town in Gubio LGA of Borno State arrested three suspected collaborators, namely: Modu Ibrahim, Abubakar Bunu and Tujja Mairami and captured three vehicles from them.

On 13 October, troops at Miyanti in Bama LGA of Borno State received three individuals who surrendered to troops with one FN rifle, two magazines and 14 rounds of 7.62mm x 51mm ammunition.

A separate raid in Benisheikh town, Kaga LGA of Borno State on 13 October led to the arrest of five suspected collaborators and the capture of one Dane gun.

“On 13 October 2026, one Abacha Akura surrendered to troops in Monguno town, Monguno LGA, with one AK-101 rifle and 31 rounds of 5.56mm ammunition following his escape from a terrorist camp located at Tumbunma Village, near Bukar Meriam in Marte LGA of Borno State.

Similarly, on 15 October 2026, one Abba Bukar also surrendered to troops in Monguno from the same location.

On 12 October, terrorists approaching from the Lar axis attacked troops at Hong LGA of Adamawa State. Troops countered the attack, neutralised one terrorist and discovered an AK-47 rifle.

During subsequent exploitation on 13 October 2026, troops discovered one PKT machine gun with three ammunition links containing 67 rounds, six AK-47 rifles, 11 magazines, 157 rounds of 7.62mm NATO ammunition, 120 rounds of 7.62mm special ammunition, one 60mm mortar bomb and other equipment.

Additionally, four terrorists’ bodies were found during troops patrol to cover the general area.

On 14 October 2026, troops received two surrendered terrorist fighters and their spouses from Bula Daloye in Bama LGA of Borno State, with two AK-47 rifles, four magazines and 14 rounds of 7.62mm by 39mm ammunition.

Eight additional terrorist family members surrendered to troops at Banki Junction, Bama LGA of Borno State, on the same day.

In a separate clearance operation at Nguma village, Biu LGA of Borno State, on 14 October 2026, troops neutralised a suspected terrorist who attempted to flee.

On 15 October 2026, troops rescued two abducted persons, identified as Bello Ibrahim and Ibrahim Adamu, around the Kuranabasa axis in Gwoza LGA of Borno State.

In the North West geopolitical zone, troops of Operation Fansan Yamma, on 9 October 2026, while operating around the Galadimawa area, sighted three suspected terrorists fleeing with a kidnapped person. Troops engaged the suspects and forced them to abandon the victim.

“On 10 October, troops responded to reports that a local resident travelling from Dogon Dawa to Takama Village in Birnin Gwari LGA of Kaduna State was under attack by an unknown armed group.

On arrival, the responding troops engaged the assailants and captured an AK-47 rifle with 15 rounds of 7.62mm ammunition. Following continued tracking and monitoring, troops apprehended a suspect named Yusuf Iliya Sani at Maraban Kakini on 10 October 2026, alleged to be involved in kidnapping, extortion, sexual assault and killings in Birnin Gwari LGA of Kaduna State.

“On 12 October 20026, troops on patrol from Fatika made contact with suspected terrorists at Farin Dutse, along the Dogon Marte area of Giwa LGA of Kaduna State.

A search of the area led to the discovery of an AK-47 rifle loaded with 30 rounds of ammunition. The same day, troops at Binji responded to a distress call of suspected terrorists at Soruro Village, Tangaza LGA of Sokoto State.

The responding troops engaged and neutralised one suspected terrorist and recovered an AK-pattern rifle, one magazine and 27 rounds of 7.62mm ammunition.

On 15 October 2026, troops conducted a clearance operation in Waria Forest, Tangaza LGA of Sokoto State. During the operation, troops made contact with suspected terrorists, neutralised one and recovered two AK-47 rifles and two magazines.

The operation formed part of ongoing efforts to disrupt terrorist activity and deny armed groups freedom of movement in the area.

In the North Central, troops of Operation Enduring Peace conducted a covert operation in Mangu and Barkin Ladi LGAs of Plateau State and arrested one suspected arms fabricator at Heipang, Barkin Ladi LGA.

Three other suspects were also arrested over alleged involvement in illegal arms trafficking.

Troops recovered one locally fabricated revolver rifle, one fabricated pistol, one fabricated AK-47 barrel, one AK-47 magazine and 42 rounds of 7.62mm by 54mm rimmed ammunition.

On 10 October 2026, troops arrested a suspect (Yusuf Suleiman) at Barkin Ladi Main Market. He was allegedly linked to the attack on Kassa community on 24 September 2026, as well as kidnapping, armed robbery and the killing of a resident, Mr Gyang, on 16 April 2026.

Also, on 14 October 2026, troops raided a suspected kidnappers’ hideout at Ruga in Methodist Kisahyip, Agingin, Bassa LGA of Plateau State and arrested 2 suspects.

Troops of Operation Savannah Shield on 9 October 2026 took custody of one Sidi Kamaki voluntarily surrendered to troops in Audu Fari in Borgu LGA of Niger State.

He claimed to have spent about two years with an armed group he described as part of Darul Salam associated with the Shekau faction.

He claimed to have participated in six operations in Borgu and the Republic of Benin.

“On 10 October 2026, troops at Eruku, working with local security groups, responded to a distress call concerning the abduction of residents from their farmlands in the Eruku–Egbe–Koro Forest area of Ekiti LGA of Kwara State.

Troops pursued the abductors, who abandoned the victims and fled into the forest. The operation resulted in the rescue of 18 kidnapped victims.

Troops captured two AK-47 magazines containing four rounds of 7.62mm Special ammunition.

In the Niger Delta, troops of Operation Delta Safe on 11 October 2026, while on routine patrol along the Okene–Okpella Road, rescued one Mrs Halima Ibrahim. The kidnappers fled on sighting the advancing troops, abandoning the victim.

Also on 11 October, troops and other security agencies conducted an operation in Sasaro Forest, Akoko-Edo LGA, Edo State, following a tip-off and rescued an abductee named Prince Michael Akao.

During the operation, troops neutralised three suspected kidnappers and captured three locally fabricated firearms, nine cartridges and other items.

In the South East geopolitical zone, troops of Operation Udoka on 14 October 2026, arrested three suspects at Atan–Ihechiowa Village in Arochukwu LGA of Abia State.

The suspects were identified as Ozioma Mark, a suspected IPOB kingpin, Kalu Obasi and Kamba Igwu Ogbonna. Two motorcycles and cash were captured during the operation.

On 14 October, a suspected IPOB member was handed over to troops in Lilu, Ihiala LGA of Anambra State, by local security volunteers.

Furthermore, Onoja said, “The Chief of Defence Staff, General Olufemi Oluyede, appreciates the resilience of all security personnel, urging them to maintain operational momentum, remain fiercely vigilant, and deny criminal elements all freedom of action.

“The Chief of Defence Staff calls upon all security agencies to deepen their collaborative intelligence-sharing frameworks to enhance operations against criminal elements across the nation.

“He also charges the media to project accurate, patriotic reportage to bolster national morale, and implores traditional rulers, community leaders, and relevant stakeholders to sustain their vital partnership with the military by exposing subversive elements within our communities.

“National security is a collective civic responsibility, and together, through unwavering unity and resolve, we shall secure a peaceful and prosperous future for our great nation.”

World.title: Trump signs executive order waiving new Russia sanctions, tariffs
World.content:
(Photo by ALEX WONG / GETTY IMAGES NORTH AMERICA / Getty Images via AFP)

President Donald Trump signed an executive order Friday that waived sweeping US sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia’s energy revenues after signing them into law last month.

The Lindsey Graham Act — named after the deceased US senator who sponsored the bill — allowed Trump the authority to impose duties up to 100 percent on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.

“As described further in section 4 of this order, I am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions, and duties provided for in the Graham Act,” the executive order said.

The law targeted Russia’s energy and defense sectors, President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials, as well as Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to circumvent Western sanctions.

Trump’s reversal on the Russia sanctions comes in after a controversial deal he struck with Putin that would allow Russia diesel exports in exchange for US sanctions relief.

Relations between Kyiv and Washington have soured since the deal, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky calling it a “weak decision” and Ukrainian forces resuming attacks on Russian oil refineries.

AFP

World.title: Drug Addiction: Arrest is not recovery – Prof Daniel Ikpechukwu
World.content:
*Why Nigeria must connect accountability for drug-related offences with access to treatment, rehabilitation and sustained support for young people

By Sola Ogundipe

Punished but not healed

Nigeria’s revolving door of arrest, release and relapse

According to Ikpechukwu, drug use does not occur in isolation. For many young people, it intersects with unemployment, economic pressure, trauma, peer influence, family stress and social exclusion.

In his presentation, Ikpechukwu’s argument brought the intersection of public health and justice into focus. A young person’s encounter with the justice system, he showed, can become either a revolving door of arrest, release and repeat offending or a turning point towards assessment, treatment and recovery.

He challenged the country to rethink its response to youth drug addiction and the intersection between substance use disorders and the criminal justice system.

In his presentation, Ikpechukwu posed a question that went to the heart of the debate: “Which pathway better protects the young person, the family and society?”

His argument was not that drug-related offences should be excused or that addiction should become a blanket defence against criminal responsibility. Rather, he called for a response that recognises the distinction between criminal accountability and the treatment of a health condition.

“Not excusing crime. Not criminalising illness. Not abandoning accountability,” Ikpeachukwu stressed in framing the purpose of a more effective response. The goal, he explained, should be to “identify addiction early”, “assess risk and need”, “hold people accountable”, “treat what is treatable” and “support recovery”.

His words “Not every person who uses drugs has an addiction..Not every offence committed by a person who uses drugs is caused by addiction.”

For Nigeria, where drug use and the consequences of substance use disorders remain significant public health concerns, he explained that this distinction has implications for the police, courts, correctional institutions, health authorities and agencies responsible for drug control.

It also raises a difficult question about what happens after enforcement: when a young person is identified as needing help, is appropriate treatment available, and who ensures that the person can access it?

Price of treating illness as crime

Ikpechukwu asked: ‘Do we wait for addiction to become a crime problem before treating it as a health problem?” The question resonates with public health and drug prevention messaging associated with the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) and the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA).

The scale of the challenge was underscored by the UNIDOC’s national drug-use survey, conducted in 2018 and published in 2019. The survey estimated that 14.3 million Nigerians aged 15 to 64 had used drugs in the previous year. About one in five people who used drugs had a drug use disorder, while nearly 40 per cent of high-risk drug users who wanted treatment were unable to obtain it.

“These are historical estimates rather than current prevalence figures, but they point to a longstanding concern: the gap between the need for treatment and access to care.”

For young people, he noted, substance use may intersect with trauma, family strain, unemployment, economic pressure, peer influence and social exclusion, but these circumstances do not excuse offending, but they can complicate recovery.

“Where services are scarce, treatment is unaffordable or follow-up support is weak, a young person may leave custody without the care needed to sustain recovery or the practical support needed to rebuild a life.”

Ikpechukwu’s presentation challenged authorities to look beyond arrests and prosecutions and ask whether the system is producing better outcomes.

Who ensures that a young person referred for treatment actually receives it? What happens when rehabilitation is recommended but suitable services are unavailable? Who follows up after release to determine whether treatment continues and whether the individual is reintegrating into the community?

In his view, these responsibilities cannot rest on law enforcement alone, they require coordination among health authorities, justice institutions, drug-control agencies, qualified treatment providers, families and communities. They also require clear measures of progress, including access to treatment, completion of appropriate programmes, continuity of care after release, successful reintegration and reductions in repeat offending.

“Treatment itself must be more than a referral or a court order. Where clinically appropriate and legally permissible, it should involve proper assessment, medical and psychological care, relapse prevention and continuing support.

“Depending on the individual’s circumstances, recovery may also require help returning to education, developing employable skills, securing work and rebuilding damaged family relationships.”

Ikpechukwu cautioned against treating rehabilitation as a box-ticking exercise. His warning was direct: “Mandate treatment carefully. Never mandate poor treatment. A court order cannot create treatment facilities where none exist, guarantee qualified care or ensure that support continues after release.”

Any diversion or treatment programme must therefore be based on clinical need, lawful criteria, due process and appropriate safeguards, while protecting public safety.

“Ultimately, the issue is not whether Nigeria should choose treatment over accountability. It is whether the country can make both work together, responding firmly to offending while ensuring that young people who need treatment are not left without help.”

When youth addiction becomes a justice problem

As he put it, “The measure of success is not simply fewer arrests, it is fewer young people trapped in addiction, crisis and repeat offending.”

That requires authorities to measure not only how many people are arrested or prosecuted, but also whether those who need care can obtain it, whether treatment continues after release and whether young people have a realistic chance of returning to their families and communities without falling back into the same cycle.

His closing message captured the challenge facing Nigeria’s justice and public health systems: “Justice should hold young people accountable, but where addiction is part of the problem, recovery must become part of the solution.”

The real test is whether Nigeria can turn that possibility into a functioning system, one in which treatment is accessible, accountability is meaningful and recovery is treated not as an afterthought, but as part of the solution.

Vanguard News

World.title: DSS, military, police arrest 5 over NYSC members kidnap
World.content:
…As 3 others escape with gunshot injuries

By Soni Daniel

Operatives of the Department of State Services (DSS), the military and police have arrested five suspected members of a criminal gang allegedly responsible for the abduction of 20 prospective National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) members in Imo State on Nigeria’s 66th Independence Day.

Five other suspected members of the gang, however, escaped with gunshot injuries prompting a massive manhunt for them.

The suspects were apprehended during a series of intelligence-led operations conducted at different locations in Rivers and Abia States. However, in the course of the operation, three other suspects escaped with varying degrees of injury.

Security sources disclosed that the operations were carried out between October 10 and 14 in Port Harcourt, Rivers State and Aba South LGA. Abia State.

Recall that 20 NYSC members were abducted by armed men along Owerri–Onitsha Expressway in Imo State on October 1, 2026, as they travelled to their assigned orientation camps in Abia and Akwa Ibom states.

The victims were subsequently rescued on October 7, 2026, during a joint security operation at Amakohia Ubi Village.

The string of operations mark a significant breakthrough in efforts to track down the perpetrators, dismantle the criminal network allegedly responsible for the abduction and bring those involved to justice.

A security source described the development as a major relief, noting that security agencies had sustained a wide-ranging manhunt for the abductors.

“This is a huge sigh of relief. Security agencies have been on a manhunt for the abductors, and we are elated that they have been captured. We strongly believe they will be charged to Court by DSS and the corps members will get justice,” the source said.

World.title: NFF Normalisation Committee: FIFA keeps Nigeria waiting
World.content:
The Nigeria Football Federation (NFF) is still awaiting clarification from FIFA following Thursday’s FIFA Council meeting in Zurich, Switzerland, amid expectations that the country’s football leadership crisis would be on the front burner.

The FIFA Council held its 37th meeting on October 15, 2026, with discussions covering football development funding, governance reforms and disciplinary procedures.

However, FIFA’s published statement on the meeting did not confirm whether the Council approved the proposed Normalisation Committee for Nigeria.

The absence of a public announcement does not necessarily mean Nigeria’s situation was not discussed behind closed doors.

Among the key developments, FIFA announced plans to increase football development investment to US$6.35 billion for the 2027–2030 cycle, covering its 211 member associations, confederations and other stakeholders.

The proposed framework could allow individual member associations to receive allocations of up to US$25 million, subject to applicable requirements and approval procedures.

The Council also agreed to establish a working group to examine FIFA’s governance framework and directed relevant committees to review disciplinary procedures.

The meeting attracted particular interest in Nigeria following the August resignations of former NFF President Ibrahim Gusau, General Secretary Mohammed Sanusi and members of the federation’s executive board.

A joint FIFA and Confederation of African Football (CAF) delegation subsequently visited Nigeria in September to consult stakeholders and examine possible solutions to the crisis.

One option reportedly under consideration is a Normalisation Committee to manage the federation temporarily, implement reforms and organise elections.

Earlier reports indicated that the matter could be considered under the FIFA Council’s miscellaneous agenda.

On Thursday October 15, Nigerian football stakeholders waited in vain for official clarification on whether FIFA will constitute a Normalisation Committee and issue a timetable for restoring elected leadership. But neither of these happened as at press time.

World.title: ‘I’ve intercepted 573 Benue girls from traffickers, returned over 103 from outside Nigeria since March’ — Acrivist Yaaya
World.content:
By Peter Duru, Makurdi

How old are you, because you look so young and you have taken up a task that is quite herculean?

I am 36 years old.

At 36, why did you choose to lead an anti-trafficking campaign, what is the motivation?

If you check everywhere, over time, there have been issues of insecurity and other challenges in Benue. Notwithstanding the hardship, some people have now resorted to trafficking, perhaps for profit-making and other reasons.

From the available data, Benue is the state with the highest number of human trafficking cases.

So, as a citizen of Benue state, I thought it was wise to see if I could help. I decided to campaign and create awareness so that people would know that this is happening. Aside from my inability to provide solutions to insecurity, kidnapping and other challenges, I chose to fight human trafficking and organise anti-human trafficking campaigns.

I don’t have any other motive. It is not for profit-making. I am just trying to help in my little way.

In the course of your voluntary work, how many people have you rescued since the beginning of this year?

My brother, they are many. Let me break it down for you. From March till now, I don’t like giving out my data because I work with people. I work with the police, and if I have to give out any data, I think it would be wise to go through the proper channels. But, since this is for a report, let me say that from March till now, I have intercepted 573 girls. By interception, I mean that we stopped them before they were taken out of the country.

We could intercept them at a motor park or somewhere along the route because I have people who assist me.

We have intercepted 573 girls from March till now. These are girls intercepted within Nigeria, especially in Lagos.

And these were all Benue girls?

Yes, all of them were Benue girls. I don’t have the resources to focus on people from other states. I am focused on Benue.

For those we rescued outside the country and brought back home, the number is 103.

You rescued them from outside the country?

Yes. Some were rescued from Ghana, Côte d’Ivoire, Burkina Faso and other countries.

Outside the country, I have people who assist me. In one particular Nigerian embassy, I have a Benue brother who helps me. Once I give him the location, he mobilises, goes there and helps rescue them.

So, apart from those rescued outside the country, the ones you intercepted inside Nigeria are over 500?

Yes, those within Nigeria are interceptions

If you intercept them, that means traffickers couldn’t get them outside the country?

Exactly. That is the essence of interception. This whole thing is also happening within Nigeria. For instance, in Benin, Edo and others states there are places where women and young girls are allegedly kept for prostitution.

And they are all Benue girls?

Yes, they are all Benue girls, like I said. All Benue girls. I have videos and pictures. If you want, I can forward them to you. I have many pictures. We also have about 32 who died outside the country. If you go through my social media handles, you will see that I sometimes post about Benue girls dying in Ghana.

And this record is from March 2026 till now?

Yes, just from March. That was when I started taking the issue seriously.

Are you getting any support from the government?

No, no single support.

So, you are doing this from your pocket?

From my pocket. I also have some brothers who support me. Sometimes, people who follow me on social media and see what I am doing send me messages saying they want to help. The highest support I have received so far is N500,000.

I have received N500,000, N200,000, N100,000, N10,000 and so on from individuals.

What are the challenges you have been facing in the course of your intervention?

There are a lot of challenges.

First, the traffickers and their families try to come after me and my family. That is one major challenge. Some of them even use security agencies. As I speak, there’s a petition written against me by a trafficker in Lagos.

According to her, she trafficked only three girls. But those girls told me that she took six of them to Ghana.

When I contacted her, she said she took only three and brought back two, meaning that only one is still there. When I asked her to send the remaining girl back home, she went and wrote a petition against me at Zone 2 in Lagos. In Nigeria, if you have money, you can do almost anything. That is one of the challenges.

Finance is another major challenge, and it is the biggest one. If I am well-funded, I think I can expand my work. There are victims from other states who have been contacting me. Last week, some girls from Rivers State called me from Mali for assistance.

For now, I want to focus on Benue because of some limitations and other factors. But if I have the money, why not expand the work to other states? I will.

Human trafficking is a major challenge in Nigeria, and Benue is currently topping the list, according to the data available to us.

How many of the traffickers have you been able to get arrested in the course of this intervention?

They are many. When it comes to arrests, I really appreciate the Benue State Police Command for the wonderful job it is doing. Initially, I was working with the National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons, NAPTIP, but I moved from NAPTIP to the police in March. That is why I gave you the statistics starting from March.

The number of people arrested and remanded awaiting trial is now 59.

When I arrest some of them, I sometimes give them a soft landing. That is if they bring the victims back, take them to the hospital and perhaps empower them. Some of them comply and I let the matter go.

Given the inherent dangers in this assignment, are you not scared for your life?

Of course I am very scared. I count my days every day. But I know that when you are doing what is right, God is always there for you.

What I am doing is to help the society, especially the underprivileged. So, I am not really scared in the true sense of the word.

Do you have personal security?

I don’t have the money for that for now. God is my security. When I have the money, I can get security personnel attached to me. But for now, I am doing the work and praying to God for protection.

Is the Benue State Government assisting you?

No, not at all. But I get assistance from Benue Links, the state-owned transport company, which helps to transport some of the girls back home when we rescue them.

What is your final word to young girls and traffickers out there?

My message to the traffickers is that we are getting closer to the end of the war against human trafficking. If they still want to move more people, we will enforce more measures against them. If I have what it takes, I believe you won’t see anything like human trafficking again. But I have developed strategies over time. I have developed major strategies, including working with immigration officials, people at the borders and others. If we can close all the leakages, I think we will achieve good results.

For my sisters, I am always advising them to stay at home, go to school and get educated. If you are travelling as an educated person, you should know that you need a passport and all the necessary documents before travelling. If somebody says they are offering you a job, you should be able to check the company’s website and verify everything. Make your findings very well before travelling.

I advise them to stay safe, get educated and become useful to themselves.
