World.title: INEC 2027: What Happens After We Vote?
World.content:
By Ugo Inyama

A Nigerian can transfer money on a phone and receive confirmation within seconds. Yet after spending hours in the sun to vote, the same person may spend days searching for their polling unit result and wondering whether it entered the final count.

An election is more complicated than a bank transfer. Nobody disputes that. But a citizen who has voted deserves to know what happened afterwards.

That is the question INEC must answer before 2027.

On election morning, people leave their homes with hope. Some arrive before the officials. They wait for materials, endure the heat and remain patient when voting starts late. Many stay behind for the counting because they want to hear the figures themselves.

The votes are counted. Results are announced. Party agents collect their copies. At that point, everyone present knows what happened at that polling unit.

Then the result leaves.

It passes through collation centres, where figures are added together until a winner emerges. This is where many Nigerians begin to worry. Will the figures remain the same? Will the result appear on the portal? If something changes, will anyone explain why?

People should not have to rely on a party spokesman to tell them whether their votes counted. They should be able to check.

We have spent too many elections arguing about what happened between the polling unit and the final declaration. That uncertainty gives room to people who manipulate results. It also allows candidates who lose fairly to make allegations they cannot support.

A process that people can follow would help expose both.

Before the 2023 elections, BVAS and the INEC Result Viewing Portal raised expectations. Nigerians hoped technology would make it harder to alter results without leaving evidence.

When presidential result uploads were delayed, voters kept refreshing the portal. They wanted to see the results they had watched officials count. The absence of that information created anxiety, and explanations struggled to overcome the suspicion that followed.

INEC should take that experience seriously. Public confidence is difficult to recover once people believe they have been misled.

The Electoral Act 2026 requires electronic transmission of polling unit results to IReV after the prescribed signing and stamping of Form EC8A. Where communication failure makes transmission impossible, the signed paper form remains the primary source for collation and declaration. (placng.org)

That fallback needs clear procedures.

Who records the failure? Who verifies what happened? What evidence is retained? How is the paper result protected while transmission remains impossible?

These questions should be answered before election day, when there is time to examine the arrangements calmly.

Anyone who uses a phone in Nigeria knows that network problems are real. But because they are familiar, they should be planned for. INEC should demonstrate how officials will retain results, record attempted uploads and account for delays.

“Network failure” should begin an explanation, rather than close the matter.

Buying equipment is only part of the job. Officials must know how to use it, follow the procedures and account for their decisions. Where an official deliberately breaches those procedures, there must be consequences.

INEC should publish its transmission and contingency arrangements early, submit its systems to independent technical scrutiny and test them under difficult conditions. Accredited observers and political parties should have meaningful opportunities to examine the preparations, with appropriate security safeguards.

The details matter. A replacement device should be recorded. A correction should show the original figure, who changed it and why. Polling unit results should remain traceable as they move through collation.

Communication matters just as much. If a system fails, INEC should identify the affected locations, explain the problem and provide regular updates. Leaving people staring at a blank portal invites rumours, especially when political tensions are already high.

The Commission’s independence will also be tested when powerful people demand exceptions. A governor may object. A party may apply pressure. An influential candidate may want a disputed result hurried through.

Officials must follow the same rules whoever benefits.

Political parties have their own part to play. Too often, they condemn conduct in one state and defend it in another. Their position depends on whether they are winning.

A party that demands transparency must accept what transparency reveals, including defeat.

Vote buying requires the same consistency. We readily condemn the voter who accepts money, but what happens to those who supply the funds and organise the purchase? Accountability must reach them too.

Courts will remain necessary. But Nigerians should not routinely have to wait for litigation to understand how polling unit figures became a declared result. The evidence should be available while the process unfolds.

INEC cannot persuade every losing candidate to concede. It can give citizens enough reliable information to assess the claims made in their name.

The person who stood in the sun has already fulfilled their responsibility. INEC owes that voter a clear account of what happened next.

By 2027, following a vote from the polling unit to the final declaration should be an ordinary part of a Nigerian election.

*Ugo Inyama

Email: Ugo@africandgc.org

Website: www.africandgc.org⁠

World.title: About the North’s ‘Tinubu Must Go’
World.content:
By Mobolaji Sanusi

“For to be free is not merely to cast off one’s chains, but to live in a way that respects and enhances the freedom of others.”

— Nelson Mandela(1918-2013).

The ban on political campaigns was lifted in August/September, but campaigns are only just gathering momentum. By mid-October to early November, all major political parties will be in full campaign swing, and the heat of the January 2027 elections will be felt across the 774 local government areas and the Federal Capital Territory.

The freedom offered by the electioneering window is enormous, but it comes with a clear caveat prohibiting hate speech, violence, and other activities inimical to public order.

Politicians, being creatures of mischief with often scant regard for the rule of law, have a proclivity for breaching these rules. They constantly seek ways, legal or otherwise, to outwit their opponents, with little regard for societal wellbeing as long as their selfish interests are served.

This campaign window is no exception. Politicians across the board are deeply involved in brazen breaches of electoral rules, and for want of enforcement tools, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) appears helpless. Hateful rhetoric rather than lofty policy ideas now fills the political space, and this is more rampant in the northern part of the country. Never in the history of intelligence leadership has the country had a more tolerant leadership than the Department of State Services (DSS) currently has. This is reflected in the Department’s accommodating disposition toward dissenting views, especially in the North, which in recent times has shown clear intolerance toward the current federal administration. Yet an administration that is led by a northerner is principally responsible for the current abysmal state of the nation’s general wellbeing.

Even though the current government’s economic reforms may have brought hardship felt across Nigeria, the North’s modus operandi of venting anger against the President has been contemptuous of caution and decorum.

It has become routine in the North to encounter processions promoting the ” Tinubu Must Go” movement. One such gathering was scheduled for last weekend in Kano state but was halted by the police. The convener, Abba Hikima, a lawyer, wrote on his verified Facebook page that the police sealed off the facility paid for to host what he described as a “non-partisan platform set up to sensitise Nigerians and mobilise voters against Tinubu in the 2027 elections over economic hardship.”

It is judicially settled that Nigerians have the inalienable right to assemble and to protest peacefully. In practice, however, there is often a thin line between a peaceful and a violent procession.

Citizens have a constitutional right to freely associate to exchange ideas and educate themselves on the need to vote out any administration. The concern of the state should be how they go about achieving that mission. In the convener of the Kano movement’s personal view, which may not reflect the general consensus, “Tinubu has failed,” possibly because he’s not a northerner but that does not give them licence to insist in October 2026 that the President “must go” when his current mandate runs until May 2027, and with the constitutional right to seek reelection that he is presently exploring.

Democracy provides for periodic elections precisely to allow the electorate to use their votes to retain or remove incumbents.

While the rights to freedom of speech and association are guaranteed under the Constitution, hiding under that guarantee to act in a manner capable of breaching public peace and order is unacceptable. Hikima insists they are “not criminals, not thugs, not hooligans,” but it behoves law enforcement agencies to take precautionary measures to prevent a breakdown of law and order.

All Nigerians, irrespective of region or ancestry, should endeavour to respect the rights of others, especially when it concerns the President. I sincerely believe that Nigerians, including those from the North, have a right to be aggrieved by the economic hardship. However, such grievances must be expressed within the reasonable bounds of the law.

This does not appear to be the case, judging by the routine harassment of anything associated with Tinubu in parts of the North. Last month, youths in the Jega area of Kebbi State destroyed posters and billboards of President Tinubu and Governor Nasir Idris and damaged vehicles on major roads in the town, under the pretext of venting anger against the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC).

A similar scenario occurred in Borno State recently, where persons wearing “Tinubu Must Go” T-shirts caused a breach of public peace. Five of them — Baba Aji Gremani, Mustapha Abba Yemen, Abacha Mohammed Ali, Adam Umar Gubio and Abdulhamid Mohammed — were arrested and later released by the police for printing and wearing T-shirts with the inciting inscription.

Tinubu was elected by Nigerians of all ethnic backgrounds and should be allowed to complete his constitutionally permitted tenure, just as he also has constitutionally guaranteed right to seek re-election. Only the ballot can decide his re-election or otherwise. Destroying the President’s campaign billboards, attacking his campaign vehicles, or chanting “Tinubu Must Go” in a violent street procession, is wrong and should not be tolerated. It is a dangerous trend that, if replicated in other regions, could set the country ablaze.

In realistic terms, Tinubu has done more to promote northern presidential interests than many living northern leaders. Atiku Abubakar contested the presidency under Tinubu’s Action Congress in 2007. Mallam Nuhu Ribadu, incumbent national security adviser, was given the same platform by Tinubu in 2011 to contest for the presidency. But for God and Tinubu’s political benevolence, Muhammadu Buhari would not have become President, until Tinubu yielded his strong political goodwill to him. How would Buhari have defeated Atiku in the APC presidential primary held in Lagos without Tinubu’s deft political manoeuvring? It is still difficult to understand why northerners will not direct their grievances at their own successive leaders that have left the region pauperised despite having ruled the country as both military and civilian leaders.

The poverty in the North was not caused by Tinubu. Sons of the North have governed the country longer than sons from other regions, with no visible improvement in the general wellbeing of the majority of northerners. It is curious to now see vulnerable people in the North directing misplaced anger at Tinubu.

No democrat in his right senses would argue that any leader is indispensable and this rule applies to the current situation in the country. But there’s a question begging for an answer: Are those jostling to wrest power from Tinubu that at one time or the other been beneficiaries of his political generosity and have shown no clear-cut realistic plans that are different from Tinubu’s ongoing reforms better alternatives?

For as long as it’s trite that uneasy lies the head that wears the crown, Tinubu should be held responsible for the policies and decisions of his government. The President has been consistent in defending his reforms by insisting they were done in the best interest of the country and that the dividends would be felt by Nigerians as the reforms become more rooted with time. That is his strong position that stands to be contested by whoever feels otherwise.

However, part of the consequences of his reforms is the hardship in the country, from which yours sincerely is not insulated. I doubt if President Tinubu is asking for anyone’s pity because he asked for the job. Nigerians should learn to express their displeasure peacefully. The resort to incitement, violence and impunity by some people in the North or elsewhere to express disaffection toward the president should be discouraged and not condoned.

To the sincerely and insincerely aggrieved people in the North or elsewhere: you have a right to oppose Tinubu, but what you cannot do is prevent those supporting Tinubu from campaigning in the North or anywhere else. As Eleanor Holmes Norton once said: “The only way to make sure people you agree with can speak is to support the rights of people you don’t agree with.” On this note, I rest my case for this week.

•Sanusi, former MD/CEO of Lagos State Signage and  Agency, is currently Managing Partner at AMS RELIABLE SOLICITORS. (WhatsApp only: 07011117777)

World.title: Coalition Of Parastatals CEOS: A Masterstroke For Tinubu’s Re-election
World.content:
Omonu Nelson

A political earthquake is shaking up the road to 2027: a powerful coalition of federal agency heads has officially formed to spearhead President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s re-election campaign. This unprecedented alignment of institutional heads represents the most strategic and formidable innovation yet ahead of the next general election.

Under the Forum of CEOS of Federal Parastatals (FORCEPA), these institutional heavyweights have resolved that the campaign cannot be left to the governing All Progressives Congress (APC) alone. Instead, those who execute the government’s policies must actively participate in renewing its mandate—marking a profound shift in political thinking.

For years, bureaucrats have abandoned the battlefield, cowardly hiding in the shadows. The architects of vital public programmes retreated behind ivory towers of silence, leaving their critical achievements defenseless against political crossfire and partisan sabotage. By refusing to stand and fight for their own records, these administrators have surrendered the narrative to opportunists in the opposition who would rather weaponise their hard-won results than protect the people they serve.

By engaging APC National Chairman, Prof. Nentawe Yilwatda, and the National Working Committee (NWC), the Forum—led by its Chairman and Director-General of the National Board for Technology Incubation, Dr. Kazeem Kolawole Raji—aims to close the dangerous gap between performance and perception. Their stance is simple and compelling: where the government has delivered, those achievements must be shared. After all, who is better equipped to communicate results than the people who produced them?

The strategic advantages of this coalition are monumental. While the 2023 campaign centred on promises of what President Tinubu would do, the 2027 narrative will shift entirely to accountability—what he has achieved. Winning that argument demands hard data, institutional memory, and deep grassroots mobilization. These chief executives command exactly those assets, making them indispensable to anchoring the next campaign in undeniable evidence.

They provide a complementary technical structure designed to extend the reach of the Presidential Campaign Council, not compete with it. These professionals, public-sector leaders, and political stakeholders offer deep expertise in election planning, grassroots mobilization, and strategic messaging. By leveraging nationwide networks through their parastatals, they drive government messaging into communities the central campaign machinery often misses.

In doing so, they affirm the bold nature of President Tinubu’s reforms, showing that key insiders who weigh the costs and benefits of difficult decisions remain confident enough to publicly campaign on that record. That courage is now being validated beyond Nigeria.

Five influential international institutions and rating agencies, including the International Monetary Fund (IMF), World Bank, African Development Bank (AfDB), Fitch and S&P, have acknowledged progress in Nigeria’s reform programme under President Tinubu. Their assessments point to improving macroeconomic stability, stronger external balances, better revenue mobilisation, and renewed confidence in economic policy. rewrite for high impact flow.

This external validation gives the Forum a credible foundation to build its campaign messaging on. However, as the chief executives themselves understand, the next test is to translate these macro gains into lower living costs, more jobs, rising purchasing power, and better living standards for ordinary Nigerians. That is precisely why their grassroots presence matters.

The calibre of the Forum’s leadership virtually guarantees its success, anchored by Chairman, Dr. Raji—a distinguished telecommunications authority with more than 25 years of proven success in leadership, project management, and technological innovation.

Dr. Raji, an Oyo State-born engineer affectionately known as ‘Raji KK,’ is a distinguished leader whose academic and leadership foundation was built at the prestigious University of Ibadan. During his time there, he served as the Hall Chairman of Nnamdi Azikiwe Hall (Zik Hall)—widely recognized as the most vibrant, politically active, and influential student residence in any African university.

He possesses an extraordinary academic portfolio that reflects a lifelong commitment to excellence. His qualifications span multiple disciplines, including a PhD. Combining deep technical engineering expertise, executive business acumen, and a proven track record of grassroots leadership, Raji stands out as a dynamic force in both academia and corporate management. During the 2023 general election, he drove key grassroots initiatives as the Director of National Youth Mobilisation (South-west) for the Tinubu-Shettima Presidential Campaign Council.

Another member of the forum, who embodies the suitability of this arrangement, is Otunba Biodun Ajiboye, the Chairman of the forum’s Media and Publicity Committee and Executive Secretary of the National Institute for Cultural Orientation (NICO). Ajiboye’s entry into public service is no accident. He brings the formidable expertise of a seasoned media personality and a legendary advertising leader with more than three decades of pioneering experience.

That blend of professional expertise, political loyalty, and oratorical power makes him perfectly cast for his current role. He understands that an election is won not just by mobilisation, but by messaging—and for an incumbent, that messaging must be rooted in performance.

As the CEO of NICO, he directly executes the Renewed Hope Agenda in the cultural sector while remaining one of the ruling party’s most consummate communicators. Thus, when he argued that the communication apparatus cannot be left to the PCC alone—advocating that the Forum act as a technical monitoring body to identify gaps and reinforce narratives—he speaks from both experience and authority.

Ultimately, the contribution of this coalition to the success of President Tinubu’s second-term bid in 2027 could be decisive. It provides what every incumbent needs but rarely organises early enough—a credible, coordinated, and decentralised army of validators who can speak with authority about what the government has achieved. It transforms the campaign from a purely party affair into a national project driven by those who know the work firsthand.

To dismantle the opposition’s relentless campaign of deceit and manufactured narratives, this coalition stands as an unstoppable frontline of undeniable facts, raw institutional power, and boots-on-the-ground dominance.

By deploying its members to explain, defend, and mobilise around the administration’s record — from internationally acknowledged macroeconomic reforms to everyday community impact — it ensures that the president’s long-term economic ambitions are not just understood in Washington, London and Abidjan, but felt in markets, farms and homes across Nigeria.

This is how elections are won in mature democracies—not by slogans alone, but by aligning the implementers with the campaigners. With Otunba Ajiboye providing the strategic communication leadership, the Forum has positioned itself as a critical pillar for victory in 2027.

* Omonu, a development journalist, writes from Abuja

World.title: Atiku Fit, Ready to Traverse 36 States, FCT, ADC-PCC Declares
World.content:
Says Tinubu’s refusal to campaign nationwide is arrogant, insult to Nigerians

Accuses Kwankwaso of doing president’s bidding, describes call for former VP to step down as reckless

Chuks Okocha

The African Democratic Congress Presidential Campaign Council (ADC-PCC) has declared that its presidential candidate, former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar, is fit and ready to campaign across Nigeria’s 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory ahead of the 2027 general election.

The council also criticised President Bola Tinubu over his decision not to campaign in all states, describing it as an act of arrogance and an insult to Nigerians, while accusing former Kano State Governor Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso of advancing the president’s political interests by calling on Atiku to step down for Peter Obi.

The Director of Media and Publicity of the ADC-PCC, Kola Ologbondiyan, in a statement, was quoted to have made the remarks while receiving a delegation of youths under the aegis of Young Voters for Atiku (YVA) and in a separate response to Kwankwaso’s interview on Channels Television.

Ologbondiyan argued that a president seeking re-election should be willing to engage voters directly, account for his stewardship and present his plans for the country. He said Tinubu’s reported reluctance to campaign nationwide would give the opposition an advantage.

“What President Tinubu has done is a clear act of contempt against the Nigerian people. The APC is known for its contempt for Nigerians. How can a man who wants to be re-elected as president, after failing woefully, say he does not want to visit the people he seeks to govern?” he said.

The ADC-PCC spokesman dismissed the argument that official engagements could prevent Tinubu from campaigning across the country, citing former Presidents Olusegun Obasanjo, Goodluck Jonathan and Muhammadu Buhari, as well as former United States President Donald Trump and former Vice-President Kamala Harris, as examples of political leaders who campaigned while holding or seeking public office.

He alleged that Tinubu was reluctant to face voters because of public dissatisfaction over hunger, poverty, insecurity and the state of the economy.

Ologbondiyan maintained that Atiku was physically fit, mentally alert and prepared to visit every state and the FCT to present his manifesto and seek the electorate’s mandate.

He urged Nigerians, particularly young voters, to reject the All Progressives Congress (APC) in 2027, arguing that another term for the ruling party would prolong the hardship citizens were experiencing.

He also expressed confidence that Atiku, if elected, would prioritise economic recovery, wealth creation, national security and improved living standards.

The ADC-PCC further criticised Kwankwaso for urging Atiku to step down for Obi, describing the call as reckless, self-serving and an attempt to weaken the opposition ahead of the 2027 election.

Ologbondiyan questioned why Kwankwaso was focusing on opposition leaders rather than challenging Tinubu’s administration, which the council said Nigerians were eager to vote out.

“Rather than campaigning against President Tinubu, whose administration Nigerians are eagerly working to vote out, Kwankwaso is fixated on Atiku Abubakar, the ADC candidate, whom millions of Nigerians believe can restore economic stability and make life affordable again,” he said.

He alleged that Kwankwaso’s position raised questions about his political intentions, suggesting that his actions could benefit the ruling APC by creating divisions among opposition parties.

“What Kwankwaso is doing amounts to advancing President Tinubu’s interests. It is a familiar APC strategy to use willing collaborators within the opposition to create confusion, sow division and weaken the collective efforts to bring about political change,” Ologbondiyan said.

He also argued that Kwankwaso’s political influence in Kano should not be considered indispensable to any presidential candidate seeking victory in the state. Citing the 2003 and 2007 presidential elections, he said former President Muhammadu Buhari had secured victories in Kano without Kwankwaso’s support, adding that Atiku could also win the state in 2027.

Ologbondiyan further questioned Kwankwaso’s ability to translate his regional influence into nationwide electoral support, citing his fourth-place finish in the 2023 presidential election.

He also alleged that Kwankwaso’s call for Obi’s candidacy was driven partly by personal political ambition and possible calculations ahead of the 2031 election.

The ADC-PCC director maintained that Atiku had built political relationships across Nigeria’s six geopolitical zones over more than three decades, which he said positioned the former vice-president to assemble a broad national coalition.

He urged Kwankwaso and other opposition figures to support Atiku, arguing that opposition leaders should prioritise defeating the APC rather than undermining one another.

“The task before opposition leaders is not to undermine one another for personal political advantage but to unite around the urgent national mission of rescuing Nigeria,” Ologbondiyan said.

The council also claimed that it had been politically strengthened by the inauguration of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, saying the event had not attracted endorsements from ADC members or sympathisers.

World.title: 2027: N32trn FAAC Windfall in 41 Months Puts Governors Under Spotlight
World.content:
· CSOs demand evidence of improved healthcare, education, jobs, infrastructure

· Seek greater transparency

Nume Ekeghe and Sunday Ehigiator

As the 2027 general election approaches, the performance of state governors is coming under renewed scrutiny, with states and local governments receiving a combined N31.77 trillion from the Federation Account Allocation Committee (FAAC) between June 2023 and October 2026, according to data compiled by THISDAY.

This is as Governors have been challenged to account for increased FAAC revenues by demonstrating measurable improvements in healthcare, education, infrastructure, employment and poverty reduction, amid concerns that rising public revenues have yet to translate into better living conditions for many Nigerians

The massive inflows have raised questions about how effectively the funds have translated into better infrastructure, improved public services and tangible improvements in the lives of Nigerians, particularly at the grassroots, where local governments are expected to play a critical role in development.

Despite the Supreme Court’s landmark judgment of July 11, 2024, affirming financial autonomy for local governments, many state governors have continued to wield considerable influence over funds allocated to local government areas (LGs), raising concerns about whether the ruling has delivered the intended independence.

Under the existing revenue-sharing formula, the federal government receives 52.68 per cent of distributable revenue, state governments get 26.72 per cent, while LGs receive 20.60 per cent. However, the administration of LG allocations remain a contentious issue, with questions persisting over the extent to which councils exercise effective control over their funds.

FAAC allocations to states and local governments have risen substantially since the removal of the petrol subsidy, which increased the revenue available for distribution among the three tiers of government.

THISDAY’s analysis showed that states and local governments received a combined N3.861 trillion between June and December 2023. While the 36 states received a total of N2.223 trillion in the seven-month period, LGs got N1.637 trillion. Also, in 2024, both tiers of government got N7.870 trillion, with States receiving N4.594 trillion and the LGs N3.276 trillion.

Furthermore, in 2025 both tiers of government got N10.419 trillion, in which N5.988 trillion went to the states and N4.430 trillion to the LGs. Also, in the first nine months of 2026, they received N9.618 trillion, with the States receiving a total of N5.56 trillion and the LGs N4.056 trillion. This brings the total for both tiers of government since President Bola Tinubu announced the removal of petrol subsidy to N31.77 trillion.

The September 2026 revenue which was shared by FAAC this week, further underscored the scale of the revenue windfall. A total of N2.428 trillion from the Federation Account was distributed among the three tiers of government in October 2026, representing an increase of N90 billion from the N2.338 trillion shared in September.

Of the amount, the federal government received N832.242 billion, the 36 state governments received N799.87 billion, while local governments received N560.66 billion.

Leading the call for accountability on the increased allocations actions, the Civil Society Legislative Advocacy Centre (CISLAC) and the Rule of Law and Accountability Advocacy Centre (RULAAC) urged citizens, civil society organisations (CSOs) and the media to intensify scrutiny of state finances and government performance.

CISLAC, through its Executive Director, Auwal Ibrahim Musa (Rafsanjani), expressed concern over what it described as a widening gap between increased FAAC revenues accruing to state governments and persistent poverty, unemployment, infrastructure decay and economic hardship.

“Governors cannot continue celebrating record allocations while citizens struggle with failing hospitals, deteriorating schools, unemployment, poor roads and inadequate basic services,” the organisation stated.

“The question is no longer how much states receive, but what governments have delivered with the money.”

CISLAC argued that governors should be assessed on measurable improvements in citizens’ welfare rather than political publicity, budget announcements or ceremonial project commissioning.

It identified key indicators for evaluating state performance to include the functionality of primary healthcare centres, availability of medicines and medical personnel, school enrolment and learning outcomes, completed and usable roads, access to clean water, sustainable job creation and poverty reduction.

According to CISLAC, “Development is not measured by the size of government allocations, but by the quality of life of the people.”

It called on state governments to publish accessible monthly revenue reports, quarterly budget implementation records, contract details and independently audited financial statements to enable citizens to track public funds from allocation to actual service delivery.

It urged CSOs, investigative journalists, professional associations and community-based groups to verify projects on the ground, expose abandoned or inflated contracts and compare official expenditure claims with actual conditions in communities.

It also called on State Houses of Assembly to exercise independent oversight, while urging Auditors-General, procurement authorities and anti-corruption agencies to investigate credible allegations of misappropriation, inflated contracts and diversion of public funds.

On the political implications of the increased allocations, CISLAC challenged governors to publish comprehensive, independently verifiable records of revenues received and development outcomes achieved during their tenures.

Similarly, the Executive Director of RULAAC, Okechukwu Nwanguma, said increased FAAC allocations had given state governments greater fiscal capacity, but warned that higher revenue did not automatically translate into development.

“Nigerians should judge governors by measurable outcomes, not by announcements, groundbreaking ceremonies or the number of contracts awarded,” he said.

Nwanguma said citizens should examine each state’s FAAC receipts alongside internally generated revenue, debt profile, recurrent expenditure and actual capital-budget implementation.

“The relevant question is: after salaries, debt servicing and administrative costs, how much was invested in projects and services that directly improved people’s lives?” he asked.

He identified education completion rates, the number of out-of-school children, healthcare access, maternal and infant mortality, youth unemployment, household incomes, food security, road quality, access to potable water and capital project completion rates as essential indicators for assessing governors.

Nwanguma also stressed the importance of comparing these indicators with conditions before the revenue increases, using per-capita spending and adjustments for inflation to establish whether citizens had experienced genuine improvements.

He urged CSOs to obtain and simplify state budgets, monthly FAAC receipts, procurement records, quarterly implementation reports and audited accounts, converting the information into accessible scorecards showing what governments received, budgeted, spent and delivered.

He added that communities should document abandoned or substandard projects, interview beneficiaries and use public hearings, town halls, radio programmes and partnerships with journalists to demand explanations from public officials.

Ahead of the elections, Nwanguma said, CSOs and the media should publish non-partisan performance scorecards based on verifiable evidence.

World.title: Kwankwasiyya, NNPP Petition INEC Over Kano, Oyo Guber Candidates’ Exclusion
World.content:
Protest hits Kano as aggrieved supporters challenge omissions

Tinubu reappoints Bila, nominates five new INEC commissioners

Alex Enumah, Adedayo Akinwale in Abuja and Ahmad Sorondinki in Kano,

The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) is facing mounting pressure over the exclusion of some candidates from its final list for the 2027 elections, with the Kwankwasiyya Movement and the New Nigeria People’s Party (NNPP) petitioning the commission over omissions in Kano and Oyo states, respectively, while a Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) aspirant in Ogun State has threatened legal action.

The development comes as President Bola Tinubu yesterday nominated five new officials to the electoral body and reappointed its National Commissioner representing the North-east, Dr Bala Bila, amid preparations for the forthcoming general election. The president nominated four national commissioners and two resident electoral commissioners, with the Senate expected to scrutinise the nominees.

In Kano, hundreds of supporters of the Kwankwasiyya Movement stormed the state office of INEC to protest the omission of their governorship candidate from the final list.

The protesters, led by the deputy governorship candidate, Mustapha Kwankwaso, on behalf of Aminu Gwarzo, submitted a formal petition demanding the reinstatement of the National Democratic Congress (NDC) candidate.

Responding, the Kano State Resident Electoral Commissioner, Abdu Zango, said the commission had received the complaint and would give it due attention.

“Basically, what they came to do is to present a complaint about the omission of their candidates. INEC has made the point very clear, the reason for the omission and the fact that there is a window of appeal that has been provided up to the 24th of October,” Zango said.

He added that the petition would be forwarded to the commission’s national headquarters for consideration, commending the protesters for presenting their grievances peacefully.

Zango said INEC in Kano remained neutral and urged residents to continue collecting their Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs), noting that collection would soon be extended to Registration Areas to improve accessibility.

The spokesperson for the Kwankwasiyya Movement, Dr Habib Mohammed, said the protest was not only to demand the reinstatement of the candidates but also to petition against an INEC staff member allegedly involved in the substitution of some candidates.

“We are also petitioning against a staff here, whom we believe colluded with some unauthorised people to hide a decision which led to substitution of some of our candidates,” Mohammed said.

He alleged that letters bearing suspected forged signatures had been submitted to INEC, resulting in the substitution of the candidates. He called for an investigation into the staff member’s alleged role, adding that the Resident Electoral Commissioner had assured the delegation that the petition would be escalated to the national headquarters.

Oyo NNPP Candidate Petitions INEC Chairman

In Oyo State, the governorship candidate of the NNPP, Adebiyi Adedapo, petitioned the INEC Chairman, Prof. Joash Amupitan, over the omission of his name from the final list of governorship candidates for the 2027 election.

In an open letter dated October 15, Adedapo urged the commission to investigate the omission and take corrective action in accordance with the law.

He said he emerged as the party’s duly nominated candidate following a consensus primary conducted under the supervision of its National Secretary, Oginni Sunday, in accordance with the party’s constitution and electoral guidelines.

According to him, the NNPP submitted his candidature to INEC, while his EC9 form was displayed at the commission’s Oyo State office, giving him reason to expect that his name would appear on the final list.

Adedapo said he had never withdrawn from the race and had neither submitted nor authorised anyone to submit a withdrawal letter on his behalf.

“I have never withdrawn my candidature from the Oyo State governorship election. I have neither submitted nor authorised the submission of any letter of withdrawal to INEC, the NNPP, or any person or institution acting on my behalf,” he said.

He called on INEC to disclose any document purporting to show that he had withdrawn, including its source and date of receipt, and to investigate any unauthorised withdrawal or substitution.

The candidate also urged the commission to verify his nomination records, provide a written explanation for the omission, preserve all relevant documents and apply any lawful remedies required to ensure that his name appears on the ballot.

He said he was prepared to provide evidence of his nomination, primary results, submitted particulars and party correspondence to assist the investigation.

Tinubu Reappoints Bila, Nominates Five New INEC Officials

Meanwhile, President Tinubu has nominated four new national commissioners and two resident electoral commissioners to fill vacancies at INEC arising from expiring tenures, while reappointing Bila as the National Commissioner representing the North-east.

Presidential spokesperson Bayo Onanuga disclosed the nominations in a statement on Friday, saying the nominees would be scrutinised by the Senate.

The new national commissioner nominees are Professor Mustapha Aliu, who is to replace Professor Abdullahi Zuru as the North-west representative, and Bashir Muhammed Umar, who is to replace Professor Muhammad Adamu as the North-central representative.

The president also nominated Mrs Oluwatoyin Babalola, the resident electoral commissioner in Osun State, as the South-west national commissioner to replace Professor Cornelius Ajayi, whose tenure expires on October 24, 2026.

The two nominees for resident electoral commissioner positions are retired permanent secretary Dr Samuel Akinjide Akinleye, representing Ekiti State, and Zahradden Basiru Sanusi, from Jigawa State, who is to replace Professor Saidu Ahmed Babura.

Tinubu urged the Senate to expedite confirmation of the nominees in view of the forthcoming general election scheduled for 2027.

Ogun PDP Aspirant Threatens Legal Action

In Ogun State, governorship aspirant Olusegun Peter Topa gave INEC 48 hours to publish his name as the PDP’s duly nominated candidate for the February 2027 governorship election or face possible legal action.

In a letter dated October 14 and addressed to the INEC chairman through his lawyer, Anderson Asemota of Neplus Ultra Attorneys, Topa argued that he had fulfilled the requirements for nomination and should be included in the final list.

He said he obtained the party’s Expression of Interest and nomination forms on May 12, 2026, and participated in its governorship primary conducted on May 27, 2026.

INEC published its final list of governorship candidates on October 10 but excluded the PDP from the race in Ogun State.

Topa’s lawyer maintained that his client’s name appeared as entry number 15783 on the PDP membership register submitted to INEC in compliance with Section 77 of the Electoral Act, 2026.

He argued that the commission had a statutory obligation to publish the particulars of duly nominated candidates, subject to applicable laws and any binding court decisions.

The lawyer urged INEC to verify Topa’s membership status, examine the party’s primary and nomination records, establish the basis for the exclusion and provide a written explanation.

He further asked the commission to publish a supplementary or amended list containing Topa’s name if its records confirmed his nomination and no lawful basis existed for excluding him.

Asemota warned that his client had instructed his lawyers to consider instituting proceedings before a competent court if INEC failed to provide a substantive response within 48 hours or the omission persisted without a lawful explanation.

World.title: With New Credit Rating Agency, Africa Pushes for Fairer Risk Assessment, Lower Borrowing Costs
World.content:
• Continent pays more to borrow, says WAIFEM DG

• Experts demand transparent ratings, stronger data, joint ownership of debt analysis

• IMF warns rising debt service crowding out development spending

• W’Bank mobilises $112bn in private capital, says 59m Africans gain electricity access

Nume Ekeghe in Bangkok, Thailand

African policymakers and financial experts have called for a fairer assessment of the continent’s economies, stronger debt management capacity and greater transparency in credit rating methodologies, warning that persistent risk premiums continue to raise borrowing costs and constrain development financing.

The call comes as Africa seeks to strengthen its voice in global credit assessments following the launch of the Africa Credit Rating Agency (AfCRA) in Mauritius this month, against the backdrop of mounting debt pressures, a projected global shortfall of 800 million jobs and growing demands for infrastructure and social investment.

Also yesterday, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) warned that rising debt-service burdens were squeezing development spending, while the World Bank Group highlighted the challenge of creating jobs for a rapidly growing global workforce, with a projected shortfall of 800 million jobs over the next 10 to 15 years.

Speaking at the 2026 IMF/World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned that high and rising interest burdens, particularly in low-income countries, were leaving governments with less room to finance development.

On his part, World Bank Group President Ajay Banga, stressed the need to mobilise private capital, expand infrastructure and create jobs, disclosing that the institution mobilised $112 billion in private capital last year.

The new continental credit rating agency is expected to complement existing international credit rating agencies by incorporating more African data, expertise and perspectives into assessments of the continent’s economies. However, stakeholders say its success will depend on its independence, credible methodologies, reliable economic data and acceptance by investors.

Speaking at a panel discussion on ‘The Debt Sustainability Framework, Credit Ratings and Africa’s Risk Premium,’ held on the sidelines of the IMF/World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, the Director-General of the West African Institute for Financial and Economic Management (WAIFEM), Dr. Baba Musa, said African countries had spent decades calling for their economic realities to be assessed accurately and proportionately.

He said African countries pay more to borrow than comparable economies in other regions, arguing that prevailing perceptions and external interpretations of the continent’s economic realities often placed it at a disadvantage.

“For a rating agency, the methodology should be comparable with international standards. However, what African countries have been asking for over the past 20 years is that they should be assessed accurately, their risks communicated proportionately, and their economies evaluated fairly,” Musa said.

He stressed that the demand for fairer assessments was not a call for preferential treatment or lower standards, but for methodologies that adequately reflected the diversity, resources and economic circumstances of African countries.

“Africa’s voice should be heard and the continent should be assessed fairly, just like any other region,” he said, adding that AfCRA’s success would depend on transparency, credible methodologies and its ability to capture the actual realities of African economies.

The cost of Africa’s risk premium remains substantial. The Deputy Executive Secretary and Chief Economist of the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (ECA), Dr. Hanan Morsy, estimated that persistent risk premiums cost the continent approximately $75 billion annually in excess interest payments.

The additional borrowing costs come at a time when governments face mounting pressure to finance development, improve living standards and create jobs for rapidly growing populations.

Morsy said African countries must also take greater responsibility for presenting evidence-based accounts of their economies rather than relying on others to make their case.

“If you do not advocate for yourself, no one will. This applies to individuals as well as countries. You must make your case and ensure that it is not based on words alone but backed by evidence,” she said.

She emphasised the need for reliable data to limit the room for discretion in credit assessments, warning that countries must be prepared to provide the evidence needed to support their economic outlooks.

Morsy added that international institutions had helped countries without previous credit ratings obtain them and subsequently improve their ratings, while also supporting countries seeking investment-grade status.

The launch of AfCRA is expected to broaden the information available to investors and provide additional perspectives on African economies, reform programmes and growth prospects. However, stakeholders have cautioned that the agency’s establishment alone will not automatically reduce borrowing costs without stronger economic fundamentals and institutional credibility.

Beyond credit ratings, African policymakers called for reforms to debt sustainability assessments to ensure that the models and assumptions used by international financial institutions adequately reflect national economic conditions.

Musa welcomed aspects of the revised Debt Sustainability Framework (DSF), noting that distinguishing between external debt distress, overall public debt distress and actual debt unsustainability represented progress in assessing African countries’ debt positions.

He explained that countries experiencing liquidity pressures should not necessarily be assessed in the same way as those facing solvency problems. Indicators such as gross financing needs relative to gross domestic product and government revenue, he said, could provide a more nuanced picture of countries’ debt positions.

However, he called for African governments to have a greater role in debt sustainability assessments, arguing that countries should jointly determine the assumptions and projections used to evaluate their debt positions.

Musa warned against situations in which the IMF and World Bank relied on their own projections while African governments maintained different estimates of their economic outlooks.

Former Finance Minister of Niger Republic, Hon. Ahmat Jidoud, said the revision of the DSF should not mark the end of efforts to improve debt assessment across the continent.

He called on the IMF and World Bank to engage more closely with African countries, explain the models and assumptions underpinning the framework, and provide training to officials in finance ministries and other relevant institutions.

Jidoud also raised concerns about the treatment of domestic debt under the revised framework, particularly its implications for regional economic communities such as the West African Economic and Monetary Union and the Central African Economic and Monetary Community.

For the Chief Executive Officer of the African Legal Support Facility (ALSF), Dr. Olivier Pognon, stronger coordination and knowledge-sharing among African institutions are essential to improving the continent’s engagement with credit rating agencies and strengthening debt management.

Pognon said the ALSF was developing a capacity-building platform expected to be launched in Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire, at the end of November. The initiative would support debt management offices and officials involved in public borrowing and major project negotiations.

IMF Warns Debt Burdens Squeezing Development

The debate over Africa’s borrowing costs comes as the IMF warns that rising public debt and interest payments are limiting governments’ ability to finance development and respond to economic shocks.

Speaking at the Annual Meetings Plenary, Georgieva, said low-income countries faced particularly difficult conditions, with high and rising interest burdens compounded by declining official aid.

“Too many countries carry too much debt,” she said, warning that debt-service obligations were crowding out development spending.

Georgieva said governments could not rely on economic growth alone to reverse rising debt trajectories quickly enough and called for credible medium-term fiscal plans to restore stability.

“The inescapable bottom line is that preserving stability requires fiscal consolidation in most high-debt countries,” she said.

However, she cautioned that fiscal adjustments must protect vulnerable households, limit the cost to future growth and be complemented by structural reforms that improve productivity.

World Bank mobilises $112bn in private capital

Banga, meanwhile, highlighted the need to mobilise private capital, expand infrastructure and create jobs for a rapidly growing young population.

He said 1.2 billion young people were expected to enter the labour market over the next 10 to 15 years, while the global economy was projected to generate only about 400 million jobs, leaving a potential shortfall of 800 million.

“The jobs gap is a projection. It does not have to be our future,” Banga said.

He argued that closing the gap would require countries to make better use of scarce resources by combining public finance, private investment, philanthropy and technology to support development.

Banga disclosed that the World Bank Group mobilised $112 billion in private capital last year, compared with approximately $35 billion in financial year 2022. Total financing, including the institution’s own resources, exceeded $230 billion.

However, he acknowledged that attracting commercial investment remained difficult in low-income countries, where private capital mobilisation stood at roughly $3 billion.

He said the World Bank was seeking to expand financing for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises by improving access to finance, connecting smaller businesses to larger markets and simplifying regulations that constrain growth.

Banga also identified infrastructure, human capital and regulatory certainty as essential foundations for job creation, noting that businesses needed reliable electricity, water, transport and digital connections, while workers required education, healthcare and relevant skills.

On electricity access, he said the World Bank Group and the African Development Bank were working to provide electricity to 300 million people across Africa by 2030 under Mission 300.

So far, 59 million people have gained access, with the pace accelerating from 12 million in financial year 2024 to 18 million in financial year 2025 and 28 million in the latest financial year.

“But access is only part of the challenge. Homes, mines, factories, farms, and growing cities need reliable, affordable baseload power,” he said.

Stakeholders also stressed the need for responsible fiscal policies, stronger domestic resource mobilisation, improved debt management and greater coordination between African governments and international financial institutions.

World.title: Tinubu Welcomes W’Bank’s $5.79bn Plan, Dangles $78.5bn Projects Before Investors
World.content:
Deji Elumoye in Abuja



President Bola Tinubu yesterday welcomed World Bank Group’s proposed plan to mobilise about $5.79 billion in private financing for Nigeria.

He has also taken steps to attract domestic and foreign investors to Nigeria, unveiling a pipeline of 65 bankable projects seeking $78.5 billion in investment.

According to Tinubu, the investment move was aimed at strengthening the foundation for economic growth, expanding businesses and creating jobs, with agriculture and digital infrastructure among the sectors expected to benefit from increased private capital.

Tinubu, in a post on his verified X handle, @officialABAT, extended invitation to Nigerian and international investors to explore the projects, assuring them that his administration would work to resolve obstacles and facilitate the execution of viable investments.

He wrote, “We undertook our economic reforms to build a stronger foundation for investment and give more Nigerians the opportunity to earn a better living.”



According to the President, the World Bank Group’s financing mobilisation initiative is a support for the government’s efforts to attract investment and expand economic opportunities.

“I welcome the World Bank Group’s work to mobilise up to $5.79 billion in private financing for Nigeria. This partnership supports our efforts to help businesses expand and attract investment into agriculture and digital infrastructure,” Tinubu said.

The $78.5 billion project pipeline was presented by the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, alongside the Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria, Olayemi Cardoso, at the Nigeria Investors Forum, held on the sidelines of the 2026 IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok.

The President charged investors to examine the proposed projects and engage directly with their sponsors through Projects Nigeria, the Federal Government’s platform for showcasing investment opportunities.

“Our administration will work with you to resolve obstacles and move viable investments into execution, creating jobs and expanding opportunities for our people,” Tinubu stated.

His appeal came as the government seeks to attract private-sector financing to support economic development, with the government positioning the project pipeline as an avenue for investors to participate in key sectors of the Nigerian economy.

The initiative is expected to complement efforts to expand productive activities, support business growth and create employment opportunities through increased investment in viable projects.

The President directed the investors to access details of the 65 projects through the Projects Nigeria portal at finance.gov.ng/projectsnigeria.

World.title: The 10 Kruger National Park camps with the BEST views
World.content:
Kruger National Park is famous for its wildlife, but where you stay can be just as memorable.

Some camps overlook rivers, dams or valleys, while others offer elevated views across the surrounding bushveld. Here are 10 camps to consider if scenery is high on your list.

Views for days at these Kruger camps

Camp What makes the view special Olifants Elevated views over the Olifants River Lower Sabie Sabie River and Lebombo Mountains Letaba Letaba River and surrounding bushveld Mopani Pioneer Dam and mopane-covered koppies Skukuza Sabie River and lush riverine vegetation Berg-en-Dal Rugged mountain landscape Biyamiti Mbiyamiti River and dense bush Talamati Open valley and surrounding grassland Shimuwini Letaba River and large riverine trees Sirheni Remote northern bushveld setting

1. Olifants

Olifants is probably the standout if dramatic scenery is what you’re after.



The camp sits on a hill high above the Olifants River, with lookout points overlooking the river and surrounding landscape. SANParks describes it as an “unforgettable window of Africa”.

2. Lower Sabie

Lower Sabie combines two classic Kruger views: a river in the foreground and the Lebombo Mountains beyond it. The camp sits directly on the Sabie River, making it particularly attractive for visitors who want to combine scenery with wildlife viewing.

3. Letaba

Letaba is positioned on a sweeping bend of the Letaba River. The river and surrounding greenery provide a striking contrast to the drier bushveld, while the area is also particularly good for elephant viewing.

4. Mopani

Mopani overlooks Pioneer Dam and is surrounded by mopane-covered koppies. The dam provides an additional attraction, with animals and waterbirds often gathering around the water.

5. Skukuza

Skukuza may be Kruger’s biggest and busiest camp, but its setting along the Sabie River gives it a particularly attractive side. Lush vegetation and tall trees line the river’s edge.

6. Berg-en-Dal

Berg-en-Dal is the choice for something different. SANParks describes it as the only camp set in a rugged mountain environment, with a landscape quite different from the river views at camps such as Lower Sabie and Olifants.



7. Biyamiti

For a quieter bush setting, Biyamiti is worth a look. The small bushveld camp sits on the banks of the Mbiyamiti River, surrounded by large wild fig and jackalberry trees.

8. Talamati

Talamati offers a different kind of scenery, with the camp positioned in a large open valley. The surrounding grassland attracts herds of grazing animals, while the open landscape also creates good opportunities for game viewing.

9. Shimuwini

Shimuwini is a good choice for visitors who like river scenery but want a quieter setting. The bushveld camp is associated with the Letaba River and its large riverine trees, including enormous baobabs.

10. Sirheni

Sirheni, in the north of Kruger National Park, is another option for a more secluded bush experience. It is one of Kruger’s smaller bushveld camps and is close to the Pafuri area, making it particularly appealing to visitors who want scenery, tranquillity and a different side of the park.

World.title: ‘BIGGER PLAN FAILED’ | Fannie Masemola fires back at IDAC
World.content:
National police commissioner General Fannie Masemola has questioned the motives behind his prosecution following the withdrawal of charges linked to the controversial Cat Matlala tender. Image: X

National police commissioner General Fannie Masemola has questioned the motives behind his prosecution, suggesting the Investigating Directorate Against Corruption (IDAC) pursued a bigger plan that ultimately failed.

Masemola broke his silence on Friday, 16 October, after President Cyril Ramaphosa lifted his precautionary suspension, clearing the way for his return to office on Monday.

Speaking to Business Day, Masemola suggested that IDAC’s decision to charge him may have formed part of a broader agenda targeting senior police officials.



“Maybe one day we will know what the plan was, but it did not succeed,” he said.

MASEMOLA QUESTIONS IDAC’S MOTIVES

Masemola said he did not know what motivated investigators to pursue the case but believed they had intended to achieve something beyond his prosecution.

His remarks follow the collapse of criminal charges linked to a R228 million SAPS healthcare tender awarded to Medicare24, a company owned by alleged crime boss Vusimuzi “Cat” Matlala.

IDAC charged Masemola with four counts of contravening the Public Finance Management Act (PFMA).

Prosecutors accused him of failing to take appropriate steps to prevent irregular expenditure linked to the contract.

He did not face corruption charges.



MADLANGA COMMISSION HEARS CLAIMS AGAINST IDAC

The Madlanga Commission previously heard allegations that former IDAC head Advocate Andrea Johnson had pushed for criminal charges against Masemola and other senior police officials.

IDAC state prosecutor Drushantha Ramsamy testified about alleged efforts to target Masemola and Crime Intelligence head Lieutenant-General Dumisani Khumalo.

The commission also scrutinised IDAC’s decision to include Masemola in the Medicare24 corruption case.

During her testimony, Johnson struggled to identify the legal basis for joining Masemola to the proceedings.

Commission chairperson Justice Mbuyiseli Madlanga questioned whether prosecutors had sought to damage Masemola’s reputation by associating him with corruption allegations.

The commission has not established Masemola’s suggestion of a broader plan as fact.

NPA ORDERS REVIEW OF FAILED PROSECUTION

National Director of Public Prosecutions Advocate Andy Mothibi ordered prosecutors to withdraw the charges against Masemola on 15 September.

The decision followed a review of the evidence gathered by IDAC, alongside assessments by a case assessment panel and independent senior counsel.

The National Prosecuting Authority (NPA) concluded that prosecutors had no reasonable prospect of securing a conviction.

The Pretoria Magistrate’s Court formally withdrew the charges on 22 September.

However, questions remain over how prosecutors handled the case.

The NPA referred the matter to the IDAC judge to investigate whether prosecutors committed misconduct when assessing the evidence, enrolling the case and applying the law.

The review has not established misconduct.

MASEMOLA SET FOR MONDAY RETURN

Ramaphosa confirmed on Friday that Masemola would resume his duties on Monday, 19 October, nearly six months after his suspension.

The president also thanked Lieutenant-General Puleng Dimpane, who served as acting national police commissioner during his absence.

Masemola has indicated that he intends to complete his term, which ends in 2027.

His return comes as the Madlanga Commission continues investigating allegations of corruption and criminal interference in South Africa’s law enforcement structures.

World.title: The Mrs: Who was Hyron Andrews’ wife Maiglin?
World.content:
31-year-old Hyron Andrews passed away on Friday 16 October while on tour with the Lions in France. Who is the wife he is leaving behind?

WHO WAS HYRON ANDREWS’ WIFE MAIGLIN?

Hyron was married to Maiglin Andews. The pair got engaged in September 2021. A year later, the pair tied the knot in July 2022 at the BlueBridge Event Centre in Grawn, Northern Michigan. The pair have two children together, young sons – Hendrix and Emerson. The Lions sent their condolences to Maiglin and the children in a tribute.

“Our deepest and most heartfelt condolences go to Hyron’s wife, Maighlin, their young sons, and the entire Andrews family. We hold them in our thoughts during this time of unimaginable grief and ask that their privacy be respected as they mourn,” read the statement said.



The couple maintained a very low profile, not much is known about Maiglin. She is an American medical practitioner. Her background is in emergency medicine. Maiglin is reportedly from Ironwood, Michigan, in the United States. She met Hyron while she came to Durban, South Africa to study.

“One month into my trip, I met my now husband, Hyron. We managed a long distance relationship for over 6 years, got engaged in Ireland in September 2021, and then I moved to Durban full-time in December 2021,” she wrote in a newsletter.

WHAT HAPPENED TO HYRON ANDREWS?

The Sun reports that Andrews was found unconscious in a shower cubicle at the team’s hotel on the Ile de Re, an island off France’s western coast. This has been the team’s training base since Tuesday. Emergency services were called to the scene shortly after 10am on Friday morning. Paramedics attended to the player, who was in “cardiorespiratory arrest”. Andrews was pronounced dead after medical personnel responded to the scene.



Initial reports claimed that Andrews died of a suspected heart attack. However, a statement from SA Rugby suggests that the rugby star passed away “following an accident while on duty with his team in France”.

“SA Rugby on Friday sent its condolences to the family of Lions lock forward Hyron Andrews who passed away tragically, following an accident while on duty with his team in France,” read the statement from SA Rugby.

This was just a day before the Lions Champions Cup opener against La Rochelle on Saturday 17 October. The Lions confirmed that the team would honour Andrews by fulfilling the fixture. Further details on the tribute would be communicated in due course.



Take a look at five things to know about Andrews here.

World.title: Venue for Bafana Bafana v Kenya AFCON qualifier confirmed
World.content:
Bafana Bafana are back in action next month with back-to-back 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) qualifiers against Kenya.

Pitso Mosimane’s men will host Benni McCarthy’s side on Friday, 13 November 2026, before travelling to Nairobi for the return fixture on Tuesday, 17 November 2026. Kick-off for the first encounter at Orlando Amstel Arena is scheduled for 18:00.

The two matches will carry extra significance, with McCarthy set to face his home country for the first time since taking charge of Kenya. The former Bafana Bafana striker will also have an opportunity to test himself against Mosimane on South African soil.



Bafana Bafana currently sit at the top of Group D after winning both of their AFCON qualifying matches in September. Mosimane’s charges defeated Guinea 2-1 in Johannesburg before recording a convincing 5-0 victory over Eritrea in Egypt.

South Africa also secured a 1-0 win over Egypt in Cairo during the same international window, further boosting the team’s confidence ahead of the upcoming qualifiers.

The impressive run of results has also contributed to Bafana Bafana’s rise in the FIFA rankings. South Africa are currently ranked 48th in the world and 10th in Africa.



Mosimane is expected to announce his preliminary squad in the coming days as preparations for the double-header gather momentum.

Bafana Bafana Closing in on AFCON Qualification

With South Africa sitting at the summit of Group D, the upcoming matches against Kenya could prove decisive in their bid to qualify for the 2027 AFCON tournament.

Bafana could secure qualification by winning both matches against Kenya, provided Guinea fail to beat Eritrea in at least one of their two meetings.



That scenario would put Mosimane’s men in a strong position to book their place at next year’s continental showpiece, although the final qualification picture will depend on the results elsewhere in the group.

The double-header therefore presents South Africa with an opportunity to strengthen their position at the top of Group D while dealing a blow to Kenya’s qualification hopes.

Bafana have qualified for the last two AFCONS under previous head coach Hugo Broos.

World.title: SASSA pensioners will get nothing this November
World.content:
This November, pensioners receiving an Older Person’s Grant from the South African Social Security Agency (SASSA) should expect nothing.

South Africans head to the polls on 4 November, prompting the agency to review dates. The decision was to pay pensioners earlier.

But what does that mean for those relying on the grant?



No Money Coming this November

For more than 30 days, SASSA pensioners will get zero rand and zero cents.

The announcement comes during some of the most difficult economic periods in recent history.

Now, pensioners will be forced to go one full month without getting any money from SASSA.



That is not the case for other social grant beneficiaries.

Those receiving a Disability Grant will get a payment on 2 November. Their next payment is on 3 December.

Child Support Grant beneficiaries will be paid on 3 November. Then again on 4 December.



Yet, the 4 million pensioners relying on SASSA will have to live on R75 a day in November.

This community of mainly fixed-income seniors are expected to stretch an October payment until December.

This change could devastate pensioners.

Pensioners May Need Help in the Last Days of November

Pensioners typically have 30 days between payments.



However, pensioners will wait 3 extra days, forcing pensioners to count every penny.

Pensioners should budget their money more efficiently after their October 2026 payment.

Pensioners should consider:

Buying bulk groceries that will last throughout November.

Keeping some money aside for November expenses.

Only starting to spend the October payment in November.

If pensioners can afford it, the best option will be to avoid spending the October payment until the original November date, Wednesday 2 November.



This means it resets the payment window to the original 30 days.

Pensioners who can’t do this may struggle toward the end of November and potentially need to borrow money, which can lead to unwanted deductions.

If pensioners make enough noise, SASSA may also review the December date and move it closer.

World.title: 8 South African towns you’ve probably never visited, but should this summer
World.content:
The mountains and forests around Hogsback make it one of the Eastern Cape's most scenic small towns. Image: X @hogsbackinfo

Some of the most beautiful South African towns are the ones that rarely make the travel lists.

They don’t have airports or big resorts.

What they do have is slow mornings, friendly locals and scenery that stops you in your tracks.



And most of them are only a few hours’ drive from a major city.

If you’re looking for a summer weekend getaway that’s a little off the beaten track, these eight small towns are worth adding to your list.

PATERNOSTER, WESTERN CAPE

Paternoster is a fishing village on the West Coast, about two hours’ drive north of Cape Town.

It’s known for its whitewashed fishermen’s cottages, white beaches and fresh seafood.

Things to do: Walk along the beach, watch the fishing boats come in, and visit Cape Columbine Nature Reserve.

Its lighthouse, built in 1936, was the last manned lighthouse to be built in South Africa, and it’s still manned today.



Where to stay: Guesthouses, self-catering cottages and beachfront rentals.

GREYTON, WESTERN CAPE

Greyton sits at the foot of the Riviersonderend Mountains in the Overberg, about two hours from Cape Town.

Its oak-lined streets and historic cottages make it feel like a step back in time.

Things to do: Browse the local markets, enjoy a long country lunch, or hike the Boesmanskloof Trail, which links Greyton with the town of McGregor.

Where to stay: Country guesthouses, B&Bs and self-catering cottages.

PRINCE ALBERT, WESTERN CAPE

Prince Albert lies in the Great Karoo, at the foot of the Swartberg Mountains.

It’s famous for its olives, figs and dramatic mountain scenery.

Things to do: Drive the spectacular Swartberg Pass, explore the town’s galleries and food spots, and enjoy the Karoo’s clear night skies.

Where to stay: Historic guesthouses, farm stays and self-catering cottages.

Tip: The Karoo gets very hot in summer, so plan outdoor activities for early mornings or evenings.

NIEU-BETHESDA, EASTERN CAPE

Nieu-Bethesda is a tiny Karoo village near Graaff-Reinet, with gravel roads and a quirky, creative spirit.

Things to do: Visit The Owl House, the extraordinary home and sculpture garden created by artist Helen Martins. You can also see ancient fossils at the town’s fossil centre, and stargaze under some of the darkest skies in the country.

Where to stay: Small guesthouses, cottages and B&Bs.

HOGSBACK, EASTERN CAPE

Hogsback is a misty mountain village in the Amathole Mountains, surrounded by forests and waterfalls.

Local legend says it inspired the forests in JRR Tolkien’s The Lord of the Rings, though that has never been proven.

Things to do: Hike the forest trails, chase waterfalls, and enjoy the cool mountain air.

Where to stay: Forest cabins, guesthouses and backpackers’ lodges.

PARYS, FREE STATE

Parys sits on the banks of the Vaal River, about an hour and a half’s drive south of Johannesburg.

It’s close to the Vredefort Dome, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It’s the largest and oldest known meteorite impact structure on Earth, created more than 2 billion years ago.

Things to do: Go river rafting or tubing on the Vaal, browse the antique shops, and explore the Vredefort Dome.

Where to stay: Riverside lodges, guesthouses and campsites.

DULLSTROOM, MPUMALANGA

Dullstroom is one of the highest towns in South Africa, which keeps it cool even in summer.

It’s a popular escape for Gauteng residents, about three hours’ drive from Johannesburg.

Things to do: Try fly-fishing in the local dams, browse the craft shops, and stop for a hearty meal.

Where to stay: Country cottages, guest farms and lodges.

HAENERTSBURG, LIMPOPO

Haenertsburg is a peaceful mountain village in the Magoebaskloof area, surrounded by forests and plantations.

Things to do: Hike the forest trails, visit the nearby dams and waterfalls, and explore the scenic Magoebaskloof Pass.

Where to stay: Forest cottages, guest farms and campsites.

TIPS FOR YOUR SUMMER WEEKEND GETAWAY

Book early, since small towns have limited accommodation, especially over the December holidays.

since small towns have limited accommodation, especially over the December holidays. Check road conditions before you go, since some towns, such as Nieu-Bethesda, are reached on gravel roads.

before you go, since some towns, such as Nieu-Bethesda, are reached on gravel roads. Support local businesses, from farm stalls to craft shops, since tourism keeps many small towns going.

I love that South Africa has so many small towns waiting to be explored. We really have it all.

You don’t always need a plane ticket for a proper break. Sometimes, a few hours on the road and a quiet village are all it takes.

My advice? Pick one, book early and switch off your phone for the weekend.
