World.title: Trump waives tariffs on largest buyers of Russian oil
World.content:
President Trump prevented some new sanctions on Russia and hefty tariffs on large-scale buyers of Russian oil from taking effect late Friday, waiving portions of a bipartisan law aimed at pressuring the Russian government — as Mr. Trump seeks to ease prices by tapping Russian energy.

Tariffs of 100% on the world's five largest importers of Russian crude oil and natural gas were set to take effect on Sunday under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act, which Mr. Trump signed late last month. But the law gives the president the authority to waive portions of the law if he certifies to Congress that halting the sanctions is "in the national interests of the United States," a provision that Mr. Trump invoked in an executive order Friday.

The president said he sent a notification to Congress.

He also waived the law's 500% tariffs on Russian goods, and halted certain other sanctions on Russia. He said the waivers will remain in place until administration officials "determine that further action is appropriate," and directed members of his administration to "monitor" countries that import Russian energy or evade sanctions.

An envoy to Russian President Vladimir Putin praised Mr. Trump's decision on Saturday.

"The Trump administration's suspension of the Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment," Kirill Dmitriev said in a post on social media.

The law — championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died before it was passed — largely took aim at the world's largest buyers of Russian oil and gas, including China, India and Turkey. The European Union has also historically purchased large quantities of natural gas from Russia, but it has cut imports significantly in recent years.

The Friday night waivers came one week after Mr. Trump eased sanctions on Russian diesel and announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import diesel to the U.S. market.

The moves mark an about-face for the United States, which has imposed tight restrictions on Russian oil and gas for years — and urged other countries to follow suit — in an effort to prevent Putin from using his country's energy wealth to finance his invasion of Ukraine.

But as oil prices remain high after spiking due to the Iran war, Mr. Trump has increasingly turned his attention to Russia and Ukraine, arguing that war in Ukraine has pushed up energy prices.

Mr. Trump pressed both countries to stop attacking each other's energy infrastructure last weekend, announcing an "energy ceasefire." Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy initially said he was willing to abide by an energy ceasefire, but after Russian attacks continued, he said earlier this week that Ukraine would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries.

The U.S. president has lashed out at Zelenskyy, saying he is "not a big fan."

The decision to ease sanctions has drawn pushback in Congress. Earlier this week, a bipartisan group of senators called the diesel waivers a "betrayal of the people of Ukraine," and urged Mr. Trump to enforce the sanctions and tariffs laid out in the Graham law.

"These authorities require you to apply economic pressure on Russia and the chief enablers of its war, in particular China, and thereby enhance your negotiating position to bring a swift end to this ruinous conflict," they wrote.

World.title: Oregon school shooter ID'd, used shotgun bought by mother, sources say
World.content:
The 16-year-old gunman who shot and killed three children and one 25-year-old teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday has been identified as Griffin J. John II, Bend's police chief announced in a news conference Friday.

Authorities said he was shot and killed by a bystander at the school. The suspect was a former student of Silver Rail Elementary, police said.

The attacker used a shotgun purchased by his mother, law enforcement sources told CBS News. Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said Friday that a Maverick 88 pump-action 12-gauge shotgun was located near the suspect, as well as a backpack. Krantz said that three types of ammunition were used in the shooting: birdshot, buckshot and slugs.

The suspect fired as many as 15 rounds, Krantz said Friday, and another 44 remaining rounds of ammunition were located at the scene.

A motive for the attack has not been provided. Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook said in Friday's news conference that the classroom where the shooting occurred was a special needs classroom, and he disclosed that the suspect had been a special needs student at that school.

An undated photo of Griffin J. John II, the suspected shooter who authorities said opened fire at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, on Oct. 15, 2026, killed three children and a teacher. Shauntai Nickerson/Facebook

In 2020, the suspect's mother, Shauntai Nickerson, spoke to a local television station about her then-10-year-old son, who she said had special needs and struggled to learn from home during the pandemic.

Krantz said the suspect approached the fence of the school on foot, threw the shotgun over the fence, and then climbed it himself.

When he was confronted by a man who was passing in a pickup truck, he fired on the truck, striking it at least three times, Krantz said. That driver then drove on and made the initial 911 call.

It was at that time that the bystander who would later kill the suspect, a 36-year-old man whose children attend the school, witnessed that shooting and drove into the school parking lot.

Krantz said that the suspect forced his way into the school by firing several rounds into the glass panes of a set of double doors. He then went directly into the classroom immediately to the left of those doors, where he opened fire.

"All of the victims were shot in that classroom," Krantz said.

Krantz told reporters Friday that the bystander, who was identified by his family as Kaylub Giamanco, took from his vehicle a .40-caliber pistol which he legally owned, and entered the school and classroom where the shooting was taking place.

"As he made entry through the forced open doors, he heard shooting and saw a teacher involved in a physical altercation with the suspect," Krantz said. "He then went to the classroom where the struggle was underway and fired his weapon, striking the suspect multiple times."

Krantz also praised the "heroic actions" of the teacher who engaged the suspect in the physical struggle, saying she "threw her cellphone at the suspect and then tackled him and fought to take the firearm from him."

That teacher, who was not hurt, "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed," Krantz said.

Law enforcement sources told CBS News that investigators are combing through his computer, phone, social media, search history and other online activity. They are probing whether the shooter may have been obsessed with violence, including prior mass shootings. The sources emphasized that the investigators are in the preliminary stages of their investigation.

The children killed in the shooting were ages 5, 8 and 11, Krantz said. The 5-year-old victim was identified by police and his family as Rhoam Summer. Bend police identified the 25-year-old teacher killed as Meghan Lambert. The families of the two other children have not made their names public, Bend police said.

Two others — a 7-year-old girl and a 54-year-old teacher — were wounded. The 7-year-old girl was being treated at Oregon Health & Science University in Portland, where she was in serious but stable condition, Krantz said Friday. The teacher, identified to CBS News by her family as Becky Drury, suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries, Krantz said. She was being treated at St. Charles Medical Center.

The family of Giamanco, a Bend resident with two daughters who attend Silver Rail Elementary School, issued a statement Friday, in which they said Giamanco "is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support."

Police said they responded within minutes to the 911 calls from the school and found the deceased shooter and other victims inside.

World.title: Katie Zacharia out as White House press secretary after first week
World.content:
Washington — Katie Zacharia, President Trump's new White House press secretary, is being removed from the role after just five days on the job, two U.S. officials told CBS News on Friday.

The news capped a tumultuous week for Zacharia, marked by a heavily criticized performance in the White House briefing room and growing questions over whether she had misrepresented herself as a lawyer, despite never having passed the bar.

One aide told CBS News that Zacharia spent the week unusually isolated and didn't function as a press secretary.

"No one thought she was sticking around long enough to even involve her in actual decision-making," the aide said.

Some White House staff learned about the change from news coverage. The New York Times first reported that she had been fired as press secretary. Zacharia was expected to start a new role in the administration soon, sources familiar with the discussions said.

CBS News reached out to Zacharia for comment, but she did not immediately reply. In a social media post Friday night, she wrote, "President Trump is a kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man. I wish more Americans appreciated him. No one will ever make America great the way he has and continues to. It was an honor to work for him."

She was seen at the White House as recently as Friday morning. She and her family were invited to dinner with Vice President JD Vance on Friday night.

Leaving the White House shortly before news of Zacharia's departure as press secretary broke, the president signaled her tenure could be coming to an end, saying he told her he would "reconsider" taking the job if he were in her shoes.

"They've been so nasty to her," Mr. Trump said, referring to the press. "I said, to her, 'Honestly if I were you, I'd reconsider. You think about it. But I would reconsider. You got a beautiful husband and family.' I met the family yesterday. Beautiful kids. It's like from a picture postcard. I said, 'You should reconsider. Because you don't want to go through this.'"

President Trump speaks to members of the press before boarding Marine One on the South Lawn of the White House on Oct. 16, 2026. Jim WATSON /AFP via Getty Images

The abrupt shift came one week to the day after Mr. Trump announced Zacharia as his pick to replace Karoline Leavitt, who stepped aside in August. The White House has not yet indicated who may replace Zacharia.

Zacharia's qualifications and background quickly came under scrutiny as questions arose over her résumé.

CBS News and other outlets reported that Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer over the years. She graduated from Pepperdine Law School but failed the California bar exam in 2011, a fact she acknowledged on Thursday. She told the New York Times that the president of Pepperdine University advised her at one point that she could call herself a "lawyer" but not an "attorney."

Zacharia told conservative commentator Jack Posobiec that she never described herself as an "attorney at law," and said there's a "lot of misinformation around the fact that I labeled myself a lawyer."

"I was very careful how I executed this. I never came across as someone who was an attorney at law," Zacharia said.

In her first and only press briefing on Tuesday, a visibly nervous Zacharia spoke from prepared remarks for about 10 minutes before taking questions from just three outlets — Breitbart, Fox News and the Daily Mail — for another five. She defended her performance on Fox News, saying she had little time to prepare.

Katie Zacharia conducts her first briefing as White House press secretary on Oct. 13, 2026. Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call Inc via Getty Images

"What I feel is I really stepped up to the plate to do the press conference, Sean, with very little prep time," Zacharia told Fox News' Sean Hannity on Thursday. "I received briefing materials in the morning of Tuesday and I went to deliver all of the great results that President Trump is delivering for the American people that are not often spread in the national media."

Hannity, a Trump ally, noted that her performance was "widely panned."

The about-face on Zacharia's role was reminiscent of the tenure of Anthony Scaramucci, who survived just 11 days as White House communications director during Mr. Trump's first term.

"Records are made to be broken," Scaramucci said in a post on X. "But I take no pleasure in other people's pain."

World.title: Sacramento mom says "hero" son shot, killed Oregon school shooter
World.content:
A Sacramento mother says her son acted on instinct when he confronted and fatally shot a gunman during a deadly school shooting in Oregon, an attack that killed three children and a teacher.

Police said Friday they believed the teenage gunman was targeting a class of children with special needs when he opened fire at the school.

36-year-old Kaylub Giamanco was identified as the armed bystander who pursued the shooter into Silver Rail Elementary School in the city of Bend on Thursday. Giamanco is a father of two children who attend the school.

His mother, Kenda Freeman, said Giamanco is originally from Placerville, roughly 45 minutes northeast of Sacramento, but has lived in Oregon for more than 30 years.

Freeman, a Sacramento resident, spoke with CBS News Sacramento exclusively about her son's actions and the emotional toll she said he has experienced since the shooting. She described her son as someone who cares deeply about the people around him.

"Kaylub has a genuine heart and he loves his community and his family and his children," Freeman said. "He's just a good person, in general."

Undated photos of Kaylub Giamanco. Kenda Freeman

According to Freeman, Giamanco was heading home during his lunch break when he saw the 16-year-old shooter on the school's campus.

"Kaylub knew something was not right, so he pulled up onto the grass, grabbed his gun and basically stalked the gunman back into the school," she said. "He crawled through a window that the gunman had shot out. He army crawled through the window."

Freeman said her son called her shortly after the confrontation and told her what had happened.

"He said, 'Mom, I just shot and killed somebody.' I said, 'Kaylub, tell me about it.' He said, 'A man went into my daughter's school and shot kids,' and he said, 'and I looked at him point-blank, and I shot and killed him, Mom.' "

Kenda Freeman and Kaylub Giamanco pictured together. Kenda Freeman

Giamanco works as a contractor and has been around firearms for much of his life. Freeman said he legally owns and carries his own firearm.

Freeman said the experience has left him traumatized.

"I told him he was a hero, he did what he had to do, and that he did the right thing, and that I was proud of him and that he was a hero and he saved a lot of lives," she said. "And he said, 'Mom, I couldn't save them all.' "

Three children and a teacher were killed in the shooting before Giamanco fatally shot the suspect, authorities said.

The shooter has since been identified by Bend police as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II. Law enforcement sources told CBS News that John used a shotgun that was bought by his mother. Police said Friday that that up to 15 rounds were fired by the suspect during the classroom shooting.

Another child and a teacher were wounded in the attack, and both remained hospitalized Friday. Both of Giamanco's children survived.

"It's tough because, well, I'm thankful that my babies are OK. There are babies that are not, and that's hard to swallow because my heart goes out to those families that didn't get to bring their babies home," Freeman said through tears.

Giamanco's actions have drawn praise from community members and Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek, but Freeman said her son is struggling with the idea that he could not save everyone.

"He's having a hard time with it — again, the idea of not being able to save them all, right? When he closes his eyes and the things that he thinks about: 'What could I have done differently? How could I have done it better?' " Freeman said.

Freeman said she hopes people will take the tragedy as a reminder to appreciate their loved ones: "Hug your babies, love your neighbors."

Family responds to questions about gun ownership

Shootings of this nature usually spark national discussion about gun control.

Freeman said those broader political debates are not the family's priority as they process what happened. She said Giamanco grew up hunting, has long been familiar with firearms and legally owns and carries his weapon, as many do in his community.

According to Freeman, his intention in owning a firearm was to have a way to protect his family.

World.title: Why visitors are flocking to Philadelphia's popular pigeon tour
World.content:
When tourists visit Philadelphia, they like to see the Liberty Bell, Independence Hall and the Rocky Steps. Now, there's a new attraction that can be added to the list: pigeons.

Hannah Michelle Brower and her partner, Aspen Simone, started their tour business, Philly Pigeon Tours, where they take you to visit "pigeony areas in the neighborhood."

"If you live in any city, you've probably seen them [pigeons] many times, but we don't learn to pay attention," Hannah Michelle told CBS News.

The 90-minute tour, which TripAdvisor now ranks as the third most popular in the city, answers all your burning pigeon-related questions, including why they always face the same way.

"So they're facing into the wind because their feathers streamline from front to back," Simone explained on a recent tour.

It may seem ridiculous, but just seeing Hannah Michelle's joy is worth the price of admission. And to think, she used to hate pigeons until four years ago, when she came across one that appeared to be sick or injured.

Hannah Michelle says she couldn't just leave it there, although many of us would have. Instead, she nursed it back to health, and she said that experience changed her entire outlook.

"She was so cute and scruffy and I just completely fell in love with her," Hannah Michelle said.

It is a love that never left. That pigeon, which they named Primrose, is now fully domesticated, takes baths, gets blowouts and likes to be petted.



"We constantly, every day, are like, 'There's a pigeon in our apartment,'" Hannah Michelle said. "'This is absurd!'"

The whole thing may seem crazy, but there's also a method to their madness: a much deeper lesson to their tour.

Said Hannah Michelle: "I think it's a way for people to practice getting curious about something that they pass every day."

World.title: Sean "Diddy" Combs moved to prison in Pennsylvania
World.content:
Sean "Diddy" Combs has been moved to a federal prison in Pennsylvania after reports that the hip-hop mogul was living the high life and was injured in a fight at his New Jersey lockup, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press on Friday.

The federal Bureau of Prisons is transferring Combs, 56, from FCI Fort Dix to FCI Allenwood Low, a low-security facility south of Williamsport and about 155 miles west of New York City, the person said. The person was not authorized to speak publicly and did so on condition of anonymity.

The Bureau of Prisons confirmed the move but provided no further details. The agency said it does not discuss conditions of confinement for anyone in its custody, including reasons for transfer, for privacy, safety, and security reasons.

"Decisions about inmate placement are made by the BOP, and we are not in a position to speak to the circumstances surrounding this transfer," said Combs' spokesperson, Juda Engelmayer. "Sean remains focused on moving forward, and we hope that his time at the new facility will be productive and without unnecessary disruption."

Combs is serving a four-year, two-month sentence for his conviction last year on prostitution-related charges for transporting people across state lines for sexual encounters. The case featured harrowing testimony about violence and sex parties he called "freak-offs." It was a forceful reckoning for one of music and entertainment's most influential figures.

Last month, NBC News reported that Combs was continuing to enjoy aspects of his millionaire lifestyle at FCI Fort Dix, smuggling in Hennessy, having fellow inmates cook, clean, make his bed and give him massages, and using a contraband cellphone to view social media and an ex-girlfriend's nude selfies.

On Wednesday, TMZ reported that Combs was injured in a fight with another inmate at Fort Dix and had to be taken out of the prison for treatment. In a rare rebuttal, the Bureau of Prisons refuted TMZ's report, telling the AP: "The story you are referring to is false and did not happen."

In the wake of the NBC report, Combs was placed in the prison's special housing unit, a heavily secured part of the facility away from the general population, for inmates with disciplinary issues or security concerns. He has also been docked 41 days of good-conduct credit, pushing his release date back to March 2, 2028, according to the person familiar with the matter.

In April, the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals heard arguments in Combs' bid to overturn his conviction and sentence, which his lawyers argued was too harsh. The court has yet to rule.

World.title: Teacher and 5-year-old student killed in Oregon school shooting identified
World.content:
Two of the four victims killed in the shooting at an Oregon elementary school on Thursday have been identified as 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert and 5-year-old student Rhoam Summer, police announced Friday.

Kelik Summer posted to a Facebook group Thursday night that it was "the worst day of my life. My son Rhoam was killed in a school shooting. We are broken and lost, but are surrounded by friends and family who are keeping us safe."

"Meghan was compassionate and had a huge heart," Lambert's family said in a statement that was read during a news conference Friday. "She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs. She was an incredible sister, daughter, niece and granddaughter. Her friends became her family. She was funny and opinionated, and she lit up the room."

Two other children — ages 8 and 11 — were also killed in the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School. The families of those two children have not made their names public, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said Friday.

A 7-year-old girl and a 54-year-old teacher were wounded. The 7-year-old girl was being treated at Oregon Health & Science University in Portland, where she was in serious but stable condition, Krantz said. The teacher, identified to CBS News by her family as Becky Drury, suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries and was being treated at St. Charles Medical Center.

"We are incredibly grateful for the outpouring of support, prayers, and well-wishes following yesterday's tragedy at Silver Rail Elementary," Will Drury, Becky Drury's husband, said in a statement. "The kindness and concern shown to our family and everyone affected mean more than we can express. We live in a truly special community."

The suspect was identified by Krantz as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, who was shot and killed at the scene by a bystander.

Officials said the gunman was a former student at Silver Rail. Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook said in Friday's news conference that the classroom where the shooting occurred was a special needs classroom, and he disclosed that the suspect had been a special needs student at that school.

The family of Kaylub Giamanco, who came forward as the man who shot and killed the suspect, said in a statement on Friday that he is "not seeking recognition" and instead expressed "his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support." His two daughters attend Silver Rail Elementary School.

Police also praised a teacher who "threw her cellphone at the suspect and then tackled him and fought to take the firearm from him," Krantz said. "She was not injured in that incident, but she almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed."

Memorials with flowers, balloons and stuffed animals popped up around the school, which sits in a neighborhood filled with newly built homes.

Bend, which has about 100,000 residents, is the biggest city in central Oregon. Ringed by mountains, it has grown in population over the past three decades and is a tourism and outdoor recreation hub, about 125 miles southeast of Portland.

World.content: Brewers sweep Dodgers to reach World Series The Milwaukee Brewers are heading to the World Series for the first time in 44 years after sweeping the heavily-favored Los Angeles Dodgers. Mark Strassmann has the story. More

World.title: Katie Zacharia is out as press secretary, White House says
World.content:
Katie Zacharia is out as press secretary, White House says

Katie Zacharia is "transitioning out" of her role as press secretary, according to a White House official not authorized to speak on the record, marking a stunning turn of events for the spokeswoman.

Transcript

AILSA CHANG, HOST:

From NPR News, this is ALL THINGS CONSIDERED. I'm Ailsa Chang.

SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

And I'm Scott Detrow. It was over almost before it began. The White House's newest press secretary is out after just five days on the job. Katie Zacharia started her job at the beginning of the week. She gave her first and only press briefing on Tuesday. The briefing was noticeably short and widely panned, and then questions emerged about her legal credentials. NPR's Emily Feng has been following Zacharia's rapid rise and rapid fall and joins us now in the studio. Welcome.

EMILY FENG, BYLINE: Hi, Scott.

DETROW: Let's start with this. What has President Trump said about what is happening with Zacharia's job?

FENG: So Trump was asked earlier today about this. He strongly hinted that she was leaving, but he said he was giving her the option to decide if she wanted to resign.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: I said, Katie, you know, you don't have to do this if you don't want. She said, this is a lot tougher. I said, welcome to the world of Trump.

FENG: And a senior White House official told NPR she is, quote, "transitioning out" of this very, very new job. Trump noted that she'd had a really rough time with how the media was treating her, and so he asked her if she still wanted to do this job.

DETROW: Let's talk more about this because a big part of the reason why she has faced so much scrutiny this week was this possible misrepresentation of her legal credentials. Can you explain what happened?

FENG: Yeah, so Trump has referred to her as an attorney, and Zacharia did go to law school. But there is no record of her passing the bar in any state. And when she was asked about this, she responded that she had passed when she moved to China. Now, Scott, you know, I've lived in China for the better part of a decade. It is just not possible for foreigners to take the bar there or even practice law. Zacharia later said she misheard the question about when she passed the bar, and then she defended herself last night on Fox News when questioned by Sean Hannity about her professional record.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

KATIE ZACHARIA: I graduated Pepperdine, got married in the same week, and we had all intent to move out to China. I sat for it because I didn't want to have a withdraw status.

DETROW: So if Zacharia is out after a week, that leaves the White House once again without a press secretary. How much of an issue is that?

FENG: According to Trump, it's no problem. He has shown he is very comfortable with the idea of mostly speaking for himself, regardless of whether that's good or bad for the Republican Party. There - it's been almost two months, I should note, since Karoline Leavitt, the last press secretary, left. And so there have not been regular press briefings for months now. And Trump frequently comes out and just directly takes questions from reporters at the White House, sometimes with very little notice.

And so Trump, it looks like, will continue to be his own spokesperson, but this is a really critical juncture for him right now. His approval ratings as president are at the lowest for his presidency. And yet, he's in full throttle for midterm campaigning. You know, he's hitting the road again today. He's in Georgia. He just spoke at a rally this afternoon. And he's hoping to defy polling that shows Republican candidates are really back on their heels right now in this midterm election.

DETROW: That is NPR's Emily Feng. Thank you so much.

FENG: Thank you, Scott.

World.title: Katie Zacharia is 'transitioning out' as press secretary, White House says
World.content:
Katie Zacharia is 'transitioning out' as press secretary, White House says

toggle caption i Win McNamee/Getty Images

Katie Zacharia is "transitioning out" of her role as press secretary, according to a White House official not authorized to speak on the record, marking a stunning turn of events for the spokeswoman who officially started Monday and is out by Friday.

Zacharia's first briefing was Tuesday morning where she faced scrutiny both over her performance – during which she delivered a lengthy and halting opening statement read from notes and called on only three reporters – and her legal credentials.

President Trump on Friday cast doubt on the future of Zacharia, saying he had a discussion with her just before leaving for a campaign rally in Georgia.

Sponsor Message

"I just spoke to her about it. I said, 'Katie, is this for you?'," he told reporters. "She's been treated, I would say, pretty nastily. And I said to Katie just two minutes ago, I said, Katie, you know, you don't have to do this if you don't want."

He said he was leaving the decision up to her but advised her "you should reconsider" serving in the position.

The 41-year-old graduate of Pepperdine Caruso School of Law and self-described attorney had stepped in as Trump's chief spokesperson at a moment when his popularity has fallen to record lows and Republicans are scrambling to limit potential losses in the midterm elections.

Much of the scrutiny of Zacharia focused on her credentials as an attorney. While standing with Trump, she was asked by reporters where she passed the bar exam.

"When I moved to China," Zacharia answered, an apparent reference to what she has described on her LinkedIn page as a period of time from 2011 through 2013 spent working for a prominent Beijing-based law firm called Zhon Lun.

NPR asked the White House to clarify whether Zacharia is a licensed attorney in the U.S. In a statement provided to NPR, Zacharia said she "practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials."

Sponsor Message

More recently, Zacharia has served as a communications advisor for the Trump Media & Technology Group, the firm that operates Trump's Truth Social platform. She has also been a frequent pro-Trump commentator on conservative outlets including Fox News and Newsmax.

NPR's Brian Mann contributed.

World.title: Hot flashes, night sweats, insomnia – OB-GYNS set new rules for menopause treatment
World.content:
Hot flashes, night sweats, insomnia – OB-GYNS set new rules for menopause treatment

toggle caption i BSIP/Universal Images Group/Getty Images

For the first time since 2014, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists has updated its guidelines for the treatment of symptoms commonly associated with menopause. The doctor's group, known as ACOG, recommends hormone replacement therapy alongside certain antidepressants, nonhormonal medicines, and other treatments to address symptoms like hot flashes, insomnia and mood swings.

"What's changing is the breadth of options that we now have … And the benefit of that is that we are better equipped to be able to take an individualized approach for patients," said Catherine Cansino, MD, MPH, an obstetrician/gynecologist, chair of ACOG's Committee on Clinical Practice Guidelines and co-author of the new guidance.

Sponsor Message

The guidance, released Thursday, focuses on specific menopausal symptoms and underscores that the safety of hormone replacement therapy is now "well-established," Cansino said.

In 2002, the Women's Health Initiative suggested that hormone replacement therapy increased the risk of heart disease, breast cancer, stroke and pulmonary embolism.

However, as researchers revisited that data years later, they noticed certain limitations, (including that a majority of participants were 60 years or older) making it difficult to generalize the findings to younger women experiencing menopause or perimenopause.

With more and better quality studies, physicians are able to review the evidence and make better-informed recommendations, Cansino said.

"Hormone therapy is probably the best option for symptomatic, newly menopausal women within 10 years of the final menstrual period or before the age of 60," said Robert Kauffman, MD, MSCP, a co-author of the guidelines, during a press briefing on Thursday.

In addition to hormone replacement therapy, the guidelines highlight new nonhormonal options for treating menopausal symptoms, including the drug fezolinetant, brand name Veozah, which the Food and Drug Administration approved to treat hot flashes in 2023 and elinzanetant, brand name Lynkuet, which was approved in 2025.

"What's so exciting about these treatment options is they were specifically studied based on the understanding that we have of the physiology of thermoregulation and sleep," Cansino said.

The medications work by blocking certain chemical messengers in the part of the brain that regulates body temperature and manages sleep/wake cycles, according to the guidance.

About 2 million women begin menopause each year. The average age of a woman experiencing menopause is 49.9 years, according to the guidelines. However, symptoms of menopause can begin years before a woman's final menstrual period.

Sponsor Message

The new recommendations support the use of systemic hormone replacement therapy, or HRT, with a combination of estrogen and progestogen in women with a uterus who have no contraindications to hormones.

Reasons to avoid hormone therapy include undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding, and current or past histories of certain gynecologic cancers, blood clots, stroke, heart attack, liver disease or a known or suspected pregnancy.

The reason progestogen is recommended in women with a uterus is because estrogen can stimulate growth of the uterine lining and increase the risk of endometrial cancer. Progestogen therapy helps mitigate that risk, Cansino explained.

Around half a million women have hysterectomies each year, and for women without a uterus, ACOG recommends estrogen alone.

As an alternative to estrogen-progestogen therapy, ACOG also recommends a pill, sold under the brand name Duavee, that combines estrogen and a drug called bazedoxifene. Bazedoxifene is a "selective estrogen receptor modulator," which blocks the estrogen from working in certain areas of the body, such as breast tissue, while mimicking estrogen's benefit for bone density, for instance.

Another drug recommended in the new guideline is gabapentin, an anticonvulsant typically used to treat seizures. It can also manage menopause symptoms for people who can't tolerate hormones or the other new medicines.

Cognitive behavioral therapy, mindfulness-based interventions, exercise, clinical hypnosis, and acupuncture can all improve some symptoms, ACOG says, however the guidelines also note that the evidence for these interventions is weaker than the evidence for HRT.

Still, patients may have their own preferences and goals, Cansino said.

"I live in California, and I have a practice where many patients don't necessarily want pharmacologic therapy," Cansino said. So, she tends to have a lot of conversations about non-pharmacologic treatment options with her patients.

"A healthy diet and regular physical exercise is going to go a long way. So let's start with that," and then discuss what other interventions to add to the regimen, she said.

Sponsor Message

Asked, in a follow-up email, whether Cansino recommended one medication or tool over another, she warned against "over-simplifying treatment based on tiers."

Just like with contraception, she noted that patients may choose a certain method, knowing that it's less effective. "As long as they understand the pros and cons, such a decision is perfectly OK."

Meanwhile, demand for HRT is already rising. Last year, the FDA scrapped the "black-box warning" on labels for certain estrogen therapies.

In recent months, estrogen products like transdermal patches have been hard for pharmacies to keep in stock.

"I think the shortage of transdermal estrogen therapy highlights the fact that we have all of this attention about hormone therapy, and not necessarily enough about other treatment options," Cansino told NPR.

She also stressed the need for patients to talk to trusted clinicians about the pros and cons of treatments and to avoid having "tunnel vision" about a single option.

The level of care that OB/GYNs provide by helping individual patients find the right treatment is one of the most important aspects of the new guidance, Cansino said.

"There's a lot of misinformation out there and exaggerated claims about hormone therapy, and so some people end up taking risks when they shouldn't," she added.

World.title: Amid talk of public execution, public opinion on death penalty is split
World.content:
Amid talk of public execution, public opinion on death penalty is split

toggle caption i Paul Hennessy/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images

U.S. public sentiment about the death penalty has come to the forefront after President Trump gave his blessing, then backtracked, to livestreaming an execution via firing squad.

That planned execution comes after two botched Tennessee lethal injections this year, where the state struggled to find veins to administer death-inducing drugs to Christa Pike and Tony Carruthers.

Speaking at a press conference a day after Pike's failed execution, Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee said Tennesseans were disappointed about what happened.

"The people of Tennessee have determined that the death penalty is an appropriate penalty for the most heinous crimes in this state," he said. "The people of Tennessee make that decision and my job is to make sure that those sentences are carried out."

Those Tennesseans join some two-thirds of Americans who support the death penalty for people convicted of murder, according to a Pew Research Center poll from this summer. According to PRRI, a nonpartisan nonprofit, people that favor the punishment tend to be Christian, white and vote Republican.

Sponsor Message

Daniel LaChance, a history professor at Emory University, says the overall numbers mask a wide range of opinions.

" Support for the death penalty in the United States is a mile wide and an inch deep," says LaChance, who also wrote the book "Executing Freedom: The Cultural Life of Capital Punishment in the United States."

That's because the polling is incredibly nuanced, LaChance said. When polls offer more variance in the questions, such as life without parole, 60% of Americans support that over the death penalty. The number drops even further when monetary support to the victims' family members is an option.

And separate 2025 polling from Gallup — which has been tracking support for the death penalty since 1937 — shows that 52% of Americans support the death penalty if a person is convicted of murder, the lowest share in more than 50 years.

The change in public opinion

The Death Penalty Information Center, a nonprofit that tracks the use of the death penalty but does not take a position on it, has counted 203 people since 1972 who were exonerated after being wrongfully convicted and sentenced to death.

"Those are just the ones we know about," says Robin Maher, the nonprofit's executive director. "We don't know how many innocent people were executed before we learned about their claims."

Sponsor Message

The wrongful death sentences, plus the moral efficacy, are what is swaying the public's opinion, Maher said.

"For the public to realize that the death penalty system was fallible, that it made serious mistakes, raised a lot of issues in people's minds about whether this very costly public policy, that was nonetheless rather inaccurate and unfair, should be used," Maher said.

The Pew Research Center study from July also found that while most people support the death penalty for crimes like murder, some 59% of respondents in the survey said the death penalty does not deter people from committing serious crimes – versus 39% who believe it does.

Six states were responsible for the 31 executions in 2026 — even though 27 states still legally allow the most severe form of punishment in this country. Florida led the way, with more than half of the executions this year.

Maher says that the fact that more than half the states allow capital punishment, but are issuing fewer death sentences, shows that the American people are disenchanted with the use of the death penalty.

" More often than not, they are finding it is not the right answer to violent crime," she says. "Executions on the other hand, are the result of what a handful of elected officials in just a few states are doing."

Texas accounts for the most executions since the 1970s, while Michigan holds the title for the longest-running death penalty abolition in the U.S., after banning the practice in 1847.

Out of public sight

The planned execution by firing squad is of Nidal Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist stationed at Fort Hood, Texas, who killed 13 people and wounded 32 in 2009. It's slated for December but appeals could delay it further.

While 52% of Americans support Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan's execution, 80% say his death should not be livestreamed, according to an October poll from ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos.

When Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced earlier this month that Hasan would be executed publicly, the U.S. also hadn't conducted a high-profile public execution in 90 years.

Sponsor Message

In certain parts of America, quasi-public executions drew up to 10,000 viewers in the past, said LaChance, the Emory history professor. But the growing use of medicine such as anesthesia began a negative shift in public executions.

" Pain, especially in public spaces, starts to seem scandalous," LaChance says. "It's preventable now. It starts to seem barbaric."

LaChance also said the public, especially in immigrant communities, would turn the executed into heroes. "They would claim the body and conduct little parades in Lower Manhattan, celebrating the life of the person who had been put to death," he said.

One U.S. official who spoke to NPR on condition of anonymity out of fear of retribution said President Trump was talked out of a livestream execution because it was against American values — but also because there was concern the tape would show up on Jihadi websites, leading to an increase in recruits and possible danger to U.S. forces in the Middle East.

" That's the story of the death penalty," LaChance says. "People didn't want public executions to disappear when they did. Elites did because they were becoming embarrassing carnivals."

World.title: Israeli settlers beat Palestinians and a U.S. photojournalist in West Bank attacks
World.content:
Israeli settlers beat Palestinians and a U.S. photojournalist in West Bank attacks

toggle caption i Ahmad Gharabli/AFP via Getty Images

Masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians as they were harvesting olives in the occupied West Bank on Friday, injuring several people including an American photojournalist.

The Washington Post said photographer Heidi Levine was reporting in the West Bank, wearing a protective vest clearly marked as "press," when she was beaten.

"Today I was brutally attacked," Levine said in a video filmed at a hospital and posted online."We saw in the distance, in the hilltop, I would say at least 50 masked men, slingshots. And when they came running down, I was attacked, pushed to the ground," she said, "they just kept kicking me and kicking me." They also stole her cameras and phone.

Sponsor Message

She said medical workers rushed her in an ambulance to a hospital. Washington Post Executive Editor Matt Murray said in a statement the paper was relieved that Levine received medical care and is safe, but denounced the violence against her.

"We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities," Murray said.

The Post said the attack happened when Palestinians were trying to harvest their olives. It said settlers set Palestinian olive groves on fire and hurled stones using slingshots.

toggle caption i Leo Correa/AP

Israeli police issued a statement acknowledging reports that a foreign journalist was injured and said it would investigate the incident and "bring those involved to justice."

The office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu attempted to cast some doubt on the story, asserting on social media that the facts "remain unclear and are under investigation." Murray, the Post's executive editor, quickly clarified. "To be clear: Some facts are neither in dispute nor unclear. Our photographer was clearly marked as Press. She was clearly beaten," he wrote in a quote post on X of the Israeli leader's statement.

The U.S. State Department said it was aware of the reports and that it contacted The Washington Post to offer consular assistance. "We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and support appropriate investigations as well as legal accountability for those responsible," the State Department said, without mentioning the assault of the American photojournalist.

toggle caption i Ahmad Gharabli/AFP via Getty Images

There were two dozen settler attacks on Palestinian olive harvesters Friday, leaving 20 people injured, according to the Palestinian Red Crescent Society.

Sponsor Message

The United Nations' humanitarian office for Gaza and the West Bank said settler attacks during the olive harvest season have killed one Palestinian and damaged more than 2,500 olive trees or saplings.

The attacks came as groups of Israeli settlers have stepped up their assaults on Palestinians in the West Bank. They also follow another assault earlier this month, when Israelis beat Agence France-Presse photojournalist Jaafar Ashtiyeh as he was covering settler violence against Palestinian olive farmers in the West Bank.

Sara Qudah, who handles the Middle East for the Committee to Protect Journalists, said Levine's beating was not an isolated incident for journalists covering the West Bank olive harvest. "It's part of a disturbing pattern of violence and harassment against journalists regardless of their nationalities," she said.

She added that the attackers have no reason to fear consequences because Israeli authorities fail to do anything to stop the violence.

The Palestinian Journalists Syndicate also condemned the attack as an "assault on press freedom" and a violation of rules protecting journalists during conflicts.

Nuha Musleh contributed reporting from Ramallah, West Bank.

World.title: Crowds throng New Delhi and wave Indian flags amid escalating protests
World.content:
Crowds throng New Delhi and wave Indian flags amid escalating protests

toggle caption i Vipin/AP

NEW DELHI — Thousands of Indians thronged a bustling thoroughfare in the heart of the capital, waving the national flag and demanding the resignation of the country's election chief, the latest show of public dissent against Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.

The protesters rallied in Connaught Place, one of New Delhi's busiest commercial districts, responding to a call by the youth "Cockroach" movement, whose leader Abhijeet Dipke was detained by police ahead of the demonstration. Protesters spanning generations joined the rally, reflecting broad public anger and intensifying pressure on the country's top election official.

Protests by the youth and opposition parties have intensified over an ongoing review of voter lists that has removed more than 130 million names since last year. Critics say the exercise is politically motivated, threatens to disenfranchise millions more, and has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims. They have demanded the resignation of election chief Gyanesh Kumar.

toggle caption i Prabhat Mehrotra/AP

The Election Commission and Prime Minister Narendra Modi's administration deny the allegations and say the revision is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries.

Sponsor Message

Friday's protest was part of a growing campaign that has put Modi's government under pressure and comes a week after a police crackdown on protesters in New Delhi.

The demonstrators vastly outnumbered the security personnel lining the road, while columns of riot police stood watch.

Police had earlier asked people not to join the rally and offered to let a small group gather to wave the national flag and sing the national anthem. In anticipation of the protests, authorities also closed Central Park, a green space surrounded by Connaught Place's white colonial-era buildings, on Friday and Saturday.

Modi has not publicly commented on the protests. Some of his party leaders have dismissed the demonstrators as "anarchists" and suggested, without offering evidence, that they are backed by foreign powers.

Police detained Dipke, the founder of the "Cockroach" movement, ahead of the demonstrations. He had urged supporters unable to travel to New Delhi to raise the flag and demonstrate in their own communities.

toggle caption i Channi Anand/AP Photo/Channi Anand/AP

A live video posted on the movement's Instagram account showed Dipke leaving a house and heading toward the street, where police officers intercepted him. After a brief exchange, officers hauled him into a police vehicle and drove away.

"Waving the tricolor (Indian flag) is not a crime," he told reporters Thursday.

Sponsor Message

The "Cockroach" movement began as an online satirical campaign this summer after India's chief justice compared unemployed young people to parasites. Many young Indians embraced the remark, adopting the cockroach as a symbol of resilience. It has since expanded into a nationwide protest movement of young people. Protests led by the group forced the resignation of Modi's education minister in July, a rare setback for the prime minister, who has been in power for more than 12 years.

It remains unclear whether the protests will grow into a wider political movement. Modi's government remains electorally strong, and anger over voter lists may not necessarily translate into support for the opposition, which has used the issue to criticize his Hindu nationalist government.

World.title: Sally Rooney's books will no longer be sold in U.K. after Palestinian Action support
World.content:
Sally Rooney's books will no longer be sold in U.K. after Palestinian Action support

toggle caption i Kin Cheung/AP

Irish author Sally Rooney has long been described as "the voice of a generation" for her best-selling novels that are ostensibly about millennial relationships but also explore deeper questions of class, gender and politics.

Now the 35-year-old writer's books will no longer be sold in the UK because of her own closely-held political beliefs. She had promised to donate the revenues to a pro-Palestinian group that the UK has designated a terrorist organization.

In a statement this week, her publisher explained:

"Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher."

Sponsor Message

"As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format," Faber said.

The move comes after Rooney — who has said she believes Israel is committing genocide in Gaza — announced last year she would be donating funds from the proceeds of her books to Palestinian Action, which was controversially banned in the U.K. under terrorism legislation.

Israel vehemently denies allegations of genocide.

UK-based Palestinian Action says on its website it uses "disruptive tactics" to target "corporate enablers of the Israeli military-industrial complex and seeks to make it impossible for these companies to profit from the oppression of Palestinians."

It has targeted facilities linked to an Israeli weapons manufacturer and, in a major security breach, last year managed to break into Britain's largest air force base. The activists spray-painted two aircraft at the base blood red, in what the group said was a protest against Britain's military support for Israel.

Palestinian Action was also responsible for vandalizing one of President Trump's golf courses in Scotland in March last year, when activists painted the course with the words "Gaza is not 4 sale." Reacting on social media , Trump called those responsible "terrorists."

toggle caption i Richard Shotwell/Invision/ AP

When the British government banned the group in July last year, it said it was on the grounds that Palestinian Action is responsible for "serious damage to property." It was the first time a terrorist designation had been given to an organization that does not call for violence against people.

Sponsor Message

"Its activity has increased in frequency and severity since the start of 2024 and its methods have become more aggressive, with its members demonstrating a willingness to use violence," the British government said at the time.

The government also said that the group's "activities meet the threshold of being concerned in terrorism as set out in the Terrorism Act 2000.," adding that it assessed "that Palestine Action commits and participates in acts of terrorism."

Free speech concerns

But critics questioned this assessment, saying it raised concerns about freedom of speech.

U.N. Human Rights Chief Volker Türk urged the U.K. government to rescind the decision, saying it "appears disproportionate and unnecessary."

"It limits the rights of many people involved with and supportive of Palestine Action who have not themselves engaged in any underlying criminal activity but rather exercised their rights to freedom of expression, peaceful assembly and association," Türk said.

Amnesty International UK also raised concerns, saying "the UK has a deeply flawed and overly broad definition of terrorism."

Under the U.K. law, anyone who provides financial assistance to the group could face up to 14 years in prison.

For fear of arrest, Rooney says she has stopped traveling from her home in Ireland to the U.K. to attend award ceremonies and other events since the law came into force.

But the novelist has defended her support of Palestinian Action, saying in an opinion piece in The Irish Times last year: "if this makes me a 'supporter of terror' under UK law, so be it."

It was in that op-ed that she announced she would use the British proceeds of her work "as well as my public platform generally, to go on supporting Palestine Action and direct action against genocide in whatever way I can."

Now however, her books won't be sold in Britain at all, so there will be no further proceeds.

Sponsor Message

The Normal People author was undeterred, saying in a statement shared with NPR: "I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences."

Since the ban on Palestinian Action, several thousand people in the UK have been arrested for supporting them, mainly for carrying placards and wearing T-shirts.

The ban has been challenged in the courts, with the UK's high court ruling against it in February. A court of appeal later overturned that decision. Next month, the case heads to Britain's highest court.

World.title: Teen kills 4 at Oregon school. And, DOJ sues California over alleged noncitizens
World.content:
Teen kills 4 at Oregon school. And, DOJ sues California over alleged noncitizens

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

A teenager opened fire at an elementary school in Bend, Ore., killing three children — ages 5, 8, and 11 — and a teacher, officials confirmed. A 7-year-old and a 54-year-old were hospitalized. A bystander killed the 16-year-old suspected shooter after following him into Silver Rail Elementary School, according to local officials. The suspected shooter has not been identified. Officials say he was a resident of Bend. He used a "long gun," which is similar to a rifle or shotgun, during the attack. His connection to the school — if any — remains unclear.

toggle caption i Mathieu Lewis-Rolland/Getty Images

🎧 The teenage suspected shooter was able to enter the school by firing at locked doors, according to the Bend Police Department. NPR's Arezou Rezvani tells Up First that something she found interesting on the Bend-La Pine Schools website was its emphasis on security protocols. They said they have secure vestibules for sign-in, ID checks for visitors and electronic buzz-in systems, but none of these measures stopped the gunman. Rezvani says police arrived at the school within minutes after the shooting started, but an unidentified community member shot the alleged shooter soon after the officer arrived.

Sponsor Message

The Justice Department is suing California to stop the state from counting ballots that the government claims are from noncitizens. Three weeks before Election Day, the DOJ provided a flash drive containing the names of 20,000 people it suspected of being noncitizens on California's voter rolls to Los Angeles County's top voting official. The DOJ gave him 48 hours to investigate the names or face a lawsuit, which was filed yesterday.



🎧 California and many election experts doubt the administration's noncitizen voting claims, citing President Trump's history of misinformation around the topic and flawed data analysis that can produce false positives, NPR's Miles Parks says. With vote-by-mail ballots already sent out for upcoming elections, the DOJ is seeking to segregate ballots linked to these claims for investigation so they don't get counted. Parks says it would be surprising if the DOJ succeeds in this lawsuit, as the Constitution clearly states that states manage elections.

Trump administration lawyers will argue today at a federal appeals court that White House papers belong to Trump rather than the American people. The case could end up in front of the conservative-leaning Supreme Court. The White House's claim comes after a series of actions during Trump's second term that challenged the limits put on the president after the Watergate scandal. For some 200 years, presidents could personally decide what to do with the papers they created in office. Then, Congress established the Presidential Records Act following disputes with Richard Nixon. Until this year, every president has followed this records law. Six months ago, the Trump administration moved to invalidate it. The move came after Trump was indicted on obstruction-of-justice charges for allegedly possessing classified documents at Mar-a-Lago, although a federal judge dismissed the case for technical reasons and the Justice Department later dropped it after Trump won reelection.

Sponsor Message

Behind the story

by Monika Evstatieva, senior producer on NPR's Investigations team

toggle caption i Collage by Jackie Lay/NPR

It all began with a tip. A colleague of mine had a friend in Ann Arbor who needed help. When I called her, she told me her elderly mom had been walking through a mall when a salesperson approached her with an eye cream sample. She went into a store called Beauty Essentials in Ann Arbor, Mich., and came out with $5,000 in skincare products she didn't want, tried to refuse, and couldn't return. But, she said, it wasn't an isolated incident. She posted on Facebook and connected with more than 30 people with complaints about the store. She asked me to look into it.

And so began an investigation that took place over more than a year. My reporting partner, Caley Fox Shannon, and I found similar complaints all over the country. We followed the trail, and found a network of mall skincare stores that systematically targeted older adults and people with disabilities across the United States. There was a link between them: one company, the California-based Mazal Group.

Over the past year, we spoke with more than 50 people, including customers who say they were taken advantage of, their family members and former employees. We looked at state and federal court lawsuits, hundreds of online reviews and nearly 500 consumer complaints we got through Freedom of Information Act requests. We went to stores selling products from Mazal Group in Virginia, Maryland and California, as well as the company's Chatsworth, Calif., headquarters.

You can read about what we found in NPR Investigations' whole report here, watch our documentary or listen on Consider This.

Weekend picks

toggle caption i Nintendo

Check out what NPR is watching, reading and listening to this weekend:

🍿 Movies: Other Mommy, starring Jessica Chastain, follows a 7-year-old who is visited by a mysterious entity that takes the form of her mother. Pop Culture Happy Hour describes it as an intense horror film filled with dark family secrets.

Sponsor Message

📺 TV: The Lowdown is back for its second season, featuring Ethan Hawke as a freelance investigative reporter entangled with a prominent Tulsa family.

📚 Books: The Two Saddest Kitchens is a comic conversation between cartoonists Roz Chast and Jason Adam Katzenstein about their fear and shame over their apartment kitchens and their disinterest in cooking.

🎵 Music: Remi Wolf's new album, Mud, emerged from a period of significant personal change, including a breakup and becoming sober. Watch her talk about it and perform some songs on World Cafe.

🎮 Gaming: NPR's James Perkins Mastromarino got to play The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time early, ahead of its Nov. 5 release. He says, "The game's poised to ensnare old fans and entice new players."

❓ Quiz: This week featured changes at the White House, a child reality star's comeback and Elon Musk. If you kept up, you might score perfectly.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Mario Tama/Getty Images

The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating suspicious mailings, some of which contained a white powdery substance, to state election officials and congressional offices. Trump has canceled the livestream of Nidal Hasan's execution. The former Army psychiatrist killed 13 people and wounded 32 at Fort Hood, Texas. The Smithsonian National Zoo welcomed five cheetah cubs this month. You can watch them grow and snuggle with their mom on a 24-hour livestream cheetah cam.

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: Carney warns 'stakes are high' at pro-Confederation rally in Edmonton
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney received loud cheers and applause at a pro-Confederation rally in Edmonton Friday night as he urged Albertans to vote for their province to stay in Canada.

"The stakes are high," he told a large crowd during his speech at Edmonton's Expo Centre. "This referendum comes at the worst possible time. The world is becoming more dangerous and divided."

"There are some outside our borders who are working to break us."

Friday's speech came ahead of Monday's provincial referendum, in which Alberta's place in Canada is one of 10 questions on the ballot. The other nine questions ask Albertans to vote on issues relating to immigration, services for newcomers to Alberta and constitutional matters.

In his speech, Carney told Edmontonians he believes voter turnout will play a massive role in the outcome of the referendum and pleaded with rally attendees to encourage their friends and family to show up on voting day.

"Vote like Canada's future depends on it, because it does," he said.

Carney spoke about his government's desire to work with Alberta to build major infrastructure projects, such as the Pacific Link oil pipeline. He said voting in favour of a binding referendum on Alberta independence simply to "send a message" is a "dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians."

Before Carney took to the stage, Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack, pro-Confederation campaigner Thomas Lukaszuk and Edmonton Oilers hockey legend Kevin Lowe spoke to the crowd.

A crowd gathers at Edmonton's Expo Centre on Friday where Prime Minister Mark Carney urged Albertans to vote to stay in Canada in a provincial referendum. (Emma Zhao/CBC News)

Lukaszuk, a former deputy premier of Alberta who leads the Forever Canadian campaign, said he believes separation is not the answer to the province's challenges and said future generations will judge Albertans for how they voted in the referendum.

"Send a strong signal to the world that Canada is united, independent and will never become a 51st [U.S.] state," he said. "The world right now is looking to Canada for leadership."

Carney emphasized how proud he is to have grown up in Edmonton and Alberta.

"I grew up here," he said. "This city, this province, this country, have given me everything — my family, my education and my values."

Carney and Smith make joint pitch for unity

Ea rlier in the day, Carney appeared with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith at a pro-unity event at a brewery in Red Deer.

Smith said she and the prime minister are on the same page when it comes to staying in Confederation.

" We often disagree quite publicly on several things," she said. "But today we can all agree that on Question 10, we are voting for Option 1 to remain in Canada ."

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith are seen at a national unity rally in Red Deer, Alta., on Friday. (Lina Elsaadi/CBC News)

Albertans are set to get to polls on Monday for a 10-question referendum. On Question 10, Albertans will choose either Option 1, to remain in Canada, or Option 2, to begin the process to hold a second, binding referendum on separation.

Smith j oined Carney in Red Deer as he passed through central Alberta on his way from Thursday's Forever Canadian rally in Calgary to Friday's rally in Edmonton .

" This is now a time, a moment in Canadian history, where we are going to be able to work side by side," Smith said. "I feel for the first time in a long time, Alberta and Canada are walking together. "

Carney said Alberta's trust in the federal government has been tested, but the interests of the province and Ottawa are now aligned.

"As a country, we are co-operating again," he said. "Canada is working again. We are coming together. "

WATCH | United we stand: Premier says Alberta and Canada 'walking together' for first time in a long time | Duration closed caption 3:15 At a campaign stop with Prime Minister Mark Carney, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said she and Carney can agree on voting to remain in Canada in the upcoming referendum, but 'there is still more to come' and she is going to vote yes to the nine other questions on the ballot. 'I have bad news for you, prime minister - all of the premiers are interested in talking about immigration reform,' Smith said.

Both leaders urged Albertans to vote and listed examples of what their recent co-operation has achieved, including the announcement of the Pacific Link pipeline and agreements on water, housing and defence.

There are more shared wins to come, Smith said, noting the Supreme Court of Canada agreed Thursday to hear an appeal of the federal ban on single-use plastics.

Smith and Carney split on other referendum questions

While Carney and Smith agree on a united Canada, Smith wants Albertans to vote "yes" on nine referendum questions that would give the province more control over immigration and a mandate to pursue constitutional changes to wrest power from Ottawa.

Prime Minister Mark Carney attends a national unity rally in Red Deer alongside Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on Friday. (John Ulan/The Canadian Press)

Carney, meanwhile, has urged Albertans to say "no to the nine.”

Smith said Friday she will work to change his mind.

Near the end of his brief comments, Carney held up a pair of red, knitted mittens, calling them a symbol.

They were made in Red Deer with a pattern by an Ontario designer and yarn from New Brunswick. He cited the mittens as an example of the "threads that link us as a country.”

"What we're facing on Monday is, in part, a reflection of that.”

Both leaders called out notable politicians in the crowd, including former Alberta premier Ed Stelmach and former MP Monte Solberg, who served in Stephen Harper's cabinet . Matt Jeneroux, the MP for Edmonton Riverbend, was also there.

A number of current and former municipal leaders also attended the event, like Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas, former Edmonton mayor Amarjeet Sohi, Sylvan Lake Mayor Megan Hanson, Airdrie Mayor Heather Spearman and Red Deer Mayor Cindy Jefferies.

Red Deer residents weigh in

"I don't think Red Deer's seen this kind of attention for some time," Jefferies said.

She added that when she attended a Liberal caucus retreat a month ago, she told federal politicians that she had noticed them paying more attention to Alberta recently and that she doesn't want that to stop when the referendum is over.

Prime Minister Mark Carney is seen at a national unity rally at a brewery in Red Deer, Alta., on Friday. (Lina Elsaadi/CBC News)

Jefferies had co-signed a statement with Edmonton Centre MP Eleanor Olszewski last month calling for Albertans to vote for Option 1 on Question 10.

"I hesitated to take a position on it," she told CBC News. "But listening to businesses in the community, many of them were having concerns around recruiting and retention of staff because of the uncertainty created in our province with respect to this referendum and the discussion that's going on."

"I want stability," she said.

While the brewery was filled with people who support Alberta staying in Canada, some people could be seen across the road waving an "Alberta strong" flag, and one person told CBC News they support the idea of an independent Alberta.

Red Deer resident Kelsie Petersen said she came because she "never had a chance to see a prime minister before." She said she will vote for Option 2 on Question 10 because, even though she would rather not separate, she wants to get "a better deal for Alberta."

Pro-remain supporters gather outside of Red Hart Brewing in Red Deer, Alta., on Friday. Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith spoke inside the brewery, making a pitch for unity before the Alberta referendum on Monday. (Lina Elsaadi/CBC)

Smith was later expected to head to Calgary to speak at the Canada Strong and Free Network conference. Earlier Friday, Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre made his pitch for unity at the same conference.

World.title: Trump pauses sanctions package targeted at Russian economy
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump on Friday signed an executive order that puts on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause was in the national interest.

Trump personally signed the legislation last month and his move came just two days before a deadline set in the law itself for its implementation. Named after late South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham, it had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fuelling the war against Ukraine.

Trump's unexpected move comes a week after he stunningly said the U.S. had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine in its war with Russia.

An AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll published Oct. 1 found that Americans disapprove of the president's handling of the Iran war and blame him for higher prices. Trump's approval ratings have sunk to near-historic lows and pressure is mounting as Republicans try to hold control of both chambers of Congress on Election Day on Nov. 3.

Graham, a close ally and friend of the president, had just returned from Ukraine when he unexpectedly died in July. He had advocated for stricter U.S. sanctions against Russia as a way of pressuring it to end its war in Ukraine.

His colleagues in Congress responded with bipartisan support after his death and Trump attached his signature to the legislation — then changed his mind Friday.

The package had been meant to starve Russian President Vladimir Putin of the resources Moscow needs to continue its war in Ukraine after invading its neighbour more than four years ago. The bill, also drafted by Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal, sanctions Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving.

It also directs Trump to impose up to 100 per cent tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15 per cent of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.

Democratic Virginia Rep. Don Beyer noted on social media shortly after the announcement of the sanctions being suspended that he and others had "warned" Trump might make such a move. The veteran congressman, who spoke out against the bill as it was debated, called on Congress to "fix this flawed law to stop Trump from capitulating to Putin and ensure that it truly supports Ukraine."

The White House did not immediately explain how pausing the sanctions was in the national interest.

The decision was posted on the White House website late in the evening, and the notification noted that the report explaining the decision had been submitted to Congress.

Still, it comes as Trump has increasingly lashed out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, blaming him for failing to make a deal with Putin to end the fighting.

The Trump administration has remained mostly quiet since the recent passage of the bill with large bipartisan majorities in the U.S. House and Senate after Graham's sudden death — with lawmakers urged ahead by Zelenskyy.

Follows deal after Putin call

The U.S. president's latest action also followed him announcing last week that he had reached an agreement with Putin.

WATCH | Trump, the price of diesel and a deal with Russia: The broken math of Trump's diesel deal with Putin | About That | Duration closed caption 14:36 U.S. President Donald Trump says a new diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin will ease soaring fuel costs and lower inflation. Andrew Chang breaks down the agreement and what it means beyond the pump.

Trump said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and one million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote.

Trump's decision to strike a deal with Putin on diesel on the world market has been pilloried by Republicans and Democrats alike who say it will help Russia execute its war against Ukraine — without making a different to global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Trump's war on Iran.

The sanctions that Trump has now suspended, meanwhile, also had become a campaign centrepiece for Sen. Darline Graham, the late senator's sister appointed to serve out the remaining months in his current term, who is also running to replace him in the Senate more permanently.

In a debate earlier this week with Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, Graham — who has Trump's endorsement and is expected to campaign with him in South Carolina next week — said she had been "so proud" to help get the measure passed but acknowledged it was the president's purview as to how he implemented it.

"It gives the president tools that he can use if he so chooses, to end the war through economic sanctions," Graham said Sunday during a debate in Columbia, S.C.

"So, that's up to him as to whether or not he wants to use it, or whether he wants to use something else, but I think the purpose of it is to bring down the gas prices and ultimately end the war. And when the war ends, gas prices will fall."

World.title: ‘Crypto King’ spent $16.3M of investor funds on cars, credit cards, jets, security, accountant testifies
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A forensic accountant who audited Aiden Pleterski's bank accounts testified the 27-year-old never sent investors' money to the the trading platform their contracts said he’d use on their behalf.

'Crypto King' bank records show he spent nearly half of investors' $36.3M on himself

Self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski spent nearly half of the $36.3 million investors gave him on himself and paid out about the same amount to investors as returns between 2020 and 2022, according to a senior forensic accountant who testified at his trial in Toronto’s Superior Court on Friday.

Albert Ciorma, who works for the Ontario Securities Commission (OSC), told the court that none of the funds Pleterski received from investors were ever sent to FXChoice — the trading platform their contracts said he’d use on their behalf. And only about $113,000 was ever sent to other foreign exchange and cryptocurrency platforms.

Instead, Ciorma said his forensic audit found Pleterski spent about $5.6 million on luxury vehicles, $4.9 million on credit card bills, $870,000 on travel and private jets, $598,000 on security, and Pleterski gave nearly $3.7 million to his parents. He also took $609,000 in cash advances from a credit card. Altogether, those expenses total more than $16.3 million.

Pleterski also paid out another $16.1 million to investors from the funds he received, according to Ciorma.

The 27-year-old has pleaded not guilty to fraud over $5,000 and money laundering. Pleterski was charged in May 2024 after a lengthy investigation by the OSC and Durham Regional Police.

Albert Ciorma, a senior forensic accountant, testified about self-described 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski's bank accounts at his fraud and money laundering trial on Friday. (Pam Davies/CBC)
