Shortly after the Mexico City mayor’s office jumped the gun (officials shared the announcement through the government’s official X account before deleting the post), Garbage confirmed the gig on Instagram.

“Well. The news got leaked so here we are — a little off balance and rushing to catch up,” the band wrote. “We were going to announce this show tomorrow, but someone has beaten us to it.”

Overcoming the spilled beans, Garbage — which has sold 17 million albums worldwide — declared they were enthusiastic about the invitation.

“We are so immensely proud and deeply honoured to have been invited by the Mexican Government to play in Mexico City on the 14th of November at Mexico City’s most prestigious venue – The Zócalo,” the band said.

Manson also heaped praise on the band’s Mexican fans for supporting the group since their first visit in 1996. Since then, Garbage has played in Mexico 16 times, including three shows last year (April 4 in Zapopan, Jalisco; April 6 in Monterrey and Nov. 14 in Mexico City).

“We are one of the most fortunate bands in the world to have enjoyed playing in Mexico since we first arrived on the scene but this is the absolute cherry on the top of what has been a passionate and 30 year long love affair,” the Instagram post said.

Formed in 1993 in Madison, Wisconsin, the band’s four-member line-up has remained unchanged: the Scottish lead singer Manson and American musicians Duke Erikson (guitar, bass, keyboards), Steve Marker (guitar, keyboards) and Butch Vig (drums, percussion).

With reports from El Financiero, Consequence, Chilango and Billboard

World.title: Mexico reduces fishing restriction area by 86% to focus on vaquitas’ known habitat
World.content:
Mexico has reduced the zone where gillnets are banned by 86%, saying the smaller area will ease restrictions on fishermen while focusing conservation efforts on protecting the nearly extinct vaquita.

The new rules, which went into effect Thursday, shrink the restricted area in the Upper Gulf of California from 11,106 square kilometers (roughly the size of Jamaica) to 1,562 square kilometers (slightly larger than Mexico City).

Last year, scientists estimated that just seven to 10 vaquitas remained in the Upper Gulf of California — the species’ only habitat across the globe. The vaquita is the world’s smallest porpoise.

President Claudia Sheinbaum praised the change as a way to protect biodiversity while supporting fishing communities whose livelihoods have been constrained by the restrictions.

The Environment and Natural Resources Ministry (Semarnat) said the boundaries follow recommendations from the International Committee for the Recovery of the Vaquita, based on sightings and monitoring over the past two decades — such as a 2019 count showing 22 remaining vaquitas.

The population collapse from about 600 in 1997 has been driven by vaquitas becoming entangled and drowning in gillnets, large mesh nets that are often set illegally for totoaba, a fish whose swim bladder is prized in China.

Within the newly revised zone, fishermen may use only approved gear — no gillnets.

Within the larger area, a 225-square-kilometer Zero Tolerance Zone will retain its boundaries and total ban on fishing, but the new decree authorizes a transit channel for qualifying, small fishing boats. Gillnet fishing remains prohibited along that route.

The agreement also requires boat monitoring systems and identification markings for gillnets used outside the prohibition zone.

Lorenzo Rojas-Bracho, a marine biologist and senior adviser at the San Diego–based National Marine Mammal Foundation, said that concentrating enforcement could help save the species.

“It is difficult to enforce a ban over a very large area, which includes vast areas with no recent records of vaquitas,” he told Reuters. “If you lose a ring, you don’t search your entire house. You focus on where you lost it.”

However, another scientist, biologist Gerardo Ceballos of the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM), told Reuters that authorities lacked the technical and logistical capacity to enforce even the smaller zone.

The changes come after a July meeting in which UNESCO gave Mexico six months — until Feb. 1, 2027 — to report on concrete steps to protect its Gulf of California World Heritage site, including the vaquita, and address threats from proposed liquefied natural gas (LNG) projects.

However, the new decree does not cite UNESCO as its impetus.

It explicitly links the revisions to Mexico’s commitments under CITES, an international treaty intended to ensure wildlife trade does not threaten species’ survival. The document cites a Feb. 5 decision for Mexico to pursue the revisions, before UNESCO’s July meeting.

Adult vaquitas grow to roughly 1.5 meters (5 feet) and weigh about 30 to 55 kilograms (65 to 120 pounds).

A training expedition in May recorded sightings and acoustic detections; however, the next full observation survey isn’t planned until May 2027.

With reports from Reuters, Reforma and SDP Noticias

World.title: Rotting meat stench from US-backed screwworm fly plant triggers protests in Chiapas
World.content:
Residents of a small Chiapas town took to the streets again on Thursday to demand the relocation of the sterile fly production plant used to control the New World Screwworm (NWS).

Protesters in Metapa de Domínguez have complained about the smell emanating from the plant since it began operating in June. Locals describe the foul odor as akin to rotting meat and say the plant’s proximity to homes and schools poses a health risk.

En #Metapa, #Chiapas, pobladores protestan y exigen la reubicación de la planta de moscas contra el gusano barrenador, construida por #México y #EUA. Acusan grave contaminación, daños a la salud y afectaciones a la vida cotidiana. https://t.co/F2lzS8yvcH — Cheché Torres (@Chechetc) October 15, 2026

They ended a three-day sit-in in early September after government officials agreed to address their complaints.

Residents told Reuters that the smell now regularly wafts across the town, even disrupting classes at nearby schools.

Mercedes Becerra de la Cruz, a local truck driver, said protesters want the plant relocated.

“We don’t care about the investment; we want this plant moved, because the smell is overwhelming,” Becerra told Reuters.

The protest comes less than four months after President Claudia Sheinbaum and U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins inaugurated the US $51 million facility, a key part of the bilateral effort to ​halt a screwworm outbreak that has disrupted the cross-border cattle trade since November 2024.

The Mexican government described the sterile fly plant as critical to protecting Mexico’s livestock industry, public health, the environment and the food sovereignty of both nations.

Millions of pest flies are raised inside the controlled, biosecure laboratory, where their larvae are fed a nutrient-rich mixture (e.g., eggs, milk and powdered hemoglobin) that mimics an animal’s open wound. The pupae, or adult flies, are treated with radiation to make them sterile.

Because female screwworm flies mate only once, mating with a sterile male results in no offspring, eventually crashing the wild population.

Sterile flies are the main defense against screwworm, a parasite that burrows into the flesh of warm-blooded animals and can be fatal if untreated.

As the smell has worsened, reaching ranches several kilometers away, residents said the government has not kept its September promises leaving them no choice but to protest again.

“We hope the commitment to reduce the fetid odors will be fulfilled no later than Dec. 16, otherwise we might be forced to undertake road blockades and other pressure tactics,” one resident told Diario del Sur newspaper.

With reports from Reuters, Diario del Sur and Forbes México

World.title: Mexico’s telecom sector shifts again as Televisa buys AT&T for US $2 billion
World.content:
In a major, though expected, telecom shake-up, Grupo Televisa and Fintech Holdings have agreed to acquire AT&T’s mobile telephony business in Mexico for US $2 billion.

The announcement was made on Oct. 13, though the deal is subject to regulatory approval. However, the parties expect to finalize the transaction during the first quarter of 2027.

When they do, a consortium will be formed in which Televisa and Fintech — the latter an investment firm owned by Mexican businessman David Martínez — will each hold a 50% stake.

The move had already been anticipated by industry members. For a year, the U.S. subsidiary had signaled its intention to sell its Mexican franchise as part of a broader strategy to concentrate its investments in the United States, where it seeks to expand its fiber-optic and 5G mobile networks.

According to Televisa, AT&T will receive the payment in cash upon the closing of the transaction, subject to adjustments and other contractual and contingent benefits. The buyers will finance the acquisition through a combination of their own funds and secured debt, with no recourse against the consortium.

For Televisa, the transaction represents an opportunity to incorporate a large-scale mobile operation into its existing portfolio of fixed-line connectivity and pay-TV services. AT&T Mexico has approximately 24.7 million subscribers and ranks as the second-largest mobile operator in the country.

The deal could turn the media giant into the first company to achieve a setup known as “quadruple play,” meaning it would offer bundled internet, television, fixed-line, and mobile services. The aim would be to strengthen its competitive position against Telcel, which is part of América Móvil, owned by business tycoon Carlos Slim.

“[Televisa’s] position is significantly strengthened by this transaction, with a view to the coming years,” head of Spectrum Intelligence Rolando Alamilla told the newspaper El País.

The telecommunications market in Mexico is now concentrated among a handful of companies. More than half of all mobile phone users are served by Telcel, followed by AT&T, Movistar and Grupo Walmart (Bait).

During her Thursday morning press conference, President Claudia Sheinbaum said she viewed the transaction as “a good thing,” and explained that the acquisition of AT&T by Televisa and Fintech Holdings will help competition and improve internet services in the country.

“What we want is for there to be competition, for investment to take place, and for the internet to be better,” added Sheinbaum.

With reports from El País and Forbes

World.title: El Jalapeño: Foreigner who opens message with ‘buenas tardes’ accidentally gains three aunts
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

SAN MIGUEL DE ALLENDE, Guanajuato — A recently arrived resident of San Miguel de Allende who attempted to adhere to local etiquette by opening a WhatsApp message to his neighbor with a proper “buenas tardes” found himself fully integrated into a local family structure, added to a multi-generational group chat and assigned three distinct aunts within two hours.

Arthur Pendleton, 38, had originally intended to send a brief text asking for the phone number of a reliable plumber to look at a slow-draining sink. Remembering advice from an online guide to Mexican social norms, Pendleton typed “Buenas tardes, Don Héctor, espero que se encuentre muy bien” before posing his question.

“I expected a phone number or a quick thumbs-up,” Pendleton said Monday, adjusting to the rapid expansion of his domestic commitments. “Instead, Don Héctor called immediately, invited me to Sunday lunch, introduced me to his sister Doña Rosa, and within 20 minutes she had brought over a container of caldo and called me mijo.”

By 3 p.m., Pendleton had been added to a WhatsApp group titled “Familia García y Amigos 2026,” which generates roughly 140 messages a day consisting primarily of animated morning greetings and detailed updates regarding regional weather patterns.

According to family members, the transition was a direct consequence of basic civil protocol.

“If someone sends a message that simply says ‘Send plumber number,’ you give them a number,” explained Doña Rosa, who confirmed she considers Pendleton family despite having only interacted with him once prior when he was standing near a gas truck. “If someone takes the time to say buenas tardes, that is family; and you cannot let family fix a sink on an empty stomach.”

Sociologists who study diplomatic integration note that while foreign residents often fear social isolation upon moving abroad, the primary hazard in Mexico is accidentally agreeing to attend a child’s first communion within 45 minutes of asking for directions.

At press time, Pendleton confirmed he had been assigned to bring extra ice to Christmas dinner, with Doña Rosa reassuring him that he only needed to show up “si se puede, no te preocupes,” an expression that legal scholars confirm leaves zero grounds for absence.

World.title: US commerce secretary’s resistance to cutting tariffs stalls trade talks with Mexico
World.content:
Listen to this article

Mexico’s trade talks with the United States have stalled as a direct result of U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s opposition to tariff cuts, The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday.

Citing people familiar with the negotiations, the Journal said talks were at an impasse due to disagreements ​over the U.S. tariffs on vehicles, steel and aluminum from Mexico.

The report said Lutnick has opposed significant cuts to the 25% tariff on Mexican cars and the 50% tariff on steel, aluminum and derived manufactures (finished products made of steel and aluminum). Such levies were imposed by the Trump administration for what it called national security reasons and are administered by Lutnick’s department.

Mexico is on record as citing tariff relief as its top priority in trade negotiations with the U.S.

The Journal traces Lutnick’s intransigence to pressure from U.S. domestic industry, which has told the Trump administration that reducing tariffs would harm businesses and lead to layoffs.

Lutnick is not leading the negotiations with Mexico, but according to the Journal his presence is creating tension with the man who is — U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.

It is the second time Lutnick has disrupted advanced negotiations with a North American partner, the report said, apparently referring to Canada. But he has now re-inserted himself into Trump’s trade agenda after being sidelined through most of 2026 as Greer gained more prominence.

Sources told the newspaper that the two countries appeared close to finalizing a deal that would have reduced the U.S. tariffs in exchange for a series of concessions from Mexico.

Mexico had already agreed to suspend for five years the 10% tariff it applied to imports of parts and components intended for vehicle assembly. This concession also seeks to reduce assembly costs, attract investment in new production lines and strengthen supply chains, especially as the automotive industry has been contracting.

Finalizing this bilateral deal would pave the way for further talks on renewing the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement, which is currently under review.

Officials from both countries denied that the bilateral talks had stalled. Mexican officials and numerous business executives had expressed optimism about an imminent agreement.

On Wednesday, Mexico’s Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard updated federal deputies about the perceived progress in the bilateral trade talks.

During his meeting with members of the Social Economy and Cooperativism Promotion Committee and the Economy, Commerce and Competitiveness Committee of the Chamber of Deputies, Ebrard told the lawmakers that President Claudia Sheinbaum’s leadership had helped Mexico consolidate itself as the country with the best conditions for accessing the U.S. market.

Just two weeks earlier, after meeting with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer at the National Palace, Ebrard declared that “Mexico is ever closer to reaching new trade agreements with the United States and does not expect to lose the favorable position it maintains with other Washington partners.”

Ebrard was scheduled to meet with the same two legislative committees on Friday.

With reports from The Wall Street Journal, El Universal, Reuters, El Economista, LopezDoriga.com, La Silla Rota and The Latin Times

World.title: Officials urge caution as Category 3 Hurricane Trudy approaches Pacific coast: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🌀 Hurricane Trudy to approach Pacific coast this weekend: Fabián Vázquez, head of the National Meteorological Service, said the Category 3 storm will pass about 65 kilometers off the coast of Colima and Jalisco on Saturday night or early Sunday. He urged coastal residents to stay alert, warning that “any movement to the right or the left can change meteorological conditions a lot.”

Fabián Vázquez, head of the National Meteorological Service, said the Category 3 storm will pass about 65 kilometers off the coast of Colima and Jalisco on Saturday night or early Sunday. He urged coastal residents to stay alert, warning that “any movement to the right or the left can change meteorological conditions a lot.” 🏥 Sheinbaum says IMSS developing “comprehensive program” for healthcare workers: The president said IMSS director Zoé Robledo is evaluating a plan that would include a bigger pay raise “within the limits of what’s possible,” plus the regularization of positions. Workers rejected an offer of a 2.9% pay rise and a 3.9% increase in benefits on Wednesday, and are seeking a 10% pay raise. Sheinbaum didn’t say whether IMSS would meet that demand.

The president said IMSS director Zoé Robledo is evaluating a plan that would include a bigger pay raise “within the limits of what’s possible,” plus the regularization of positions. Workers rejected an offer of a 2.9% pay rise and a 3.9% increase in benefits on Wednesday, and are seeking a 10% pay raise. Sheinbaum didn’t say whether IMSS would meet that demand. 💻 Sheinbaum predicts tech exports will keep growing: Asked about the UN forecast that Mexico’s export revenue will rise 26% in 2026, the president pointed to electronics, with plants being expanded to meet U.S. data center demand. She also said Mexican auto industry export revenue had partially recovered despite U.S. tariffs.

Why today’s mañanera matters

A hurricane off Mexico’s Pacific coast, a plan to address public healthcare workers’ demands and strong growth in Mexican exports were among the important topics discussed at President Sheinbaum’s Friday morning press conference.

According to the U.S. National Hurricane Center, Hurricane Trudy was about 380 kilometers southwest of Acapulco, Guerrero, at 9 a.m. Mexico City time on Friday. Trudy — a Category 3 hurricane at 9 a.m. — is forecast to approach the coast of western Mexico this weekend.

⚠️ #Trudy se mantiene como #Huracán categoría 3 ⚠️ ▪️Se prevé que en el transcurso de este día el sistema se intensifique a huracán de categoría 4

▪️Su centro se localizó a las 09:00 h a 380 km al suroeste de Acapulco, #Guerrero, y a 525 km al sur-sureste de Manzanillo, #Colima.

▪️Vientos sostenidos de 195 km/h, rachas de 240 km/h y desplazamiento hacia el nor-noroeste a 7 km/h. 🌧️ Lluvias previstas:

– Puntuales intensas: #Guerrero (centro, este, sur y sureste) y #Oaxaca (norte, centro, oeste y sur).

– Puntuales muy fuertes: #Colima y #Michoacán (oeste, centro y sur).

– Puntuales fuertes: #Jalisco (oeste y sur). 🌊 Oleaje de 4 a 5 metros de altura en costas de #Guerrero y #Michoacán. — Coordinación Nacional de Protección Civil (@CNPC_MX) October 16, 2026

Meanwhile, the Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS) is working on a plan to respond to the grievances of healthcare workers, who protested across Mexico on Tuesday to demand higher pay, better work conditions, increased funding for healthcare and an end to shortages of medicines and medical supplies.

Sheinbaum indicated that IMSS would improve its pay offer, but didn’t say whether it would agree to the 10% raise workers are seeking.

Late in the press conference, she offered an upbeat assessment of Mexico’s export sector, which is a significant contributor to GDP.

Hurricane Trudy to approach Mexico’s Pacific coast this weekend

Fabián Vázquez, head of the National Meteorological Service, reported that Hurricane Trudy was “relatively far” from Mexico’s Pacific coast on Friday morning.

However, Trudy will approach the coast of Colima and Jalisco on Saturday night or early Sunday as a Category 3 hurricane, he said.

“It’s going to be very close, it’s going to be 65 kilometers from the coast,” Vázquez said.

“We have to be very careful because any movement [of the hurricane] to the right or the left can change meteorological conditions a lot,” he said, warning of strong winds and large swells.

Vázquez called on residents of coastal areas of Colima and Jalisco to take care and stay alert over the weekend “because on Sunday there could be a major hurricane off the coast.”

Sheinbaum: IMSS is working on a ‘comprehensive program’ to respond to healthcare workers’ demands

A reporter asked the president whether she was confident that the government could soon reach an agreement with IMSS employees, who, in a vote on Wednesday, formally rejected an offer of a 2.9% pay rise coupled with a 3.9% increase in benefits.

Sheinbaum noted that IMSS and the National Social Security Workers Union (SNTSS) held talks on Thursday, adding that IMSS director Zoé Robledo is “evaluating” a “comprehensive program” in response to the demands of workers.

She said the IMSS proposal would include not only a bigger salary increase, “within the limits of what’s possible,” but also “the regularization of positions” — i.e. making temporary jobs permanent — and measures to address other worker demands.

In a video message on Thursday morning, Robledo said that IMSS and the SNTSS would “analyze alternatives to develop a better proposal within the framework of what’s possible.”

Sheinbaum predicts that Mexico’s tech exports will continue to grow

A reporter noted that the United Nations Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean is forecasting that Mexico’s export revenue will increase 26% in 2026, the second highest projected growth among 33 countries in the region. She asked Sheinbaum what the growth in exports means for the Mexican economy, which recorded 1.2% annual growth in the first six months of 2026.

“The export of electronics has increased a lot and plants in Mexico are being expanded due to the demand from data centers in the United States,” Sheinbaum said without explicitly answering the reporter’s question.

“And [electronics exports] will probably keep growing,” she added.

Sheinbaum also said that “a part of the [Mexican] automotive industry” had “recovered” in terms of export revenue, “despite [U.S.] tariffs” on vehicles.

She highlighted that Mexico isn’t just exporting to the United States, but also to European countries and Japan, among other nations.

Mexico exported goods worth a record US $549.4 billion in the first eight months of 2026, a year-over-year increase of 29.3%.

Mexico News Daily reported last month that, despite the record performance, analysts point out two concerns: the predominance of the U.S. as Mexico’s main buyer and the country’s reliance on Asia as an indispensable supplier for the fast-growing computer industry.

World.title: MND Local San Miguel de Allende: New forum, migrant aid and local honors
World.content:
Collaboration is on the agenda for a new community organization, a local NGO recommends ways to help migrant children, a photography exhibit from Cervantino is in town, and the city and a local Red Cross team recently won major awards.

Here’s the latest on some of the many community activities happening in and around San Miguel de Allende.

San Miguel Forum aims to link philanthropy, NGOs

A new community organization focused on addressing challenging social issues by enhancing collaborative efforts held its bilingual inaugural event Oct. 6-9 at the Instituto Allende in San Miguel.

The San Miguel Forum drew 88 invited attendees evenly split between foreigners and Mexicans, said Larry Cooley, one of the group’s cofounders. Participants included international philanthropists, implementers and policy-makers interested in scaling solutions to societal challenges in six areas.

These areas — dropout prevention, hospice/palliative care, girls’ empowerment, youth employment, and water and watersheds — were joined by the overarching issue of community cohesion, which Cooley said turned out to be the most popular theme.

“It seemed important (due to) the gentrification of San Miguel, so some sense of belonging and some sense of community identity didn’t get lost in the shuffle,” he said. “It has different manifestations in different places. With people from outside, it was different than within San Miguel.”

According to a media release issued after the inaugural event, the forum’s goal “is not simply to identify problems, but to connect people and resources around solutions that can grow to match the scale of the need while remaining locally appropriate and sustainable.”

Cooley said foreigners who attended the inaugural event had an interest in scaling efforts, as well as an interest in Mexico, and that organizers wanted to focus on issues that were “really topical for Mexico now.”

Private philanthropy is being called upon to do a lot more these days, he said, and it needs to find ways to collaborate with government and the private sector to solve societal problems at scale.

“Mexico is ahead on many, many things but is behind on that part,” Cooley said. “Philanthropy’s role at scale is trying to find ways to influence what governments are doing but doing it better and include people who are not being included.”

The San Miguel Forum is planning a second gathering in San Miguel in November 2027. For more information, contact info@sanmiguelforum.org.

Ways to help migrant children, courtesy of local NGO

The San Miguel-based Latin American Relief Fund (LARF) is recommending a number of ways to assist migrant children in both Mexico and the United States. As the group’s October newsletter discusses, thousands of children have been separated from their families when parents are either detained or deported from the U.S.

LARF recommends supporting the ABBA migrant shelter in Celaya, which will celebrate its 11th anniversary next month. ABBA provides children with education, rehabilitation and therapy, while helping them acquire the documents required to enroll in school or access other services in Mexico.

LARF also recommends these U.S. organizations that help migrant children:

The Young Center for Immigrant Children’s Rights, which supplies trained staff and volunteers to act as independent child advocates.

The Acacia Center for Justice , which provides lawyers for unaccompanied children.

Each Step Home , which funnels donations to a commissary account for families held in a Dilley, Texas, detention camp.

Centro gallery hosts photography exhibit from Cervantino

The 54th annual Cervantino Festival in Guanajuato, held Oct. 3-18, is again sharing artistic offerings with other cities in Mexico. Last year, San Miguel was a host city for live music performances and film screenings from the festival’s Cervantino Circuit schedule.

This time, a photography exhibit called “Habitando la imagen” (“Inhabiting the Image”) features the work of Yolanda Andrade Salas. Her photography reveals “the complexity of urban life, popular culture, diverse identities, and the everyday gestures that construct collective memory.”

The exhibit will be shown through Jan. 10, 2027, at Galería Meridiana 101º inside the Instituto Allende, Ancha de San Antonio 22 in Centro.

Condé Nast Traveler readers rate San Miguel 4th-best city

The 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards from Condé Nast Traveler magazine ranked San Miguel No. 4 on the list of the 10 Best Small Cities in the World. It was rated No. 5 last year.

Victoria, Canada, was No. 1 on this year’s list, followed by Puerto Vallarta; Florence, Italy; San Miguel; Lucerne, Switzerland; Dubrovnik, Croatia; Porto, Portugal; Amalfi, Italy; Venice, Italy; and San Sebastian, Spain.

San Miguel did much better in Travel + Leisure magazine’s 2026 World’s Best Awards, coming in at No. 1 for the second year in a row.

Local Red Cross team shines in national competition

Cruz Roja Mexicana, the local Mexican Red Cross organization in San Miguel, was recently named No. 7 across the country in a National Vehicular Rescue Competition. The competition tested emergency rescue team members on their rapid response, technical skill and preparedness.

Team members were challenged with a timed simulated motor vehicle accident and had to use extraction equipment, apply patient care techniques and work together to achieve the desired results. They were congratulated by municipal and community leaders for the impressive national achievement.

Cathy Siegner is an independent journalist based in San Miguel and Montana. She has journalism degrees from the University of Oregon and Northwestern University.

— Why it matters Colombia’s lines can carry about 450 megawatts, roughly a tenth of Ecuador’s peak demand, while the shortfall is put at 1,200 to 1,300 megawatts.

— Why now Ecuador’s Mazar reservoir sat about eight metres above its critical level on Friday, and thousands of companies face scheduled power cuts.

— What happened On Friday 16 October President Daniel Noboa thanked Colombia’s Abelardo de la Espriella for restarting energy dispatch after no commercial exports since 7 September.

— What it means for you US investors, exporters and travellers face power-cut risk that Colombian supply only partly offsets, and the volume and price are still unpublished.

— Power Index Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 51.9 points (October 2026 edition).

Colombia resumes Ecuador power sales, President Daniel Noboa announced on Friday 16 October, as Ecuador’s dry season deepens. For US investors, exporters and travellers, the link matters because Ecuador’s industry faces cuts of up to 72 hours a week.

Noboa thanked Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella on X for restarting energy dispatch and promised that Ecuador would help Colombia in hard times. Neither the volume nor the price of the new supply has been published, El Comercio and Infobae noted.

Why Colombia Resumes Ecuador Power Sales Now

Ecuador’s grid operator, Cenace, showed Colombian power flowing again on Friday, although the readings differ. Primicias read 132 megawatts at 11:00, while Infobae cited 347 megawatts and Expreso 347 megawatt hours by 09:00.

Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The sources reviewed do not reconcile the units or show the scheduled supply. Colombia’s rules allow it to cut or suspend shipments whenever its own system requires, Expreso notes.

On Thursday 22 January Colombia’s energy ministry suspended sales, citing energy sovereignty and climate variability, after Ecuador announced a 30% security levy on Colombian imports, Vistazo reported. Sales restarted on Wednesday 5 August with a forecast of 8.6 gigawatt hours a day, more than 8% of Ecuador’s demand, according to Más Colombia.

Commercial exports stopped again on 7 September, when regulator CREG’s Circular 343 of 5 September put shortage-risk rules into force after four straight months of below-average river inflows, Ecuador Chequea reported. Under CREG Resolution 101 127 of 27 August, power may be exported only after domestic demand is met, CREG’s supporting document and Ecuador Chequea show.

How Deep Ecuador’s Power Shortfall Runs

Ecuador’s Mazar reservoir stood at 2,123.15 metres above sea level at midday Friday, about eight metres above its critical level of 2,115 metres, according to Celec figures in El Comercio. Mazar feeds the Paute hydroelectric complex, which Infobae describes as central to national generation.

El Comercio puts the national shortfall at 1,200 to 1,300 megawatts, so Colombia’s 450-megawatt line can cover only part of it. Fernando Salinas of the Foro Energético Ecuador says Colombia supplied 5% to 6% of Ecuador’s consumption before the cut, about 6 to 7 gigawatt hours a day.

Since 22 September the government has disconnected medium and high-voltage industry in turns, starting at 24 hours and reaching 72 hours a week from 12 October, Expreso reported. On 14 October the government called a seven-day disconnection order an error, and high-voltage group AV1 could draw normal power again from 15 October, El Universo reported.

The government says the industrial cuts aim to keep homes free of the rationing seen in 2023 and 2024. Even so, Extra reported recent outages in parts of Quito, Guayaquil and other cities, as covered in Ecuador Blackouts Hit Homes Despite Pledge.

Colombia’s Own Risk From El Niño

Colombia has its own supply worries, which is why it closed the export window. CREG recorded river inflows at 74.5% of the average in August, a reservoir below its threshold and record demand, Más Colombia reported.

The risk period has no end date and ends only when reservoirs recover or CREG judges conditions have improved. El Comercio says the energy now sent comes from thermal plants burning liquid fuels, which cost more, although CREG’s rules also allow surplus solar, wind and spilled hydropower.

On 5 August Ecuador’s energy minister, Juan Carlos Blum, said the import contract averaged US$0.33 per kilowatt-hour. El Comercio recalls that prices under former president Gustavo Petro had risen to US$0.65 and almost US$1.00.

Earlier shortages are covered in Ecuador Power Cuts Hit Industry Over 9 October Holiday and in Ecuador Explained: The Country, the Security Crisis, the Economy and What to Watch. No price has been published for the supply that restarted on Friday.

What It Means for You

For US investors and importers, the supply matters because industry carries the scheduled cuts, which can slow factory output and export schedules. The National Chamber of Aquaculture warned of job losses and asked the government for more transparency, El Espectador reported.

Travellers and residents should expect possible local outages in Quito, Guayaquil and other cities, since Colombian power does not guarantee supply. Companies should plan for backup generation, because the government has told firms to run their own plants during the cuts.

Colombian supply and rain over the Paute basin could ease the strain, but neither is assured. Blackouts of up to 14 hours a day in September 2024 show what a deeper shortage can mean, El Espectador recalled.

What Is Not Known

The volume is unclear, because Cenace readings reported on Friday differ (132 megawatts at 11:00 per Primicias, 347 megawatts or megawatt hours earlier per Infobae and Expreso) and no official schedule has been published. The price, the contract terms and the duration of the supply have also not been announced.

The sources reviewed contain no statement from the Colombian government or from XM, Colombia’s grid operator, on the restart. They rely on Noboa’s post and on Cenace data, so the Colombian side of the decision is not documented here.

Colombia has not said how long it will export, since the CREG risk period has no end date. Ecuador has announced no change to the industrial cuts, so it is not known whether they will ease.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Colombia selling electricity to Ecuador again?

President Daniel Noboa said on Friday 16 October that Colombia had restarted energy dispatch. Cenace data showed Colombian power flowing that morning, but no volume or price has been announced.

Why did Colombia stop selling power to Ecuador?

Colombia’s regulator CREG put shortage-risk rules into force on 7 September because El Niño had cut river inflows. The rules let Colombia export only after its own demand is met.

How much power can Colombia send?

The interconnection can carry about 450 megawatts, roughly a tenth of Ecuador’s peak demand. Actual flows depend on Colombian availability and have not been published.

Will Ecuador’s industrial power cuts end?

The sources reviewed show no announced change to cuts of up to 72 hours a week for medium and high-voltage industry. Relief depends on Colombian supply and on rain feeding the Mazar reservoir.

How low is the Mazar reservoir?

Celec put it at 2,123.15 metres above sea level on Friday 16 October. That is about eight metres above the critical level of 2,115 metres.

What does Colombian electricity cost Ecuador?

In August the energy minister said imports averaged US$0.33 per kilowatt-hour. The price of the supply that restarted on Friday has not been published.

World.title: Colombia Protest Decree 1525 Faces Lawsuit
World.content:
Marchers on a Bogotá street during the national strike of 28 May 2025, under the previous government. Archive photo. (Photo: ProtoplasmaKid, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

COLOMBIA · PROTEST RULES

Key Facts — The country Colombia, where President Abelardo de la Espriella took office in August, has new national rules for how police handle street protests, marches and road blockades.

— Why it matters Decree 1525 lets police skip dialogue steps against people who use violence, and opposition lawmakers say only Congress can limit the right to protest.

— Why now The decree was signed on Tuesday 13 October, about 12 hours before the first national march against the new government.

— What happened The president signed Decree 1525 on 13 October, and opposition lawmakers announced a lawsuit at the Consejo de Estado on 14 October.

— The numbers The decree has 26 articles, sets five response levels and keeps police escorts at least 4 metres from marchers. The government counts 62,000 marchers on 14 October.

— What it means for you Travellers and companies in Bogotá, Cali and Medellín should expect march-day detours, and investors should watch the court case.

— Still open Whether the Consejo de Estado suspends or annuls the decree, and how the revived Esmad riot squad behaves at the next march.

— Prediction markets Polymarket gives Flávio Bolsonaro a 77% chance and Lula a 23.5% chance of winning the Brazilian presidency (17 October, 2:27 a.m. ET). Polymarket puts Flávio Bolsonaro’s chance of winning at 77% and Kalshi at 77% (Lula: 24% and 21% ), as of 17 October, 3:20 am ET ; prices are bets, not polls.

— Power Index Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 51.9 points (October 2026 edition).

The Colombia protest decree, known as Decree 1525 of 2026, rewrote police rules for street marches when President Abelardo de la Espriella signed it on Tuesday 13 October. Opposition lawmakers announced a lawsuit the next day at the Consejo de Estado, Colombia’s top administrative court.

For US readers, the rules matter because US companies, travellers and aid workers in Colombia depend on how marches, strikes and road blockades are policed. The signing also comes as De la Espriella, a public supporter of Flávio Bolsonaro, follows the Brazil election 2026 runoff on 25 October.

Brazil’s Brasil de Fato calls the measure a criminalisation of protest, and La Silla Vacía says the rights group Temblores fears it could stigmatise marchers. The decree text amends a police protocol and says the violent acts it targets are already crimes.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Brazil ranks 1st of 14 with 75.0 points. Strongest pillar: military means (100); weakest: state capacity & security (56). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What the Colombia Protest Decree Changes

The decree has 26 articles and amends Decree 003 of 2021, a protocol written after a 2020 Supreme Court order to curb arbitrary police force at protests. It applies from publication in the Diario Oficial, and the government first used it on 14 October.

Under the Colombia protest decree, police must respond in five levels, from local dialogue managers up to the riot squad. Levels four and five need an order from the area’s first police authority, except in cases of imminent danger to life or imminent crime.

Against people who carry weapons or firebombs, hold others against their will or attack journalists from the start of a march, officers need not first try levels one to three when those steps are not materially possible. A command post must record why each level was skipped and inform the Public Ministry at once, and dialogue continues with peaceful marchers.

The Colombia protest decree says blocking a road does not make a march violent by itself, and dispersal is allowed only in exceptional cases. The decree also bars potentially lethal force to protect property.

Police must keep an escort team at least four metres from the march, with exceptions where the site makes that impossible. Information gathered in the dialogue stage cannot be used for intelligence work or to profile marchers.

Brasil de Fato says officers may shadow marchers at less than four metres, but the decree sets a minimum distance of four metres. The copy reviewed sets no new penalties or offences, and its article on protecting inventoried property says it does not limit or condition the right to strike.

Eight grounds end the dialogue stage, among them blocked ambulances, weapons, attacks on journalists and a verified shortage of food, water, fuel or medicine. Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara, who co-signed the text, called it protective of rights and democratic, La Silla Vacía wrote.

The First Test on 14 October

Caracol Radio reported that the decree was signed about 12 hours before the first national march against the new government. Unions, Indigenous organisations and other groups called the 14 October protests, DW reported.

De la Espriella said that night that 62,000 people marched nationwide and that 98% of the protests were peaceful. His government counted six police interventions, in Bogotá, Ibagué, Popayán and Medellín, and six arrests for alleged vandalism in Montería, Ibagué and Pasto.

The president described the incidents as small disturbances that ended when the riot squad arrived. These are government figures, and the sources reviewed contain no independent count of turnout.

La Silla Vacía wrote that fears of heavier police force did not materialise on the first day. That judgment covers only the first day of marches.

We previewed the draft in Colombia Readies Protest Decree Before Rallies and the call to march in Colombia Unions and Teachers March on 14 October. For the wider political map, see Colombia Politics Explained, Who Holds Power in 2026 and Who Dominates Colombia, Elites and Regions Explained.

The Court Challenge and the Return of the Esmad

Senator Jennifer Pedraza announced the lawsuit on 14 October, calling the decree regressive and unconstitutional. She argues that only Congress, through a statutory law, can set limits on the right to protest under article 37 of the Constitution.

Pacto Histórico lawmakers Daniel Monroy and Laura Beltrán announced a nullity suit and a tutela, and Senate second vice president Alejandro Ocampo filed another nullity suit on 14 October, El Espectador wrote. Beltrán and Monroy asked for the decree to be suspended while the court studies the case, and the Pacto Histórico is the left-wing party of former president Gustavo Petro.

The sources reviewed show no ruling by the Consejo de Estado on the Colombia protest decree yet. They also show no formal government reply in court.

The UN human rights office in Colombia, which gave technical help to the Interior Ministry on the text, said the government accepted some of its recommendations, El Espectador reported on 16 October. It welcomed the split between violent and peaceful marchers and the solidarity corridors, but warned that the broad definition of violence and some rules ending dialogue could weaken dialogue in practice.

Separately, police Resolution 03226 of 13 October created the Unidad Nacional Antidisturbios and revived the Esmad name, La Silla Vacía wrote on 16 October. It replaces the Undmo unit created in 2022 and gives the force 90 days to adopt its new structure.

The Esmad, the Mobile Anti-Riot Squad, drew complaints of excessive force in past protests, including the death of Dilan Cruz, La Silla Vacía noted. The new resolution tells the unit to respect human rights standards on the use of force and to carry out dialogue work.

The Link to Brazil’s Runoff

De la Espriella has openly backed Flávio Bolsonaro, the conservative who won Brazil’s first round on 4 October. On 7 October he gave Bolsonaro his first interview as president, which the Brazilian candidate published on his own channels.

In it he said he would be happy to attend a Bolsonaro inauguration but had promised not to leave Colombia for four years, offering a bilateral meeting in Colombia instead. Brasil de Fato calls him an ally of Flávio, which is that outlet’s own description.

Flávio faces President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the runoff on 25 October, and our guide to the Brazil runoff date explains how to follow it. The sources reviewed show no link between the Brazilian race and the content of the decree.

What It Means for You

Travellers in Bogotá, Cali or Medellín should check march dates and allow extra time, because Bogotá’s city government warned of TransMilenio detours on 14 October. Police escort teams are meant to stay at least four metres from marchers, so keep clear of crowds and follow local guidance.

Companies with plants, depots or shops can expect formal records of blockades, including lost income and blocked workers, under the new articles. Investors tracking Colombian political risk will watch the court case over the Colombia protest decree and whether marches stay peaceful.

What Is Not Known

The sources reviewed do not show whether the Consejo de Estado will suspend the decree or how long a ruling could take. They also give no independent count of the 14 October turnout, so the 62,000 figure rests on the government.

One Colombian lawyer told Brasil de Fato that police used violence against marchers in Bogotá after the march ended, and the other sources reviewed do not confirm it. Whether the revived Esmad will change how police act on the street is not yet clear.

The full list of plaintiffs may be longer than the lawmakers named in the coverage reviewed. The decree text was read in a copy linked by El Espectador, not in the Diario Oficial.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket prices Flávio Bolsonaro at 77% and Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva at 23.5% to win Brazil’s presidency on Saturday 17 October (2:27 a.m. ET). Flávio’s contract has traded about US$21.4 million, and the whole Brazilian presidential event about US$185 million.

These are real-money bets, not polls, and they cover the Brazilian race rather than the Colombian decree. Our Brazil election odds page tracks the live prices.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Colombia’s Decree 1525?

Decree 1525 of 2026, the Colombia protest decree, amends a 2021 protocol that governs how police respond to protests. President Abelardo de la Espriella signed it on 13 October 2026.

Does the decree make protest a crime?

The copy reviewed sets no new offences or penalties, and its preamble says the violent acts it targets are already crimes. Critics argue it could still stigmatise marchers and lets police skip dialogue steps.

Who is challenging the decree in court?

Senator Jennifer Pedraza and other opposition lawmakers announced a lawsuit at the Consejo de Estado on 14 October. They argue that only Congress can limit the right to protest through a statutory law.

What happened at the 14 October marches?

The government says 62,000 people marched and 98% of the protests were peaceful. It counted six police interventions and six arrests, and the figures are not independently confirmed.

What is the Esmad?

The Esmad is the Mobile Anti-Riot Squad of Colombia’s National Police. A resolution of 13 October restored the name inside a new National Anti-Riot Unit.

Why does Brazil’s election come up?

De la Espriella has publicly backed Flávio Bolsonaro, who faces Lula in the runoff on 25 October. The sources reviewed show no link between that race and the decree.

World.title: Flávio Vows Payroll Tax Relief 9 Days Out
World.content:
Avenida Faria Lima in Sao Paulo, the centre of Brazil's financial industry (Photo: Themium, CC0 via Wikimedia Commons)

ELECTION 2026 · BRAZIL

Key Facts — The country Brazil, Latin America’s largest economy, picks a president in a runoff on Sunday 25 October between President Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro.

— Why it matters Flávio now promises payroll tax relief to help companies absorb a shorter work week, but he has not said what it costs or who pays.

— Why now The promise aired in his television campaign slot on Friday 16 October, the day Congress promulgated the end of the 6×1 schedule and nine days before the vote.

— What happened On Friday 16 October Flávio said a government of his would make up the difference by cutting taxes, lowering interest rates and relieving the payroll.

— The numbers The weekly limit falls from 44 to 42 hours after 60 days and to 40 hours a year later. One industry estimate puts the extra cost at up to R$267 billion (about US$52.5 billion).

— What it means for you US firms with Brazilian staff face a 5×2 week and a 42-hour cap within 60 days, whoever wins on 25 October. A payroll cut would need a new law.

— Still open How the relief would work, which wages and sectors it covers, what it costs the budget and whether Congress would pass it.

— Prediction markets Polymarket gives Flávio Bolsonaro a 77% chance of winning the 25 October runoff and Lula 24% (17 October, 2:31 a.m. ET). Polymarket puts Flávio Bolsonaro’s chance of winning at 77% and Kalshi at 77% (Lula: 24% and 22% ), as of 17 October, 2:40 am ET ; prices are bets, not polls.

— Power Index Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 75.0 points (October 2026 edition).

Flávio Bolsonaro, the conservative candidate in the Brazil election 2026 runoff, promised payroll tax relief on Friday 16 October to help companies pay for the end of the 6×1 work week. For US readers, the pledge matters because American firms with Brazilian staff face a shorter week within 60 days, and the plan has no price tag.

He used a 30-second spot in his televised campaign programme and gave no detail on how the relief would work, InfoMoney reported. The vote falls on the Brazil runoff date, Sunday 25 October, against President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of the left-wing Workers’ Party (PT).

What Flávio Bolsonaro Said on Friday

“Our government will make up the difference by cutting taxes, lowering interest rates and relieving the payroll,” he said, in our translation from Portuguese. He added that Brazil will prosper and workers will have more time for their families.

WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Flávio is a senator for Rio de Janeiro and the candidate of the Liberal Party (PL), Brazil’s main conservative party. He is the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.

The spot also said his proposal is for people to “work one day less without losing pay,” in our translation. InfoMoney noted that this is not the first time he has floated payroll relief.

On Thursday 20 August he told his weekly YouTube show the idea was a progressive payroll relief, InfoMoney reported. He asked Daniella Marques, who coordinates his economic plan, to explain how it would work, and she did not.

Maximum weekly working hours under Constitutional Amendment 141, promulgated on 16 October 2026, with no cut in pay. Source: Agência Senado and Agência Brasil.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

How Flávio Moved From Critic to Backer of a Shorter Week

Until last week Flávio called the amendment, known as a PEC, opportunistic and preferred pay by the hour worked. On Tuesday 13 October he said he would vote for it and that the government must bear the cost because employers are stretched, Estadão Conteúdo reported.

The Senate passed the amendment on Wednesday 14 October by 75 votes to 1, as set out in Brazil Senate Passes 5-Day Week, 75 to 1. Congress promulgated it on Friday 16 October as Constitutional Amendment 141, covered in Brazil Enacts End of Six-Day Work Week.

Sixty days after promulgation, employers must run a 5×2 schedule with two rest days and cap the week at 42 hours, Agência Senado reported. A year later the cap falls to 40 hours, with no cut in pay.

The turn in his position is told in Brazil’s Flávio Backs Ending 6X1 Work Week. The payroll pledge adds a mechanism to his earlier call for the government to compensate employers.

What Payroll Tax Relief Would Mean for Employers

In plain terms, payroll tax relief lowers the charges employers pay on top of wages, which makes each worker cheaper to hire. The spot did not say which charges, which wages or which sectors would be covered.

CNI, the national industry confederation, estimates that the shorter week could add up to R$267 billion (about US$52.5 billion) to production costs. It also projects a 0.7% fall in GDP and average inflation of 6.2%, Agência Brasil reported on 15 October.

Ipea, a federal research institute, estimates a smaller effect of about 1% of total costs in commerce and industry, and up to 6.6% in security and surveillance. Studies disagree, and some find only a small residual loss, Agência Brasil noted.

Payroll tax relief would shift part of that cost from firms to the public purse, which US investors watch through the budget deficit and the real. The spot gave no figure for the lost revenue or the spending cuts that would pay for it.

Finance Minister Dario Durigan said on Friday 16 October that the government is studying credit lines and training for affected firms. He announced no payroll tax cut or other direct compensation for employers, Agência Brasil reported.

Where Lula and the Liberal Party Stand

Lula, who made the shorter week a campaign flag, said at the ceremony that nobody wants a company to go bankrupt but nobody wants a worker to die from lack of rest. Opposition leaders did not attend the session, Agência Brasil reported.

Sóstenes Cavalcante, the Liberal Party leader in the Chamber of Deputies, told TV Jovem Pan that, if elected, Flávio should approve PEC 12/2026, which provides for a contract “per hour worked”. The hourly model Flávio once preferred is therefore still alive in his party, Agência Brasil reported.

Runoff poll results are collected in Brazil election polls, and the 6×1 issue is now common ground for both sides. The fight is over who pays, which is where the payroll pledge enters.

What It Means for You

If you employ staff in Brazil, the 5×2 schedule and the 42-hour cap apply 60 days after promulgation whoever wins on 25 October. A payroll cut would follow only if the winner sends a bill and Congress passes it, and the spot named no bill or date.

Investors in Brazilian equities and real-denominated bonds should read the pledge as a statement of intent, not a costed policy. It adds to fiscal questions about the next government if it is not matched by spending cuts, and none have been described.

We convert reais at the central bank’s PTAX sell rate of R$5.0826 per US$1 on Friday 16 October. For the wider picture, see What Brazil’s Election Means for US Investors and Lula vs Flávio: Where They Stand on 7 Issues.

São Paulo, Brazil’s largest city, has a page in our São Paulo expat city guide. Our What to Do in São Paulo in October 2026 lists what is on this month.

What Is Not Known

The spot did not say which payroll charges would be cut, for which wages or sectors, or from when. It also gave no estimate of the revenue the state would lose.

It is not known whether Congress, where the amendment passed 75 to 1 after the opposition freed its senators to vote, would back a payroll cut after the runoff. The sources reviewed also give no figure for the government’s own credit lines.

No poll reviewed here measures whether the payroll pledge changes votes. Prediction-market prices move on many events, so they cannot show its effect alone.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket’s Brazil presidential election market priced Flávio Bolsonaro at about 77% and Lula at about 24% at 2:31 a.m. ET on Saturday 17 October. Over the previous day Flávio’s price slipped about 2 points while Lula’s gained about 3.

The event has traded about US$185 million in total, and these prices are bets, not polls. Our Brazil election odds page tracks the live prices on both platforms.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Flávio Bolsonaro promise on 16 October?

He said a government of his would make up the cost of ending the 6×1 schedule by cutting taxes, lowering interest rates and relieving the payroll. The spot gave no detail on how.

What is the 6×1 work schedule?

It is a pattern of six working days followed by one rest day, which Constitutional Amendment 141 replaces with a 5×2 week. The change was promulgated by Congress on Friday 16 October.

When does the 5×2 week start?

The 5×2 schedule and a 42-hour weekly cap start 60 days after promulgation. A year later the cap falls to 40 hours, with no reduction in pay.

What is payroll tax relief?

It lowers the charges employers pay on top of wages, which makes hiring cheaper for companies. The cost falls on public revenue unless it is matched by spending cuts.

How much could the shorter week cost companies?

The industry confederation CNI estimates up to R$267 billion (about US$52.5 billion) in extra production costs. Ipea, a federal research institute, estimates about 1% of total costs in commerce and industry.

Who is Flávio Bolsonaro?

He is a Rio de Janeiro senator for the conservative Liberal Party and the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. He faces President Lula in the runoff on Sunday 25 October.

World.title: Mexican Peso Falls 9 Centavos to 18.50
World.content:
The Banco de México building in Mexico City, decorated with the national colours. File photo. (Photo: Mauricio Campos Gallardo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

MEXICO · MARKETS

Key Facts — The country Mexico is a top US trading partner, so the value of its currency touches US travellers, importers and investors.

— Why it matters The Mexican peso lost ground for a sixth straight week, which makes trips and Mexican costs cheaper in dollars but signals investor caution.

— Why now The currency closed the week on Friday 16 October after a hot US inflation reading and growing bets on a Federal Reserve rate rise.

— What happened The peso closed at 18.5045 per dollar on Friday, 9 centavos weaker than the 18.4111 close on 9 October, which lifted the dollar 0.51%.

— The numbers Banxico’s reference rate (FIX) for Friday 16 October was 18.4930, up from 18.4163 a week earlier; the weekly high for the dollar was 18.6090, a level last seen in November 2025.

— What it means for you A rent of MXN 20,000 (about US$1,081) costs about US$5 less than a week ago, while Mexican exporters and dollar borrowers face more pressure.

— Still open Whether the Federal Reserve raises rates, and whether Mexican inflation data next week keep Banxico on hold or open the door to a cut.

— Prediction markets Polymarket gives 76% to no change in Banxico’s rate at its November decision and 20.1% to a 25-basis-point cut (17 October, 2:50 a.m. ET).

— Power Index Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 71.4 points (October 2026 edition).

The Mexican peso ended the week at 18.5045 per dollar on Friday 16 October, 9 centavos weaker than last Friday’s close of 18.4111, Banxico data cited by El Economista show. For US readers, a softer peso makes Mexican trips and bills cheaper in dollars, yet it also signals nervous investors in a top US trading partner.

Mexico’s central bank, Banxico, publishes the official numbers behind this move, and the picture is more nuanced than one headline figure. Below is what the closing rate, the FIX reference rate and the market drivers each say.

How the Mexican Peso Lost 9 Centavos This Week

The peso fell 0.49% on Friday, or 9.03 centavos, from Thursday’s close of 18.4142, El Economista reported. Over the full week the loss was 9.34 centavos, or 0.51%, against the 18.4111 close of Friday 9 October.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 with 71.4 points. Strongest pillar: economic relationships (90); weakest: state capacity & security (46). Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

During the week the dollar reached 18.6090, a level El Economista says Mexico had not seen since November 2025. On Friday itself the rate moved between 18.3425 and 18.5157.

El CEO counts this as the sixth weekly loss in a row, the longest run since the weeks from 19 July to 30 August 2019. A centavo is one hundredth of a peso, so nine centavos is about half a US cent (US$0.005) at the Friday rate.

The Mexican Stock Exchange (Bolsa Mexicana de Valores) and office towers on Paseo de la Reforma, Mexico City. File photo. (Photo: Juan Carlos Fonseca Mata, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

What the Banxico FIX Rate Shows

Banxico also sets a daily reference rate called the FIX, which the Official Gazette (DOF) publishes on the next business day for settling dollar obligations in Mexico. Banxico’s statistics database puts the FIX determined on Friday 16 October at 18.4930 pesos per dollar, against 18.4163 in the Gazette listing of Monday 12 October, which carries the FIX of 9 October, a rise of 7.67 centavos or 0.42%.

The FIX is set during the trading day rather than at the close, so it can differ from the final quote, as it did on Friday (18.4930 against a close of 18.5045). The Gazette listing dated 16 October, 18.4250, is Thursday’s FIX, and Friday’s will appear in the listing of Monday 19 October.

FIX readings of 18.4888 on Wednesday, 18.4250 on Thursday and 18.4930 on Friday show that the slide was uneven rather than a straight line. The weekly FIX gain of 0.42% for the dollar is a little smaller than the 0.51% rise in the closing rate.

Why the Dollar Is Winning

US inflation set the tone on Wednesday 14 October, when September consumer prices rose 3.7% from a year earlier, with the monthly pace of 0.6% the fastest in five months, MéxFin chief executive Juan Carlos Cruz told El Economista. The peso lost 0.61% that day and traded as high as 18.60 per dollar, its weakest level since November 2025, El Economista reported.

Traders now bet on a Federal Reserve rate rise, with the CME FedWatch tool giving 71.7% to a 25 basis-point increase at the 8-9 December meeting, El Economista reported. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh declined on Friday at the IMF meetings in Bangkok to signal any decision, El Financiero reported, ahead of a meeting on 27-28 October listed in the Fed’s calendar.

Higher US rates narrow the gap with Mexican rates, which weakens the carry trade, where investors hold higher-yielding pesos funded with cheaper dollars. Banxico’s own target rate has stood at 6.50% since its 24 September decision, the central bank’s website shows.

Minutes of that meeting indicate that part of the board would cut the rate if inflation improves, El Economista reported. El Economista says Mexico’s inflation data for the first half of October are due next week and may shape that debate.

Felipe Mendoza of EBC Financial Group also pointed to HR Ratings cutting Mexico’s long-term sovereign rating to BBB, with a stable outlook, El CEO reported. That downgrade is explained in HR Ratings Mexico Downgrade Reasons Explained, and its Pemex fallout in Pemex Rating Cut Follows Mexico’s Downgrade.

Earlier moves in this slide are tracked in Mexican Peso Falls Past 18.40 on Central Bank Minutes. Friday’s stock-market side is in Mexico Stocks Rise 1.87% on Broad Rally | Mexico Market Report, Oct 16.

What It Means for You

A rent of MXN 20,000 (about US$1,081 at Friday’s Banxico close) costs about US$5 less than a week ago, when the same rent was about US$1,086. Travellers and remote workers paid in dollars gain a little purchasing power, but the gain is small.

Banamex quoted its counter rates on Friday at 17.93 pesos per dollar to buy and 18.95 to sell, El Financiero reported. A visitor who sold US$100 at 17.93 would receive MXN 1,793 (about US$97 at the Banxico close), so the bank spread costs more than the weekly move.

US companies that pay Mexican staff, suppliers or rent in pesos see those costs ease in dollars. Mexican households and firms with dollar debts or imported inputs face the opposite pressure.

The move is small, about half of one percent in a week, and far from a currency crisis. Banxico’s 6.50% rate still pays investors more than US rates do, which is the main cushion for the peso.

What Is Not Known

The Federal Reserve meets on 27-28 October and 8-9 December, and the 71.7% odds quoted apply to December, so what traders expect for October is not known. Nor is it known how much of the weekly slide came from US data and how much from Mexico’s rating cut.

The explanations quoted here come from market analysts, who are opinions rather than official findings. The first-half October inflation figure next week is unknown, as is Banxico’s next move.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket’s market on Banxico’s November decision priced no change at 76%, a 25-basis-point cut at 20.1% and a 25-basis-point rise at 2.6% on Saturday 17 October (2:50 a.m. ET). The market has traded about US$68,300 in total, and these are real-money bets, not polls.

The question concerns Banxico’s rate rather than the exchange rate, so it shows what traders expect from policy. Thin volume means prices can swing on small orders.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did the Mexican peso fall this week?

The peso closed at 18.5045 per dollar on Friday 16 October, 9.34 centavos or 0.51% weaker than the 18.4111 close of 9 October. It touched 18.6090 during the week, its weakest level since November 2025.

What is the Banxico FIX rate?

The FIX is a daily reference rate set by Banxico and published in the Official Gazette (DOF) for settling dollar obligations in Mexico. The Banxico database shows 18.4930 pesos per dollar for Friday 16 October.

Why is the Mexican peso weaker?

Analysts quoted by Mexican outlets point to hot US inflation, bets on a Federal Reserve rate rise and a cut to Mexico’s sovereign rating by HR Ratings. These are explanations from analysts, not official findings.

Is Mexico cheaper for US visitors now?

A weaker peso gives dollar holders slightly more pesos, so hotels, meals and rent cost a little less in dollars. Bank counter rates can cost more than the weekly move, so compare exchange spreads.

When is the next Mexican inflation reading?

El Economista says the first-half October inflation figures are due next week. They will shape expectations for Banxico, whose target rate is 6.50%.

Will Banxico cut interest rates in November?

Polymarket traders give 20.1% to a 25-basis-point cut and 76% to no change at the November decision. Those are bets, not forecasts from Banxico, and the market is thinly traded.

World.title: Peru Banks Eye Stablecoin FX, 0 Launched
World.content:
Towers in the San Isidro district of Lima, Peru (Photo: Protontorniyo, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

BANKING · PERU

Key Facts — The country Peru has no specific crypto law, so BCP’s bitcoin and USDC pilot runs in a sandbox authorised by the banking regulator, the SBS.

— Why it matters Dollar-linked tokens such as USDC and tether could open a new channel for dollar exchange and for money sent to Peru from abroad.

— Why now On Friday 16 October a senior payments consultant said many Peruvian banks can start turning soles into stablecoins to earn exchange fees.

— What happened No bank has announced a stablecoin exchange; the pilot in the coverage is CriptoCocos at BCP, launched in October 2025 for at most 3,000 clients.

— The numbers The pilot caps each trade at US$999 and each client at US$3,000 in purchases, with a 1% fee on every buy or sell.

— What it means for you Readers sending money to Peru see no change today, and a bank launch would still need clear fees and regulatory approval.

— Still open Which bank moves first, under what licence, and whether the regulator backs a wider rollout of the BCP pilot.

— Power Index Peru ranks 5th of 14 in Peru ranks 5th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 54.7 points (October 2026 edition).

Peru banks could earn fees by swapping soles into dollar-linked stablecoins, a Boston Consulting Group (BCG) executive said in remarks published by Gestión on Friday 16 October. No Peruvian bank has announced such a service, so the newspaper’s headline describes a possibility, not a launch.

For US readers the story is about the dollar, because USDC and tether are pegged to it and Infomercado describes USDC’s issuer, Circle, as a US-regulated company. A bank that routes soles through such tokens would add a dollar channel to Peru’s exchange and remittance flows.

What Peru Banks Are Weighing on Stablecoin FX

Gonzalo Troncoso, a managing director and partner at BCG who leads its payments and fintech practice in Latin America, named digital assets as one of three trends. The other two are artificial intelligence and the use of AI agents inside banks.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Peru ranks 5th of 14 with 54.7 points. Strongest pillar: military means (71); weakest: future resources (37). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

On Peru, he said many banks can begin to think about converting soles into stablecoins such as tether, a token linked to the US dollar. That, he said, would generate exchange commissions and then support the handling of remittances.

He presented this as an option for banks to consider, and he named no bank that plans it. Gestión’s own summary says banks “will evaluate” the idea, which is weaker than the headline’s “will launch”.

Troncoso also pointed to Nubank, which recently announced an international multi-currency account for fee-free transfers between more than 35 countries. He said the market still has to decide how to adopt it, but expected established banks to try to move in a similar direction.

BCG says artificial intelligence has lifted revenue at payment companies by 5% to 10%. It estimates that payment firms adopting it could raise profits by 20% to 30% in the short term.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What the BCP CriptoCocos Pilot Shows

Banco de Crédito del Perú (BCP), which calls itself Peru’s largest bank, launched CriptoCocos in October 2025 with the custody firm BitGo. It offers bitcoin and USDC in a closed circuit, with no transfers to outside platforms.

The SBS, the banking, insurance and pension regulator, authorised the pilot, and Infomercado reported that it sits inside the SBS regulatory sandbox. The same outlet reported that up to 3,000 clients may trade.

BCP’s own page sets a limit of US$999 per trade and US$3,000 in cumulative purchases per client during the pilot. It charges a 1% commission on each purchase or sale.

In December 2025 BCP executive Jorge Jenkins told Gestión that 2,000 people had registered but only a minimal number had started trading, since applicants first take a crypto knowledge test. Purchases were small, averaging about US$250, with 70% in bitcoin and the rest in USDC.

The pilot trades bitcoin and USDC, and the coverage reviewed does not describe it as a foreign-exchange or remittance service. Jenkins said BCP needs a favourable SBS opinion, which he estimated for October 2026, before deciding at the end of 2026 whether to open it to the public.

Why Stablecoins Are Gaining Ground in Peru

Forbes Perú reported in January that Peru has no specific crypto law, so BCP’s pilot runs in a sandbox. The main rule is an SBS anti-money-laundering resolution that requires virtual asset service providers to register with the financial intelligence unit, and it does not restrict trading or custody.

The same report cited a blockchain-analytics estimate of 1.28 million Peruvian crypto users, about 3.7% of the population, for the year to June 2025. At the exchange Buda.com stablecoins rose from 31% of traded volume in October 2024 to more than 50% in October 2025.

A Visa survey of more than 1,000 Peruvian consumers, covered by Gestión on 2 October, found that half of remittance operations are now digital. It also found that 50% of Peruvians know stablecoins and that 77% would use them if fraud protections were strong.

José Arango of the remittance firm Jet Perú told Gestión that stablecoin use today is mostly between companies, because few local products accept them. A neighbour’s step is covered in Brazil Clears Visa, Mastercard Stablecoin.

Regional background is in Stablecoins Are Digital Dollars. Latin America Uses Them More Than Any Other Region.

What It Means for You

If you send money to family in Peru from the United States, nothing changes today, because no bank has announced a stablecoin transfer service. If one launches, compare its fees, its exchange spread and its regulatory status before using it.

For investors, the signal is competition for dollar flows, not a proven bank product. The only evidence so far is a capped pilot whose average trade was about US$250 in December 2025.

The wider setting is covered in Who Runs Peru’s Economy, the Key Players in 2026. Peru banks operate under SBS supervision, so any new service would need the regulator’s consent.

What Is Not Known

No Peruvian bank has named a date, a product or a licence for a stablecoin exchange, and Troncoso did not name any bank. The SBS had not commented on the idea in the coverage reviewed.

Whether the SBS has given its opinion on CriptoCocos, which Jenkins expected around October 2026, is not stated in the coverage reviewed. The text of the Gestión article names only the BCP pilot as a local example.

Forbes Perú gave no date for the SBS anti-money-laundering rule it described, and the SBS website could not be read by our tools. The pilot’s current user numbers after December 2025 are also unknown.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are Peru banks launching a crypto exchange?

No bank has announced one. A BCG executive said on 16 October that many banks can start thinking about converting soles into stablecoins to earn exchange fees.

What is CriptoCocos?

It is a pilot at Banco de Crédito del Perú that lets approved clients buy and sell bitcoin and USDC. The SBS authorised it, and BCP launched it in October 2025.

What limits does the BCP pilot set?

Each trade is capped at US$999, and each client can buy up to US$3,000 in total during the pilot. BCP charges a 1% commission on every purchase or sale.

Is crypto legal in Peru?

Peru has no specific crypto law, according to Forbes Perú. An SBS anti-money-laundering rule requires virtual asset service providers to register with the financial intelligence unit.

What are stablecoins such as USDC and tether?

They are digital tokens whose value is linked to the US dollar. USDC is issued by Circle, which Infomercado describes as a US-regulated company.

Will stablecoins change remittances to Peru?

Not yet, because no bank has launched such a service. A Visa survey found that 77% of Peruvians would use stablecoins if fraud protections were strong.

Sources: Gestión, 16 October 2026; Gestión, 29 December 2025; Gestión, 2 October 2026; Forbes Perú, 5 January 2026; Infomercado, 7 October 2025; BCP CriptoCocos page; BCP launch release, October 2025.
