Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally, is seeking to become France’s next president on a hardline anti-EU platform, pledging to cut the country’s contributions to the EU budget and end funding for Ukraine.

 

On Ukraine, Le Pen has repeatedly pledged to end financial assistance. Speaking to reporters in Brussels on Wednesday, she said that if elected, France could only sustain funding for six months because of the “perilous” state of its public finances.

“This funding will stop, and it is a matter of honesty to tell [Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy] the truth,” she told Euronews.

Zelenskyy hit back in an interview with the Financial Times on Thursday. “The price to pay is not as high as the value of people’s lives,” he said. “That is why I think Ms Le Pen is not fully familiar with certain details.”

He added that, if Le Pen were elected president, she should have access to “the most powerful European system that works”, stressing that Ukraine’s battlefield experience could benefit European countries.

Le Pen has also called for an end to EU sanctions against Russia, while saying France could continue training Ukrainian troops and supplying military equipment to Kyiv.

Her comments signal that Le Pen is prepared to take a hardline stance, pledging to end French funding for Ukraine in a position similar to that of US President Donald Trump.

Her stance also contrasts sharply with that of Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who is often compared to Le Pen but has advocated continued support for Kyiv.

Speaking in the Italian Senate on Wednesday ahead of an EU summit in Brussels, Meloni delivered a forceful defence of Ukraine’s right to self-defence.

“Supporting Ukraine is not an alternative to peace, it’s what makes it possible,” Meloni said. “The peace we want is one that is sustainable, just and also safeguards Europe and our interests.

“Therefore, the position of this government will not change: support for Ukraine, pressure on Russia and Euro-Atlantic unity.”

‘France’s support for Ukraine goes far beyond aid’

“France’s support for Ukraine goes far beyond aid alone. It is primarily diplomatic,” Elie Tenenbaum, director of the French Institute of International Relations’ Centre for Security Studies, told Euronews.

He highlighted France’s leading role in initiatives such as the Coalition of the Willing, launched alongside the United Kingdom, as well as other mechanisms that “help keep Ukraine afloat”.

These include the €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan (USL), whose implementation and disbursement depend on the political backing of major countries, including France.

Tenenbaum stressed that cuts to EU-level funding would have a greater impact on Ukraine than a reduction in France’s bilateral aid.

“If France were not only to stop providing bilateral aid and contributing to the EU budget, but also to actively oppose these kinds of mechanisms, then the entire framework of European assistance to Ukraine would be put at risk.”

According to figures from the German think tank Kiel Institute, France has committed an estimated €27 billion to Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. This includes €7.9 billion in bilateral aid and €19 billion through European mechanisms.

Germany remains Europe’s largest provider of aid to Ukraine in absolute terms, having pledged more than €50 billion since February 2022, well ahead of France, Italy and the Netherlands. Relative to GDP, however, Denmark and Estonia provide the highest levels of bilateral aid.

Cutting France’s contributions to the EU budget

With six months to go before France’s presidential election, Le Pen is campaigning on a platform centred on tighter immigration controls, greater national sovereignty and measures to tackle the cost-of-living crisis, as rising fuel prices fuel public discontent.

Her party has backed capping France’s net contribution to the EU budget at €5 billion a year, down from €8 billion, according to figures published by the French Senate. Such a move would mark a departure from recent years, during which France’s contributions have generally increased, despite annual fluctuations.

Under President Emmanuel Macron, France has backed a larger EU budget, unlike countries such as Germany, which favour tighter spending limits. Paris has also called for new EU own resources, meaning additional sources of revenue beyond member state contributions.

Although France is a net contributor to the EU budget, it also receives substantial funding for its farmers through the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP).

“France stands out among the major contributors as it is the only one that has so far supported an ambitious EU budget,” Eulalia Rubio, a senior research fellow at the Jacques Delors Institute, told Euronews.

She said Le Pen’s proposals reflected a “lack of understanding” of EU institutions.

“Spending varies slightly every year, so you can’t say, ‘We’re only going to pay €5 billion every year from now on’,” she commented.

Rubio warned that if France overcame the legal obstacles to cutting its contributions, other member states would have to make up the shortfall. Such a prospect could prove particularly contentious given that France is the largest recipient of farming subsidies.

On Wednesday, France’s National Assembly rejected the National Rally’s proposal to unilaterally reduce the country’s contributions to the EU budget for 2027, instead backing the government’s planned level of funding.

Thierry Chopin, an adjunct professor of European studies at Sorbonne University, said a National Rally victory could mark a break with France’s traditional role as a driving force within the EU and with the “intellectual contributions championed by Paris” in recent years, which had gained traction in response to global events.

Chopin pointed to France’s role in promoting European sovereignty, strategic autonomy in defence and trade protection measures. However, he said France’s influence had waned during Macron’s second term as its economic credibility declined.

“This credibility was not particularly strong to begin with, but it has worsened given the country’s budgetary situation, public debt and the difficulties facing its public finances. And then, once again, there are political considerations, because the executive branch has been weakened,” he said.

EU budget for 2028-2034

Speaking to the Financial Times on Wednesday, Le Pen described efforts to reach an agreement on the EU’s 2028-2034 budget by the end of 2026 as "anti-democratic."

She accused the European Commission of undermining “democratic processes” by advancing the budget ahead of elections in France, Spain, Italy and Poland.

Ahead of the vote, Macron has moved to secure key positions, including at the central bank, by appointing allies. On Thursday, the French president told EU leaders during a closed-door meeting that Paris favours reaching a deal this year.

Beyond the timeline, Le Pen is also focused on the substance of the EU budget. Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, she said she hoped to “build new coalitions” with like-minded parties to challenge what she described as an anti-growth mindset in Brussels.

She also suggested that the European Central Bank (ECB), led by Christine Lagarde, should revise its mandate to give greater weight to economic growth. The ECB is independent and its primary mandate is to maintain price stability.

Experts told Euronews they are sceptical that member states would support another major overhaul of EU fiscal rules following the sweeping reform of the Stability and Growth Pact in 2024.

“In my view, member states show little appetite for another major reform,” Andreas Eisl, a senior research fellow in European economic policy at the Jacques Delors Institute, told Euronews.

He added that “future changes are likely to involve reinterpretations of the existing rules rather than a fundamental overhaul of their legal foundations”.

Le Pen has repeatedly criticised EU regulations and standards, describing them as “regulatory hell” or a “regulatory shantytown”, and has pledged to strip them back to the bare minimum. Such an approach could undermine the bloc’s legal framework if adopted across member states.

“Obviously, if every member state does this, the EU can no longer function as a union based on the rule of law,” Chopin said.

The National Rally leader has also vowed to “stop” the European Green Deal, the EU’s flagship programme to cut emissions and achieve climate neutrality by 2050.

Le Pen argues that the Green Deal undermines economic growth. She has also proposed abolishing institutions such as the European Committee of the Regions (CoR), an advisory body representing local and regional authorities involved in implementing EU policies, including climate measures.

“The dismantling of the European Green Deal is already underway. If Marine Le Pen were to be elected, this would only be further accentuated, according to certain analyses,” Phuc-Vinh Nguyen, head of the Energy Centre at the Jacques Delors Institute, told Euronews.

Maria Tadeo contributed to this report

World.title: Trump signs executive order waiving new Russia sanctions package
World.content:
US President Donald Trump on Friday signed an executive order to waive a new package of sanctions and tariffs on Russia shortly before it was due to take effect, telling Congress it was in the US' national interest.

 

Trump had signed the "Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026" into law in September in a push to increase pressure on the Kremlin and the Russian economy.

The legislation - named in honour of the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, who championed the measures - had sought to impose sanctions on Russian government and military officials, major banks, and vessels in Russia's shadow fleet. It also provided for duties on Russian goods and goods from certain countries continuing to buy Russian oil and gas.

The move to put the sanctions on hold comes amid increasing criticism from Trump of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

It also follows a controversial announcement from Trump, who is gearing up for the US' midterm elections, earlier this month on a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin for Russia to release large flows of diesel into global markets in an effort to bring down fuel prices.

"It was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter," Trump wrote in a post on his Truth Social account. "Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel."

Zelenskyy in Brussels

The Ukrainian leader has been in Brussels this week, where he has been meeting with European leaders to discuss the ongoing war.

Taking questions from the media on Friday, Zelenskyy was asked whether he felt he had been made a "scapegoat" for Trump's "own problems" ahead of November's midterms.

He gave a wry smile and said: "This is my answer."

Addressing the US-Russia diesel deal, Zelenskyy added that Ukraine "can’t accept diesel deals, because gas deals will come next."

"I’m absolutely sure of that," he said. "After gas, sanctions will be lifted on other things. It will eventually extend to the banking system, specific individuals, and the chemical industry. And there are risks around the frozen assets. If I don’t defend that through diplomacy – who will do it for us?"

World.title: France braces for tense day of protests as security concerns take centre stage
World.content:
The French government and security forces are on high alert ahead of major protests scheduled across France on 17 October. Unions and citizens branding themselves as "yellow vests" will take to the streets to denounce the cost-of-living crisis and rising fuel prices, with large numbers of student protestors also expected to join.

 

According to a source close to France's Interior Ministry, 500 actions are planned across the country on Saturday, alongside 90 estimated protests. The protests follow four weeks of student demonstrations over a range of issues, including teacher absences, overcrowded classrooms and outdated facilities.

Most student protests have been peaceful, but there have been clashes involving rioters and widespread criticism of alleged police brutality and violence.

Ahead of Saturday's protests, authorities are anticipating possible violence in Paris and other major cities. The source told Euronews that the far-left movement could seek to provoke confrontations with law enforcement and attempt to breach security perimeters along protest routes.

The source also warned that blockades of key transportation routes and essential infrastructure would "not be tolerated."

Meanwhile, French President Emmanuel Macron said on Friday that whilst the right to protest "is fully respected," it "must be accompanied by respect for people and property."

"That is why I call for calm and respect: these rights must be preserved," he said.

Mounting scrutiny of police actions

French law enforcement authorities have faced increasing scrutiny in recent weeks amid several allegations of police violence.

In one case, a 15-year-old schoolboy allegedly lost an eye after being struck by a police rubber bullet. In a separate incident, a 14-year-old reportedly lost his hand after picking up a police stun grenade. The circumstances surrounding both cases remain under investigation.

Following the latter case, France suspended the use of certain types of stun grenades.

Yet, in an interview on Friday, France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that the use of stun grenades would be allowed on 17 October should "serious urban violence" occur on the sidelines of demonstrations, whilst cautioning that stun grenades were "never used when things are going well."

Nuñez told France's Senate on Tuesday that 36 investigations into alleged police violence during student protests had been opened. He said that four of these cases related to mutilating injuries and six to significant injuries, whilst the others were related to alleged blows, insults and reported sexual violence.

There has been speculation that the 17 October demonstration could mark the return of the yellow vest grassroots movement, which emerged in 2018 in reaction to a planned government fuel and diesel tax hike.

For months, yellow vest protestors gathered every weekend to block roundabouts, motorways, and fuel depots across the country, with tense police clashes also occurring.

Meanwhile, the French government is grappling with a major public debt crisis as it attempts to pass a budget containing austerity measures through a hung parliament.

Police union lodges complaint against state for 'endangering lives of others'

French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said on Thursday that 937 police officers and gendarmes had been injured since the start of the protests. He also reported injuries among 248 students and 149 teaching staff members, which he said was the highest number of injuries ever recorded by France's Education Ministry.

Lecornu warned that the “secondary school student movement” was transforming into a “wave of urban violence."

Meanwhile, Alliance Police Nationale, one of France's largest police unions, announced in a statement on Tuesday that it would lodge a complaint against the state "for endangering the lives of others."

The union denounced what it qualified as "contradictory orders" given to police officers, who have been "exposed to violence and left at the mercy of public hostility" over the course of secondary school protests.

“After the president’s [French President Emmanuel Macron] expressions of empathy towards rioters and emphasis on dialogue, we are now faced with vague instructions, contradictory orders and superficial public statements!"

"The discrepancy between Laurent Nuñez’s public statements and the verbal instructions passed down through the chain of command has become unbearable," the union said.

The hard-left France Unbowed party has been accused by the government and political opponents of encouraging violence and stoking unrest through inflammatory language.

In a speech delivered on 30 September, the party's leader, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, urged his supporters to "stand up to police brutality," adding that "there will be neither forgetting nor forgiveness for anyone."

He later qualified his comments, stating that he backed peaceful protest methods.

World.title: The world’s biggest fine jewellery factory: How Pandora aims to make more and pollute less in Vietnam
World.content:
Pandora has opened what it calls the world’s largest fine jewellery crafting facility in Vietnam, expanding production while seeking to reduce its environmental footprint.

 

The factory in Ho Chi Minh City is expected to employ 7,000 people when fully operational.

It will produce up to 60 million pieces of jewellery a year, increasing the Danish company’s manufacturing capacity by 50%, according to its opening announcement.

The site is Pandora’s fourth factory globally and its first outside Thailand.

"This gives us flexibility to craft all our collections, our assortments in all our materials and crafting techniques," said Pandora CEO Berta de Pablos-Barbier.

The Danish jewellery maker sold 112 million pieces in 2025, equivalent to more than three every second. It describes itself as the world’s largest jewellery brand.

Expanding production, reducing emissions

Pandora invested $150 million (€132mn) in the Vietnam factory, which it says will operate entirely on renewable electricity. The company also switched to using 100% recycled gold and silver in its jewellery production in 2024.

As it increases manufacturing capacity, de Pablos-Barbier said Pandora would continue growing "in a sustainable manner".

Gold is particularly suited to repeated reuse, according to experts.

"In many ways, it is designed for a circular economy. It doesn't oxidise. That's why it's so valuable," said Saleem H. Ali, lead researcher for critical minerals and the inclusive energy transition at the United Nations University.

"We still have the gold from the ancient Egyptians in pretty good shape."

Using recycled metals still requires energy. Refining involves heating and separating metals from other materials to remove impurities.

Pandora’s ambition is to extend renewable electricity use beyond its own operations to suppliers involved in producing its jewellery.

Challenges in a growing jewellery market

Jewellery unit sales are forecast to grow by 4.1% annually between 2025 and 2028 — around four times the rate of clothing, according to The State of Fashion 2026, a report from McKinsey and The Business of Fashion.

Pandora’s rise from a small Copenhagen jewellery shop, founded in 1982, was built around manufacturing in Thailand, which began in 1989. Its charm bracelet, launched in 2000, helped drive international expansion before its Copenhagen stock exchange listing in 2010.

But the growing jewellery market does not guarantee an easy path for Pandora.

Pandora warned in its August 2026 results that US import tariffs would continue to weigh on profitability.

The tariffs affect sales to the United States, Pandora’s largest market, where inflation and economic uncertainty are also weighing on demand for its jewellery.

Past labour disputes have also drawn scrutiny to conditions behind its production. Danish investigative outlet Danwatch reported in 2020 that a Thai labour court had ruled in May 2019 that union activity had contributed to workers’ dismissals at Pandora’s Bangkok factory.

Pandora said the cuts reflected restructuring and employee performance.

As Pandora expands in Vietnam, it remains to be seen whether it can increase production while reducing emissions and protecting workers’ rights.

World.title: Trade unions push for EU law to address menopause at work
World.content:
The European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC), which represents 45 million members across 41 European countries, is pushing for menopause to be recognised in EU workplace law, arguing that a lack of support is costing women earnings, career opportunities and pension income.

 

“Women’s work-related health risks remain largely ignored by the law, which remains orientated around male-dominated jobs,” said ETUC Deputy General Secretary Isabelle Schömann. “It’s high time that the law caught up with the reality of the whole workforce today and the risks facing them.”

The push comes as the European Parliament examines a report calling for menopause to be treated as an economic, employment and social issue, while the European Commission has stopped short of proposing a dedicated EU menopause strategy.

Menopause, which typically occurs between the ages of 45 and 55, affects a significant proportion of the workforce. Around 30% of women experience symptoms that affect their capacity to work, including fatigue, sleep disruption, hot flushes, joint pain, anxiety and difficulties concentrating. Around 85 % of women experience at least one of those symptoms.

Research cited by the confederation found that women's earnings in Norway fell by 7.4% by the fourth year after a menopause diagnosis, with reduced working hours, sick leave and missed promotions contributing to the decline.

“Loss of pay, lost promotions, and lower pensions is the price being paid by millions of women for the failure to adapt work to the menopause,” Schömann said.

Pressure builds for EU action

The campaign comes amid growing recognition of menopause in the EU's gender equality agenda, although concrete workplace protections remain largely a matter for national legislation and employers.

In November 2025, Equality Commissioner Hadja Lahbib said the Commission was not planning a dedicated EU strategy on menopause, while pointing to research projects funded through Horizon 2020 and Horizon Europe addressing its medical and social impacts.

The Commission has since included menopause in its Gender Equality Strategy 2026-2030, published in March. The strategy commits to exchanging national best practices on tackling menstrual and menopause poverty and to a study, planned for 2028, on the economic and societal benefits of closing the women's health gap, including menopause.

The commitments mark a shift towards recognising menopause in the EU's wider equality agenda, but stop short of proposing dedicated legislation setting out workplace rights for menopausal employees.

The European Parliament is seeking to push the issue further. Spanish Socialist MEP Lina Gálvez is leading a draft report titled Menopause beyond a health issue: turning menopause into an economic, working and social priority.

The draft, which will be further discussed at the plenary session only next year, calls for a dedicated EU strategy, broader research, public campaigns to challenge stigma, better workplace support and improved access to healthcare.

“It is therefore essential to have an EU strategy that includes broader and more inclusive EU research, evidence-based public campaigns to change the social perceptions, improved workplace support and improved access to healthcare,” Gálvez wrote in the draft report. “It is time for the EU to tackle menopause.”

The report remains a parliamentary initiative, rather than adopted EU policy.

Unions want changes at work

For the ETUC, the priority is to ensure that menopause is reflected in the way workplaces are organised and regulated.

Its demands include risk assessments covering workplace temperature, ventilation and facilities; flexible hours and remote working; training for managers and human resources staff; and physical adjustments such as temperature controls and ergonomic equipment.

The confederation also wants menopause policies negotiated with trade unions, then implemented and monitored, alongside free menstrual and menopause products at work.

“The way work is organised can make a crucial difference in deciding the impact of the menopause,” Schömann said, adding that unions are already negotiating collective agreements covering workplace adjustments and flexible arrangements.

World.title: Smashing pumpkins: Annual squash festival draws thousands to Brussels castle
World.content:
Some call them pumpkins, for others they're simply squashes, or jack o'lanterns when carved creatively, however you dice or slice them - pumpkins have taken over a castle near Brussels, Groot-Bijgaarden, for its annual pumpkin festival.

 

Sourced from across Belgium and as far away as Portugal and Germany, the pumpkins come in all shapes and sizes — including a giant weighing 772 kilograms.

The festival offers more than a display of the autumn harvest. Visitors can try their hand at pumpkin carving ahead of Halloween, while some of the largest pumpkins have been turned into makeshift kayaks.

Despite a difficult harvest following a hot summer, the event continues to draw families and pumpkin enthusiasts for a celebration of autumn, with organisers expecting around 50,000 visitors this year.

World.title: Europe’s sponge cities are turning rain from waste into a valuable resource
World.content:
Wild weather swings have turned water into a dual threat for Europe’s cities. When storms hit, there’s too much of it. When droughts come, there’s too little.

 

But some experts believe that the ‘sponge city’ model – a nature-based approach to urban planning pioneered in China two decades ago – could help cities put a new spin on the old saying ‘save for a rainy day’.

The model involves retrofitting urban areas with green spaces, permeable surfaces and water storage systems to absorb, retain and reuse rain rather than letting it drain away. This eases pressure on drainage systems and conserves water to use during dry spells.

“One of the most impactful ways cities can adapt is by reversing a century of urban design that treated rainfall as waste rather than as a valuable resource,” says Justin Abbott, fellow and Europe water leader at engineering consultancy Arup.

What is a ‘sponge city’?

The sponge city model was developed in the early 2000s by Chinese landscape architect Kongjian Yu.

He proposed using features such as ponds, wetlands and planted drainage channels to catch rainfall before it rushed into sewers and rivers. Slowing the runoff would reduce flood risk during storms, he argued, while rainwater could be used to replenish groundwater supplies or irrigate parks during dry spells.

The greenery would also help cool city streets during heatwaves, and in some cases, healthy soil and wetlands could help protect against wildfires.

After catastrophic flooding killed 79 people in Beijing in 2012, his ideas gained greater attention.

In 2014, China adopted national guidelines for sponge city development, and the next year the country launched a 16-city pilot programme, including Wuhan, Xiamen and Chongqing. Another 14 cities, including Shanghai and Shenzhen, were added in 2016.

By 2030, China now aims to have 80 per cent of its built-up urban areas function as sponge cities.

Could sponge cities make Europe more resilient?

Europe has been experimenting with similar water management projects for decades.

Between 1998 and 2002, the southern Swedish city Malmö transformed its flood-prone Augustenborg neighbourhood by installing green roofs, wetlands, retention ponds and six kilometres of water channels. During major storms in 2007 and 2014, it suffered much less flood damage than other neighbourhoods.

In the Netherland’s Rotterdam, the Benthemplein water square – opened in 2013 – doubles as a basketball court and recreational space in good weather, but during heavy rains, its three basins temporarily hold up to 1.7 million litres of water.

Opened one year later in Denmark, Copenhagen’s Tåsinge Plads collects water from nearby rooftops using underground storage and rain gardens – shallow, planted areas that allow rain to soak into the soil.

The European Commission hopes to expand projects like these across the continent. Its 2025 Water Resilience Strategy called for more sponge cities, as well as to restore more wetlands, and now the bloc is developing a ‘Sponge Facility’ to help develop them.

The changes won’t necessarily be easy. Protected buildings, crowded streets and buried utilities make it difficult to retrofit historic city centres. But Abbott says that’s no excuse for failing to think outside the box.

“These challenges should encourage better targeting, not inaction,” he says, suggesting smaller interventions such as removing courtyard paving, planting more trees and installing green roofs partially or completely covered with vegetation.

Sponge cities are a ‘powerful’ tool but not a fix-all

Even the greenest city can only absorb so much rain, though. During extreme storms, soil becomes saturated and storage systems fill up, leaving excess water nowhere to go.

The catastrophic floods around Valencia in 2024 revealed the tragic consequences that can occur when extreme rainfall overwhelms a city’s defences like this.

“Sponge measures are powerful, but they cannot address every challenge independently,” Abbott explains.

Cities also need conventional drainage systems, larger reservoirs and designated routes that can carry floodwater away when rain gardens and wetlands reach capacity, he says.

That’s a matter of more than engineering. Abbott argues that city authorities, water utilities, developers and landowners all have a responsibility to manage rainfall. Decisions made by one entity, he explains, can affect entire neighbourhoods.

“In planning and designing cities, we need to put water first,” he says. “We need to ‘design with water’.”

World.title: Latest news bulletin | October 17th, 2026 – Morning
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: India news: 'Cockroach' party founder Abhijeet Dipke under preventive arrest
World.content:
10/17/2026 October 17, 2026 CJP's Dipke arrested after detention — reports

The 'Cockroach' movement has called Dipke's detention a 'kidnapping' Image: Rafiq Maqbool/AP Photo/picture alliance

Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) Founder Abhijeet Dipke has been arrested, following his detention on Friday when he stepped out to participate in a rally he had called in New Delhi, media reports said.

Dipke was arrested to ‌prevent a ⁠breach ⁠of the peace and will be taken before a Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) court later today, news agencies ANI and PTI reported.

CJP legal affairs head Ratna Singh also said that Dipke had been arrested, adding that he would appear before the SEM court in central Delhi's Mandir Marg at 12 p.m. (630 UTC).

Singh claimed that Dipke's lawyers had not met him.

The 'Cockroach' movement said early on Saturday that they did not know where their founder had been detained, calling his detention a "kidnapping."

"Until now, neither his parents nor his lawyers and not the CJP team have been given any updates about his location," the CJP said on X, as it published a video of CJP leader Ajinkya Shinde asking about Dipke's whereabouts.

Dipke was detained publicly on Friday as he left the house in Jhandewalan where he was staying to take part in CJP's 'Lehra Do Tiranga' (Wave the tricolor) protest rally in Connaught Place.

Videos of his detention showed the CJP founder being told by a police official that he was being placed under "preventive detention" before he was taken to a police car.

Dipke was seen displaying India's flag as police and media personnel surrounded him. Some supporters were seen trying to block the police vehicle from driving away with Dipke.

Just hours earlier, a group of Delhi Police officials had visited the 31-year-old at the Jhandewalan residence and served him a notice barring the Friday protest.

The Delhi Police had previously reiterated that Section 163 of India's criminal procedure law, which prohibits any form of assembly or protest, was in force in the Connaught Place area.

"The manner in which he was picked up from right outside his residence, no information about his whereabouts, and the fact that even his lawyers have been unable to meet him raise serious concerns about due process and fundamental rights," Singh wrote on X.

Even after Dipke's detention, hundreds of protesters turned up in Connaught Place defying the heavy security deployment. The protesters were seen waving the Indian national flag as part of the CJP's 'Tricolor' rally. According to police, some 150 protesters were detained during the demonstrations.

The fresh protests came after CJP co-conveners Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were sent to a five-day detention in jail on Wednesday for alleged violation of prohibitory orders and breach of a peace bond after they attempted a demonstration. They too were carrying the Indian tricolor and the flag has since been at the center of CJP's campaign.

The Indian flag "belongs to the 1.3 billion people of this country and not the Delhi police. We will wave it where we want!" the movement has said.

Dipke, Das and Ranka were earlier detained on October 10 from a plane as they arrived in the capital for a protest march calling for the resignation of India's Chief Election Commionser Gyanesh Kumar over alleged manipulation of voter lists.

They were released after nearly 24 hours.

World.title: US: Homes burned in California as wildfires rage
World.content:
Multiple mansions have been engulfed in the fires raging in California while firefighters continue to douse the blaze.

At least six expensive properties have been engulfed by fast-spreading wildfires on the southern coast of California, prompting thousands of people to evacuate.

The Orange County Fire Authority said on X that the so-called Norte fire had scorched about 465 acres (188 hectares) and that at least four homes had been impacted in the affluent San Juan Capistrano municipality.

Black smoke billowing from the hills was visible for miles as firefighters tried to contain the fast-moving blaze.

The agency said firefighters were "aggressively attacking the fire from ground and air" and repeatedly requested people to stay away from the area.

Danger of fire spreading remains as thousands without power

The Norte fire started in the coastal city of San Clemente and wind drove it into San Juan Capistrano.

The National Weather Service warned of "high risk for large fires and rapid fire growth," especially over Los Angeles and Ventura counties, as well as the mountains and foothills of San Luis Obispo and Santa Barbara counties

The wildfires have continued to worsen due to the intense Santa Ana winds, low humidity and unseasonably high temperatures.

Firefighters have been trying to douse the Norte Fire Image: Apu Gomes/AFP

According to forecasters, wind gusts of up to 50-70 miles (80-110 kilometers) per hour were recorded in the mountains, with coastal and valley areas seeing gusts between 35 and 55 miles per hour.

Authorities have turned off the electricity supply to reduce the risk of electrical sparks that the heavy wind gusts could carry, leaving thousands of people in the state without power.

World.title: Oregon school shooting: Police praise 'heroism' of those who intervened to stop more killing
World.content:
US police have praised the actions of three people who cut short a deadly shooting at a school in the state of Oregon. Three children and a teacher were killed in the attack, carried out by a former pupil at the school.

Police in the northwestern US state of Oregon have identified a teenage gunman who shot dead four people at a school as a former special needs student there, while praising people who stepped in to stop more killings.

Three children aged 5, 8 and 11 lost their lives in Thursday's rampage, along with a 25-year-old female teacher, before the shooter was shot dead by a father of two pupils at the school, located in the town of Bend.

Another young child and a teacher were also injured in the attack.

Who intervened to prevent more deaths in Oregon?

A man in a vehicle outside the school who was shot at and missed by the 16-year-old gunman was the first to alert police to the danger.

Before they arrived, however, a female teacher tackled the shooter after he had already killed the victims with a pump-action 12-gauge shotgun in the school's special needs classroom.

While the two wrestled with each other, a man identified by family as Kaylub Giamanco, a 36-year-old father of two girls at the school, rushed in with his legally held weapon and shot the gunman dead.

"He heard shooting and saw a teacher involved in a physical altercation with the suspect ... and fired his weapon, striking the suspect multiple times," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz told reporters.

"When someone is willing to risk their own life for others, we recognize that. The teacher who is willing to stand and fight for her children ... incredible. That is true heroism, and we don't see that a lot in society," he said.

The shooting has shocked the Bend community Image: ABC affiliate KOHD/Handout/REUTERS

Praise from Trump as gun control debate revived

Giamanco's mother told the local branch of Fox News that she was "very proud" and that her son was "an absolute hero."

US President Donald Trump also hailed Giamanco's actions.

"It's a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it," he told reporters.

The shooting in Bend has triggered the usual responses from both sides in the everlasting debate about gun control laws in the US.

The National Rifle Association (NRA), one of the main and most powerful opponents of tighter laws on the possession of weapons by civilians, hailed the actions of the armed bystander.

"Yesterday's terrible act of violence in Oregon serves as another reminder of the importance of a law-abiding armed citizenry," the NRA said in a post on X.

Gun control advocates, however, once more condemned the relative ease with which firearms can be procured in the US, which they see as the main factor in the country's high rate of gun-related deaths compared with most other developed countries.

"America's gun violence crisis is killing our babies. Enough is enough," gun-control group GIFFORDS said.

According to an analysis by the education information portal Education Week, there have been 26 shootings at US schools so far this year that have resulted in injuries or deaths.

More than 360 mass shootings have been recorded across the country this year, according to the Gun Violence Archive.

It defines mass shootings as incidents in which at least four people are shot, excluding the shooter.

World.title: Trump puts new Russia sanctions on hold
World.content:
The US president cited national interests for his decision to sign a waiver on sanctions Congress voted to place on Russia.

US sanctions on Russia will not take effect as planned after President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Friday waiving them for national security reasons.

"As described further in section 4 of this order, I am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions, and duties provided for in the Graham Act," the executive order said.

"I have submitted to the Congress ​a certification that ‌the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the ​United States," ⁠Trump said in the order released by the White House.

Can Trump’s diesel deal bring down US fuel prices? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The White House did not immediately explain how Trump's decision to pause the sanctions will serve the national interest.

The White House posted the decision on its website late in the evening. It noted that the report explaining the decision had been submitted to Congress.

According to the order, the waiver will remain ​in effect until Trump or his top officials determine that "further action is appropriate."

Trump's controversial deal with Russia

The Lindsey Graham Act, which was named after the deceased US senator who sponsored the bill, had found bipartisan support in Congress and was passed in September.

It allowed the Trump administration to increase pressure on Russia over its war against Ukraine by imposing duties up to 100& on major buyers of Russian oil.

The sanctions were meant to starve Russian President Vladimir Putin of the resources needed to continue its war in Ukraine. The bill aimed to penalize Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving.

Trump announces 'energy ceasefire' in Ukraine war To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

​India, one of the biggest buyers of Russian oil, was among the countries that raised concerns about the Russia sanctions.

Now, the move to waive the sanctions against Russia comes a week after Trump said the US had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try and bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine in its war with Russia.

With US midterms just around the corner, the sanctions on Russia could have risked raising oil prices even further while Americans are already grappling with increased costs largely because of the US-Israeli war on Iran, analysts have said.

Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat who also drafted the bill with sanctions against Russia, said Trump was turning his back on "the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, and our European allies."

"These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin," Blumenthal said.

World.title: Brazil: Amazon deforestation lowest in nearly 40 years
World.content:
The latest figures show that 3,335 square kilometers of the Amazon rainforest were cleared in the year ending in July, the lowest level since 1988. The drop has been described as an "historic achievement."

Brazil has recorded the lowest level of deforestation in the Amazon rainforest in nearly 40 years.

According to data released by the Brazilian space research agency Inpe on Friday, between August 2025 and July 2026, 3,335 square kilometers (1,288 square miles) of forest were cleared, the lowest level witnessed since records began in 1988.

The numbers showed a nearly 42% decrease from last year's figure of 5,731 square kilometers.

The Amazon is the world's largest tropical rainforest and one of its most biodiverse ecosystems, most of which lies in Brazil.

It also extends into parts of Peru, Colombia and other South American countries. Deforestation and the illegal exploitation of resources have been pushing it closer to a climate tipping point.

The Amazon is the world's largest tropical rainforest Image: Pablo Porciuncula/AFP

Drop hailed as 'historic achievement'

"It's an absolutely stratospheric drop...it's like a dream," said Environment Minister Joao Paulo Capobianco at a press conference in the capital, Brasilia.

"Our goal is to achieve zero illegal deforestation by 2030," said President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in a post on X.

"The figures released today are a historic achievement," said Marcio Astrini, executive secretary at climate advocacy group Observatorio do Clima.

"They put Brazil at the forefront of the forest protection agenda and show the world that, with political will, it is possible to stop the chainsaws and curb greenhouse gas emissions," Astrini said on his organization's website.

Observatorio do Clima said the figures were the result of a "sustained commitment" to protecting the environment by the government, which introduced greater monitoring and stiffer penalties for illegal logging.

The news comes ahead of the October 25 runoff election between Lula and conservative senator Flavio Bolsonaro with the two running neck and neck according to polls.

World.title: Ukrainian President Zelenskyy speaks at EU summit amid spat with Donald Trump
World.content:
EU leaders reaffirmed support for Ukraine at the Brussels summit. But souring relations with the US over Russia and Starlink and a big hole in the budget will make for a difficult winter for Ukraine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was applauded by EU leaders when he appeared at this week's summit in Brussels. But getting what he needs from Europe will be tough, and a public dispute with US President Donald Trump has put him in a very difficult position.

Speaking to press at the summit, he said that "Putin wants to destroy us" and that Ukraine must prepare for a hard winter.

Experts view the upcoming cold season as a rough one for Ukraine as well.

"Ukraine is arguably entering the most difficult winter since [Russia's] full scale invasion," Olena Prokopenko, a senior fellow at the German Marshall Fund of the United States, a nonpartisan think-tank, told DW.

Three painful topics were on the table at the summit for discussion between Zelenskyy and EU leaders: US relations with Russia, Starlink ― and money.

Is the US siding with Russia?

Zelenskyy's visit to Brussels comes at a time when he needs European support more than ever. That's because his relationship with the US is worsening. Worries are growing in the EU and Ukraine that the US is growing more sympathetic to Russia.

President Trump told US news channel Newsmax: "I think I find Zelenskyy to be more difficult to deal with than [Russian President Vladimir] Putin."

Trump struck a deal to buy Russian diesel on October 12, which signifies a step back from sanctions placed on Russia and a blow for Ukraine.

When Zelenskyy ordered Ukrainian forces to conduct fresh strikes on Russia's oil refineries, Trump labelled the Ukrainian leader's decision as "a disgrace."

How Russia turned sanctions into a diesel deal To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

At the press conference at the summit on Friday, Zelenskyy told reporters that he knows that US-built missiles "are being sent to the Middle East, so it is no secret that we are not a priority."

He is asking Europe instead to supply the military power Ukraine needs to get through the winter.

Since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the US has been the biggest military donor to Ukraine. But the relationship between the two countries has become more difficult since the start of Donald Trump's second term in the White House.

The Starlink slowdown

Ukraine uses Starlink, a satellite Internet service developed by tech billionaire Elon Musk. The country also uses Starshield, the military-grade version, for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territory and interceptor drones, though not for long-range strikes in Russia.

At the summit, Zelenskyy spoke of his "deep and unpleasant" surprise upon finding out that Ukraine was experiencing disruptions to the systems. He said this has hobbled Ukraine's ability to defend itself.

Both Elon Musk and the White House say they are not responsible for the slowdown.

The EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told the press at the summit before the talks began: "Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine and unfortunately in [the] short term Europe can't replace this capability."

Prokopenko said that this was the reason "why Ukraine's most credible medium-term solution here is to continue relying on the US. And the EU is critical in this context in terms of backing Ukraine's requests for the US administration to keep those technologies on offer" for Kyiv.

Speaking to journalists at the summit, Zelenskyy said the speed of Starlink had still not been fully restored but had improved. He said Ukraine is cooperating with various countries, including France, to search for a partial solution.

Did someone order Ukraine's high-speed Starlink shutdown? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ukraine's budget problem

Zelenskyy urged EU leaders Friday to keep backing Kyiv financially as well, asking for nearly $80 billion (€70 billion) more next year.

"This is a realistic amount and I ask you to find this support," Zelenskyy said. "It will help us hold Russia back."

The EU gave Kyiv an approximately $100 billion (€90 billion) loan last year, making the EU Ukraine's biggest international backer. But the Ukrainian government is saying it needs more.

"The war is becoming objectively more expensive, and the Ukrainian economy is increasingly affected by the Russian strikes, leading to a drastic decline in tax and customs revenues," Prokopenko said. "So the needs will continue growing."

So will Ukraine get what it needs? Closing the summit, President of the European Council Antonio Costa said that Ukraine "remains a priority" and asked the European Commission to come up with a proposal to pull together more funds for the country in 2027.

Essentially, it looks as though the EU will try to find a way to meet Ukraine's cash demands ― though it is not yet clear how.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen promised the EU will "continue to lead" but urged international partners to step up as well.

Ukraine to 'keep living and fighting with dignity'

Zelenskyy will leave Brussels without concrete promises or numbers, but with renewed commitments for support from Europe.

The Ukrainian president concluded his press conference with an emotional statement: "We will keep living and fighting with dignity."

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

World.title: West Bank: US journalist injured by Israeli settlers
World.content:
Washington Post journalist Heidi Levine said she was beaten by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank. Reporters Without Borders slammed the attack as "brazen violence."

Washington Post journalist Heidi Levine was injured on Friday after being attacked by a group of Israeli settlers while on assignment in the occupied West Bank, according to the publication.

The Post said that the incident took place near the village of Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah, and involved "dozens of masked Israeli settlers" who attacked Palestinian villagers gathering the autumn olive harvest.

Washington Post says Levine clearly identifiable

Matt Murray, the paper's executive editor, called for an investigation into the incident.

"This morning, a Washington Post photographer, Heidi Levine, was attacked by Israeli settlers while reporting in the West Bank,” Murray said. Levine is a US citizen.

"She was wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist. While we are relieved that Heidi has received medical care and is safe, we are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities."

Speaking from a hospital bed later, veteran photojournalist Levine, who is in stable condition, said: "I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn't even be here, because they just kept kicking me and kicking me."

Blogger Andrey Khrzhanovskiy filmed the incident and told The Post that the settlers beat Levine with sticks while journalists and villagers were forced back.

West Bank olive harvest under attack To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Netanyahu's office says facts 'remain unclear'

The office of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu issued a statement saying it was not yet clear exactly what had happened.

"The facts surrounding the confrontation near Abu Falah, during which Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine was allegedly assaulted, remain unclear and are under investigation.

Netanyahu's office went on to say there were reports that "some 200 Arabs and far-left activists confronted approximately 40 Israeli youths." It said that there was footage of masked individuals from both sides "hurling objects."

"Other footage appears to show Levine knocked down and immediately helped to her feet by the same unidentified individual. The investigation must establish the facts, including who initiated the violence," Netanyahu's office said.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said that both the IDF and the Israel Border Police attended the scene.

"Foreign media personnel were present at the scene and a female journalist was injured during the confrontation. All details of the incident will be examined. Upon arriving to the scene, the forces acted to disperse the confrontation using riot dispersal means," the IDF said in a statement on X.

"The IDF strongly condemns this incident. Attempts to incite friction between populations undermine security in the area," the IDF said.

Palestinian American watches as West Bank house under siege To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US condemns 'criminal violence'

The US said it condemned "criminal violence by any party" in the occupied West Bank.

"We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and support appropriate investigations as well as legal accountability for those responsible," the AFP news agency quoted a State Department official as saying, on condition of anonymity, without directly criticizing the settlers.

"The Department has reached out to the Washington Post to offer consular assistance," the official told AFP.

US Democratic Senator Chris Coons of Connecticut, in a post on X, called the attack "appalling" and said "there must be swift justice and accountability for perpetrators of violent extremism in the West Bank, which stands in the way of regional peace and is escalating an already unpredictable and dangerous situation."

EU to impose new sanctions against Israeli settlers To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Attack condemned by press association and advocacy group

The Foreign Press Association represents international media in Israel and the Palestinian territories and said Levine's passport, phone, wallet and equipment were stolen by the attackers.

"This is the latest in a long line of violent attacks by Israeli settlers against journalists and other civilians in the occupied West Bank," it said.

"Yet our repeated calls for action to confront this lawlessness have been ignored by Israeli authorities," it added.

International press watchdog Reporters Without Borders strongly condemned the attack and called on Israeli authorities to "put an end to this impunity and prosecute the perpetrators of this heinous assault."

"This brazen violence... is evidence of the impunity with which extremist Jewish settlers operate, often under the protection of Israeli armed forces," added the advocacy group, known by its French initials RSF.

World.title: White House press secretary Zacharia exiting role after short tenure
World.content:
Zacharia, having served only five days in the role, is now the shortest-serving press secretary in White House history. Her departure follows a rocky debut at the podium and controversy surrounding her background.

New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is on the way out from her position, The New York Times and other US news outlets reported on Friday.

Zacharia's departure leaves Trump without a key spokesperson with a little over two weeks before November's midterm elections.

Zacharia's week on the job

Zacharia started her new role just five days ago, taking over for Karoline Leavitt. She had a nervy first White House briefing with journalists on Tuesday, fielding just three questions and leaving the podium after fewer than 14 minutes.

The White House website said later that day that "Katie Zacharia delivered a commanding inaugural press briefing as the 37th White House Press Secretary."

Earlier on Friday, President Donald Trump suggested that Zacharia might be leaving. "I told her: 'I think you're better off being happy, and I'm not sure you can ever be ​happy in this stuff.' There's nothing easy about this stuff," Trump ​told reporters.

He added: "I said to her honestly, 'If ​I ‌were you, I'd reconsider... think about it. But I would reconsider.'"

Controversy over Zacharia's legal background

Last Friday, Trump announced Zacharia's appointment as the new press secretary. However, she became embroiled in controversy when it was revealed that her earlier claims of being a lawyer were false.

Until last week, Zacharia was a commentator for conservative outlets Fox News and Newsmax. She also advised Trump Media and Technology, the company behind Trump's Truth Social platform.

Zacharia has also long described herself as a lawyer, but her credentials remain unverified. While she graduated from law school, neither she nor the White House has provided evidence that she passed the bar exam in any state or in China, where she worked for a large law firm years ago.

According to her LinkedIn profile, Zacharia was an associate at Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from 2011 to 2013. She was also a general counsel at Fix California, an advocacy group founded by Trump ally Richard Grenell, from 2024 to 2025. Grenell served as acting director of national intelligence in 2020.

Zacharia earned her law degree from Pepperdine University in 2011. While nearly all licensed US lawyers first obtain a law degree, law school graduates cannot legally practice law in the US without first being admitted to a state bar.
