World.title: Dinamo Beats Anderlecht With 96th-Minute Penalty
World.content:
Dinamo beat Anderlecht 1-0 in the second round of the Europa League, with Dion Drena Beljo scoring the only goal from the penalty spot in the 96th minute. It was Dinamo’s first goal in this season’s Europa League, after a goalless draw with Israel’s Hapoel in the opening round.

Dinamo started strongly and pressed the visitors from the first whistle. Anderlecht soon settled, however, and there were good chances at both ends in the first half.

Luka Stojković had the first in the 15th minute. Left unmarked after a Hoxha cross, he was in an excellent position ten meters from goal, but the ball took an awkward spin off an Anderlecht defender and he could not make clean contact.

What followed was a spell in which Anderlecht could easily have scored more than once. In the 21st minute the Belgian side hit the crossbar twice in the same attack, with Dinamo goalkeeper Dominik Kotarski getting a touch to the second effort.

In the 28th minute Tristan Degreef shot from close range, unmarked, but Kotarski again reacted superbly to keep it out. Dinamo responded towards the end of the half, when Iker Almena found himself well placed from a cut-back but failed to hit the target.

Dinamo created three very good chances in the second half. The best fell to Arber Hoxha in the 81st minute, who was through on goal before Anderlecht full-back Barry got back to knock the ball away from behind him. The home side still found a winner at the death.

Substitute Dani Rodríguez struck the arm of Anderlecht left-back Oleg Reabciuk, and after a VAR review Dinamo were awarded a penalty, which Beljo sent down the middle.

The goal and the win go a long way to improving the picture for Dinamo. They are now 14th in the table, a play-off place, with six matches still to play in the league phase. For Anderlecht, it was a second defeat in this season’s Europa League.

World.title: Hero from Omiš Who Saved 60 People From a Fire Receives Bravery Award
World.content:
October the 16th, 2026 – A hero from a small coastal settlement near Omiš who saved 60 people from a massive fire has received a well-deserved bravery award.

Milan Balić, a young man from Stanići near Omiš, selflessly saved around 60 people with two boats when the fire broke out back in August. He has since received the Croatian Grand Security Award for bravery. Index reports that the ceremony in Opatija he modestly said that he simply found himself at the scene of the fire and emphasised that many other people also took part in the rescue. The recognition was presented to him as part of the 20th Conference of Croatian Security Managers at the Hotel Ambasador in Opatija.

The Croatian Association of Security Managers (HUMS) otherwise awarded prizes in 14 categories, and among the winners are also the City of Split, the State Hydro-meteorological Institute, APIS IT, the City of Zagreb and RTL Danas.

“it was sheer horror”

“What can I tell you, is that it was sheer horror. It was pure horror. Everything started from the upper side of the road and we hoped it wouldn’t cross to the lower side. But the fire passed across. People were running towards the sea, which was the most logical thing to do in that situation,” Balić said at the time.

“My house is among the first by the shoreline and I tried to save it as much as I could. Luckily, nothing happened to it. People were coming down to the beach, everyone was. Older people, young people, children. I decided then and there during the fire to take my boat and try to help them” he added. He set off on the rescue with two vessels. He tied the smaller boat to the larger one and loaded a total of 60 people onto them, among them children, elderly and injured persons. “I put the older men in the small boat, and the women, children and elderly people in the large one. There was really great panic,” Balić said.

“people were screaming from the beach”

The journey to Omiš was extremely dangerous. A strong bora was blowing, and because of the dense smoke visibility was almost non-existent. During the voyage Balić was especially afraid for the people in the smaller boat he was towing. “After we boarded, people were still shouting from the beach. I would have liked to help everyone, but there simply wasn’t any more space. While we were towing the smaller boat, I was most afraid that it wouldn’t sink, because there were also injured people in it,” he said. The drama did not end even upon arrival in Omiš. When docking in the town harbour the smaller boat capsized and people ended up in the sea.

“Everyone fell into the sea. Luckily, the army and special police were there and helped us pull them all out,” Balić said. For the bravery shown during that action he has now received the Croatian Grand Security Award in the category Brave Act in the Service of Security. At the award presentation, he modestly thanked all those gathered for the recognition, stressing that at the moment of the fire he simply found himself at that place. He emphasised that credit for the rescue also belongs to numerous other colleagues who took part in the action.

World.title: Croatia Should Never be a Cheap Destination, Claim Experts
World.content:
October the 16th, 2026 – Croatia should under no circumstances ever be permitted to be a cheap Mediterranean destination claim experts, but just how far has it gone the other way?

Poreč has become the centre of discussion on the direction of Croatian tourism, with a special emphasis placed on the role of hospitality operators in the development of the tourism sector. Boris Bilas reports for Glas Istre that the Parentium Plava Laguna hotel was the host of the 38th Congress of Hospitality Operators and Tourism Workers of the Croatian Chamber of Trades and Crafts (HOK). It gathered together a record number of crafts owners, tourism sector leaders and numerous high-ranking state officials.

istria generates a third of total croatian tourist traffic

The central themes of this year’s three-day gathering focused on preserving profitability in conditions of strong growth in input costs, the chronic shortage of qualified labour, and upcoming legislative changes. Opening the congress, HOK president Dalibor Kratohvil pointed out that 12,094 crafts currently operate actively in the Guild of Hospitality Operators and Tourism Workers, which is 140 more than last year. Nevertheless, he warned of the harsh economic reality on the ground.

“Hospitality operators are the last in the price-formation chain and do not realise any extra profits. While input costs of energy, supplies and labour are relentlessly rising, our margins are constantly falling. We have not raised prices in order to get rich, but exclusively for bare survival and the preservation of jobs,” Kratohvil said, emphasising that HOK continues to insist uncompromisingly on the introduction of the right to a full old-age pension while continuing to perform a craft activity.

The host of the meeting, president of the Chamber of Trades and Crafts of Istria County Robert Momić, proudly highlighted the role of Istria, which generates as much as one third of total Croatian tourist traffic with 29.5 million overnight stays realised in the first nine months.

“In the area of Istria we have almost 12,000 craftsmen, of whom 1,200 are directly in hospitality. Top-quality tourism does not happen here by chance; it is created, and our enogastronomy sector is a key motive for guests’ arrival. Thanks to synergy with local self-government and tourist boards, we have a clear strategy for a bright future of the profession,” Momić stated. Deputy County Prefect of Istria Jessica Acquavita addressed the far-from-easy reality of the labour shortage, emphasising that foreign workers have become an economic necessity without which the tourism system could no longer function.

language issues in istria

“We’re currently facing the complex challenges of language barriers and preserving the recognisable Istrian hospitality. In Istria County we are thinking seriously about this and have launched an initiative to establish a regional support network for foreign workers. We want these employees to become part of the local community as quickly and painlessly as possible, because by facilitating their integration we are directly investing in the stability of your business and preserving authenticity. Sustainable tourism is a balance between economic growth and social responsibility,” Deputy County Prefect Jessica Acquavita said.

tourists are spending more and more

Director of the Croatian National Tourist Board (HTZ) Kristjan Staničić stressed that the success of the season must no longer be measured exclusively by the number of arrivals and overnight stays, but by the overall economic effects on the economy. In doing so he exclusively presented the first data from the new comprehensive TOMAS survey that HTZ conducted in cooperation with the Institute for Tourism.

“The average daily expenditure of tourists in Croatia has risen to €160 per person per overnight stay, which is an increase of as much as 16 percent compared to a few years ago. Absolute record holders are guests from the USA who on average spend around €280 per day, followed by the British with €248. This justifies our strong investments in air traffic and digital promotion towards those emitting markets,” Staničić revealed. He also highlighted that as many as 68 percent of tourists choose mid-price restaurants, which means that “value for money” must remain at the centre of the offer.

The most important political message of the congress came from State Secretary in the Ministry of Tourism and Sport Monika Udovičić, who directly responded to the discontent of hospitality operators regarding complicated administrative obligations and the constant updating of price lists that was imposed on the sector this summer.

price increases remain a serious issue

“We’ve heard your voice and your opinion. The state’s intention was to prevent uncontrolled price increases that also affect you yourselves through procurement, but decisions in practice must not be unenforceable nor further stifle your business. That is precisely why those disputed rulebooks have been put out of force. New acts are being prepared and we will ensure enough time for us to discuss them together,” Udovičić announced.

She also addressed stories about Croatia’s expensiveness and prices in tourism and sent a clear message that Croatia must under no circumstances be the cheapest country on the Mediterranean.

“Croatia should not and must under no circumstances be a cheap destination on the Mediterranean. Our competition such as Italy or Greece is investing strongly and investing a lot. We must be a destination in which the price is fully justified by top quality and an authentic experience, and that is precisely what our craftsmen offer in their taverns and restaurants,” the State Secretary concluded, announcing that the new Hospitality Activity Act, which enters into force at the beginning of 2027, will bring a more effective fight against unfair competition and unregistered business, as well as simpler, digital procedures for all legal craftsmen.

istria’s 180-year-old tourism brochure

Poreč Mayor Loris Peršurić recalled a historical curiosity, a fascinating 180-year-old tourist brochure kept in the Poreč museum, proving that the tradition of hospitality across the region of Istria has some very deep roots. “Behind the success of Poreč stands not only natural beauty, but primarily local people, people who own crafts and their warm hospitality,” Peršurić concluded.

World.title: Turks to Purchase Uljanik for €12.05 Million
World.content:
October the 16th, 2026 – The Turks are set to purchase Uljanik for €12.05 million. The Kuzey Star Shipyard will now officially take over 97.13% of the shares of Brodogradnja 1856.

With the agreement on the transfer of business shares, Morski reports that the moves brings the months-long sales process to a close and opens a new chapter in the revitalisation of Pula’s shipbuilding industry.

The aforementioned Turkish company offered a purchase price for Uljanik of €12.05 million, which is higher than the initially sought €11.08 million. CERP therefore readily accepted Kuzey Star’s binding offer at the beginning of September, while the second received offer from the Luxembourg company Mira Finance Holding was not accepted because the payment of the prescribed guarantee wasn’t recorded in CERP’s account. Given that the buyer is from a country that is not within the EU, before the actual conclusion of the contract, it was also necessary to carry out a foreign investment screening procedure in order to determine whether the investment poses a risk to national security and public order.

the continuation of shipbuilding has been ensured

The key condition of the contract concerns the retention of the core shipbuilding activity, the construction, repair and overhaul of ships and floating objects, across the entire area of the maritime domain under concession. By taking over the company, the Turkish investor obtains the existing shipbuilding infrastructure and concession rights for the use of the maritime domain in the Bay of Pula, but not ownership of the entire land and sea space.

Minister of the Economy Ante Šušnjar emphasised the importance of this decision for this previously less than stable Croatian industry: “By signing this contract, Croatia is approaching the completion of the process of revitalising the shipbuilding industry in the Pula area. Through its decisions the Government has preserved the possibility of continuing shipbuilding in Pula. The further development of Uljanik will depend on the business decisions, investments and contracted work of the new investor.”

experience and existing business ties

The director of Uljanik Brodogradnja 1856, Samir Hadžić, assessed as positive the fact that the new owner comes precisely from the shipbuilding sector. The Kuzey Star group owns shipyards in the Turkish cities of Tuzla and Yalova and has extensive experience in the construction, overhaul, maintenance and conversion of ships, as well as in projects related to the energy sector.

In addition, the Turkish company is already well acquainted with the possibilities of the Pula shipyard. Namely, Kuzey Star and Uljanik are already cooperating on the project to complete Newbuilding (Novogradjna) 526 (a livestock carrier which had a hull that had stood unfinished for years), which gave the Turkish partner direct insight into the available infrastructure and the capacities of the workers. In a series of works, the Pula shipyard maintained production activity also through work on yacht hulls and the completion of a fishing vessel.

Kuzey Star is otherwise already present on the wider Croatian market, work on an additional re-gasification module intended to increase the capacity of the floating LNG terminal in Omišalj was carried out at their shipyard. In the recent period Uljanik Brodogradnja 1856 employed around 230 workers, while together with subcontractors between 250 and 300 people participated in production.

World.title: Estonia's Soviet-era summer cottage culture to become museum exhibit
World.content:
Built to strict Soviet rules, they stand apart from what came before and after, embodying both state leisure and private dreams.

Nearly 50,000 were built between 1950 and 1980. Now art historians from the Estonian Academy of Arts and ethnologists from the University of Tartu have joined forces to understand this heritage — what people built, and how they spent their time there.

The classic Soviet-era suvila design followed very strict dimensions. Source: ERR

"The privately owned summer cottage is a type of building constructed en masse during the Soviet era that shows how the state sought to create opportunities for working citizens to enjoy leisure time," said Epp Lankots, dean of EKA, on "Tähelepanu! Tegemist on teadusega."

Dagmar Ingi, head of rural architecture at the Estonian Open Air Museum, stressed the human-centered approach. "For me as an ethnologist, it is extremely important that we study the person and their relationship with their summer cottage," she said.

Another standard suvila design was this A-frame variety. Source: ERR

The researchers spend their summers across Estonia, talking to owners and documenting history. Interviews are free-form, closer to conversation than survey. They examine the whole property — garden beds, small structures, interiors — and spatial specialists measure and draw up plans. "We photograph them if people allow us to, inspect the interiors and draw up site plans so that, at some point, if someone wants to study this subject, all this material will have been properly preserved," Ingi said.

They also dig into archives for rare types, like terraced summer cottages. Owners bring out old photo albums, receipts and construction plans kept for decades — insight into everyday building practices and people's ingenuity.

A more idiosyncratic design of suvila. Source: ERR

The researchers approach every participant without prejudice. "For us, it does not matter what work they do or what kind of life they have lived. Every person's story is important, significant and interesting precisely as they have lived it," Ingi said.

The work is limited by time and the subjectivity of memory. Decades-old events arrive filtered through nostalgia, lending emotional color but diminishing factual accuracy.

The knowledge won't gather dust. "The aim of this project is actually to find a Soviet-era summer cottage that can be relocated to the Open Air Museum, where we can tell the story of a summer cottage built in the 1960s or 1970s, together with the story of the person who owned it, what they dreamed of and what they needed the summer cottage for," Ingi concluded.

World.title: Wind farm bonus unconstitutional, NGO says as ministry pushes plan
World.content:
An NGO says a planned bonus to for local governments for developing wind-farms within their jurisdictions is unconstitutional.

MTÜ Kinnisvara Kaitseks is arguing the bonus breaches local government autonomy. Economic Affairs Minister Erkki Keldo (Reform) says communities that back wind parks should be paid.

Onshore wind has stalled at local level, something which the bonus attempts to address

"I've been working as a lawyer for nearly 30 years, and in my view such a regulation is unconstitutional," said Tiia Raudmägi, board member of MTÜ Kinnisvara Kaitseks. "This directly conflicts with local government autonomy, which is enshrined in the constitution."

"This directly conflicts with local government autonomy, which is enshrined in the constitution."

"The wind bonus money goes to improving the local community's living environment and services. Investments go into sports facilities, education, culture — but that's for the local community to decide, because that community is ready to contribute to the country's general welfare and supply security," Keldo said.

Estonia has been pursuing wind energy and other renewables in an effort to break away from fossil fuel sources and at present has around 700 MW of onshore wind farm capacity. However no new parks are due to complete this year or next, and some regions have rejected plans to construct wind farms. For instance Järva Municipality at the start of 2025 rejected 109 turbines after 1,600 signatures while later that year, authorities in Haapsalu opposed a 10-turbine park near the Matsalu nature reserve.

World.title: Pärnu to swap public recycling for curbside pickup in 2027
World.content:
Pärnu is switching to curbside pickup for sorted household waste in 2027, eliminating public paper and recycling dumpsters from across the city.

Pärnu City Council unanimously approved the city's 2027–2031 waste management plan on Thursday, paving the way for a new system that shifts recycling from public dumpsters to curbside pickup.

Under the new plan, only public glass collection dumpsters will remain. Deputy Mayor Robert Kiviselg said producer responsibility organizations (PROs) will cover much of the cost of the new system.

"Under state rules, [households] will have to pay 50 cents per quarter for paper and cardboard and another 50 cents for the remaining mixed packaging," he said.

Residents will be free to choose between special bags and dedicated recycling bins.

Public recycling dumpsters have often been plagued with issues, including considerable amounts of waste being dumped in the wrong dumpsters. Curbside pickup, however, will make it easier to ensure residents are sorting their waste correctly.

Ivo Jaanisoo, deputy secretary general at the Ministry of Climate, said many households across the country have already gotten better at sorting their waste.

"Since last year, we've been offering separate biowaste pickup right from people's homes, and that's already shown results," he said.

Pärnu's new waste management plan will take effect next fall.

World.title: Bedroom window requirement upheld by justice chancellor
World.content:
Estonia's justice chancellor has found that requiring bedrooms to have openable windows and natural light is constitutional, even in homes with mechanical ventilation.

Then-justice chancellor Ülle Madise, now Estonia's president, issued the opinion after attorney Carry Plaks challenged a regulation requiring every living room, bedroom, workroom and kitchen to have at least one openable window and natural light.

Plaks argued the rule excessively restricted property rights and imposed unnecessary architectural and financial burdens, preventing windowless interior spaces even in buildings with mechanical ventilation from being used as bedrooms.

In her response, Madise said the requirement serves a clear and important purpose: ensuring a safe and healthy living environment suitable for round-the-clock use.

"People's health can change, and someone who is ill may have to spend much of the day in their bedroom or remain in bed for an extended period," she explained, noting that natural light and the ability to open a window to air out the room are especially important in such cases.

An openable window also serves as a backup if the mechanical ventilation system fails.

Costs do not make the rule unconstitutional

Plaks also noted that the regulation, issued by the economy and infrastructure minister, sets no minimum window size. Madise stressed, however, that the requirement is not a formality: it calls for sufficient natural light, ruling out token solutions that fall short of accepted building practices, such as attic-style spaces.

She acknowledged that windows can affect a building's layout, construction costs and how a property can be used. But such costs do not by themselves make a requirement unconstitutional.

"All building requirements — whether for fire safety, accessibility, ventilation or energy efficiency — can increase construction costs or limit how space is used," the justice chancellor said.

She said the Ministry of Climate, as the policymaker which oversees the sector, could assess whether advances in construction technology and modern housing practices might eventually allow windowless living spaces.

World.title: MP: Eesti 200 should 'lick its wounds' and sit out 2027 elections
World.content:
Eesti 200 MPs Ando Kiviberg and Toomas Uibo say their struggling coalition party should skip next March's Riigikogu elections and instead focus on rebuilding for 2031.

Kiviberg told ERR he has not decided whether to run for reelection in March, but if the party decides to run, he would have to act as a team player.

Still, he sees little sense in the party throwing money away at this point, believing Eesti 200 should sit out the 2027 elections instead.

"The party should lick its wounds, do a little soul-searching and commit to preparing properly for 2031," Kiviberg said. He added that he has already discussed the issue with other party members but expects a final decision to be made at Sunday's party council meeting.

Party whip Toomas Uibo, meanwhile, said voters have already made up their minds about Eesti 200, as their rating hit a historic 1.3 percent low in Norstat polls earlier this month.

"I don't know if miracles like this happen, but right now I don't see any point in wasting taxpayer money on running in the elections," he admitted.

While members may still decide on a different course on Sunday, Uibo likewise believes Eesti 200 should instead regroup and focus on the 2031 elections.

Toomas Uibo. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

Potential Greens merger raises questions

Eesti 200 and the nonparliamentary Estonian Greens are discussing a possible merger, but Kiviberg said this may not necessarily be the right move. "Several party members I've spoken with share my views," he said.

Uibo noted he was unsure whether the two parties have enough in common to unite.

"Of course, you can't expect two different parties to come together and agree on absolutely everything," he said, adding that the question is whether both parties are willing to set enough aside and compromise. "It's still unclear how much common ground we have."

Kiviberg nonetheless ruled out running on another party's ticket next spring and said he has received no such offers. He said he remains committed to Eesti 200 because he believes its ideas are necessary and sound, and will ultimately benefit the country. The question, he said, is how effectively the party has put those ideas into practice.

While Uibo and Kiviberg argued that Eesti 200 should sit out the upcoming elections, fellow MP Peeter Tali told ERR he currently intends to run.

"A politician has to run," Tali said. "If they're no longer a politician, then they don't have to."

World.title: Defense official: Front heats up, energy truce fails as US-Kyiv strain grows
World.content:
The recent US–Russia diesel deal and a failed energy truce have strained ties with Kyiv at a time when fighting has been escalating at the front, the defense ministry said.

The ministry's intelligence review points to growing friction between Washington and Kyiv as battlefield intensity rises alongside the stalled energy ceasefire.

Speaking at the regular Ministry of Defense Friday press conference, Gert Kaju, head of the ministry's defense readiness department, said a number of significant events had taken place at the strategic level over the past week. He said it became known last Friday that the U.S. had issued the Russian Federation a temporary permit to supply diesel fuel to its market and to the global markets. "According to the expectations of the U.S. leadership, Russia should supply 3 million tons of diesel fuel as quickly as possible, which the U.S. leadership believes should lead to a decline in fuel prices on the U.S. domestic market," Kaju said.

Just over a week earlier the U.S. president had announced a ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia so far as attacks on energy facilities went, but it later emerged that this was a ceasefire arrangement which neither side had agreed to.

Ukraine did attempt to observe the energy ceasefire and refrained from striking Russian oil refineries for three days on the condition that Russia stop attacking Ukraine's electricity generation facilities and transmission networks.

Russia, however, interpreted the agreement as a suspension of attacks only on oil refineries and fuel transportation infrastructure only, and continued striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure. According to Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, the energy ceasefire proposed by President Donald Trump had not been specified in detail.

The U.S.-Russia diesel supply agreement drew international criticism, some of it from Kyiv. In response, the U.S. raised the question of the need to hold elections and change the government in Ukraine. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy agreed to hold elections on the condition that a 60-day ceasefire be established, but Moscow refused. Russia's leadership believed Ukraine would use the ceasefire to rebuild its forces, and according to Peskov, Moscow was prepared to establish a ceasefire for only 24 hours.

Since Russia had not observed the energy ceasefire, President Zelenskyy announced on October 15 that Ukraine would resume strikes against Russian oil refineries, saying it would be prepared to consider suspending such strikes only if it received assistance in strengthening its missile defense capabilities.

Ukraine counterattacked in the Lyman and Sloviansk sectors in Donetsk oblast

Nearly 230 combat engagements took place per day on the front line over the past week, a rise on the previous week. The most intense fighting took place in Donetsk oblast in the Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka directions, followed by the Huliaipole direction in Zaporizhzhia oblast, the Southern Slobozhanshchyna direction in Kharkiv oblast and the Lyman sector in Donetsk oblast.

Ukrainian counterattacks took place mainly in the Lyman and Sloviansk directions in Donetsk oblast, the Oleksandrivka area in Dnipropetrovsk oblast and in Sumy oblast. Ukrainian forces pushed back Russian units in the Sloviansk and Kramatorsk sections and strengthened the front line in that sector.

The Russian armed forces' objective remains to reach the borders of Donetsk, Luhansk and Zaporizhzhia oblasts and restore their positions in Dnipropetrovsk oblast, while simultaneously attempting to expand the territory under their control in Sumy and Kharkiv oblasts. At the same time, the Russian Federation lost an average of 1,600 military personnel per day. Russian armed forces' losses remained above 10,000 troops per week, marking the seventh consecutive week that losses had reached this level, the ministry said.

The fighting was also accompanied by extensive airstrikes despite the recent stalled truce. The Russian Federation attacked various targets in at least 19 Ukrainian oblasts (out of a total of 24). Targets of long-range precision strikes included critical infrastructure, residential buildings, government, commercial, educational and medical institutions, the transportation system, the fuel industry and the energy system.

Russia intensively attacks energy infrastructure

The number of strikes against Ukraine's energy infrastructure has steadily increased in recent weeks and multiplied in Kyiv. Between October 4 and 11, Russia attacked Ukraine's energy infrastructure 196 times and its fuel infrastructure 20 times, while Ukrainian energy workers restored electricity supplies to 1.9 million households.

Intensive attacks continued overnight on October 13-14 in Kyiv and Kharkiv oblasts, where 26 energy infrastructure facilities were damaged, including three combined heat and power plants in Kyiv, and according to President Zelenskyy, 600,000 people were left without electricity.

Ukraine responded with extensive long-range strikes. Between October 8 and 10, attacks hit Russian oil refineries in Omsk oblast, Bashkortostan and the Komi Republic, an oil terminal in Rostov oblast and a distribution station in Samara oblast. Attacks resumed on October 15, when a long-range strike hit the Ryazan oil refinery.

In the 242nd week of the war, Ukrainian long-range strikes targeted Yandex data centers in Ryazan, Kaluga and Vladimir oblasts and a Sberbank data center in Saratov oblast for the first time.

Ukraine also attacked companies important to Russia's military-industrial complex in Tver, Nizhny Novgorod and Rostov oblasts, as well as military targets and transport routes in occupied and border areas.

Away from the front line, Russia continued its hybrid activities against countries supporting Ukraine. The Danish Security and Intelligence Service also warned that Russia had launched operations against Danish companies supporting Ukraine in repelling the aggression.

"At the same time, the Finnish Security Intelligence Service noted that Russia poses a real, although not yet immediate, threat to the country's defense industry, which the agency considers an expected development, as Finnish companies operate in the same security environment as the rest of Europe," Kaju added.

World.title: Pärnu named European City of Sport for 2027
World.content:
Pärnu has been awarded the European City of Sport 2027 title by the European Capitals and Cities of Sport Federation, the city announced.

This means a second Estonian city has been awarded the title in three years, after Tallinn held the role last year.

Mayor Siim Suursild said the recognition reflects work done so far but that the most important work lies ahead, with a focus on getting more people active.

"We are very pleased and have reason to be proud! The European assessment committee has given Pärnu the European City of Sport 2027 title. This is recognition of our work so far and confirms that we are moving in the right direction. But the most important work is still ahead," Suursild said via the city's website.

"For us, the European City of Sport title is not an end in itself. What matters is what we can do better in Pärnu through it — bring more people out to move, support our sports community and create opportunities for an active lifestyle to be a natural part of everyday life," he continued.

Pärnu has been awarded the title for next year. Source: Pärnu City Government.

The title is awarded by the European Capitals and Cities of Sport Federation, which works as a partner of the European Commission. It recognizes cities with strong sports infrastructure, the capacity to host sporting events and diverse opportunities for residents to take part in sport.

In early October, the federation's assessment committee visited Pärnu, toured its sports facilities and met local sports representatives.

"We got a very good overview of Pärnu and its sporting opportunities. Both the sports facilities and Pärnu's superb natural environment impressed me, creating very good opportunities for movement. Pärnu has a lot to offer as a sports city," said committee member and federation secretary general Hugo Alonso.

The European City of Sport is an annual recognition awarded by ACES Europe, a Brussels-based non-profit that works with EU institutions to promote sport, and is one tier of a scheme that also names European Capitals of Sport for larger cities and Towns or Islands of Sport for smaller communities. Tallinn was European Capital of Sport in 2025.

World.title: 52nd OIC Council of Foreign Ministers convenes in Baghdad with 55 nations
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The 52nd session of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) officially opened in the Iraqi capital, Baghdad, on Saturday, October 17, 2026. Convening under the banner of advancing regional solidarity, peace, and sustainable development, the two-day summit brings together diplomatic delegations representing 55 member states and observer nations.

The spokesperson for the 52nd ministerial session, Ambassador Hassanein Kamil, announced in a formal statement that proceedings commenced following the arrival of all participating international delegations in Baghdad.

The commencement follows an announcement by the Iraqi Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Friday confirming the completion of all logistical, technical, and security arrangements required to host the high-profile multilateral convention, which runs through October 17–18.

Baghdad’s stewardship of the OIC foreign ministers’ summit reinforces Iraq’s proactive diplomatic posture aimed at bridging regional divides and serving as a neutral convening hub for dialogue.

Ministerial agendas across the two-day meetings are set to address collective security frameworks, cross-border economic integration, humanitarian response mechanisms, and coordinated diplomatic strategies to de-escalate ongoing conflicts across the wider Islamic world.

World.title: AI is coming for every company, Nvidia boss says
World.content:
Stockholm – Artificial intelligence will ultimately become a key aspect of all companies, the head of AI chip giant Nvidia said during a visit to Stockholm, where he urged Europe to ramp up its AI industry.

“Every single company will be an AI company eventually. Every single industry will be impacted by AI,” Jensen Huang told an event late Thursday, part of a European tour that includes a Nvidia-hosted conference in Berlin next week.

“The important thing for us is to recognise that Europe needs to build out the entire stack,” he said, referring to the AI technology chain from data centres to chatbots and other apps.

Speaking later to AFP, Huang said his company had invested $8 billion in Europe over the past year.

“We’ve strategically invested in different parts of that ecosystem, really high quality companies that we believe could help lift it, the whole ecosystem in Europe,” he said, citing the British data centre and AI cloud provider Nscale and the Dutch cloud provider Nebius as examples.

“In the last one year, we’ve invested $8 billion already. We have another couple of billion dollars in the pipeline,” he added. “We’re helping Europe create the AI ecosystem.”

Huang was in Stockholm for the launch of Sferical One, a Swedish supercomputer using Nvidia chips that will keep sensitive Swedish data and expertise in the country.

During his visit, Volvo Cars also announced it was expanding its partnership with Nvidia to improve safety technology in its planned self-driving vehicles.

World.title: Chelsea captain James has knee surgery
World.content:
London – Chelsea captain Reece James has undergone successful knee surgery, the Premier League club announced on Friday.

The England international has missed Chelsea’s past two league games — a 3-0 defeat by Brentford and a 5-1 win over Bournemouth.

“The 26-year-old was absent from Saturday’s 5-1 victory over Bournemouth at Stamford Bridge while medical assessments took place following the injury suffered in training,” the club said in a statement.

“Those assessments confirmed surgery would be the required course of action.

“Reece has already begun his road to recovery and will be supported by the club’s medical department at Cobham during this rehabilitation phase.”

Chelsea are sixth in the Premier League ahead of Saturday’s visit to Everton.

World.title: Asian stocks rise as tech bounces from rout, Warsh upbeat on AI
World.content:
Hong Kong – Most Asian markets bounced Friday after the previous day’s tech rout fuelled by concerns over the AI boom, which Federal Reserve boss Kevin Warsh said offered huge benefits to the global economy.

Seoul and Tokyo enjoyed healthy gains in early exchanges boosted by chipmakers SK hynix and Kioxia, after having been pummelled Thursday as investors bailed out of the once-dominant AI sector.

The selling had been fuelled by forecast-beating US inflation data that ramped up bets on Fed interest rate hikes, as well as concerns about the financial health of data centre operator CoreWeave owing to its huge debt pile.

The New Jersey firm — which has borrowed heavily to finance hefty purchases of pricey semiconductor chips from Nvidia — tanked 15.5 percent Wednesday in the US as yields on some of its bonds soared, reflecting heightened angst over its future.

That added to concerns about the whole AI-tech complex, but Nvidia chief Jensen Huang on Thursday lifted spirits by defending the company and its health.

“CoreWeave’s strength is improving every day,” he told Bloomberg. “I’m optimistic. Their cost of capital is actually decreasing.”

CoreWeave’s shares climbed almost six percent.

Huang’s “defence of CoreWeave’s financial position was enough to pull the NeoCloud complex off the floor, drag AI equities higher and give the broader market something resembling a pulse”, wrote SPI Asset Management’s Stephen Innes.

“One moment the market was pricing the possibility that the AI financing machine had started eating its own tail, the next it was listening to the high priest of the boom explain that the patient was getting stronger.

“AI Jesus had entered the trading room and, for a while at least, the machines found religion again.”

Seoul jumped more than two percent and Tokyo around 1.8 percent, though they slumped 7.6 percent and 4.9 percent respectively Thursday.

Hong Kong, Shanghai, Singapore, Taipei, Mumbai, Bangkok and Manila were also up.

Paris and Frankfurt opened higher but London fell.

Fed chief Warsh said Friday that AI was the “most consequential change” to the global economy in his lifetime, predicting its effects would be positive but the path forward “bumpy”.

At an event at the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok he said the AI investment boom would drive prices up in the short term, but “there really is, I think, a huge benefit to the global economy, to the US economy over the horizon”.

He also reiterated his previously stated belief that the technology would “make economies and countries that put it to good use more productive”.

But he added: “The path from where we are to there is likely to be a very bumpy one, bumpy in our understanding of the technology, bumpy because we really don’t know what the market structure is going to be of these new technologies.”

Shares in Jakarta tanked more than 11 percent — its heaviest loss since 1998 — after index compiler MSCI said it was “no longer appropriate” to maintain Indonesia’s emerging-market status, fuelling fears of an exodus of foreign investment.

The US firm said earlier this year that investors had raised concerns about “ongoing opacity in shareholding structures” as well as co-ordinated trading behaviour that affected price information.

Authorities said they had carried out changes but MSCI said Friday that investors had indicated the “sufficient progress has not been observed consistently across the Indonesian equity market”, adding “it considers Indonesia’s continued classification as an Emerging Market no longer appropriate”.

World.title: Trump’s new press secretary says China lacked ‘proper’ toilets
World.content:
Washington – White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia, who was appointed less than a week ago, said China lacked “proper toilets” in an interview that aired on Thursday.

Zacharia, 41, is already under scrutiny over her legal credentials, after giving an inconclusive answer about where she had passed the bar exam, a prerequisite for practicing law in the United States.

The press secretary, who previously lived in China, recalled in an interview that the perception in 2016 was that China would soon overtake the United States.

“We were all being told Hillary (Clinton) was going to win. The golden days or the glory days of America were over. That China was on the horizon,” Zacharia told right-wing influencer Jack Posobiec.

“I remember this very distinctly, having just come from China, thinking, ‘How is China the next country on the horizon? They don’t even have proper toilets,” she added.

There was no immediate comment from Chinese authorities.

Trump has boasted about his “great relationship” with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

During a Washington summit in September, the two leaders discussed topics ranging from AI and trade to the stalled war in Iran, and confirmed that they would meet for a third and fourth time this year.

Zacharia held her first White House press briefing on Tuesday and only answered questions from three journalists.

She succeeded Karoline Leavitt, a loyal Trump supporter and often combative spokesperson, who stepped down in August to care for her young children.

Zacharia has described herself as a lawyer and listed herself as general counsel of a California-based conservative nonprofit. She also said she had worked at a law firm in Beijing.

Asked about her legal background on Thursday, Zacharia said she had registered to take the bar exam but was then “distracted and overwhelmed” by plans to move with her husband to China.

Zacharia said that she did not retake the bar exam upon returning to the United States due to the birth of her first child.

World.title: Indonesian stocks dive 11% as MSCI weighs market reclassification
World.content:
Jakarta – Indonesian stocks plunged more than 11 percent Friday as index compiler MSCI said it was “no longer appropriate” to maintain the country’s emerging-market status, fuelling fears of an exodus of foreign investment.

The US firm said earlier this year that investors had raised concerns about “ongoing opacity in shareholding structures” as well as co-ordinated trading behaviour that affected price information.

Authorities in Jakarta said in April they had completed reforms, hoping to avoid the downgrade, which could deal a blow to government efforts to kickstart Southeast Asia’s biggest economy, and have a significant impact on investment decisions.

But on Friday MSCI said investors had indicated the “sufficient progress has not been observed consistently across the Indonesian equity market”.

“Despite the announced reforms, significant concerns remain around market dysfunction, including continued suspected coordinated trading behaviour and lack of evidence of meaningful enforcement.

“Accordingly, MSCI considers Indonesia’s continued classification as an Emerging Market no longer appropriate and is launching a consultation on a proposal to reclassify Indonesia as a Standalone Market.”

“A reclassification to Frontier Markets would not properly recognise the depth of the market problems,” it said.

A standalone classification could force investment funds tracking the MSCI’s emerging market indexes to sell Indonesian holdings.

Argentina, Lebanon and Palestine are among the markets with the designation, with none in Asia, according to Bloomberg.

The Jakarta Composite Index collapsed eight percent at the open, sparking a trading halt. When trading resumed it was down 11.1 percent, its heaviest fall since early 1998 and sitting at its lowest level since 2020.

The index has now fallen more than 40 percent since the start of the year.

– Rupiah weakens –

In reaction to the news, the Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) said it “respects MSCI’s independence in assessing and determining market classification based on its proprietary methodology”.

“However, considering the various progress and reform measures that have been taken, the IDX will request further clarification from MSCI regarding the basis for the considerations and assessments behind this announcement.

“We also need to emphasise that this MSCI announcement is still part of the consultation process, with input being accepted until April 30, 2027, and does not constitute a final decision.”

The rupiah dropped about 0.8 percent against the dollar to sit at around around 18,060, having hit 18,209 in June, its weakest level on record.

Erwin Gunawan Hutapea, the Indonesian central bank’s head of monetary management and securities, said the bank would take action to ensure stability of the rupiah, which had already tumbled around eight percent this year to a record low.

“Amid rising global risk-off sentiment, which has driven US dollar strengthening and put pressure on domestic financial markets, capital outflows from domestic portfolio assets are expected to continue.

“Bank Indonesia is committed to maintaining a presence in the market to uphold Rupiah exchange rate stability in line with its fundamentals and to ensure that market mechanisms function properly.”

The central bank had carried out several rate hikes earlier in the year to shore up the rupiah, after it came under pressure over the state of Southeast Asia’s biggest economy.

The bank is due to hold its next monetary policy meeting on Wednesday.

New York-based MSCI produces international indexes used by investors as a benchmark to balance their portfolios.

It has a significant impact on investment decisions through its flagship emerging markets index, which contains 1,200 companies with a market capitalisation more than $10 trillion.

Fund managers worldwide keep a close eye on what countries are included or excluded in MSCI’s indexes as that can trigger adjustments to their portfolios.

World.title: Iraq’s parliament approves new cabinet ministers
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — On Thursday, Iraq’s parliament confirmed 11 cabinet nominees and three deputy prime ministers, including Laith al-Khazali, a key member in Iran-backed Asaib Ahl al-Haq who faces US terrorist sanctions.

The nomination is a politically risky decision for Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi, whose administration is dealing with strained regional ties and severe economic challenges as a result of the continuing US-Israeli war against Iran.

Al-Khazali is the brother of Qais al-Khazali, the commander of Asaib Ahl al-Haq, which Washington listed as a foreign terrorist organization in 2020.

Both brothers were classified as specially designated global terrorists, and the US Treasury sanctioned them individually in 2019 for suspected participation in violence against Iraqi demonstrators.

Their US designations also included references to assaults on American troops, such as a 2007 operation that killed five US soldiers.

The parliamentary decision raises concerns about al-Khazali’s nomination and its ramifications for Baghdad’s relationship with Washington, especially as al-Zaidi wants to reinforce Iraq’s sovereignty and manage ties with neighboring nations.

Following the voting, Al-Zaidi advised the newly appointed ministers and deputy prime ministers to do their duties with competence and integrity.

The appointments come as Iraq faces a deteriorating economic crisis, with oil export interruptions and liquidity shortages putting strain on the government’s budget.

Al-Zaidi has declared a significant depreciation of the Iraqi dinar, warning that the government confronts unprecedented economic and security problems.

The presence of a US-sanctioned militia member in the government’s high leadership may hamper Baghdad’s attempts to preserve fruitful relations with Washington.

World.title: ‘Mixed feelings’: AI cracks centuries-old ciphers
World.content:
Tokyo – Napoleon Bonaparte ordered the wartime missive written in code, creating a puzzle that went unsolved for more than 200 years — until AI cracked it in a matter of hours.

Artificial intelligence is helping non-specialists unlock the secrets of historical sources, a trend described as a “turning point” in a field previously the preserve of scholars and dedicated hobbyists.

One new sleuth is Carter Church, a 27-year-old AI engineer who decrypted a 19th-century letter to one of Napoleon’s generals.

Without digital tools, the task could have taken weeks, but the latest model from ChatGPT-maker OpenAI broke the cipher in just six hours.

“What AI mostly brings is persistence,” Church told AFP, saying he felt “an unbelievable sense of satisfaction and excitement when I saw the result”.

The message from 1809 — detailing French and allied troops’ positions in two dozen lines of symbols, numbers and letters — had lain ignored in an online academic archive.

Because traditional, low-tech methods to crack ciphers are effective but time- and labour-intensive, historians “have more important problems to solve, so many ciphers like this often sit unattended”, said Church.

To find the solution, Church, who works at US cybersecurity firm SentinelOne, needed to learn “very little” about code-breaking techniques or the historical period.

He spent some evenings going over it, then consulted Japanese patent engineer Satoshi Tomokiyo, who maintains an online list of unsolved ciphers, to verify it.

“2026 will be remembered as a turning point for codebreaking of historical ciphers,” Tomokiyo wrote on his website Cryptiana, a go-to resource for the small but enthusiastic global community of amateur cryptographers.

– ‘Mixed feelings’ –

Researchers were already developing AI models to break ciphers, but the public release of state-of-the-art generalist tools has unleashed dozens of new solutions.

Although Church used OpenAI’s most powerful model, GPT-6 Astra, other people have used top offerings from rival US lab Anthropic instead.

Tomokiyo said that since mid-September, most of the ciphers on his list have been cracked using AI.

“There remain some tough problems” which could stay an enigma for years to come, because there is less relevant data available to help AI figure them out, the 58-year-old told AFP.

“I’m excited long-time problems are now solved, but on the other hand, I have mixed feelings, because AI seems to have solved these difficult problems so easily,” he said.

With technology draining the satisfaction of being first to crack a cipher, a fellow code-breaker told Tomokiyo: “I feel useless.”

AI is surpassing human abilities in pursuits from mathematics to computer programming, while threatening to alter or even eradicate many jobs.

The technology is transforming the work of historians not only by decoding documents, but also by analysing millions of medieval manuscripts or helping read ancient scrolls.

Too fragile to be unrolled without risking destruction, the Herculaneum Papyri — hundreds of papyrus scrolls carbonised in the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 AD — are now being X-rayed and analysed by AI to reveal the hidden writing inside.

Researchers in Italy announced in June the first complete virtual unrolling of a scroll, which turned out to be a treatise on ethics.

– ‘Facebook of the past’ –

AI is also being used to build a huge, searchable collection of previously inaccessible sources on Jewish history and culture by transcribing 10 million pages of Hebrew manuscripts.

“It’s gigantic. No human being could process such a quantity” of data, said project leader Daniel Stoekl Ben Ezra, of the Ecole Pratique des Hautes Etudes in Paris.

Researchers hope the databases created using the digitised text — which he likens to a kind of “huge Facebook of the past” — could help bring to light links between people, places and ideas.

And at the French capital’s Notre Dame Cathedral, an AI system has been trained to transcribe 14,600 Latin pages from the church’s medieval archives — a task not dissimilar to code-breaking.

“These are minutes drawn up by notaries who abbreviate their decisions. The script is highly administrative, very pragmatic… with rather technical vocabulary,” said historian Julie Claustre, who leads the e-NDP project.

With character recognition rates ranging between 88 and 94 percent, the project has revealed information about the cathedral’s daily life, its building work, its staff and the care of abandoned children.

Doing the same by hand would take “several decades”, said Claustre, but “it’s not just a time-saver”.

Automation enables “inquiries that were not previously possible; it transforms the conditions of research.”

World.title: ‘Gyanesh Kumar must be removed’: DMK demands CEC’s ouster, backs student protests
World.content:
DMK passes resolution demanding CEC's ouster, backs student protests

DMK recalls opposition to SIR

Party backs student protests

DMK targets Congress, TVK over SIR stance

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

DMK MPs to petition President for electoral reforms

NEW DELHI: Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) on Saturday demanded the immediate removal of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and an inquiry into his conduct, accusing him of overseeing the systematic disenfranchisement of legitimate voters through the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The party also extended its support to student protests against the exercise and resolved to seek the scrapping of the SIR and a return to paper ballots.The resolutions were adopted at a meeting of the DMK Parliamentary Party, chaired by party president and former Tamil Nadu chief minister MK Stalin at the party headquarters, Anna Arivalayam, in Chennai.The meeting adopted four resolutions, including one demanding Kumarâs removal, another extending solidarity to student organisations protesting against the SIR, and a third accusing the Congress and Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) of maintaining double standards on the issue.The DMK's demand comes amid a wider political campaign against Kumar, with opposition groups calling for his resignation and announcing a Tiranga march.News agency ANI reported citing resolution that Stalin had opposed the SIR in July 2025 after reports emerged of large-scale voter deletions in Bihar, the first state where the exercise was introduced. He also participated in the Voter Adhikar Yatra in Bihar, accompanied by DMK deputy general secretary and parliamentary party leader Kanimozhi Karunanidhi.The party said Stalin subsequently raised concerns after the Election Commission announced on October 27, 2025, that the SIR would be conducted in 12 states, including Tamil Nadu. He alleged that the BJP was seeking to extend the exercise to Tamil Nadu as part of a conspiracy to disenfranchise voters.The DMK also objected to conducting the revision during November and December, citing the monsoon and festive seasons. Its MPs, the resolution said, had repeatedly raised concerns in Parliament over the exercise and its potential impact on eligible voters.Referring to the 2025 Bihar Assembly election results, the party recalled Stalin's November 15 remarks on problems within the opposition alliance, including disagreements over seat-sharing and candidates from alliance partners contesting against one another. However, Stalin had maintained that these political difficulties did not justify alleged lapses by the Election Commission.The resolution said public confidence in the poll body had fallen to an unprecedented low.In a separate resolution, the DMK extended full solidarity to student organisations protesting against the SIR and reiterated its demand for Kumar's removal.The party said Stalin was among the first leaders in Tamil Nadu to condemn the exercise and accused the CEC of disregarding the Constitution, acting unilaterally and exceeding his authority. Stalin also reiterated his criticism during by-election campaigns in Dharapuram and Madurantakam, the resolution said.The party maintained that its position remained unchanged: the SIR should be scrapped and Kumar removed from office. It also pledged support to protests organised by democratic groups seeking these demands.In its third resolution, the DMK accused the Congress and TVK of double standards over the electoral revision.The resolution criticised the Congress for opposing the SIR at the national level while, according to the DMK, remaining reluctant to raise similar concerns in Kerala and Tamil Nadu. It argued that allegations of irregularities should be addressed consistently across states.The party also questioned the TVK's position, asking why its leader, actor Vijay, had not publicly opposed the SIR or demanded Kumar's removal despite democratic groups sharing a platform with the party during protests.The DMK further alleged that certain individuals associated with the Congress were praising the TVK for personal benefits. It accused both parties of misleading the public and warned against attempts to provoke a political confrontation with the DMK, which is not part of their alliance.Under its fourth resolution, the DMK decided that its MPs would submit a formal petition to the President of India seeking electoral reforms under Stalin's guidance.The party's demands include the complete scrapping of the SIR and the use of pre-SIR electoral rolls for all upcoming elections. It also called for discontinuing electronic voting machines and restoring the traditional paper ballot system, arguing that the move would help rebuild public confidence in the electoral process.(With inputs from ANI)

World.title: Behind the lights and grandeur: What it takes and costs to build a Durga Pujo pandal
World.content:
Long before the first beat of the dhak, a Durga Pujo has already been decided, priced and partly built. The goddess arrives in autumn, but the people who bring her to a neighbourhood start months earlier, with a theme, a budget and a list of permissions that must be collected one office at a time.

To the crowds who walk through a pandal's gates, a pujo is a few days of colour, light and sound. To the club that puts it up, it is a yearly project that runs on money raised from the neighbourhood, a small circle of skilled craftsmen and a large number of people who all have to be in the right place on the right day. In West Bengal that project is repeated in locality after locality, each with its own ledger.

The quiet work before the dhak

The ledger is not small. A medium-scale pujo costs several lakh rupees, and the biggest share does not go to the idol at the centre of it all.

It goes to the structure built around her. Most visitors never see the figures, the deadlines or the people behind them, and that is exactly how the organisers want it. A pujo is meant to arrive as a finished thing.

The budget

Nirmal, a pujo organiser from West Bengal who has run one for the past 10 years, knows that ledger well. "A medium scale pujo in West Bengal would cost somewhere between 10 to 15 lakhs," he says. "Every year the budget increases as per the market inflation."





That second sentence matters as much as the first. A committee that spent a certain amount last year should expect to spend more this year on the same pujo, before it adds a single new ambition. For a club working with money collected from its neighbours, the target keeps moving upward, and the neighbours are asked to keep up with it.

The pandal takes the biggest share

Ask him what costs the most and the answer is immediate. "The pandal costs the most," he says.

Not the lighting, not the idol, not the food. He puts the pandal at around Rs 3 lakh to Rs 5 lakh for a medium-scale pujo, which makes it the line the rest of the budget has to work around.

The idol costs a fifth

Next to the pandal, the idol is a modest line. "Whatever the pandal costs, the idol costs its one-fifth," Nirmal says. For a medium-scale pujo, that works out to around Rs 80,000.

It is a striking ratio. The figure at the heart of the festival, the one every visitor has come to see, costs a fraction of the structure that shelters her.

Within the idol's cost, the most expensive element is gold. Certain gold items are designated for it, among them an ornament that is given by the club organising the pujo. The ornament comes from the organisers themselves, which makes it a different kind of expense from the rest.

A theme, decided half a year early

A pandal needs a theme, and the theme needs time. "The theme is decided at least six months ago," Nirmal says, meaning at least six months before the pujo.

That is a long lead for a festival that lasts only days.

Who decides it varies. In some committees, he says, there is a specific person whose sole job is deciding the theme. In others, the pandal makers can decide it too. The choice matters for more than looks, because the budget is also decided through the theme. Once the idea is fixed, the cost of building it can be worked out, and the money follows.

This is why the calendar starts so early. A theme chosen six months out leaves room to price the work, find the right artisan and settle the budget before construction begins.

By the time the neighbourhood sees the first bamboo go up, the important decisions have already been made.

Two months, or more

Construction is where the calendar turns uncertain. Asked how long a medium-scale pandal takes to build, Nirmal is candid. "It depends on the workers, to be honest," he says. "Some can build the same pandal in two months, whereas some will require more time."

Six months, one theme, lakhs of rupees

The reason, as he describes it, is a shortage of skill. "The skilled pandal makers are not a lot in number.

Mostly there is just one skilled artisan and a lot of people work under him."

That structure explains a good deal. The quality of the pandal and the speed at which it rises rest heavily on one person, with a large crew following his lead. For an organiser, choosing a pandal maker is therefore as much a scheduling decision as a financial one. A maker who is slow, or one who is booked elsewhere, can put the whole timeline at risk.

Where the money comes from

The funding model is local. "Every area or colony has a designated club which builds a pandal," Nirmal explains. "And then they get chanda, donations, s that ultimately make the pujo what it is."

There is also help from the state. This year, he says, the West Bengal government is providing Rs 1 lakh to small-scale pujos, and electricity is completely free. Free power removes a bill that would otherwise sit beside the lighting and the pandal.

The Rs 1 lakh grant, though, is meant for small-scale pujos. Set against a medium-scale budget of Rs 10 lakh to Rs 15 lakh, most of the money still has to come from the neighbourhood, from donors and from advertisers.

The people who are paid

Some costs are smaller but just as fixed. The priest's expenditure, Nirmal says, is around Rs 30,000 to Rs 40,000. The dhaki, whose drumming is as much a part of the pujo as the idol, is paid around Rs 10,000.

On top of that, he gets free food, lodging and clothes.

What it costs to raise a Durga Pujo

Those extras are part of the arrangement. A dhaki who is housed and fed for the duration of the pujo is a cost the committee carries beyond the headline fee. Nirmal was also asked about bhog expenditure, but his answer covered only the priest and the dhaki.

What the numbers leave out

Add up the lines Nirmal named, the pandal, the idol, the priest and the dhaki, and the total lands somewhere between roughly Rs 4.2 lakh and Rs 6.3 lakh.

His estimate for the whole pujo is Rs 10 lakh to Rs 15 lakh.

The gap is considerable. It covers everything else a pujo needs, including the lighting and food he named only to rule them out as the biggest expense. Nirmal did not break down how that money is divided.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Everything, from beginning to end

Asked about the biggest challenge organisers face, Nirmal does not name a single expense. "The biggest challenge is that everything from the beginning to the end is completed properly," he says.

That includes permissions. "You have to get proper permissions like the police and the fire department," he says, "and it takes a lot of people to complete a pujo and to make a pujo what it is."

The pandal maker and his crew, the artisan working on the idol, the priest, the dhaki and the club members collecting funds are all working towards the same date. Seen this way, the Rs 10 lakh to Rs 15 lakh is only part of what a pujo demands. The rest is coordination, and much of Nirmal's decade in the job has gone into it.

For the people who walk through the gates, the pujo arrives as a finished thing. For the club behind it, it began at least six months earlier with a decision about a theme, and it will begin again next year at a higher cost.

World.title: 'Internet access is fundamental right': SC suggests ‘child mode’ for social media accounts
World.content:
Blanket restrictions are not the answer

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Building on earlier rulings

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Saturday declared access to and use of the internet a fundamental right for every individual, including children, under Articles 21 and 19(1)(a) of the Constitution, observing that âThe safety of our children and their freedom are not at odds with each other. âThe bench of Justice JB Pardiwala and Justice K Vinod Chandran also suggested that childrenâs online safety should be strengthened through measures such as a âchild modeâ for social media accounts, rather than denying them access to the internet altogether, LiveLaw reported.A bench comprising Justice JB Pardiwala and Justice K Vinod Chandran made the observations while issuing directions to strengthen mechanisms for detecting and removing child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) from social media platforms and other online services.According to LiveLaw, the bench said: "..we have no hesitation in saying that the right to access and use the internet is a fundamental right of every individual under Article 21 read with Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. Our children, irrespective of their age enjoy the same rights, and to deny the same altogether would be as absurd as saying children below a certain age do not have a conscience worth protecting or a freedom of speech worth expressing.The safety of our children and their freedom are not at odds with each other. Our children are entitled to both."The bench acknowledged that the internet, in its present form, poses safety risks to children. However, it said restricting children's access because online platforms had failed to detect and remove harmful material would amount to mistaking the victim for the problem.The court examined whether children should be completely shielded from the internet and social media in the interest of their safety. It noted that the right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) includes the right to know, receive and impart information and ideas.Describing the internet as a marketplace of ideas, creative expression and information, the court said its value extended beyond the material available online to the opportunities it provided for learning, communication and access to information."For many children, particularly in remote areas, it is often the only source of learning and information," the court observed.It also noted that the internet could be particularly important for children with special needs, for whom online platforms might be the only place to find companionship with others facing similar circumstances.The bench referred to the Supreme Court's 2020 judgment in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, which held that "the freedom of speech and expression and the freedom to carry on any trade or business through the medium of the internet is constitutionally protected as a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution."In that judgment, the court had refrained from expressing a view on whether the right to access the internet, by itself, constituted a fundamental right.The bench also referred to the 2025 judgment in Pragya Prasun & Ors. v. Union of India, in which the court recognised the right to digital access as a fundamental right under Article 21.

World.title: YouTuber Dhruv Rathee faces court warrants over 2018 video targeting BJP IT cell
World.content:
NEW DELHI: A Delhi court has issued bailable warrants against YouTuber Dhruv Rathee in a 2018 defamation case, PTI reported.

The case stems from a video published by Rathee in May 2018, in which he allegedly claimed that the Bharatiya Janata Partyâs (

) Information Technology cell had attempted to bribe a man to defame him.

The video was posted on Ratheeâs social media account and later retweeted by Arvind Kejriwal, who was then the Delhi chief minister.

The complainant, Vikas Sankrityayan, also known as Vikas Pandey, subsequently initiated defamation proceedings against Rathee and Kejriwal over the video and its circulation.

Earlier, on October 12, Judicial Magistrate Rahul Jain of the Saket court ordered fresh summons to Rathee after the complainant submitted that repeated attempts to serve him had remained unsuccessful since the proceedings began.

The complainantâs counsel, advocate Samaksh Sharma, told the court that the summons had remained unserved for several years as Rathee primarily lived abroad. The court was informed, however, that Rathee was then in India and residing at an address in Gurugram, Haryana.

The magistrate noted that Rathee had first been summoned on July 23, 2019, and that the complainant had continued to pursue service of the summons.





The court allowed Pandey to accompany the process server and directed him to deposit the process fee within two days. The next hearing was scheduled for October 17, 2026.

Separately, Rathee is facing a defamation suit before the Saket court over a video that allegedly claimed Lord Ram and Goddess Sita consumed meat and alcohol during their exile.

The complainants, who identified themselves as Hindu devotees, alleged that the video hurt their religious sentiments. They have also sought an ex-parte ad-interim injunction restraining Google from restoring, hosting, uploading, sharing or disseminating the video, or any video with identical or similar content, after notice and verification of the URL, during the pendency of the suit.

World.title: ‘He spoke to Putin to buy diesel’: Ex-diplomat Fabian after Trump waives sanctions over Russian oil
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Former diplomat KP Fabian on Saturday questioned the rationale behind the US tariff pressure on India over Russian oil purchases, arguing that Washingtonâs own decision to waive sanctions-related duties under the Lindsey O.

Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act exposed a contradiction in its approach.

His remarks came after US President Donald Trump earlier today waived sanctions-related duties under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act.

Speaking to ANI, Fabian said, âTrump himself spoke to Putin to buy diesel. If America itself is buying, either it should sanction itself, which is ridiculous."

He also argued that the tariff threats against India were a negotiating tactic aimed at securing a favourable trade deal rather than a genuine response to New Delhiâs energy purchases from Russia.

âCertain tariffs were imposed, and the court in the United States said that Trump had no business."

Fabian said Trump had avoided directly confronting Chinese President Xi Jinping over Russian oil purchases because China was a major buyer of Russian exports and Washington wanted closer engagement with Beijing.

âContrary to the Lindsey Graham Act, President Trump did not dare to mention it to Xi Jinping because China is a top buyer, 50 per cent of Russiaâs exports.





India comes next at 37 per cent,â he told ANI.

Trump pauses sanctions

However, Trump earlier on Saturday paused provisions of the Graham Act that could have imposed tariffs of up to 100% on goods imported into the US from the five largest buyers of Russian crude oil or natural gas, including India and China.

The move comes against the backdrop of rising diesel prices in the US ahead of the November midterm elections and a reported agreement under which Russia would supply diesel fuel to Washington.

Trump invoked Section 115 of the Act, which authorises the US president to waive certain sanctions-related provisions and restrictions involving foreign entities.

âI have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver is in the national interests of the United States and a report explaining the basis for the certification, consistent with section 115(b) of the Graham Act,â Trump said in the order.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

What it means for India

Russia continues to be the single largest supplier of oil for India. A waiver of tariffs of up to 100% which may have come into place in the coming days means that India can continue importing oil in large numbers from Moscow without any economic fallout.

If 100% tariffs had been imposed by the Trump administration, then it would have hit exporters as the US is the largest trading partner for India. At the same time, any sanctions may have rendered Russian crude economically unviable which would have added to the supply crunch at a time when Middle East tensions continue.

World.title: Indian woman jailed over son’s fatal stabbing faces possible deportation from UK
World.content:
An Indian woman jailed for helping her son after he fatally stabbed an 18-year-old student in Southampton could face deportation to India following her early release from prison, British authorities have indicated.

According to new agency PTI, the UK Home Office said it would seek to deport foreign criminals at the earliest opportunity, although it did not refer specifically to Kiran Kaur, 53. Foreign nationals sentenced to at least 12 months in prison are generally considered for deportation, subject to exceptions and legal challenges.

Kaur was sentenced to three years in prison in July for assisting an offender by removing the weapon used by her son, Vickrum Digwa, to kill Henry Nowak on December 3, 2025.

She is expected to be released early under a government scheme aimed at reducing overcrowding in British prisons.

Digwa, 23, was sentenced to life imprisonment in June, with a minimum term of 21 years before he becomes eligible for parole.

Both Kaur and her son have been granted permission to challenge their sentences, with their appeals scheduled to be heard by the UK Court of Appeal on November 5.

Kirpan argument sparks controversy

The case drew widespread attention after Digwa sought to invoke a religious self-defence argument involving the kirpan, a ceremonial knife that Sikhs are legally permitted to carry in the UK.





During Kaurâs sentencing, Justice William Mousley stressed that the kirpan was a symbol of religious faith and was not intended to be carried for offensive purposes. He said any use of the weapon in self-defence would have to be justified by circumstances involving great seriousness and urgency.

The judge also criticised Kaur for removing the weapon rather than challenging her sonâs actions and encouraging him to do the right thing.

He acknowledged that she had experienced a difficult life in India before marrying and moving to the UK nearly 30 years ago. He said she had acted to protect her son rather than for personal gain and was unlikely to reoffend, while making clear that her actions warranted punishment.

British Sikh organisations and parliamentarians subsequently condemned what they described as the misrepresentation of the kirpan, stressing that religious protection did not justify the violence in this case.

Police conduct under investigation

The killing also triggered scrutiny of police conduct after body-worn camera footage showed officers handcuffing Nowak following Digwaâs allegations that he had been subjected to racism. Those allegations were subsequently rejected in court.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct is investigating the officersâ handling of the incident amid allegations of âtwo-tierâ policing, referring to claims that different communities were treated unequally.

The case has heightened tensions in Southampton and the wider Hampshire and Isle of Wight area.

Kaurâs potential deportation remains subject to the applicable immigration process, while the outcome of the appeals against her sentence and Digwaâs life term is awaited.

World.title: ‘Foreign-inspired terrorism no longer visible’: Home Secy Govind Mohan on changing internal security landscape
World.content:
Home Secy Govind Mohan speaks on changing internal security landscape
