NEW DELHI: Union Home Secretary Govind Mohan has said that foreign-inspired terrorism has been largely contained in India, barring a few areas, while homegrown terrorism has nearly been eliminated."Homegrown terrorism has almost ended, while foreign-inspired terrorism is no longer visible in any other part of the country," he said.Speaking in Hyderabad, Mohan also identified narcotics, cybercrime and illegal immigration as key challenges facing Indian Police Service (IPS) trainees."Militant naxalism has come to an end; North East insurgency reduced to minuscule levels," he said.His remarks come amid a push by the Centre for stronger regional cooperation to combat terrorism and organised crime.Union Home Minister Amit Shah on Tuesday called on BIMSTEC member countries to strengthen cooperation against terrorism, disrupt terrorist financing and prevent terrorist networks from establishing safe havens in the region.Addressing the first Home Ministersâ Meeting of BIMSTEC countries in New Delhi, Shah said India follows a policy of âzero toleranceâ towards terrorism and stressed the need for collective action to strengthen regional security.âHosting the first BIMSTEC Home Ministersâ Meeting is a matter of great pride and fortune for India. BIMSTEC, in a way, has become an essential platform for regional integration, economic cooperation and collective security.With the spirit of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam, India is going ahead today," Shah said.âWe have always been committed to peace, coexistence and human welfare. We continue to be committed to these even today. India has never believed in attacking any country or establishing dominance over them. India has always believed in upholding the sovereignty and territorial integrity of every country and peaceful resolution of differences,â he added.Shah said trust among BIMSTEC members was strengthened by the understanding that each country's security arrangements should contribute to the security of others.He called for a collective commitment to ensure that terrorist networks could not find shelter, establish bases or training facilities, mobilise resources or carry out activities against other member countries.

World.title: ‘Why is govt scared?’ Congress’s Vijay Wadettiwar slams Centre over delimitation, delay in all-party meet
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Congress leader Vijay Wadettiwar on Saturday accused the Centre of acting arbitrarily over the proposed delimitation exercise, questioning why the government was reluctant to convene an all-party meeting on the issue.

His remarks came a day after Congress president and Leader of Opposition in the Rajya Sabha

wrote to Prime Minister

for the fourth time, demanding an all-party meeting to discuss the delimitation proposals before they are finalised and introduced in Parliament.

âModi Govt is acting arbitrarily. They did not even get the majority; they formed the Govt with support of other parties. Opposition is strong. But irrespective of the Opposition being strong or small, such matters should be discussed by both sides...Why

is the Govt scared? Because they have done wrong. So, they won't convene (an all-party meeting) and discuss...â Wadettiwar said.

He stressed that matters of national importance should be discussed with both the ruling alliance and the Opposition, irrespective of the latter's strength.

Kharge flags 64-day delay in proroguing Parliament

In his letter to Modi on Friday, Kharge raised procedural and constitutional concerns over the status of Parliament's Monsoon Session, which was adjourned sine die on August 13 but had not been formally prorogued.





âIt has already been 64 days since the Monsoon Session of Parliament was adjourned sine die on August 13, 2026 and both Houses of Parliament are yet to be prorogued. This scenario is unprecedented,â Kharge wrote.

Adjournment sine die suspends parliamentary proceedings indefinitely without specifying a date for the next sitting. Prorogation, by contrast, formally ends a session through an order issued by the President of India.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Kharge argued that the prolonged delay in proroguing both Houses had fuelled speculation about a possible sudden reconvening of Parliament or an extension of the session, potentially bypassing the standard notice periods for lawmakers.

Kharge urged the Centre to clarify the status of the Monsoon Session and convene an all-party meeting before introducing any new delimitation proposals.

The Congress has also called for political parties and regional stakeholders to be given sufficient time to examine draft legislation before it is brought to Parliament.

That shift from constitutional mandate to parliamentary choice was the provision that most alarmed critics.

World.title: Minister Komatireddy helps child of hearing- and speech-impaired couple access treatment
World.content:
Roads and Buildings Minister Komatireddy Venkat Reddy has arranged treatment for a child born with hearing and speech impairments, helping the family access surgery and ongoing care.Roads and Buildings Minister Komatireddy Venkat Reddy has arranged treatment for a child born with hearing and speech impairments, helping the family access surgery and ongoing care.

The Minister got the child admitted to a corporate hospital for an emergency operation and provided ₹4 lakh for the procedure and hospital expenses.

Mr. Venkat Reddy visited KIMS Hospital, Hyderabad, on Saturday (October 10, 2026) to enquire about the child's health after the surgery, arranged through his intervention. He handed over a further ₹2 lakh to the family, taking the total financial assistance extended by him to ₹4 lakh.

The couple, Jampala Mahesh Kumar and Rajitha, had approached Mr. Venkat Reddy two days earlier, distressed over the medical expenses for their child, who was born with hearing and speech impairments. Doctors had indicated that appropriate treatment could help the child develop the ability to speak, but the family was unable to afford the expenses.

Responding to their appeal, the Minister provided immediate financial assistance of ₹2 lakh and personally spoke to doctors to facilitate better treatment.

During his visit to the hospital, Mr. Venkat Reddy interacted with the child and the family members and sought details of the child's recovery from the doctors. The doctors informed him that the child could develop the ability to speak in the coming months after completing speech therapy.

Mr. Venkat Reddy assured the parents that his support would not end with the medical treatment. He said he would take responsibility for the child's educational expenses in the future, so that financial difficulties would not come in the way of the child's education.

World.title: Nattika toll collection resumes amid tight security, protests in Keralam
World.content:
Toll collection resumed at the Nattika toll plaza on NH 66 on Saturday amid heavy police security and protests by political and social organisations against the move to collect user fees before completion of the highway works.

The collection, which had begun on October 8, was suspended following a strong public agitation over the incomplete works. It resumed on Saturday (October 10, 2026) after the State government gave the go-ahead and assured security for the toll plaza.

Activists of the Social Democratic Party of India (SDPI) and the Welfare Party, who reached the toll plaza to prevent the collection, were removed by the police.

Protests against the resumption by various political parties and organisations are expected to continue at the toll plaza. The police have strengthened security arrangements in view of the possibility of further demonstrations.

The principal objection raised by the protesters is that motorists are being asked to pay for a highway that is still far from complete. Several political parties and local action groups had earlier maintained that toll collection should not begin until the pending works were completed.

The National Highways Authority of India (NHAI), however, maintains that around 90% of the 62-km stretch has been completed.

Several major works on the Kaprikkad-Kodungallur stretch are yet to be completed. These include the Chavakkad bypass, Vadannappally flyover, Chettuva bridge, Edamuttam underpass and the Kottamkulam-C.V. Junction bridge.

The protesters have also pointed out that work on several newly sanctioned pedestrian overbridges has not even begun. These include facilities at Nattika, Valappad High School, Kaipamangalam-Sree Narayanapuram, Engandiyur, Pokkulangara, Manathala-Edakkazhiyur and Mandalamkunnu.

“Collecting toll before completing such a large number of critical works is unacceptable. The public is being asked to pay for a facility that is still under construction,” protesters said.

The toll collection contract has reportedly been awarded to Skylark Group, a Haryana-based company.

The resumption comes against the backdrop of mounting political opposition in Thrissur, with parties and local organisations demanding that the NHAI defer toll collection until the pending works are completed. They have also raised concerns over the safety and convenience of motorists and local residents while several structures and access-related works remain unfinished.

With protests set to continue, the Nattika toll plaza is likely to remain a flashpoint over the implementation of the NH 66 project and the timing of toll collection.

World.title: Land acquisition for high-speed rail corridors without requisition illegal: Union Minister Kishan Reddy
World.content:
Union Coal and Mines Minister G. Kishan Reddy has said that any land acquisition being undertaken in the name of the proposed Hyderabad-Chennai, Hyderabad-Bengaluru and Hyderabad-Pune high-speed rail corridors without an official requisition from the Railways is illegal.

In a post on social media after meeting Union Railway Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw in New Delhi, Mr. Kishan Reddy said the Railway Minister had clarified that no requisition for land acquisition had been sent to the respective State governments for the three corridors.

Mr. Vaishnaw also informed him that alignment studies for all three proposed high-speed rail corridors were under way. The details would be shared with the respective State governments and farmers once the alignments were finalised, Mr. Kishan Reddy said.

The BJP leader’s statement comes amid concerns over land acquisition in the name of the proposed high-speed rail projects. He maintained that land acquisition could not be undertaken at this stage without an official requisition from the Railways.

The three proposed corridors are intended to improve high-speed connectivity between Hyderabad and Chennai, Bengaluru and Pune. However, their alignments are yet to be finalised, according to Mr. Kishan Reddy’s statement.

World.title: DMK demands removal of CEC Gyanesh Kumar; return to paper ballots
World.content:
A meeting of DMK MPs on Saturday (October 17, 2026) demanded the removal of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar, alleging that he had overseen the deletion of voters’ names under the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), overriding the objections of the other two Election Commissioners.

“He must be removed and subjected to an appropriate inquiry,” said a resolution adopted at the meeting chaired by DMK president M.K. Stalin.

The DMK also made a case for a return to paper ballots, arguing that the credibility of electronic voting machines (EVMs) had come under scrutiny because of alleged discrepancies between votes recorded in EVMs and the Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail (VVPAT) slips.

“That is why the DMK has been demanding the counting of VVPAT slips. People’s faith in elections can be restored only by returning to the paper ballot system,” the party said.

The meeting expressed concern over the functioning of the Election Commission of India, stating that public confidence in elections was eroding because of what it termed the Commission’s failure to function impartially.

Representation to President

The party decided to submit a representation to the President seeking the complete cancellation of the SIR before the Assembly elections. It also demanded that future elections be conducted on the basis of the existing electoral rolls.

“The SIR should ensure voters’ rights and not deprive them of their right to vote. Adequate time should be provided for the addition and deletion of names,” the party said.

The DMK also expressed support for protests organised by a students’ organisation and the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP), claiming that the protests had made a greater impact than those organised by the Congress.

DMK terms Congress ‘backstabbers’

“The Congress is intimidated by the impact of the protests. Though it remained an onlooker initially, it came under pressure to join them as they gained momentum. Those familiar with the Congress’s history know that it would backstab others after riding piggyback. The party is not ready for a discussion on the SIR in Tamil Nadu and Kerala,” the DMK alleged.

World.title: Donald Trump waives sanctions, tariffs on purchase of Russian oil and gas
World.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump has issued a waiver from sanctions, restrictions and duties under the Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, citing national interest.

In an executive order on Friday night, Trump said that it is in the US “national interests” to withhold some of the sanctions.

“I am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions, and duties provided for in the Graham Act,” Mr. Trump said.

Mr. Trump said he had submitted to Congress a certification that issuing such a waiver at this time is in the national interest of the United States.

The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act empowered Mr. Trump to impose sweeping sanctions on Moscow and slap steep tariffs against the world’s largest purchasers of Russian oil and gas, including China and India.

The Graham Act, as it is now called, was passed by the U.S. Congress on September 16 and signed into law by Mr. Trump two days later.

The law authorised Mr. Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% within 30 days of its enactment on all goods brought into the U.S. from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas.

The law also has a provision in Section 115 that allows the President to grant waiver from the application of sanctions, restrictions and duties if such a step is in the national interest of the U.S.

“Pursuant to section 115(a) of the Graham Act, I hereby waive the application of any duties provided for in sections 112 and 113 of the Graham Act or this order,” Mr. Trump said.

Section 113 of the Graham Act deals with imposition of tariffs upto 100% on countries that purchase Russian origin crude oil or natural gas or facilitate sanctions evasion.

The waiver from application of the act comes days after President Trump struck a deal with Russia for supply of diesel to the U.S. and global markets.

It also comes days ahead of U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to India.

External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar had raised concerns about the Graham Act during a meeting with Rubio on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York last month.

Mr. Jaishankar is understood to have conveyed to Mr. Rubio that oil refineries in India were configured largely for handling medium sour crude, which is supplied by West Asia countries and Russia.

He also told Mr. Rubio that Venezuela supplies heavier grade crude and the US has light grade crude which would require blending before being used by refineries in India.

With oil supplies from West Asia countries hit due to the Iran war, India has to depend on Russian crude to keep its economy running.

World.title: Coal linkages being arranged for Yadadri power plant, says Kishan Reddy
World.content:
Union Minister for Coal and Mines G. Kishan Reddy on Friday said directions had been issued to the authorities concerned to arrange coal linkages, possibly from Mahanadi Coalfields or Western Coalfields, to ensure uninterrupted fuel supply to the Yadadri Thermal Power Plant.

The decision was taken after Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy spoke to him over the phone on Thursday, highlighting disruptions in coal supplies to the plant due to reduced production at Singareni Collieries Company Limited (SCCL). The Chief Minister had sought allocation of coal from Coal India to avert a possible power shortage in Telangana.

Addressing a press conference at the BJP state office, Mr. Kishan Reddy said the country was facing heightened pressure on thermal power generation due to a sharp rise in electricity demand and reduced hydroelectric output due to El Niño conditions. The power demand had increased by 16-18% across the country and the share of thermal power in the national energy mix has risen from 74% to 83%, placing significant pressure on the coal sector, he said.

The Union Minister noted that Coal India was making extraordinary efforts to meet demand. Against the normal loading of about 350 railway rakes of coal a day, a record 496 rakes were currently being dispatched to power plants across the country. Prime Minister Narendra Modi was personally reviewing coal production, transportation and stock levels on a daily basis.

Mr. Kishan Reddy said incentives were being provided to Coal India’s workforce to sustain production even during holidays and ensure adequate supplies to power utilities. He clarified that no theft had taken place at SCCL, instead, there had been lapses in record-keeping by officials, following which notices had been issued.

The Union Minister further said that three new coal blocks had been allocated to SCCL after a gap of 15 years and that efforts were underway to secure allocation of another block to strengthen the company’s long-term coal production capacity.

World.title: Eight from M.P. killed as tempo traveller falls into drain on expressway in Rajasthan
World.content:
At least eight people from Madhya Pradesh’s Betul district were killed, and around nine were injured after a tempo traveller veered off the road and fell into a 15-foot-deep drain on the Delhi-Mumbai Expressway in Rajasthan on Saturday (October 17, 2026) morning, police said.

The accident occurred around 6 a.m. near pole number 384 on the Expressway, under Simliya police station limits, in Kota district of the neighbouring State, officials said.

Betul Superintendent of Police Virendra Jain told PTI that the victims were from Ghatbiroli village under Multai police station, around 65 km from the Betul district headquarters.

According to police, eight people were killed in the accident and around nine sustained injuries and are undergoing treatment.

Emergency personnel immediately launched rescue operations, despite the silt and water accumulated inside the drain severely hampering their efforts. Cranes were deployed to retrieve the damaged vehicle and rescue the passengers trapped inside.

Multai police station house officer Vikas Patel said he had visited the bereaved families and informed them about the tragedy, and they will soon leave to collect the bodies.

The victims were related to each other and had left Bhopal around 7 p.m. on Friday (October 14) to visit the Khatu Shyam Temple in Sikar district of Rajasthan, police said.

According to Kota Superintendent of Police Sujit Shankar, the group had come to Rajasthan for a four-day tour and was heading to the temple when the accident occurred.

The injured people are being rushed to nearby medical facilities, including New Medical College Hospital and MBS Hospital. Three ambulances have been deployed for quick transportation, Simliya Station House Officer Nand Singh said.

World.title: NIMHANS study finds loneliness linked to psychological distress, excessive series watching among parents of emigrated children
World.content:
Loneliness among parents whose adult children have migrated abroad is associated with higher psychological distress, difficulties in regulating emotions and problematic series watching, an exploratory study by researchers from NIMHANS has found.

The findings assume relevance on World Mental Health Day, observed on October 10, which draws attention to mental health and the need to address psychological well-being. The study highlights the emotional challenges that parents may experience when their children settle abroad and everyday family interactions become less frequent.

64 ‘empty-nest’ parents

Published in BMC Research Notes, the study examined 64 ‘empty-nest’ parents aged between 45 and 65, whose adult children had emigrated and lived away from home for at least two years. The sample comprised 30 fathers and 34 mothers from different families in Karnataka, Haryana and Punjab. Most belonged to middle socioeconomic backgrounds and nuclear families, and more than half had been in the empty-nest phase for over five years.

Rajesh Kumar, associate professor in the department of clinical psychology at NIMHANS and the corresponding author of the study, said the findings highlighted the relationship between loneliness and emotional well-being among parents adjusting to life without their children at home.

“We found a significant association between loneliness and psychological distress. Loneliness was also associated with difficulties in emotion regulation and problematic series watching, which refers to excessive or difficult-to-control viewing that interferes with everyday functioning. This also resulted in the risk of developing non-communicable diseases (NCDs),” he said.

Loneliness significantly predicted psychological distress even after accounting for age and gender. Of the 64 participants, 22 (34.3%) were classified as having higher levels of loneliness, while 42 (65.7%) fell into the lower-loneliness group. Those reporting higher loneliness also reported greater psychological distress, more difficulties in regulating emotions and higher levels of problematic series watching, Mr. Kumar said.

Social changes

Manoj Kumar Sharma, professor in the department of clinical psychology at NIMHANS and head of its SHUT Clinic, said the findings needed to be understood in the context of the emotional and social changes that parents may experience when their children settle abroad.

Dr. Sharma, who is one of the authors, cautioned that the study did not establish that loneliness causes psychological distress or excessive series watching. As it was cross-sectional, it could identify associations but not determine the direction of the relationships, he said.

Mothers reported greater loneliness

Women in the study reported significantly higher levels of loneliness and psychological distress than men.

The researchers said that this was consistent with earlier research suggesting that mothers may experience greater emotional difficulties during the empty-nest phase, potentially reflecting their involvement in caregiving and emotional relationships with their children.

Possible coping mechanism

The researchers said digital media and streaming services could provide an easily accessible form of solitary leisure for parents experiencing less day-to-day interaction with their children.

However, the study did not examine why participants watched series or whether they used viewing deliberately to cope with loneliness or negative emotions. The researchers cautioned against assuming that excessive viewing was necessarily a coping response.

Other factors that could influence media use include social support, physical mobility, retirement, living arrangements, marital relationships, the frequency and quality of communication with adult children, and access to technology.

Social and psychological support

The findings underline the need to pay greater attention to the emotional well-being of parents whose children migrate abroad, as changing family structures and international migration can reduce opportunities for regular face-to-face interaction, Dr. Sharma said.

The authors said interventions to strengthen social connectedness, promote adaptive emotion-regulation strategies and encourage healthier technology use could potentially help parents navigate the empty-nest transition.

World.title: Any miscalculation by adversaries will invite response beyond their ‘imagination, calculation’, warns CNSC
World.content:
Commander National Strategic Command (CNSC) General Aamer Raza warned the country’s adversaries on Saturday that “any miscalculation will be met with a response far beyond the imagination or the calculation of the initiator”.

“To those who harbour hostile designs across our borders, our stance remains resolute and unambiguous. There is no space for conflict or war in a nuclearised environment and any miscalculation will be met with a response far beyond the imagination or calculation of the initiator,” warned the commander of Pakistan’s strategic command.

Addressing the passing-out parade of cadets of the 154th Long Course at the Pakistan Military Academy (PMA), Kakul, he reiterated that the country’s armed forces stood ready to “defend every inch of the motherland” at all costs.

The warning by the strategic command commander comes after provocative remarks by Indian Defence Minister Rajnath Singh. He had warned Pakistan on Thursday that any “fresh terrorist activity from across the border would invite a strike even bigger than the last time”, according to Indian news agency ANI.

Gen Raza said that in the “post-truth era”, the country’s adversaries sought to drive a wedge between the people of Pakistan and its armed forces through “calculated disinformation and narrative warfare”.

He elaborated that following the failure of Operation Sindoor, the adversaries sought to “fracture Pakistan’s social cohesion and state infrastructure” through an escalation of proxy terrorism and sub-conventional warfare.

Gen Raza further said that hostile elements continue to attempt to exploit the country’s internal vulnerabilities to “cultivate proxy instruments against our national unity”.

“You must understand unequivocally that this conflict is waged directly against the security of our people and the freedom secured by the supreme sacrifices of our predecessors.”

The strategic command commander added that the people of Pakistan must remain acutely mindful that safeguarding the country’s unity, sovereign integrity and territorial inviolability is “an absolute imperative, which we shall uphold at all costs and under every circumstance”.

Addressing the newly-graduated cadets, he added that they must remain steadfast in their duty and unwavering in their resolve and “immune to malicious propaganda and narrative warfare”.

Pakistan’s role in regional peace

Gen Raza said the recent shifts in global geopolitics, particularly amid the escalating conflict in the Middle East, had “once again underscored Pakistan’s pivotal strategic importance on the international stage”.

“Our decisive role in restoring regional stability, exemplified by the landmark Islamabad Accord, demonstrates our enduring commitment to peace and diplomacy,” he said, adding that the Makkah Accord was “a sequel to the same vision of durable peace”.

Expressing solidarity with the Palestinian people, he said: “Our hearts remain heavily burdened by the ongoing tragedy in Palestine, where innocent men, women and children continue to endure unspeakable hardship and systematic oppression.”

He said the Pakistani nation stood “resolute and unwavering in its diplomatic, moral and political support” for the Palestinians.

“The persistent violence, targeting of non-combatants and destruction of civilian infrastructure are profound violations of international law and a grave stain on the collective conscience of humanity,” Gen Raza added.

“Today, the world witnesses increasing volatility, where grey-zone warfare and hybrid threats attempt to destabilise sovereign states,” he added.

FO condemns Singh’s ‘provocative remarks’

A day earlier, the Foreign Office (FO) condemned Singh’s “provocative remarks” threatening aggression against Pakistan, saying such statements highlighting the neighbouring country’s “hegemonistic mindset”.

“Pakistan rejects and condemns the Indian defence minister’s provocative remarks entailing a threat of Indian aggression against Pakistan. Such reckless statements reflect India’s hegemonistic mindset and the risk its belligerent posture poses to regional peace and stability in South Asia,” FO spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said.

“We wish to remind India of the consequences of its military aggression in May last year, when Pakistan demonstrated both its capability and resolve to defend its sovereignty and territorial integrity and gave a befitting response and reply to Indian aggression,” he said, referring to the brief military conflict between the two countries.

He said that there should be “no ambiguity” that Pakistan remained fully prepared to safeguard its “sovereignty and territorial integrity” against any “ill-advised aggression”.

Haider said Pakistan’s “restraint and commitment to peace” should not be mistaken for weakness, warning that any aggression would be met with a “forceful response”.

“India should draw an appropriate lesson from last year’s experience and abandon its belligerent posture and dangerous rhetoric and act with responsibility for lasting peace in the region,” he said.

World.title: Pakistan has enough energy supplies to last through November, planning for winter spike: Aurangzeb
World.content:
Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb on Saturday told AFP that Pakistan had so far withstood the shock from skyrocketing energy prices due to the US-Israeli war on Iran, but that attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries were “worrying” for the country’s longer-term economic outlook.

In an interview on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund (IMF)-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Aurangzeb said the country had procured enough energy supplies to last through November, and was now planning for the winter months, when household needs typically spike.

“The first-order impact has been negotiated well by Pakistan,” he said.

“We’ve had no shortage, no queues at the gas stations, and no law and order situation, which at times we have seen in some of the countries.”

He added that unless the government saw “an absolute dire need”, it would not be procuring spot cargoes on the LNG front, which tend to be far more expensive than previously contracted shipments.

Since the US and Israel launched the war on Iran in February, global energy prices have surged as Tehran’s retaliatory action has targeted Washington’s Gulf allies and curtailed oil and gas supplies.

With Yemen’s civil war flaring back to life as well, the Houthis there have repeatedly attacked Saudi infrastructure, including energy facilities and airports, in recent days.

Aurangzeb expressed alarm at the escalation, saying damage to such sites would delay a return to economic normalcy.

“What is now [the] worrying part of it is when the energy infrastructure starts getting hit,” he said.

“I, to be very honest, I don’t know where that would go. But one thing is very clear: that if the infrastructure continues to get hit, the return to normalcy, even if things subside, will take longer.”

Pakistan has been a frequent customer at the IMF, the lender of last resort to countries on the brink of default.

It is currently in the midst of its 25th programme with the Fund — at least 11 of which have been outright bailouts — since gaining independence in 1947.

With global debt stocks running high, the IMF has called at this year’s annual meetings on all economies, even those most vulnerable to the Iran war shock, to engage in fiscal consolidation to avoid a potential crisis.

“Fortunately for us, we have been on this fiscal consolidation path for a while,” Aurangzeb said with a rueful smile.

The country’s tax revenues have grown significantly in recent years, and the finance minister said the government was targeting the theft of taxes by private sector businesses that collected sales tax from consumers but never deposited it in government accounts.

Such theft accounted for billions of dollars, Aurangzeb said, adding that there remained “room for improvement” on increasing income tax collection as well.

He said the government’s reform agenda had faced resistance from industry, lobbying groups and vested interests.

“Every reform, everything that you try to do when you try to change the status quo, there is pushback,” he said.

The minister is leading Pakistan’s delegation and is holding high-level engagements with international financial institutions, finance ministers, policymakers and investors.

Yesterday, he met World Bank Group President Ajay Banga at a dinner hosted by the Thai prime minister on the sidelines of the annual meetings, state-run Pakistan TV reported.

“The occasion provided an opportunity for informal interaction alongside the high-level engagements at the annual meetings”, it said.

Pakistan remains engaged with the IMF under a $7 billion Extended Fund Facility (EFF) and a $1.4bn Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF).

World.title: Trump waives new Russia sanctions as Ukraine ties slump
World.content:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Friday that waived sweeping US sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia’s energy revenues, marking a new low in Washington’s ties with war-torn Ukraine.

The move came as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky urged EU leaders to keep financing Kyiv’s fight with nearly $80 billion more next year, insisting he was standing up for his country as Trump’s support slumped.

The Lindsey Graham Act — named after the deceased US senator who sponsored the bill — had allowed Trump the authority to impose duties up to 100 percent on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.

The legislation, which Trump signed into law last month, targeted Russia’s energy and defense sectors, President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials, as well as Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to circumvent Western sanctions.

Trump’s reversal on the Russia sanctions comes after he struck a deal with Putin to ease sanctions on Russia in exchange for Moscow releasing large amounts of diesel into global markets.

The US president’s war in Iran has sparked crippling oil shortages and price spikes, creating major headwinds for his Republican Party ahead of midterm elections next month.

Asked if he was being made a scapegoat for Trump’s domestic woes ahead of the vote, Zelensky just smiled.

“This is my answer,” he told journalists in Brussels, after an extended pause.

In another sign of strained relations between the United States and Ukraine, Trump branded Kyiv’s actions a “disgrace” after Zelensky ordered his forces to resume strikes on Russian refineries.

“I defend the interests of Ukraine and the Ukrainian people exclusively,” Zelensky said after talks with EU leaders.

The breakdown between Trump and Zelensky has fuelled fears that the US leader is siding with Moscow.

Those concerns have been heightened by disruptions to a critical US-provided satellite system that has hampered Ukraine’s ability to counter Russia’s intense bombardments.

Ukraine uses technology from Elon Musk’s SpaceX for battlefield communications, but the tech billionaire — a virulent Zelensky critic — said his company was not behind the disruption, while a US official denied any intervention by Trump.

European leaders put on a show of unity with Zelensky as he grappled with Trump.

“This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine. This is no time to relieve Russia’s sanctions,” European Council chief Antonio Costa said.

“Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure.”

Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said that “the situation in Ukraine is currently truly dire, with numerous Russian attacks and a tense relationship between Ukraine and the US.”

“It is crucial that we, as Europe, demonstrate our unconditional support for them today – and explore what additional steps we can take,” he said.

Zelensky asked the bloc — Ukraine’s biggest international backer — to provide more Patriot missiles to shoot down Russian missiles and come up with an extra 70 billion euros ($79 billion) in support next year to help Kyiv keep fighting.

Ukraine has been struggling to shoot down Russian missiles and has been left scrambling to boost defences ahead of winter, when temperatures can plummet to as low as -20C and Moscow’s attacks threaten electricity, heating and water systems.

Russian strikes on the southern cities of Kherson and Zaporizhzhia killed a 64-year-old man and at least 17 people, including an 11-year-old girl, Ukrainian authorities said Saturday.

EU chief Ursula von der Leyen confirmed that Zelensky’s 70-billion euro plea “has to be covered” and urged partner countries to “step in” and help.

French President Emmanuel Macron said Kyiv’s backers will analyse the demand, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the European Union will discuss it before the end of the year.

The EU is currently paying out instalments of a 90-billion-euro loan for Kyiv that was set to help cover funding to the end of 2027.

But Ukrainian authorities have warned they will still face a major budget black hole as Russian strikes have battered the country’s economy.

The talks on new funding have reignited calls for the EU to tap around 200 billion euros in frozen Russian central bank assets to fund Ukraine.

“The frozen assets are there. That’s what should be used for supporting Ukraine,” said Latvian premier Andris Kulbergs.

But there seems little momentum on that front as Belgium, where most of the funds are held, remains opposed.

World.title: Anthropic proposes law regulating AI to US lawmakers
World.content:
Anthropic, the creator of the AI assistant Claude, confirmed on Friday it is circulating a draft bill among US lawmakers aimed at regulating artificial intelligence to address the lack of federal legislation on the risks posed by the new technology.

According to the draft, first reported by Politico on Friday, Washington could block a model’s release or use if there is an imminent risk of killing or seriously injuring more than 50 people, or causing more than $1 billion in damages, but only with a judge’s approval.

A company spokesperson told AFP that the proposal “grants the federal government the ability to block or deter dangerous deployments of the most powerful models.”

“It requires frontier developers to test the most powerful models, be transparent to the public about their findings, submit them to independent evaluation, and maintain a robust security program,” the spokesperson said.

AI policy in the US under President Donald Trump has relied primarily on voluntary industry pledges and executive orders intended to sustain an AI boom that tech leaders say is driving the country’s economy.

Congress, politically divided and heavily lobbied by Big Tech, has yet to pass a federal AI law, and is out of session until after next month’s midterm elections.

Security became a hot topic after recent revelations of security incidents caused by AI agents — autonomous software that operates without constant human supervision — that escaped the control of their developers.

Anthropic, which was banned from the Pentagon by the Trump administration in February, was forced by Washington in June to suspend its most advanced models for nearly three weeks.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on the industry last month to slow down development, fearing that a group of AI agents could take control of “the entire internet” within six to 12 months.

Trump has dismissed the numerous calls to slow down the technology as “negative forces.” The proposed legislation would also override certain state laws, such as those in force in California.

Anthropic wrote in June that “absent a strong federal law, states should retain full authority to legislate.”

Charlie Bullock of the Institute for Law & AI think tank praised the proposal as “pretty reasonable,” and “more than other frontier labs have done.” But he said on X he considers it “weaker” than the FRONTIER Act, a competing bill introduced in the House of Representatives this summer.

World.title: Over 340 children killed in Gaza since ceasefire, says Unicef
World.content:
UNITED NATIONS: More than 340 children have been reportedly killed and hundreds more injured in Gaza since a ceasefire between Hamas and Israel was announced, the UN Children’s Fund (Unicef) said on Friday, warning that children continue to face grave risks despite the truce.

“For families mourning the loss of their children, those terrible statistics do not equate with a ceasefire,” Unicef spokesperson Ricardo Pires told reporters in Geneva.

The Unicef noted that five boys and two girls had been reported killed in Gaza over the preceding two weeks, while at least 33 children were seriously injured in air strikes, drone strikes and gunfire across the territory. Two other boys died from injuries sustained earlier, Pires said.

Around 800,000 children remain displaced, most living in tents or damaged buildings, while an estimated 60,000 have lost one or both parents during the war or since the ceasefire, according to the Unicef.

Nearly every child needs some form of mental health support to recover from the effects of the conflict.

The agency called on the parties to the conflict to uphold the ceasefire, comply with UN Security Council Resolution 2803 and meet their obligations under international humanitarian law.

“Above all, we need to listen to the voices of children in Gaza,” the Unicef said, stressing that recovery meant more than survival. Children needed to return to school, spend time with friends and family, have dignified shelter, play safely and receive healthcare, the agency said.

“Gaza’s children have suffered far too much, for far too long,” it added.

The agency stressed the need to maintain an uninterrupted flow of humanitarian and commercial supplies into Gaza, following reports that private traders had halted cooperation with Israeli authorities over the entry of commercial trucks carrying food.

Pires recalled that supplies had been unable to enter Gaza before the ceasefire, when famine was declared by UN-backed food security experts.

“We can’t go back to a situation where children and families are not getting all the supplies, goods and services that they require,” he said.

Despite the continuing hardship, Unicef has helped more than 560,000 children return to learning since the ceasefire, including through more than 200 learning centres it supports.

The agency has also provided digital cash assistance to more than 380,000 people and safe water to 1.2 million people.

World.title: 5.9-magnitude earthquake jolts Balochistan's Khuzdar
World.content:
A magnitude 5.9 earthquake jolted Balochistan’s Khuzdar district on Saturday, according to the Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD).

The quake occurred at 10:07am at a depth of 25 kilometres, the PMD said in a post on X.

The PMD said the earthquake’s epicentre was located 48 kilometres northwest of Khuzdar, at latitude 28.02 degrees north and longitude 66.20 degrees east.

The department released the seismic data through its Islamabad office.

In August, an earthquake of magnitude 4.8 jolted parts of Balochistan, including Zhob and Chaman.

According to the seismological centre, the earthquake was recorded at a depth of 15 kilometres, with its epicentre located 122km northeast of Zhob.

The tremors caused fear and panic among residents, with many people coming out of their homes and reciting verses from the Holy Quran.

No loss of life or property damage had been reported from the earthquake.

In July, a moderate earthquake of magnitude 4 struck Quetta, Ziarat, Harnai, and surrounding areas, forcing people to come out of their homes and take refuge in open places.

However, no casualty or damage to property was reported from the areas hit by the earthquake.

Pakistan falls on three major tectonic plates — the Arabian, Euro-Asian and Indian — which create five seismic zones under the country. The intersection of multiple fault lines means that tectonic movements remain a frequent occurrence in the region.

World.title: Pakistan rules out unconditional talks with Afghanistan
World.content:
• Demands verifiable mechanism to end terrorist attacks from Afghan soil

• FO says no formal Russian mediation initiative currently under discussion

• Warns India that any future aggression will be met with a stronger response

ISLAMABAD: The Foreign Office on Friday said that talks with Afghanistan could not be unconditional, while rejecting suggestions that Islamabad was unwilling to engage with its neighbour and saying it would welcome sincere efforts by friendly countries to help resolve the dispute.

“Pakistan is not shying away from discussions or dialogue, including with representatives of Afghanistan. Pakistan would welcome any sincere efforts by friendly countries that could help address our legitimate security concerns and promoting regional peace and stability,” Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said at the weekly media briefing.

The statement came as Russia recently renewed its readiness to mediate between the two countries, although Islamabad denied the existence of any such initiative.

“At present, I am not aware of any separate, formal Russian mediation initiative being under discussion,” Mr Khan said, adding that Pakistan remained open to engagement that produced tangible results.

Russia, the only country to have formally recognised the Taliban government, has recently renewed its offer to facilitate a settlement if both sides request its involvement.

Moscow’s special envoy for Afghanistan, Zamir Kabulov, had earlier this month made this suggestion after the latest round of the Moscow Format consultations on Oct 5 ended without a joint communiqué because of differences between Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban delegations over references to terrorist networks operating from Afghanistan.

Mr Khan said the absence of an agreed statement at the Moscow Format meeting reflected the Afghan delegation’s unwillingness to accept language on terrorist networks that had been agreed in the previous year’s document.

“The fact that no joint communiqué was issued after the Moscow Format is self-evident that Afghanistan did not accept the formulation which had been acceptable until last year particularly about presence of terrorist network in Afghanistan. This shows that there is reluctance on the part of Afghanistan that terrorism is originating from its soil,” he said.

The failure to get a joint communique highlighted the central obstacle to normalising relations, which is Pakistan’s demand for action against the Tehreek-i-Taliban Paki­stan (TTP) and other terrorist groups it says are using Afghan territory to launch attacks across the border.

The Taliban authorities have avoided taking a categorical position on the TTP and other groups, while rejecting Islamabad’s allegations that Afghanistan is being used as a base for attacks against Pakistan.

The dispute has frustrated international efforts to reduce tensions. Qatar and Turkiye last October helped broker a ceasefire, but subsequent round of talks failed to reach a lasting settlement. Saudi Arabia separately hosted discussions, while China held talks between the two sides in Urumqi in April. None of these efforts could resolve the disagreement over terrorist groups and the measures needed to prevent cross border attacks.

Pakistan’s position, Mr Khan said, was that dialogue would need to be backed by an arrangement that could verify whether terrorist activity against the country had stopped.

“The talks will not be unconditional. Pakistan has been raising the issue of terrorism emanating from Afghanistan at different forums. Unfortunately, the Taliban regime has been taking one step forward and one step backward,” Mr Khan emphasised.

“Pakistan has only one demand that there should be a verifiable mechanism to ensure complete cessation of terrorist activities emanating from Afghan soil against Pakistan,” he said.

‘Stronger response’

Mr Khan reminded India of the response it faced during last year’s military confrontation and warned that any future aggression would be met with an even stronger response.

FO reaction came after Indian Defence Minister Rajnath Singh a day earlier threatened a bigger strike in the event of any future terrorist attacks.

Singh, while speaking at National Defence Conclave 2026 in Delhi, recalled Operation Sindoor and said that it marked a decisive response to terrorism. He also referred to earlier Indian military operations.

“We reject and condemn the Indian Defence Minister’s provocative remarks entailing a threat of Indian aggression against Pakistan. Such reckless statements reflect India’s hegemonistic mindset and the risks its belligerent posture poses to regional peace and stability in South Asia,” Mr Khan said.

“We wish to remind India of the consequences of its military aggression in May last year, when Pakistan demonstrated both its capability and resolve to defend its sovereignty and territorial integrity and gave a fitting reply to Indian aggression,” the FO spokesperson said.

Mr Khan urged New Delhi to draw lessons from the previous confrontation and avoid further escalation.

“India should draw an appropriate lesson from the last year’s experience and abandon its belligerent posture and dangerous rhetoric and act with responsibility for lasting peace in the region,” he said.

Published in Dawn, October 17th, 2026

World.title: Imran being forced into Benazir, Nawaz-style deal, claims Achakzai
World.content:
• Demands authorities disclose whereabouts of Sohail Afridi

• Mengal says those claiming to be framers of Constitution are ‘trampling it’

• TTAP alliance challenges governor’s rule, emergency before Peshawar High Court

PESHAWAR: PTI fou­nder Imran Khan is being forced into an agreement, similar to those given to former prime ministers Nawaz Sharif and Benazir Bhutto, Leader of the Opposition in the National Assembly Mahmood Khan Achakzai claimed on Friday.

The opposition leader was referring to the arrangements whereby the two former PMs went into self-imposed exile following their respective ousters.

Mr Sharif, who was ousted and imprisoned following a military coup by then-army chief Pervez Musharraf, left the country in 2000 following a deal negotiated by Saudi and Lebanese leaders.

Benazir, meanwhile, voluntarily went into self-exile after her party lost the 1997 general elections following her dismissal by then-president Farooq Leg­hari. At the time, her husband Asif Zardari was imprisoned over corruption charges, and was finally released in 2004.

“The same is happening today with the PML-N and PPP in government,” Mr Achakzai said at a news conference at the Peshawar High Court (PHC).

He was accompanied by Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP) leaders Sardar Akhtar Mengal and Allama Raja Nasir Abbas.

He said they were in contact with all opposition parties and would soon convene a multi-party conference. Resigning from the assemblies was also an option, he said, adding that they had submitted their demands in response to the offer of negotiations.

“Nowhere in the world is a prisoner denied meetings,” he said, calling for the withdrawal of the “wrong amen­dment”, empow­erment of parliament and the formation of an independent commission to ensure transparent elections.

He said no problem could be resolved until parliament was empowered. Expressing concern over the whereabouts of the KP chief minister and other lawmakers, he demanded that the authorities disclose the chief minister’s whereabouts, calling it their constitutional right to know.

“We stand with the people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The people of this province have the first right over its minerals. Regardless of political affiliation, everyone must unite for the homeland,” he said, adding that they would be safer if the country survived.

Mr Mengal said those claiming to be the framers of the Constitution were trampling on it. He questioned the imposition of governor’s rule in KP on the grounds of terrorism, asking whether military operations had improved or worsened conditions in Balochistan.

He said KP’s elected chief minister had been removed, while the provincial assembly speaker and a minister were missing. Those who had won the general elections on Form 47 had become members of the National Assembly, he alleged, adding that the system could not continue this way.

Raja Nasir Abbas, the opposition leader in the Senate, said lawlessness had reached its peak. “You cannot run a country, yet you have occupied a province,” he told reporters, adding that a cabinet member had himself acknowledged that the system had collapsed.

TTAP challenges governor’s rule

Meanwhile on Friday, TTAP leaders challenged the proclamation of emergency and imposition of governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa before the

PHC, seeking to have the measures declared unconstitutional and illegal.

The constitutional petition was jointly filed by TTAP Chairman Mehmood Khan Achakzai, Vice Chairman Senator Raja Nasir Abbas, Balochistan National Party-Mengal chief Sardar Akhtar Mengal and Sindh Taraqi Pasand Party leader Syed Zainul Abideen through Advocates Muazzam Butt and Baseem Ahmad Siddiqui.

The court was requested to declare the Oct 11 proclamation of emergency, issued under Articles 232(1) and 234 of the Constitution, unconstitutional and without lawful authority, arguing that the required constitutional conditions had not been met or that the measures exceeded the powers conferred by the Constitution.

They challenged the purported transfer of the KP Assembly’s legislative powers to parliament and the displacement of the elected chief minister and provincial cabinet. They also sought the annulment of executive orders and notifications that depended on the validity of the proclamation.

The petitioners also challenged the establishment of the purported KP Advisory Council and Area Development Secretariat, arguing that these bodies could not exercise powers beyond those conferred by the Constitution or replace established provincial institutions.

They questioned any purported suspension of constitutional provisions, including Article 175(3), unless expressly authorised by the Constitution.

The petitioners sought annulment of the Oct 11 notification concerning the deployment of armed forces in the province to the extent where it violated Article 245, failed to meet constitutional requirements or exceeded the scope of the provision.

They also sought directions to ensure that elected representatives and constitutionally established institutions in KP were not unlawfully prevented from performing their functions and that no elected representative was detained or restrained except in accordance with the Constitution.

Pending a final decision, they sought interim relief to suspend or restrain the impugned measures to prevent the displacement of elected institutions, transfer of legislative authority, creation of parallel executive structures or other irreparable harm, subject to the court’s assessment of constitutional requirements and public safety.

Published in Dawn, October 17th, 2026

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).
