World.title: Turkmenistan urges support for Ashgabat Climate Dialogue initiative
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 17. Turkmenistan has called on interested countries and international partners to support its initiative to establish the Ashgabat Climate Dialogue, a multilateral platform for cooperation on climate change and environmental protection.

This was reflected in a press release published by the press service of the Turkmen government citing President Serdar Berdimuhamedov’s speech at the 7th Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) in Baku.

“Turkmenistan is putting forward an initiative to establish the Ashgabat Climate Dialogue - a multilateral platform for exchanging experience and coordinating approaches to climate change adaptation, combating desertification and drought, the rational use of water resources and the promotion of green solutions,” Berdimuhamedov said.

The president stressed the importance of strengthening international cooperation on climate change and environmental security, including through the rational use of water resources, the introduction of modern environmental technologies and efforts to improve the resilience of national economies to global climate change.

He also said that CICA had significant potential to support joint projects and promote effective solutions for sustainable environmental development.

Meanwhile, Turkmenistan has been seeking to expand international cooperation on climate change, water security and combating desertification. In July 2026, the government announced plans to establish the Ashgabat Climate Dialogue, alongside regional centres for climate technologies and combating desertification in Central Asia. The proposed interdepartmental commission would coordinate these initiatives with foreign partners and financial institutions.

Water management is a key element of the country's climate agenda. In June 2026, the government, the United Nations and international development partners held a dialogue on long-term water availability scenarios for Turkmenistan through 2050, examining potential implications for agriculture, food security, employment and ecosystems.

Turkmenistan is also participating in regional climate adaptation initiatives supported by UN agencies. These include efforts to strengthen scientific monitoring and cooperation on the impacts of climate change on Central Asia's cryosphere and transboundary water resources.

World.title: Uzbekistan, AIIB explore transport, energy and water projects
World.content:
Photo: the Ministry of Economy and Finance of Uzbekistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 17. Uzbekistan and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) discussed expanding cooperation on road and railway networks, logistics corridors, energy infrastructure and water systems during a meeting in Bangkok on October 15.

This was reflected in the statement by the Uzbekistan Ministry of Economy and Finance, following a meeting between Uzbekistan’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance Jamshid Kuchkarov and AIIB President Zou Jiayi on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank Group.

The discussions focused on Uzbekistan’s macroeconomic trends, economic development priorities and opportunities to expand cooperation with the bank.

Particular attention was given to infrastructure projects aimed at supporting sustainable economic growth. The parties discussed developing road and railway networks, logistics corridors, electricity transmission infrastructure, water supply systems and digital infrastructure.

These projects are expected to improve connectivity, expand business opportunities and create conditions for greater production of higher value-added goods.

Additionally, the officials exchanged views on potential public-private partnership (PPP) projects to develop road infrastructure, as well as initiatives to improve rural infrastructure and modernize public school facilities.

The meeting was attended by AIIB Managing Director General for Investment Operations (Region 2) Konstantin Limitovskiy, Deputy Chairman of the Central Bank of Uzbekistan Nodirbek Ochilov, Adviser to the Minister of Economy and Finance Jasur Karshibayev and other officials.

The parties agreed to expand cooperation, develop new initiatives and continue discussions on the issues raised during the meeting.

World.title: Azerbaijan, Vietnam consider launching direct air links
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 17. Azerbaijan and Vietnam are considering establishing direct air links, including potential flights by Vietjet Air to Baku and regional airports in Azerbaijan.

According to a post on social media by Samir Rzayev, chairman of the Board of Azerbaijan Airlines (AZAL), he met on October 16 with representatives of Vietnam’s Vietjet Air, Sovico Group and Vingroup.

During the meeting, the parties discussed prospects for launching direct air services between Azerbaijan and Vietnam, Vietjet Air flights to Baku and Azerbaijan’s regional airports, and potential cooperation with Azerbaijan Airlines.

“Expanding the international route network, attracting new airlines and diversifying air links are among our strategic priorities,” Rzayev said.

Will be updated

World.title: Azeri Light oil price falls to $116.26 per barrel
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 17. The price of Azerbaijan's Azeri Light crude oil on a CIF basis at Italy's Augusta port fell by $2.78, or 2.33%, from the previous level to $116.26 per barrel, a source in the oil market told Trend.

The source said that the price of Azeri Light crude on a FOB basis at Türkiye's Ceyhan port decreased by $3.07, or 2.83%, to $105.42 per barrel.

The price of Urals crude fell by $1.08, or 1.29%, to $82.32 per barrel. The price of North Sea Dated Brent crude decreased by $9.39, or 7.45%, to $116.59 per barrel.

Azerbaijan's state budget for 2026 is based on an average oil price of $65 per barrel.

According to Trading Economics, crude oil prices exceeded $100 per barrel on Friday.

“Prices have risen by more than 11% over the week amid supply constraints and strong fuel demand from the shipping sector. Producers are facing higher freight rates and risk premiums for shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, increasing uncertainty over future oil supplies from the region. Iranian strikes on oil tankers in the strait have sharply reduced oil flows. In the week ending October 13, average daily oil flows fell to 11.62 million barrels from the previous baseline of 17.15 million barrels.

Security risks in the Persian Gulf have had a significant impact on rising oil prices. At the same time, Ukrainian drone attacks on oil refineries in Russia have further constrained fuel supplies. In addition, US crude oil inventories fell by 8.56 million barrels in the week ending October 9,” the report said.

World.title: Tajikistan, Kuwait meet on renewable energy cooperation
World.content:
Photo: Press Service of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Tajikistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 17. Tajikistan’s Ambassador to the State of Kuwait, Khusrav Noziri, met with Kuwait’s Minister of Electricity, Water and Renewable Energy, Subaih Abdul Aziz Abdul Muhsen Al-Mukhaizeem, on October 15, 2026, to discuss expanding cooperation in renewable energy, according to the Tajik MFA.

During the meeting, the parties discussed the current state and prospects for expanding mutually beneficial cooperation between the two countries in areas of mutual interest.

The parties emphasized Tajikistan’s strategic role and importance in shaping the region’s water resources, as well as its potential and capabilities in hydropower generation.

Furthermore, they also discussed contributions to the global use of clean renewable energy.

Meanwhile, Tajikistan has significant hydropower potential due to its mountainous terrain and extensive river network. Hydropower plays a central role in the country's electricity generation, while the development of renewable energy sources remains an area of potential cooperation with international partners.

Kuwait is working to expand the role of renewable energy as part of its efforts to diversify its energy mix and meet growing electricity demand. Cooperation with countries possessing substantial renewable energy resources could provide opportunities for exchanging expertise and exploring potential joint initiatives.

International cooperation in renewable energy can support the development of cleaner electricity generation, the exchange of technical knowledge, and the implementation of projects aimed at improving long-term energy sustainability.

World.title: Uzbekistan, IsDB sign agricultural mechanization deal
World.content:
Photo: the Ministry of Economy and Finance of Uzbekistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 16. Uzbekistan and the Islamic Development Bank (IsDB) have signed an agreement for an agricultural mechanization project aimed at expanding farmers’ access to modern, efficient and climate-smart machinery, during a meeting on October 15 in Bangkok.

This was reflected in the statement by the Uzbekistan Ministry of Economy and Finance, following a meeting between Uzbekistan’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance Jamshid Kuchkarov and IsDB President Muhammad Al Jasser, on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank.

The discussions focused on priority areas for cooperation, support for Uzbekistan’s ongoing economic reforms, the development of key economic sectors and opportunities to advance joint projects.

Particular attention was given to modernizing agriculture and expanding access to modern agricultural machinery and equipment. The parties also discussed potential projects involving irrigation systems, road infrastructure, rural development, mortgage market financing and agricultural lending.

The Agricultural Mechanization Development Project is designed to increase agricultural productivity, improve resource efficiency and support the development of agricultural value chains through greater access to modern machinery.

Moreover, the talks covered support for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), the development of Islamic finance instruments and opportunities to expand their use in Uzbekistan’s financial sector. The parties discussed financing mechanisms such as Murabaha and Ijarah.

The meeting was attended by IsDB Vice President for Operations Rami Ahmad, Deputy Chairman of the Central Bank of Uzbekistan Nodirbek Ochilov, Adviser to the Minister of Economy and Finance Jasur Karshibayev and other officials.

The parties agreed to strengthen cooperation and continue working on the initiatives discussed during the meeting.

World.title: Tajikistan, UN General Assembly president discuss 2028 Water Conference
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 17. Tajikistan’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Jonibek Hikmat, met with the President of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, Khalilur Rahman, on October 16, 2026, to discuss preparations for the 2028 UN Water Conference, according to the Tajik MFA.

"During the meeting, the parties discussed further implementation of the mandate of the President of the General Assembly in accordance with resolution A/RES/80/304 concerning the modalities for holding the 2028 UN Water Conference," the statement said.

Particular attention was paid to the appointment of two co-coordinators to conduct intergovernmental consultations on the outcome document, the Dushanbe Water Framework, as well as to holding a high-level preparatory event for the conference at the UN Headquarters in New York in March 2027.

Tajikistan’s Permanent Representative to the UN also emphasized the importance of close cooperation in preparations for the 2028 UN Water Conference and reaffirmed Tajikistan’s commitment to close engagement with the Office of the President of the UN General Assembly.

In turn, the President of the General Assembly expressed his readiness to support and assist in preparations for the conference.

Meanwhile, the UN Water Conference provides a platform for countries to discuss global water-related challenges, strengthen international cooperation, and promote progress toward sustainable water management. Preparatory consultations help participating countries coordinate priorities and develop proposals for addressing issues related to water resources, access to safe drinking water, and sanitation.

World.title: Uzbekistan signs five MoUs in Malaysia on semiconductor training
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 17. Uzbekistan and Malaysia have signed memorandums of understanding to develop semiconductor industry skills, expand technology research and strengthen cooperation between universities and industry, during a meeting on October 16 in Malaysia.

This was reflected in the statement by the Uzbekistan Ministry of Economy and Finance.

The first phase of the visit took place in Kuala Lumpur, where the delegation visited Malaysia’s IC Design Park complex and MIMOS Berhad, a key technology research partner in the semiconductor sector.

The delegation toured MIMOS Berhad’s laboratories and examined its technological infrastructure for semiconductor wafer production, microelectronic device prototyping, integrated circuit testing and reliability assessment.

The Uzbek officials also attended the Selangor AI & Semiconductor Summit 2026, where they held meetings with organizations operating in the semiconductor and artificial intelligence sectors to discuss potential areas for cooperation.

As part of the visit, ToshTech Technical University signed MoUs with Malaysia’s ASEM Academy and Great ASIC. Uzbekistan’s Cyber University also signed agreements with Asia e University (AeU), Asia Pacific University of Technology & Innovation (APU) and AlphaSwift.

The agreements are intended to support the training of qualified semiconductor specialists, advance research and practical projects, facilitate the exchange of expertise in advanced technologies and strengthen links between higher education institutions and industry.

The second phase of the Uzbek delegation’s visit is underway in Penang, another key stop in efforts to expand cooperation with Malaysia’s technology sector.

World.title: Police release e-bike rider image in 'sexual touching' case, increase patrols
World.content:
Police have increased patrols on walking trails surrounding a lagoon in Sydney's northern beaches after multiple women reported being "sexually touched" allegedly by a man on an e-bike.

The incidents, which number six to date, took place between October 1 and October 12 in broad daylight while the women were walking or running at Narabeen Lagoon and in the surrounding bushland.

The incidents took place between October 1 and October 12 in broad daylight. (ABC News)

In an update on Saturday afternoon, Superintendent John Duncan said it was alarming that women were being harassed.

"We take these matters very, very seriously," he said.

"In consultation with State Crime Command and the Sex Crime Squad, we've got a number of overt and covert activities.

"We have a number of our uniformed and plain-clothed officers in the area."

Most of the alleged offending occurred between 4pm and 6pm.

In some cases several incidents occurred on one day, which according to police "tends to suggest it's probably someone who is local and someone nearby".

Police say the man is believed to be aged under 25 years and of Caucasian appearance. (Supplied: NSW Police)

Earlier, police released an image of a man they would like to speak to.

He is riding an e-bike and is described as "being of Caucasian appearance, believed to be aged under 25 years, about 175cm tall and of medium build".

Police believe just one person is involved, but are "keeping their options open".

"I'd imagine that person, or their families or friends, will actually know who that is," Superintendent Duncan said.

"And we encourage them to come forward and help with our investigations."

'Rode away on an e-bike'

The first reported incidents happened on October 7 and October 8.

"In each incident, a male allegedly approached women on walking trails, sexually touched them and then rode away on an e-bike," police said in a statement.

"In one of the incidents, the man also made inappropriate sexual comments."

The first incidents reported to police took place on walking trails near the lagoon. (ABC News)

After a public appeal for information on October 12, police received an additional three reports — one dating back to the first of that month.

The woman alleged she was approached by a man near South Creek Road at Wheeler Heights about 4.30pm and allegedly sexually touched before he rode away on an e-bike.

On October 12, in two separate incidents between 5pm and 5:30pm, two women reported being sexually touched by a male riding an e-bike.

There have been no reports since then, Superintendent Duncan said, but he feared there may be more cases.

"We do believe that there are probably more victims out there that may have some information or may have been a victim of this particular crime," he said.

"And we'd like them to come forward and contact either Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 or Dee Why Police Station."

Anyone with dashcam footage is also urged to contact police.

World.title: More teens arrested over alleged assault of 15yo boy
World.content:
Two more teenagers have been arrested over an alleged group assault in the western Victorian town of Stawell earlier this month.

Police say a 15-year-old-boy was attacked by a group of teenagers near the intersection of Wakeham and Doye streets about 5:45pm on October 5.

They allegedly stole his shoes and clothing before running away.

The boy was taken to hospital but has since been released.

On Saturday, police said a 14-year-old boy had been charged with several offences, inlcuding recklessly causing injury, while a 16-year-old girl was also expected to be charged.

It follows the arrests of two 15-year-olds and a 14-year-old on Tuesday. They were charged with affray, robbery, recklessly causing injury, and theft.

They will appear in the children's court at a later date.

A spotlight on security

The incident comes as community pressure grows on the Northern Grampians Shire Council to install CCTV in police-identified crime hotspots at Stawell.

The alleged assault has renewed the conversation about public safety in Stawell. (ABC News: Sarah Mullins)

After the three initial arrests made earlier this week, Mayor Karen Hyslop said the council's policy had not changed "for now", but "priorities can be re-evaluated".

She said council had looked into "the financial cost and privacy concerns", and found CCTV installation would involve "allocating hundreds of thousands of dollars from the budget".

But Stawell resident Jessica Lees, who, alongside two other mothers, ran an online survey earlier this year to collect data in support of cameras being installed, was not happy with that response.

She said more than 300 people filled out the survey and had questioned why the council had not explored every option, including available state government grants for the cameras.

"If other councils across Victoria can find ways to fund CCTV, why can't we?" she asked.

World.title: Australia's first Vietnamese heritage museum opens in Melbourne
World.content:
Before the days of bánh mì takeaways and discount flight holidays, to most Australians Vietnam was known only for the horrors of conflict and conscription.

That was to change with the end of the Vietnam War.

Thousands of Vietnamese refugees made the perilous journey to Australia in the mid-1970s, saying an abrupt goodbye to Saigon and an apprehensive hello to Melbourne's Sunshine and St Albans or Sydney's Cabramatta and Canley Vale.

Tammy Nguyen's parents escaped Vietnam on a perilous six-day, seven-night boat journey. (Supplied)

Five decades on, refugee beginnings and generational achievement were recognised with the opening of the nation's first museum dedicated to Vietnamese-Australian history.

Constructed on a council car park in Sunshine, the unveiling of Vietnamese Museum Australia marked the culmination of a decade-long campaign to establish a permanent monument to the community's pioneering generation.

The parents of the museum's chief executive, Tammy Nguyen, escaped Vietnam on a perilous six-day, seven-night boat journey.

"There are more than 350,000 people of Vietnamese-origin living in Australia and everyone has their own unique story to tell," Ms Nguyen said.

" This museum is a living monument to all those who courageously left their homeland behind — often as refugees on overcrowded and unseaworthy boats — seeking freedom and a better future. "

The project has received bipartisan support, with Victorian Premier Ben Carroll officially opening the centre on Saturday alongside MPs from across the political divide.

Both the federal and Victorian governments contributed millions to the project, alongside grassroots community contributions.

The Vietnamese-Australian community worked for more than a decade to establish the museum. (Supplied)

Liberal MP Trung Luu, who represents the Western Metropolitan Region in the state's upper house, said the museum's opening was a significant day for the Vietnamese community.

"As someone who came to Australia as a refugee from Vietnam, today is deeply personal for me," he said.

"This museum honours the courage of every family who made that journey."

Lan Anh Hoang says racial anxieties lingered due to the legacy of the White Australia policy. (Supplied)

University of Melbourne development studies professor Lan Anh Hoang said public attitudes towards Vietnamese refugees in the 1970s and 1980s were mixed as the nation adjusted to life post-White Australia policy.

"In the immediate aftermath of the fall of Saigon, there was a great deal of sympathy and compassion, particularly because of Australia's own involvement in the war," she said.

"But as boat arrivals continued towards the end of the 1970s, concerns grew about uncontrolled migration, and the legacy of the White Australia policy meant that racial anxieties still lingered."

Professor Hoang said Vietnamese migrants to Australia who relocate in 2026 find themselves in a more welcoming environment.

But she added that they also tended to be more educated or skilled, with better English proficiency than the refugees who came in the 1970s.

"Many describe the kindness and generous support of churches and community organisations (in the 1970s)," she said.

"At the same time, Vietnamese families and their children faced more than their fair share of racism in the community and at school.

"It was not easy to be a Vietnamese kid growing up in Australia at that time."

Flashback: Members of the Vietnamese community pay their respects to Malcolm Fraser at the former prime minister's 2015 funeral. (ABC News: Clement Paligaru)

University of Technology Sydney sociology professor Andrew Jakubowicz said the mid-1970s intake of Vietnamese-Australians under the Fraser Government was the first real test of the post-White Australia policy consensus.

Malcolm Fraser became a champion of the Vietnamese-Australian diaspora and members of the community paid tribute to the ex-PM at his 2015 funeral.

"(Vietnamese-Australians) were admitted as the first big group of refugees from a group that had almost no prior presence," Professor Jakubowicz said.

"Initially, most were Catholic southerners and pro-Saigon. Their actual travel to Australia was traumatic — they were the first modern boat people.

"They arrived in the shadow of the end of White Australia into a country that was trepidatiously ready to accept Asians.

"Before then, most Asians admitted after 1967 were English-speaking professionals."

World.title: Breaking: Ohope Wins euthanased after nasty fall in Caulfield Cup
World.content:
New Zealand mare Ohope Wins has been euthanased after a fall in the Caulfield Cup that also included 2025 Melbourne Cup winner Half Yours.

With about 200 metres to go in the 2,400m race, which was won by Gavin Bedggood's Kingswood, Half Yours was in the middle of the pack when there appeared to be contact with Kings Valley.

Half Yours went down hard, sending jockey Mark Zahra into the turf, with Ohope Wins also coming down after Jye McNeil was unable to avoid the fallen McEvoy Racing product.

Ohope Wins (highlighted right) fell over the top of Half Yours (highlighted left) in the back straight. (Supplied: Racing.com)

Racing Victoria Stewards later confirmed Ohope Wins, from Chris Waller Racing, was euthanased by the on-course veterinarian.

"The mare was unable to be saved due to the nature of the injury sustained," a Racing Victoria (RV) statement read.

"RV extends its condolences to Yulong, the owners of Ohope Wins, her trainer Chris Waller and their stable staff who cared for the horse and are deeply saddened by their loss."

Half Yours got up and continued the race, eventually crossing the finish line without a jockey.

The stewards said Half Yours would undergo a "thorough veterinary examination" after falling in "a racing incident", which would be subject to an inquiry.

Half Yours got up after the fall and crossed the line without jockey Mark Zahra. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Half Yours returned to his stall, while stewards said Zahra and McNeil were both "conscious and alert" and transported to hospital for further assessment.

Trainer Tony McEvoy said after the race that Half Yours had suffered some abrasions but looked OK, all things considered.

"That was terrible to watch," McEvoy said.

"The horse, he's got a couple of lacerations, he seems bright, he seems composed in himself.

"He's got a laceration under his arm, he's got a laceration on a hind leg. They look superficial."

The final race of the day at Caulfield was delayed.

World.title: Australia's deadliest asylum seeker boat disaster remembered 25 years on
World.content:
Mourners have gathered at a national memorial in Canberra to mark the 25th anniversary of Australia's deadliest asylum seeker boat disaster, the sinking of the SIEV X.

On October 19, 2001, 353 people died when the fishing boat, heading to Christmas Island, sank in international waters off the coast of the Indonesian island of Java.

Of the dead, 146 were children.

The 20-metre-long boat, which was carrying more than 400 people, capsized and sank when its engine failed in heavy seas.

More than 20 hours after the vessel went down, 45 survivors were rescued by Indonesian fishing boats.

The name SIEV X is a naval acronym, standing for Suspected Illegal Entry Vessel X.

Mourners gathered at the SIEV X Memorial on the shores of Lake Burley Griffin in Canberra for the 25th anniversary of the disaster. (ABC News: Caitlin Maloney)

While the vessel sank 70 kilometres south of Java, not in Australia's waters, the disaster occurred in a border protection surveillance area temporarily designated by Australia.

Questions still remain about the SIEV X tragedy 25 years after it occurred, with many of the victims never publicly identified and no full judicial inquiry ever taking place.

The victims are remembered at the SIEV X Memorial in Canberra's Weston Park, where each wooden pole — decorated by school, church and community groups — marks one person who died.

Advocacy group Refugee Action Campaign (RAC) Canberra organised the 25-year memorial service along the shores of Lake Burley Griffin to honour the lives lost in the "preventable tragedy".

The SIEV X Memorial covers 400m of shoreline at Weston Park along Lake Burley Griffin. (Supplied)

The RAC said the service also allowed attendees "to stand in solidarity with [the victims'] loved ones, and to show support and compassion for refugees and people seeking asylum".

"In today's environment in which migrants and refugees are being blamed by politicians with nothing else to offer for the failures of governments to prioritise the needs of ordinary people, the SIEV X Memorial remains as relevant as ever," Refugee Action Campaign Canberra said.

A political message 25 years on

In August 2001, more than 400 asylum seekers were rescued by Norweigian ship the Tampa, sparking a national and international crisis. (AAP)

The SIEV X tragedy occurred just weeks after the Howard government refused the entry of Norwegian freighter MV Tampa, which was carrying more than 400 rescued asylum seekers.

The Tampa affair sparked intense debate leading up to the 2001 federal election campaign, as the government hardened its stance on asylum seekers.

Memorial co-founder Steve Biddulph said on the fifth anniversary of the disaster, the Howard government opposed the memorial on Commonwealth land, and so those who gathered for the service held the memorial's poles upright.

People gathered in 2006 on the fifth anniversary of the SIEV X boat disaster and established a temporary memorial. (ABC TV)

He said a year later, with the support of John Stanhope, the then ACT chief minister, permission was given to make the memorial permanent.

"It sends a signal that ordinary Australians are not terrified of refugees, they're not terrified of people from other countries," he said.

"We're essentially a loving, caring nation, and we were being sold an image of ourselves that was completely wrong.

"And so it's a message of hope, really, that love is stronger than fear."

Co-founder Steve Biddulph says the memorial was created to show the SIEV X victims were remembered as people and not just numbers. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

President of the SIEV X Memorial Association ACT Paul Meyer said the disaster remained political 25 years on, when people were "turning against migrants in general".

"Many of us have come here ourselves; a huge proportion of Australians have at least one migrant parent, if not a grandparent, so we all know that Australia's a country that welcomes people to come as long as we can contribute to it," he said.

He said as people gathered around the memorial today, more than 100 names of the drowning victims had not been made public — something both he and Mr Biddulph sought to rectify.

Paul Meyer of the SIEV X Memorial Association says the memorial's message is even more important now as the political climate is "turning against migrants in general". (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

"We tracked down around 220 of the names, and they're written on the poles, but they should all be named ... we could really do the right thing there," Mr Biddulph said.

Mr Meyer said he hoped the memorial continued to act as a beacon of compassion.

"And it's a defiance of what today would be the Hansonite approach [of], 'Oh let's be terrified,'" he said.

World.title: Cosmetics company data breach affects 340,000 clients
World.content:
Cosmetics company Napoleon Perdis has been hit by a data breach, affecting almost 340,000 customers.

In an email to customers, the company said it was informed in June that a third party it had used to store customer records, Retail Express, had been hit by a cyber attack.

"In August 2026, Retail Express confirmed the unauthorised party had access between November 2025 and June 2026, affecting approximately 339,055 customer records," the email said.

The brand was launched in Sydney in 1995 by makeup artist and businessman Napoleon Perdis. (AAP)

"The incident has been contained and the system permanently shut down."

Napoleon Perdis said the breach affected its customers from pre-June 2025.

The information accessed included customer names, dates of birth, email addresses, phone numbers, postal addresses and purchase histories.

"This system did not hold your bank account or card details, or the password for your napoleonperdis.com account.

"Our current online store … was not affected."

Napoleon Perdis warned customers to be wary of scam calls or emails impersonating the company and advised them to monitor their bank transactions.

The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner has been notified.

World.title: Crows snap Suns' winning run to climb into AFLW finals spots
World.content:
The Crows are back in the AFLW finals frame after ending the Gold Coast's six-game winning streak in Adelaide.

Led throughout by Irish sisters Grace (three goals, 12 disposals) and Niamh Kelly (two goals, 20 disposals), and 18-year-old Chloe Bown (one goal, 25 disposals) in the final quarter, the Crows scored back-to-back wins for just the second time this season in a 10.3 (63) to 7.11 (53) win.

The bad news for the Crows was the loss of influential midfielder Maddi Newman who went down twice with a knee injury.

She stayed down after a non-contact incident midway through the third quarter and got subbed off to have her left knee strapped before coming back onto the field.

Later in the term, she was hit hard by Gold Coast's Charlie Rowbottom and was carried off again, later appearing on the sidelines on crutches with ice on the back of her knee.

The win left the Crows eighth on the ladder with five wins and five losses, equal on points with Hawthorn, and four points ahead of Fremantle, West Coast, Port Adelaide and Richmond, although the Dockers, Eagles and Power all have a game in hand.

World.title: La Bola Negra star Milo Quifes has never acted before, but now he is all in
World.content:
As an out and proud author who has published a gay romance novel, Spanish actor Milo Quifes can't quite believe his luck at making his screen debut as an actor in Cannes-feted film and Oscar-contender, La Bola Negra.

The sweeping historical fiction is extrapolated from an unfinished fragment by revered Spanish poet and playwright Federico García Lorca and written and directed by Los Javis — Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi — and casts Quifes as Carlos, the beating heart behind one of three intertwined stories.

What: La Bola Negra, a queer Spanish Civil War drama Directed by: Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi Starring: Milo Quifes, Penélope Cruz, Glenn Close, Carlos González When: In cinemas now Likely to make you feel: Like you should always follow your dreams

"All those months creating Carlos and La Bola Negra with Los Javis, it was an honour," he tells ABC News. "This opportunity to scratch the surface of an unfinished work, and to bring Lorca's writing to life."

He found resonance in Lorca's writing.

"My belief is that acting is a way to explore myself," Quifes says of recognising the fraught trials of coming out or not. "I could feel all these little things, in reading Lorca, that helped me play Carlos."

Seeing is believing

At school, Quifes studied Lorca alongside other members of Spain's celebrated Generation of '27 writers, including Jorge Guillén and Rafael Albert. But it was only after landing the part of Carlos following six auditions across two months that he set about devouring everything available.

" It was amazing, rediscovering Lorca," he says. "I spent all summer reading the unfinished works, the poetry, the theatre, everything. "

And yet all that research couldn't prepare Quifes for his first day on a major film set.

Milo Quifes's character Carlos is devastatingly rejected by the old guard of his father's casino for his rumoured homosexuality. (Supplied)

Quifes's character Carlos is a handsome young man from a well-to-do family in Granada. He has the world at his feet, even as distant drums beat inexorably towards the Spanish Civil War. And yet, all his privilege cannot open one door: that of the luxurious local club, or casino, of which his domineering father is a long-time member.

Why? Because this is 1932, and Carlos's closeted homosexuality, a poorly kept secret, is a black mark against his name in unaccepting times.

On Quifes's first day on set, he was overwhelmed by the throng of cast and crew and dazzled by the baroque-inspired casino set, realised by production designer Roger Bellés, art director Oriol Guardiola and set decorator Judit Ferrer.

"I'm in the middle of that lavish casino set and you cannot imagine all the little details," Quifes says, wide-eyed once more.

"I mean, you read the script, and you imagine that space, but you cannot grasp it until you are actually there. The art team were amazing."

The baroque palace is crowned by a great glass dome from which hangs a glittering crystal chandelier. Elegantly looping brass tracks cup this astonishing space, along which the titular back balls roll, the voting method used to block Carlos's membership.

The 25-year-old novelist and actor Milo Quifes immersed himself in the texts of Lorca in the summer before filming. (Supplied)

It was almost too much, but once Quifes donned his immaculately tailored suit, as visualised by costume designer Ana López Cobos, his confidence grew exponentially.

"As soon as I pulled on that jacket, my back straightened," he says. "From there, it was step-by-step, little-by-little, day-by-day, but I had very good directors, in Los Javis, and a great team around me."

Face the Cruz and dance

The filming took novice actor Quifes from the lofty world of a casino to the astounding beauty of Granada's snow-capped Sierra Nevada mountain range.

He loved it, even if Carlos's stylish suits were hardly suitable attire for diving into snowdrifts.

"Sometimes you have to suffer for your art," he chuckles, thinking back to how freezing he was, shooting take after take, damp and shivering.

" My mind was so chaotic, but you have to focus and get it right. I remember lying in the snow, looking at the sky, and thinking, 'This is amazing.' "

Each of La Bola Negra's three storylines, set in different locations and timeframes, were filmed separately.

Quifes didn't meet many of his fellow cast members until it premiered at Cannes, where it was nominated for the Palme d'Or and the Queer Palm, with Los Javis taking home best director.

Glenn Close plays a US academic who helps 2017-era queer character Alberto on his research journey. (Supplied)

Quifes was in Madrid when co-star Carlos González was filming a key scene with Glenn Close, but the hectic schedule prevented him from meeting the American legend. Sadly, Close couldn't make the Cannes premiere, so he's still patiently waiting to meet an actor he admires and adores.

"I don't know if she's aware of my existence," he laughs.

You lose some, you win some.

Quifes did get to meet another of his heroes, Spanish superstar Penélope Cruz, when she shot her spectacular club sequence in an abandoned theatre in Sigüenza.

"Penélope was amazing," he beams. "She was very down-to-earth, caring, loving and funny all at the same time."

A film still from La Bola Negra featuring Penelope Cruz. (Supplied: Netflix)

Like Cruz, Quifes also delivers a show-stopping dance number in the movie, revealing it was one of the trickiest days on set.

"I don't have any sense of timing," he says of his clumsy footwork. "So my amazing choreographer Belén Martí Lluch had to teach me how to feel the freedom with my body, and I practised a lot."

It turns out Lluch was the perfect teacher. "We shot that scene three times, but the one that's in the film is my first take."

And the Oscar goes to …

While voting for the Oscars is yet to begin, with the shortlists announced mid-December, the buzz around La Bola Negra is hard to ignore, with the streamer Netflix throwing its campaign muscle behind its horse in the race.

As far as Quifes is concerned, it's too soon to talk awards season potential. "I can't think about that," he insists, covering his eyes bashfully.

It was wild enough going to Cannes with Los Javis, Cruz and co. "I was disassociating."

While he may be modest, Quifes hopes that this is just the beginning, with his passion for acting flourishing on set.

"If I can take this space to ask directors to call me, I will," he says, flashing a wide smile. "Now that I have discovered this world, that makes me so happy, I want to do it again. I want to be this happy again."

La Bola Negra is in cinemas now.

World.title: Stewards to hold inquiry into tragic Caulfield Cup fall; favourite beaten in Everest stunner
World.content:
Racing Victoria has issued a veterinary statement following the tragic falls in the Caulfield Cup today, which resulted in the death of Ohope Wins. Half Yours, the 2025 winner, avoided serious injury after also falling during the race.

RV said Ohope Wins, a mare, was attended to immediately but couldn’t be saved and the on-course veterinarian euthanised her.

Half Yours regained his feet and was undergoing a thorough veterinary examination.

RV offered its condolences to the connections of Ohope Wins and said stewards would conduct an inquiry into the incident. The incident would also be reviewed by RV veterinary services as is standard practice.

World.title: The Bledisloe Cup used to be a great rivalry. This year proved it no longer is
World.content:
Analysis SportRugby UnionWallabies The Bledisloe Cup used to be a great rivalry. This year proved it no longer is Tom Decent October 17, 2026 — 6:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

After a period of promise under new coach Les Kiss, whose first five matches in charge of the Wallabies produced an unbeaten run, the bubble has well and truly burst. The casual Australian fan will always judge the Wallabies by how they fare against the All Blacks, and this latest abject showing – a 43-21 defeat in Sydney – not only confirms that the Wallabies are struggling, but suggests the once-great rivalry between the two rugby nations is in peril, too. Wallabies fullback Tom Wright after Saturday’s loss to the All Blacks. Getty Images Afternoon sunshine is the perfect backdrop for running rugby – the stuff the Wallabies were renowned for in their golden years – and there was plenty of it early as Australia burst through holes down the right edge to signal their intent. But when Rob Valetini slipped off a tackle on Josh Moorby in the 12th minute, and wily All Blacks veteran Beauden Barrett crossed five minutes later, it was abundantly clear there would be no let-up from the Kiwis with the Bledisloe Cup already secured for another year.



Wallabies fullback Tom Wright said his side had “faced the music” after last week’s horror 50-19 loss in Auckland. You shudder to think what is in store for them after one of the most shambolic first halves of rugby in Australia’s history. There was once a time when 13 consecutive defeats to the All Blacks would have been considered unacceptable. Spread over six years, the underwhelming run of results has passed with barely a raised eyebrow. Perhaps Wallabies fans have simply become immune to more pain. Damian McKenzie makes a break for the All Blacks on Saturday. Getty Images The aggregate margin of defeat, 53 points across Auckland and Sydney, was the highest in a two-match Bledisloe Cup series. The previous highest was a combined 44 points in 1996, when the Wallabies lost 43-6 in Wellington and 32-25 in Brisbane.



For Australia to make any impression at next year’s World Cup on home soil, they must quickly learn the lessons from this match, in which they were comprehensively outclassed and out-enthused. Perhaps the only consolation is that a loss to the All Blacks in the pool stages would likely see Australia avoid South Africa – who, on the evidence of this year, are more ruthless than ever. Beauden Barrett scores for the All Blacks. Getty Images Some Wallabies supporters walked out at the 20-minute mark. Not out of the stadium itself, but presumably to the bar for an alcoholic beverage to make the next 60 minutes somewhat more palatable. As Nine and Stan Sport commentator Sean Maloney aptly put it: “New Zealand are in a mood.”



That was an understatement. But certainly not the biggest of the day. That honour belonged to the Wallabies’ social media accounts, which declared at half-time, with Australia trailing 36-7 and having already conceded six tries, that there was “work to do after the break”. When all the cogs in the All Blacks machine are working in harmony, it is beautiful to watch. Even with their goal-kicking slightly off – Damian McKenzie missed three of his first four attempts – they bulldozed their way through gaping holes in Australia’s defence. And when they couldn’t go around the Wallabies, they simply went straight over the top. All Blacks No.8 Wallace Sititi’s decision to peel off the back of a scrum down the blindside and run straight over Ryan Lonergan for his side’s fifth try deserves consideration as one of the softest tries Australia have ever conceded.



Put Moorby’s untouched effort in the 43rd minute in that same category as Lonergan and Max Jorgensen appeared to look at each other, wondering why the other hadn’t bothered to make a tackle. That comically bad effort drew a filthy look from Kiss, who threw his hands down in disgust. Wallabies No.10 Declan Meredith delivered the final pass for Jeremy Williams’ try but otherwise produced a mixed performance. With playmakers Carter Gordon and Ben Donaldson injured, Kiss’ decision not to throw experienced campaigners Bernard Foley or James O’Connor a lifeline will be debated in the days to come. Tom Wright is the epitome of a rocks-or-diamonds player, Jorgensen has flashes of brilliance but needs more support, while Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii had nine runs for just 10 metres gained. None of that should detract from the brilliance of an All Blacks side battle-hardened by their tour of South Africa and boasting an impressive tackle completion rate of 91 per cent.



Related Article Wallabies Will the Wallabies win the Bledisloe Cup again? The margin flattered Australia, given the result was a fait accompli by half-time. Not conceding a try in the final 37 minutes was a small consolation the Wallabies can take into their upcoming spring tour of Europe. The men in gold have won their fair share of Bledisloe Cup dead rubbers over the years, but this was not one of those days. It was as sombre as a rugby Test can be on home soil. Last week’s defeat confirmed a 24th year of Bledisloe Cup misery, while Saturday’s capitulation gave further credence to the argument that Australia might have to wait another 24 years to win it again.

World.title: Consumers again foot the bill after surcharge shuffle
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Amid the uproar at the removal of the credit card surcharge, no one appears to be investigating how banks can make $1.6 billion from fees and charges. I use a debit card and object to paying extra for the right to use my own money, so it’s usually cash or eftpos (“Cash is king in business backlash”, October 11). Yet again we are seeing the costs of business being stripped out and passed on to consumers as banks make ever more obscene profits. Perhaps if businesses refused cards and consumers used cash, the extra cost on banks to transport and handle cash might cause a rethink. Wayne Duncombe, Lilyfield

So “cash is king”. You try to find an ATM machine these days to get cash out. They’ve disappeared! You have to spend money driving to find one. I’m paying an extra 20¢ for my coffee – and that’s with cash! Graham Watson, Woollahra

Dying breed? ATMs are becoming harder to come by. Louie Douvis

All the wailing over the RBA’s ban on surcharging credit cards shows up only one thing: that business has been slugging consumers with a hefty surcharge every time one goes to buy something. Now all the businesses have to do is adjust their prices and they are back to square one and the consumer knows exactly how much they are paying. Furthermore, businesses can now shop around and get the best rate for their credit card transactions, which previously were hidden but must now be published by the banks. Also, all transactions are now cheaper by half a per cent on credit cards for all businesses. What’s not to like? There is transparency when a customer purchases something and savings for businesses. Pamela Wood, McMahons Point

Pay up and smile

I hope that private school parents do not expect sympathy for the exorbitant cost of their children’s private school tuition (“Parents facing $800k in private school fees”, October 11). They already receive massive federal funding, parental building grants, restoration projects and buy-up plans for city blocks, and student fees are increased almost yearly – all while perfectly presented public schools stand nearby at a small percentage of the costs. For some, it is prestige and influence above all in the choices we make. No sympathy here. Janice Creenaune, Austinmer

World.title: Powerbrokers, influencers, safari suits descend on Caulfield Cup
World.content:
SportRacingCBD Powerbrokers, influencers, safari suits descend on Caulfield Cup Fiona Byrne October 17, 2026 — 6:28pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Racing is a great equaliser, so industry rivalries and intrigue were set aside at Caulfield on Saturday for the running of the 150th Caulfield Cup. The centre of power and influence in Melbourne was the invitation-only committee room at Caulfield, where politicians, racing heavyweights, business identities and a smattering of celebrities rubbed shoulders. Cup colour: Bella Keltie (left) and Tayla at Caulfield on Saturday. Chris Hopkins It was a serious flex and example of pulling power by the Melbourne Racing Club, which has Caulfield in its remit. Not many doors were being knocked by politicians, as a slice of the political class took in the action at the track including Racing Minister Anthony Carbines, Deputy Opposition Leader David Southwick, shadow federal treasurer Tim Wilson and the retiring state Liberal member for Malvern, Michael O’Brien.



The Melbourne Racing Club board – comprising chair Cameron Fisher, vice chair Jonathan Munz, treasurer Alison Saville, and committee members Caitrin Kelly, Belinda Meyers, Robyn Gray, Stephen Foster, David Gambell and Frank Pollio – was out in force along with club chief executive Tanya Fullarton. Victoria Racing Club chair Neil Wilson, who recently announced he would step down after this year’s Melbourne Cup Carnival, and wife Stephanie were moving between the committee room and the mounting yard, where they were supporting friends who had runners in the big races. Michael Ramsden, current vice chairman of the VRC, was also in the power room. Alexander Merrett and Zach Merrett at the Caulfield Cup. Penny Stephens Racing Victoria boss Aaron Morrison, former Collingwood president Eddie McGuire businessman Gerry Ryan, trainer Gai Waterhouse, retired jockey Michelle Payne, award-winning actor Rachel Griffiths – fresh from the set of her new courtroom drama Slander – footy great Chris Judd, ex-jockey Tom Prebble and Mr Melbourne Martin Pakula (the former MP-turned Melbourne Grand Prix boss) were also mingling. Even former Melbourne Racing Club chair John Kanga, who resigned from his post last year, made an appearance.



Prolific racehorse owners Ozzie Kheir, Rupert Legh and John O’Neill were spotted, while Melbourne’s breakfast radio king, 3AW’s Ross Stevenson, got the day off on a winning note when his horse, Captain Maverick, won the second race in Doomben. Stevenson is a winner on the track as well as on air. Meanwhile, down in the bustling corporate enclosure, the spring fling of socialising and marquee hopping was in full flight with the top destination being The Beverly marquee – or as we here at CBD like to call it, Planet Beverly. AFL great Nathan Buckley (right) in the Sportsbet marquee. Penny Stephens Hosted by the folk behind the Beverly restaurant/bar in South Yarra, Cameron Northway and Emily Gurr, this was the cool kids’ lair. Sure, it was at the track, but whether some of the guests knew they were at the races or not was debatable.



New Hawthorn recruit Zach Merrett, the former Essendon star now carrying the banner as Caulfield Cup ambassador, was a bundle of nerves as he had a horse running in the group 1 Thousand Guineas. Merrett’s brother-in-law is a blood stock agent with leading trainer Ciaron Maher. Merrett agreed to buy a share in the horse last year and had “forgotten” until recently that he was part of the ownership group. The horse had won its past two starts. Jason Kimberley and his friend at Caulfield. Fiona Byrne “It has been a wild six weeks,” the footballer told CBD. “I’m a bit nervous. It is my first group 1 runner.” Jason Kimberley, the entrepreneur, adventurer, author and former No.1 ticket holder at the Swans, made a run for best-dressed man at the track. Forget trends – he bravely opted for a camel-coloured safari suit.



“Given most of the horses I back run like camels, I figured it was appropriate to wear a camel safari suit, sleeveless, to accommodate the very summery temperature,” he said. Adelle Petropoulos in the Beverly at Caulfield. Penny Stephens Kimberley’s fashion choice left many influencers in the shade. “Well, I haven’t spotted any influencers, I’m not sure if I’d recognise them if I saw them,” he mused. “But, look, we’re here for fun today.” Sparkly Brightonites Zana Pali and Calista Clements parked their podcasts and social media projects for the day. Clements, a fast rising loud voice in conservative media commentary, put a political spin on the day.



“I love a day at the races, but my grand final is the Victorian state election when we can see Labor never return,” Clements said. Gallery Gallery icon 26 images Caulfield Cup Caulfield Cup 2026 Pali added: “Goodbye Charlie, or should I say Ben.” Liberal MP Bev McArthur was spotted in the Sportsbet marquee with James Mathias, the executive director of the HR Nicholls Society. Former Victorian premier Denis Napthine was also among the marquee guests. Former Miss Universe Australia Olivia Molly Rogers floated through the enclosure. Nine years on from her title win, she still retains that pageant polish.



Noted hair artist Joey Scandizzo bucked fashion standards – for him a shirt was optional under his suit. Related Article Live

Spring racing carnival Stewards to hold inquiry into tragic Caulfield Cup fall; favourite beaten in Everest stunner Much was made of influencer Adelle Petropoulos attending the Cup, as she’s big in the social media space. Petropoulos, who arrived an 90 minutes late for her media call – she blamed a wardrobe malfunction for her tardy arrival – gained notice last year after she split with her fiance and wore what was to be her wedding gown to the Australian Grand Prix’s Glamour On The Grid party. She has parlayed that burst of attention into a career as a young female empowerment TikTokker. Let’s just say the bar to fame or social profile is set quite low these days. World.title: Horse’s death, reigning champion’s fall overshadow finish of the Caulfield Cup
World.content:
Breaking SportRacingCaulfield Cup Horse’s death, reigning champion’s fall overshadow finish of the Caulfield Cup Danny Russell and Andrew Wu October 17, 2026 — 6:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A tragic two-horse fall, which involved the 2025 champion and resulted in the death of another horse, has marred what should have been a fairytale finish to the 150th running of the Caulfield Cup for victorious trainer Gavin Bedggood and Irish jockey John Allen. While Bedggood and jockey Allen celebrated their first victory in the $6 million group 1 race, they were unaware of the carnage that unfolded behind them. A riderless Half Yours after the fall. Getty Images The mounting yard was sent into shock as medical staff raced to treat jockeys Mark Zahra (Half Yours) and Jye McNeil (Ohope Wins), who were left lying on the course, while galloper Ohope Wins suffered fatal injuries. Stewards were able to quickly calm worried family and connections of the jockeys by releasing a statement to say both would be taken to hospital but had escaped serious injury.



The second horse involved in the devastating tumble – Half Yours, the winner of last year’s Melbourne Cup and Caulfield Cup double – quickly regained his feet and was gathered in by a clerk of the course. Worried trainer Tony McEvoy sprinted onto the track to check up on Zahra in a dramatic finish to the Cup, and then returned to the mounting yard grim faced, but relieved to tell stressed connections his horse had suffered a laceration but was OK. Jye McNeil on Ohope Wins during trackwork in the days before the Caulfield Cup. Getty Images A green tarp was erected around the Chris Waller-trained Ohope Wins in the home straight. The mare was euthanised. Waller was not on the course. The champion trainer had stayed in Sydney to prepare his sprinter Joliestar for The Everest.



Stewards immediately opened an inquiry into the cause of the tragic fall, which blackened the day. The nervous excitement of Half Yours’ owners as the runners were being loaded into the stalls turned into disbelief two minutes later when their champion fell. Some in the ownership group were in tears, unsure of the horse’s welfare. Their emotions were in contrast to the ecstasy 12 months ago when they won the first leg of Victorian racing’s fabled Cups double. View post on X “To have the excitement and the highs we had last year and [to have] this happen today, we love the horse,” managing part-owner Jason Biasin said minutes after the race.



“You just hope he’s OK. We hope Mark’s OK.” Half Yours came down moments after Kings Valley, ridden by Jabez Johnstone, ran in as a result of a buffeting duel with Rachel King’s Green Spaces shortly after rounding the turn. Ohope Wins was unable to avoid Half Yours and fell several strides later. The moment the falls occurred in the Caulfield Cup. Channel Seven After the race, King said: “[It was] just a messy-run race from where we were.” This masthead is not suggesting that any jockey caused the fall. The stewards’ findings are yet to be determined.



Rival jockey Craig Williams turned his attention to his colleagues as he left the track. “My thoughts, most importantly, are with the horses and riders that fell,” he said. The race result was a big moment for former jumps jockey Bedggood, who has long been seen as an heir apparent to dominant trainer Ciaron Maher, as his grey Kingswood overcame a bad draw to sit three wide and win the race from Saint George and Enfjaar. Trainer Gavin Bedggood and jockey John Allen with the Caulfield Cup trophy. Getty Images “I was gutted when I saw it [the wide barrier] and thought we had to go back,” Bedggood said, unaware at that stage of details surrounding the tragic circumstances of the race.



“You speak to people that you need to speak to and I had a chat to Johnny [Allen] yesterday and said, ‘You’re riding it, you’ve drawn 17’. “I’ve ridden in races and it’s easy to sit on the sidelines and say I want you to do this, I want you to do that, but it’s not an easy task from we here drew. I pretty much left it in his hands. “We were pretty much posted three-wide all the way and everyone wanted to question the horse’s credentials at a mile-and-a-half. We couldn’t condemn him on his run here, it was on a [track rating of] heavy 9 and you had to put a line through it. It’s great to be vindicated.” He said he was grateful to former trainer Darren Weir, who told Kingswood’s owners to consider him as a training option. “He told the owners to send the horse my way, so I’m really grateful for that,” Bedggood said.



“When I got it, he told me it reminded him of Puissance De Lune, not because it’s a grey, but because it’s tough, it’s got a good constitution and it’s got a good capacity. He was bang on with everything he said.” Allen said: “Gavin, he’s a trainer going places, we’ll be hearing a lot more of him after I’m retired.” John Allen (left) rides Kingswood to win the Caulfield Cup. Getty Images Shinn makes amends Jockey Blake Shinn made up for the disappointment of being shelved for a Caulfield Cup ride on Saturday by taking out the other group 1 on the program – the $1.5million group 1 Caulfield Guineas on Saintly Dancer.



Shinn, who missed nine months of riding after breaking his leg on Melbourne Cup day last year, copped a nasty surprise during the week when told by trainer Ciaron Maher he would not be partnering Royal Supremacy in the $6 million group 1 classic. Maher told the star hoop that he had double-booked the ride, instead handing the reins to visiting UK jockey Jamie Spencer. It was a head-scratching decision considering the woeful record of international riders in our classic races. Saintly Dancer and Blake Shinn win the group 1 Thousand Guineas at Caulfield. Getty Images But Maher threw Shinn a handy consolation prize. He also trains Saintly Dancer. “[It was the] first Group 1 since I’ve been back, it certainly hasn’t been an easy road, but you just keep turning up and put the work in, and you get repaid with a big winner here today,” Shinn said after going back-to-back in the race.



“It’s all worth it and I just want to thank everyone who’s supported me and my circle and outside too for that matter, the racing industry has been wonderful so it’s nice to come back on a big day and show what we’re made of.” Shinn was also one to look forward, overlooking Maher’s choice of Cup riders when praising the trainer. “It takes a really tough horse and that’s what the Maher stable is all about, they turn up on these big days, they’re fit, and she’s put the writing on the wall all prep,” he said. The jockey’s expected $45,000 payday for the winning ride will also cover a fine from earlier in the Caulfield program. The jockey was slugged $1000 for excessive use of the whip on beaten favourite Private Eye in race 5. Maher will also have to hand over $2000 after a treatment mishap involving his imported stayer Point Of Law at the Werribee quarantine centre on Saturday morning.



Maher’s right-hand man Jack Turnbull pleaded guilty to racing stewards on behalf of the trainer for using Gastropell on the galloper – a paste to prevent gastric ulcers – which is in breach of racing rules on a race day. Point Of Law was subsequently scratched from the Caulfield Cup, which was a moot point – as the third emergency, he wasn’t getting a start. Maher’s stable hand, Samantha Waters, who usually cares for Pride Of Jenni, was also fined over the same incident after using inappropriate language towards stewards. World.title: Autumn Glow show goes on as champion cruises past $12 million
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Autumn Glow show goes on as champion cruises past $12 million Craig Kerry October 17, 2026 — 6:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Champion trainer Chris Waller marvelled at the athleticism and natural brilliance of Autumn Glow after she cruised to a two-and-a-quarter-length win in the $5 million King Charles III Stakes (1609m). The five-year-old mare, Australia’s horse champion of last season and a $1.26 favourite, went to 14 wins in 15 starts and beyond $12.8 million in earnings, holding off a brief challenge from Ceolwulf to sprint clear under James McDonald. James McDonald salutes on Autumn Glow. Getty Images “I was watching Ceolwulf and I was watching it with Darren [Beadman] and I said, ‘Oh, are we in trouble?’ And he said, ‘No’,” Waller recounted. It was a straightforward win after “an interesting week” in which Waller adjusted Autumn Glow’s training to prepare for front-running hero Pride Of Jenni, which was scratched on Thursday with a leg infection.



“Her work’s been fantastic and she’s just an absolute professional,” Waller said. Chris Waller. Getty Images “We asked to do a little bit more work this a week, expecting a wet track, expecting solid speed in the race. She just took it all in a stride, and she’s come out and done that today. “But I don’t think it really matters how you train her … she could train herself.” Autumn Glow appears likely race on to the Champions Mile at Flemington in two weeks.



It capped a big day for part-owners Arrowfield, which won the $2 million Kosciuszko with Chains Of Love. Golden chance beckons after gear change Randwick trainer Michael Freedman was looking to the $10 Golden Eagle (1500m) with $26 hope Apocalyptic after the mare lifted late to down top fancies Skyhook and Beiewacht in the $1 million Silver Eagle (1300m). The MyRacehorse talent came down the outside under Tommy Berry to beat Skyhook by a short neck, with Beiwacht a neck further back, giving her a first win since claiming the group 1 Flight Stakes (1600m) a year ago. “It’s really satisfying because for the last six to 12 months, she has been going as well as she was 12 months ago at home, but on race day she has been doing a few things wrong,” Freedman said.



“She’s been in a little bit of a mood and doing that hanging business up the straight, so we changed her gear around and put some visors on, a lugging bit on. It’s just great to see her back to what I know she’s capable of.” He said the Golden Eagle on October 31 at Randwick was next. “I can’t see any reason why we wouldn’t have a crack at a race like that because she is one of the better horses I’ve ever had anything to do with,” he said. So You Are stamps Cup credentials Trainer Bjorn Baker was looking to the Melbourne Cup with So You Are after he fought back late to add the group 3 St Leger Stakes (2600m) to his string of feature wins.



Gavin Bedggood-trained $31 chance Tempesti levelled up to favourite So You Are before Tommy Berry lifted Baker’s promising stayer over the final 100m to a three-quarter-length victory. The gritty win came after listed and group 3 victories at 2400m for Stuart Ramsey-bred and owned So You Are, which was moved to Baker’s stable in August from Armidale’s Stirling Osland. “Off the deck to get up, he’s a really, really good stayer and I can’t wait to see him over two miles,” Baker said. “I’m sure he will be able to get into the Melbourne Cup off of that and hopefully he comes through that well.” The win gave Baker an early feature double. He was eyeing a call-up in the $2 million Invitation or a shot at the group 1 Empire Rose with Unleeshing after she came from second last to mow down stablemate Pillow Fight in the group 3 Angst Stakes (1600m).



The five-year-old, with Jason Collett aboard, made up several lengths to win by three quarters of a length in the fillies and mares feature. Her Warwick Farm trainer believed both mares were only going to get better and he hoped Unleeshing could join stablemate Perfumist in the Invitation (1400m) next week at Randwick. He said the Empire Rose (1600m), a mares race over the mile at Flemington, the following week was another option. Arrowfield mare loves the fight in Kosciuszko Chains Of Love, part-owned by former broadcaster Alan Jones, produced a remarkable effort to give trainers Paul Messara and Leah Gavranich back-to-back wins in the $2 million Kosciuszko (1200m).



The four-year-old mare, trained by the team from Arrowfield Stud at Scone, was five wide or worse for the entire trip under Zac Lloyd but still had enough late to edge out Band Of Brothers by a head in an epic finish. Messara and Gavranich won the richest race for country-trained horses last year with Clear Thinking and this year combined with a Scone syndicate of slot-holders. “We were five deep, I thought we had no hope, so an amazing effort by the horse,” Messara said. Asked if he thought she was going to run second, he replied: “I thought I was going to run last.” Fillies firing for Gibbons and Sargent Dylan Gibbons came away unscathed after John Sargent-trained Beyond The Reef caught him off guard following their victory in the group 3 Reginald Allen Quality (1400m) at Randwick.



Gibbons and Sargent, who combined for victory with Global Goal in the group 1 Flight Stakes two weeks ago, pulled off an upset with $31 chance Beyond The Reef, which swept down the outside for a length and a quarter win after three placings at provincial level. Gibbons was dislodged well past the post when the filly shied, leaving him a long walk back. “It was the shadow from the trees, and she spotted it and I was too busy trying to enjoy the moment and she caught me off guard,” Gibbons said. Sargent, who trained Beyond The Reef’s mother, Miss Moana, to second in the group 3 South Australian Classic, said the filly could go for a spell and come back for the autumn after the “throw at the stumps” on Saturday paid off. Sargent and Gibbons will combine again with Global in the group 1 Spring Champion Stakes (2000m) next week at Randwick.



Lloyd lands Knockout blow for Deamer Newcastle trainer Jason Deamer praised the poise of Zac Lloyd after he gave It’s A Knockout a gun ride to take the recent addition to his stable into the $3 million Big Dance on Melbourne Cup day with victory in the wildcard (1600m). The Dynamic Syndications-owned six-year-old mare, which came to Deamer’s yard from top trainer Ciaron Maher just eight weeks ago, was put into the one-one by Lloyd before she took over approaching the 300m and powered to a two and quarter-length win. “He’s a genius, the young bloke,” Deamer said of Lloyd. “He just gave it a perfect run, just let her build into it, and asked for that effort with no weight on her back today.



“He’s just so relaxed, and he and his dad, they do their homework.” The Randwick track upgraded to a soft 6, retrospective of race one. Lloyd said post race the track felt like a Soft 6 already. The track had copped 99mm in the week prior. Gerald Ryan and Sterling Alexiou-prepared Matias was second to also make the rich mile race at Randwick. The stable also has Just Party qualified for the Big Dance, but Ryan said he may not make the trip and will race next week in the Five Diamonds Prelude at Randwick.

World.content:
LifestyleFashionThe Everest Stylish Sydney throws down the gauntlet: Everest fashion winners Courtney Thompson October 17, 2026 — 6:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The long-running Sydney-versus-Melbourne feud can be a bit overdone, but it always inevitably ends up rearing its head at some point regardless as it did today at Royal Randwick as the style set rolled in for The Everest Cup. “Sydney and Melbourne are always in competition, so why not have a bit more at the races?” asked Milana Marsh, wearing a deep burgundy Bianca and Bridgett dress. Krissy and Milana Marsh at the TAB Everest Day at Royal Randwick. Audrey Richardson “Oh look, The Everest is taking things to new heights because we’re not Melbourne, we’re Sydney, and we actually have good weather, so it actually is good for spring,” added her mother Krissy Marsh, who clearly didn’t check the coverage from Caulfield, where the sun blazed with clear blue skies. Weather aside, when it comes to racewear fashion, the difference between the two cities translates as experimental versus classic.



Kate Waterhouse. Audrey Richardson “There’s a great mix of traditional racing elegance and modern fashion, and I love seeing how everyone interprets that [at The Everest]. It’s definitely one of the most exciting days on the Sydney racing calendar for fashion,” Kate Waterhouse says. Waterhouse grew up around the racecourse, so by now, countless race days later, she can spot a fashion faux pas a mile away. Attending The Everest in Sydney and serving as a judge in the ATC Fashion Stakes, Waterhouse wore a lavender Acler dress with Ford Millinery hat to dish out her well-earned wisdom on what sets someone apart in the racewear competition. For her, the biggest style “ick” is when it’s clear someone looks out of place: “Racing fashion is a great opportunity to have fun and experiment, but you should still feel comfortable and confident.”



Montana Cox at Randwick for The Everest. Audrey Richardson Judging by the style set that moseyed around the Royal Randwick racecourse, many of them followed similar rules to Waterhouse. Model Montana Cox could wear a hessian sack and people would still probably reverse Google image search it to find out where they could get one just like it – such is the power when you’re as stunning as Cox. Supermodel superpowers aside, Cox looked striking in a blood-red strapless dress that featured a sheer floor-length skirt underneath and accessorised with a coordinating pillbox hat, which is fast becoming the headpiece of the season. Mariam Seddiq at The Everest Day at Randwick. Audrey Richardson



Another strong fashion perspective came via Mariam Seddiq, a woman who doesn’t mince her words. Related Article Live

Spring racing carnival Stewards to hold inquiry into tragic Caulfield Cup fall; favourite beaten in Everest stunner The Australian designer was assured and concise when she spoke about the lessons in racewear style she’s learnt over the years. “Anything that needs constant adjusting is a big no. You should be able to move comfortably without the outfit losing impact,” she said. But her biggest racing fashion no-no? “Heels that come off before the final race.”



Wearing a black and white dress that features a print of an artwork by Seddiq herself, the designer built her outfit around the frock. Nicely done. Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.
